### `defence-limitation-period-expired`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / library
- **Appears in:** Claim library, defences
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/docs/02l24_e.doc

```
Limitation period expired
Under s. 4 of the Limitations Act, 2002, unless the Act provides otherwise, a proceeding cannot be started after the second anniversary of the day the claim was discovered. Section 5(1) says when a claim is discovered: the earlier of the day the person first knew that the injury, loss or damage had occurred, that it was caused or contributed to by an act or omission, that the act or omission was that of the person the claim is against, and that, having regard to the nature of the injury, loss or damage, a proceeding would be an appropriate means to seek to remedy it -- and the day a reasonable person with their abilities and in their circumstances first ought to have known those things. Under s. 5(2), a person with a claim is presumed to have known of those matters on the day the act or omission the claim is based on took place, unless the contrary is proved.
```

### `defence-no-agreement-existed`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / library
- **Appears in:** Claim library, defences
- **Source:** https://www.ontariocourts.ca/scj/guides-and-service-resources/guide-to-representing-yourself/civil-resources-to-help-self-represented-litigants/steps-to-civil-case/

```
No agreement existed
The person bringing a claim generally has the burden of proving their allegations on a balance of probabilities -- including that an agreement or understanding actually existed in the first place. If that's disputed, it becomes one of the facts the plaintiff has to establish with evidence, not something assumed true by default.
```

### `defence-set-off-or-counterclaim`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / library
- **Appears in:** Claim library, defences
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/docs/980258_e.doc

```
Set-off or counterclaim
SET-OFF: under s. 111 of the Courts of Justice Act, in an action for payment of a debt, the defendant may, by way of defence, claim the right to set off against the plaintiff's claim a debt owed by the plaintiff to the defendant. Mutual debts may be set off against each other even if they are of a different nature, and if a larger sum is found due from the plaintiff to the defendant, the defendant is entitled to judgment for the balance. COUNTERCLAIM: separately, a defendant can bring their own claim as part of the same case, called a Defendant's Claim (Form 10A). Under rule 10.01(1) it may be made against the plaintiff, or against another person where the claim arises out of the transaction or occurrence relied on by the plaintiff or is related to the plaintiff's claim. The Rules say it may be ISSUED within 20 days after the day the defence is filed. Issuing and filing are different steps: a claim is issued by the court, and the 20 days runs from the day the defence was filed, not from when it was served or received. Missing that window does not end it. After those 20 days a Defendant's Claim may still be issued WITH LEAVE OF THE COURT -- permission the court gives -- at any point before trial or default judgment. After trial or default judgment, that route is no longer available. Once issued, it still has to be served on every person it is made against, and the same six-month service window that applies to a plaintiff's claim applies to it -- although the court may extend the time for service, before or after the six months has elapsed (rule 8.01(2)). How the 20 days is counted: the Rules count time by excluding the first day and including the last, and if the last day falls on a holiday the period ends on the next day that is not a holiday. "Holiday" is defined to include any Saturday or Sunday, so intervening weekends are counted and do not extend the period -- only the last day moves.
```

### `defence-waiver-release-assumption-of-risk`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / library
- **Appears in:** Claim library, defences
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/docs/90o02_e.doc

```
Waiver, release, or assumption of risk
Under the Occupiers' Liability Act, an occupier's duty to take reasonable care to see that people entering the premises, and property they bring, are reasonably safe (s. 3(1)) does not apply to risks willingly assumed by the person who enters on the premises (s. 4(1)) -- but in that case the occupier still owes a duty not to create a danger with the deliberate intent of doing harm or damage to the person or their property, and not to act with reckless disregard of the presence of the person or their property. Separately, under s. 3(3) the duty applies except so far as the occupier is free to and does restrict, modify or exclude it, and under s. 5(3) an occupier who is free to do so must take reasonable steps to bring the restriction, modification or exclusion to the person's attention. Section 4 also DEEMS some people to have willingly assumed all risks, so that only that lower duty is owed to them: a person on premises intending to commit, or committing, a criminal act (s. 4(2)); and a person entering premises listed in s. 4(4) -- rural premises used for agriculture, vacant or undeveloped, or forested or wilderness; golf courses when not open for playing; utility rights-of-way and corridors; unopened road allowances; private roads and recreational trails reasonably marked by notice as such; and portage routes -- where entry is prohibited under the Trespass to Property Act, where the occupier has posted no notice about entry and has not otherwise expressly permitted it, or where entry is for a recreational activity, no fee is paid (apart from listed exceptions) and the occupier is not providing the person with living accommodation (s. 4(3)). These provisions concern occupiers of premises.
```

### `defence-contributory-negligence`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / library
- **Appears in:** Claim library, defences
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/docs/elaws_statutes_90n01_e.doc

```
Contributory negligence
Under s. 3 of Ontario's Negligence Act, in an action for damages that is founded on the fault or negligence of the defendant, if fault or negligence is found on the part of the plaintiff that contributed to the damages, the court apportions (divides) the damages in proportion to the degree of fault or negligence found against each party. For a dog bite or attack, the Dog Owners' Liability Act has its own rule: the owner's liability does not depend on the owner's fault or negligence, but the court reduces the damages in proportion to the degree, if any, to which the plaintiff's fault or negligence caused or contributed to them (s. 2(3)).
```

### `defence-failure-to-mitigate`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / library
- **Appears in:** Claim library, defences
- **Source:** https://www.canlii.org/en/ca/scc/doc/1975/1975canlii15/1975canlii15.html

```
Failure to mitigate
A plaintiff generally cannot recover for a loss they could reasonably have avoided -- but the burden of proving a failure to do so rests on the defendant, not the plaintiff. A defendant who argues the plaintiff should have taken steps to reduce their losses generally has to prove both that the plaintiff failed to take those reasonable steps, and that taking them would actually have reduced the loss. A note on where this comes from: the case this is sourced to is a wrongful-dismissal case, and the Supreme Court of Canada stated the rule there in employment terms -- whether the dismissed employee could, with proper effort, have found other suitable work. The burden principle it sets out is a general contract-damages one, but how mitigation applies outside employment (to damaged property, for instance, or to reputation) is not something that case decides, and is not stated here.
```

### `deadline-template:court-office-closed-on-this-date`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / deadlines
- **Appears in:** The deadline section of a stage answer, when the date it counts from is known
- **Source:** _none recorded_

```
Court offices are closed on {closedOn} for {occasion}. This date is still the deadline — a closure does not move it. But anything filed online or by email that day is marked as filed on the next business day, {stampedAs}, so filing on the deadline itself would be recorded as late. Filing before {closedOn} avoids this. If that is not possible, ask the court office what to do. Source: {source}
```

### `deadline-template:court-office-closes-soon-after-this-date`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / deadlines
- **Appears in:** The deadline section of a stage answer, when the date it counts from is known
- **Source:** _none recorded_

Anything filed online or by email on {closedOn} is marked as filed on the next business day, {stampedAs}. If you are filing close to the deadline, that closure day will not count as the day you filed. Source: {source}
```

## doctrine (7)

### `doctrine:SEED_EVIDENCE_DIGITAL_CONTEXT_001`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / assistant
- **Appears in:** Guided assistant — evidence, issue and readiness answers. verificationStatus: not-verified. NOT RENDERED while it is "not-verified".
- **Source:** _none recorded_

```
Digital evidence requires context and authenticity review

Screenshots, messages, emails, and social-media evidence should be preserved with sender, recipient, date, platform, surrounding context, and original thread where possible.
```

### `doctrine:SEED_DEFAMATION_PATTERN_001`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / assistant
- **Appears in:** Guided assistant — evidence, issue and readiness answers. verificationStatus: not-verified. NOT RENDERED while it is "not-verified".
- **Source:** _none recorded_

```
Defamation cases require exact words and publication proof

A defamation-style claim is usually weak if the exact words, recipients, context, and harm are unclear.
```

### `doctrine:SEED_LIMITATION_DISCOVERABILITY_001`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / assistant
- **Appears in:** Guided assistant — evidence, issue and readiness answers. verificationStatus: not-verified. NOT RENDERED while it is "not-verified".
- **Source:** _none recorded_

```
Older events require limitation and discoverability screening

When events happened long ago or dates are unclear, the system must flag limitation, discoverability, notice, delay, and procedural timing risk.
```

### `doctrine:SEED_PUBLIC_AUTHORITY_SCREENING_001`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / assistant
- **Appears in:** Guided assistant — evidence, issue and readiness answers. verificationStatus: not-verified. NOT RENDERED while it is "not-verified".
- **Source:** _none recorded_

```
Public authority claims require threshold screening

Claims involving Crown, police, government, hospitals, ministries, courts, or public authorities require careful screening for immunity, discretion, notice, leave, jurisdiction, causation, and proper defendant naming.
```

### `doctrine:SEED_FAMILY_PARENTING_BEST_INTERESTS_001`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / assistant
- **Appears in:** Guided assistant — evidence, issue and readiness answers. verificationStatus: not-verified. NOT RENDERED while it is "not-verified".
- **Source:** _none recorded_

```
Family parenting cases must stay child-focused

Parenting and decision-making disputes should be organized around the child’s needs, stability, safety, history of care, practical schedule, communication, and evidence.
```

### `doctrine:SEED_BURDEN_PROOF_MAPPING_001`

## education-topic (339)

### `sc-topic-monetary-limit`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / intake
- **Appears in:** Intake, surfaced by recorded facts
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/docs/000626_e.doc

```
Small Claims Court's $50,000 limit

Small Claims Court in Ontario hears actions for the payment of money where the amount claimed is $50,000 or less, not counting interest and costs, and actions for the return of personal property worth $50,000 or less. A single cause of action cannot be divided into two or more actions to bring it within the limit. A claim worth more than that goes to the Superior Court of Justice, unless the person suing gives up the amount over $50,000 and files in Small Claims Court. THE LIMIT ALSO WORKS IN THE OTHER DIRECTION, which is less widely known. Since July 1, 2024, the Courts of Justice Act provides that an action WITHIN Small Claims Court's jurisdiction shall not be commenced in the Superior Court of Justice except with leave of that court, as provided in the rules of court. So for a claim under the limit, Small Claims Court and the Superior Court are not a free choice between two open doors -- starting in the Superior Court requires the court's permission first. There is an exception: that restriction does not apply to a counterclaim, crossclaim, or third or subsequent party claim where the main action was already commenced in the Superior Court of Justice.
```

### `sc-topic-limitation-period`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / intake
- **Appears in:** Intake, surfaced by recorded facts
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/page/civil-claims-suing-and-being-sued

```
Time limits on starting a claim

In most cases, Ontario's Limitations Act, 2002 gives someone 2 years from when they discovered their claim (or when a reasonable person in their circumstances ought to have discovered it) to start a claim. A person is presumed to have known of the claim on the day the act or omission happened, unless the contrary is proved. Waiting past that window can mean losing the right to sue at all, regardless of how strong the underlying facts are. There are exceptions and different rules for some claim types, so this is general information, not a determination of any specific deadline.
```

### `sc-topic-burden-of-proof`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / intake
- **Appears in:** Intake, surfaced by recorded facts
- **Source:** https://www.ontariocourts.ca/scj/guides-and-service-resources/guide-to-representing-yourself/civil-resources-to-help-self-represented-litigants/steps-to-civil-case/

```
Who has to prove what, and how much proof is needed

In a civil case like Small Claims Court, the person bringing the claim (the plaintiff) generally has to prove their allegations on a "balance of probabilities" -- meaning the evidence has to show it's more likely than not (more than a 50% chance) that their version is correct. This means the plaintiff must present evidence that will convince the judge that, more likely than not, it would be correct to rule in the plaintiff's favour.
```

### `sc-topic-demand-letters`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / intake
- **Appears in:** Intake, surfaced by recorded facts
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/page/suing-someone-small-claims-court

```
Sending a demand letter before suing

Ontario's own guidance suggests that before starting a claim, it can be worth sending a letter or talking to the other side directly to ask for payment or resolution first. This is not a legal requirement to sue in Small Claims Court -- it's a suggested step that can sometimes resolve a dispute without going to court at all, and can also become useful documentation later showing an attempt was made to resolve things directly.
```

### `sc-topic-filing-form-7a`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / intake
- **Appears in:** Intake, surfaced by recorded facts
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/document/guide-procedures-small-claims-court/making-claim

```
What filing a claim involves (Form 7A)

Starting a Small Claims Court case means filling out and filing a Plaintiff's Claim, which is Form 7A. It sets out who is suing whom, for how much, and why. Once it's filed, it generally has to be served on the other party (the defendant), and proof of that service is made with an Affidavit of Service (Form 8A). It is generally filed with the court at a later step, such as when asking the clerk to note the defendant in default.
```

### `sc-topic-six-month-service-window`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / intake
- **Appears in:** Intake, surfaced by recorded facts
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/docs/980258_e.doc

```
Serving a claim after it is issued — the six-month window

Issuing a claim and serving it are two different steps, and the second one has its own deadline. Under the Rules of the Small Claims Court, a claim must be served within SIX MONTHS after the date it is issued. The court may extend the time for service, and it may do so either before or after the six months has run out -- but that is a request to the court, not something that happens automatically. The same six-month window applies to a Defendant's Claim, which the Rules require to be served in accordance with the same provision. A note on counting: the Rules set out a general method for counting a period of time -- exclude the first day, include the last, and if the last day falls on a holiday the period ends on the next day that is not a holiday, with "holiday" defined to include any Saturday or Sunday. The Rules do not state how a period expressed in MONTHS is computed; the Legislation Act, 2006, which applies to regulations generally, has its own rule for periods in months. This content does not say how the six months is calculated in a particular case -- the date a claim was issued is on the issued claim itself, and anyone unsure how the window applies to their own dates should confirm it with the court or a licensed paralegal or lawyer.
```

### `sc-topic-collecting-after-judgment`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / intake
- **Appears in:** Intake, surfaced by recorded facts
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/document/guide-procedures-small-claims-court/after-judgment

```
Collecting money after winning a judgment

Winning a case doesn't mean payment happens automatically -- a judgment has to be enforced if the other side doesn't pay voluntarily. Ontario's guidance describes several enforcement tools, generally starting with a written request for payment, and, if that doesn't work, options like garnishment (claiming money owed to the debtor by someone else, such as an employer or bank), a writ of seizure and sale of personal property or land, or an examination hearing to ask the debtor about their finances and ability to pay.
```

### `sc-topic-general-negligence-elements`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / intake
- **Appears in:** Intake, surfaced by recorded facts
- **Source:** https://www.canlii.org/en/ca/scc/doc/2008/2008scc27/2008scc27.html

```
The elements of a negligence claim

A negligence claim generally requires proving four separate elements: (1) that the defendant owed the plaintiff a duty of care; (2) that the defendant's conduct breached the standard of care; (3) that the plaintiff sustained damage; and (4) that the damage was caused, in fact and in law, by the defendant's breach. Duty of care asks whether the relationship between the parties is close enough that one may reasonably be said to owe the other a duty not to cause injury -- a question of foreseeability moderated by policy considerations. Where the relationship falls into a type courts have already recognized as giving rise to a duty of care, precedent settles the question and a full duty-of-care analysis isn't needed -- for example, courts have long recognized that a manufacturer of a consumable good owes a duty of care to the ultimate consumer of that good. Standard of care asks whether the defendant's conduct breached the standard expected of it. Conduct is negligent if it creates an unreasonable risk of harm. Damage for this purpose includes psychological injury, not only physical injury -- but psychological injury that counts as personal injury has to be distinguished from ordinary upset. The law does not recognize upset, disgust, anxiety, agitation, or other mental states that fall short of injury; to count, an injury generally has to be serious and prolonged, rising above the ordinary annoyances, anxieties, and fears that people living in society routinely accept. Causation has two parts: whether the breach caused the harm in fact, and whether it also caused the harm in law -- meaning the harm isn't too remote to fairly hold the defendant liable for it. The factual branch is generally tested using the "but for" test: the plaintiff must show, on a balance of probabilities, that the injury would not have occurred but for the defendant's negligent act. This is a factual inquiry, applied in a robust, common-sense way -- scientific precision about exactly how the defendant's conduct produced the injury is not required. Exceptionally, liability may instead rest on showing the defendant's conduct materially contributed to the risk of the injury, -- which, as the Supreme Court of Canada noted in agreeing with the Court of Appeal, is not a test for proving factual causation but a basis for finding legal causation -- and only where two conditions are both met: the plaintiff has shown that the loss would not have occurred but for the negligence of two or more possible wrongdoers, each possibly responsible for it, and the plaintiff, through no fault of their own, is unable to show which one of them actually caused the injury, because each can point to the others. Outside that narrow situation, the ordinary "but for" test still applies even where more than one party was negligent. The legal branch of causation -- remoteness -- turns on reasonable foreseeability: whether the harm was a real risk that would occur to a reasonable person in the defendant's position, not one they'd dismiss as far-fetched. For personal-injury claims, and especially mental-injury claims, foreseeability is judged against a person of "ordinary fortitude," not the particular plaintiff's own sensitivities -- unusual or extreme reactions to a negligent act are imaginable but not reasonably foreseeable. That ordinary-fortitude threshold is a separate question from the "thin skull" rule: once it's shown that a person of ordinary fortitude would foreseeably suffer the injury, the defendant must then take the plaintiff as found for the purpose of assessing the resulting damages -- ordinary fortitude decides whether the damage is compensable at law at all, not how much compensation follows once it is. Where a defendant is shown to have had actual knowledge of a plaintiff's particular sensitivities, the ordinary-fortitude requirement doesn't have to be applied as strictly.
```

### `sc-topic-general-unjust-enrichment-elements`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / intake
- **Appears in:** Intake, surfaced by recorded facts
- **Source:** https://www.canlii.org/en/ca/scc/doc/2004/2004scc25/2004scc25.html

```
The elements of an unjust enrichment claim

A claim in unjust enrichment generally requires showing three elements: (1) that the defendant was enriched; (2) that the plaintiff suffered a corresponding deprivation; and (3) that there is no juristic reason for the enrichment -- meaning no justification in law for the defendant keeping the benefit at the plaintiff's expense. The absence-of-juristic-reason element is assessed in two stages. First, the plaintiff must show that none of the established categories applies to justify the enrichment -- those established categories include a contract, a disposition of law, a donative intent (a gift), and other valid common law, equitable, or statutory obligations. If none of those established categories applies, the plaintiff has made out a prima facie case. Second, that prima facie case can still be rebutted: the defendant may show some other reason the enrichment should be kept, and at this stage courts consider the reasonable expectations of the parties and public policy considerations. Separately, even where all three elements are made out, a defendant may have a change of position defence available -- where an innocent defendant shows they materially changed their position because of the enrichment, such that requiring them to return it would be inequitable. That defence is not available, however, to a defendant who obtained the enrichment through their own wrongdoing.
```

```
A written statement of facts that you swear or affirm is true, signed in front of a commissioner for taking affidavits, such as a lawyer, paralegal or notary. "Sworn" means you take an oath; "affirmed" means you make a solemn promise without an oath. Both carry the same weight. Courts use affidavits as evidence, especially on motions, and an affidavit of service proves a document was served. Knowingly swearing a false affidavit is a criminal offence.

- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
A court can order a bond (Form 32) to back up conditions, such as to help secure a child's return to Ontario. The bond needs at least one surety and the money must be deposited with the clerk immediately, in each case unless the court orders otherwise.
```

### `glossary:burden-of-proof`

- **Pathway / stage:** all / glossary

```
Which party has to prove something. In a civil case the party who started the case has to prove, on a balance of probabilities, every element of what they claim. If the other side thinks an element has not been proven at all, they can ask the judge to dismiss the case without calling evidence (a motion for non-suit).
```

The rules usually call a case an action.

### `glossary:case-conference`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / glossary
- **Appears in:** Glossary, "case conference"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
A meeting with a judge to move a case along: identifying what is and is not in dispute, making sure documents have been exchanged, setting a timetable, and exploring settlement. In a civil case a judge can order one at any time to sort out procedural problems without a formal motion. Small Claims Court uses settlement conferences instead.
```

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / glossary
- **Appears in:** Glossary, "case conference" (in small claims court)

Not used. The first meeting with a judge is the settlement conference.
```

```
Optional; a judge can direct one at any time, on their own or at a party's request.
```

### `glossary:case-conference:family`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / glossary
- **Appears in:** Glossary, "case conference" (in family court)
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
A judge holds at least one conference in every case where an answer is filed. The party asking for it serves and files a case conference notice (Form 17). Before it, the parties must try to talk about disclosure and a temporary resolution, unless a court order or a risk of domestic violence makes that inappropriate.
```

### `glossary:certificate-of-appointment-of-estate-trustee`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / glossary
- **Appears in:** Glossary, "certificate of appointment of estate trustee"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
The court document that appoints an estate trustee (an executor or administrator) to deal with the estate of someone who has died. People often call it probate. You ask the Superior Court of Justice for it by filing an application with proof of death and, if there is one, the will.
```

### `glossary:child`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / glossary
- **Appears in:** Glossary, "child"
- **Source:** https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/D-3.4/FullText.html

```
In family cases, a person under 18, unless the law that applies defines it differently. It can include someone a parent has clearly treated as part of their family and, in a divorce, an adult child unable to leave their parents' care because of illness, disability or another cause. Parents must support an unmarried child who is a minor, in full-time school or unable to leave their care, but not one sixteen or older who has left parental control.
```

### `glossary:child-protection-case`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / glossary
- **Appears in:** Glossary, "child protection case"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/17c14

```
A family court case about whether a child needs protection, under the child protection part of the Child, Youth and Family Services Act, 2017. Children's aid societies investigate concerns that a child may need protection and protect children where necessary. These cases have their own timelines and some special rules, for example a party can question another party as of right.
```

### `glossary:child-support-guidelines`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / glossary
- **Appears in:** Glossary, "child support guidelines"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90f03

```
The rules and tables used to work out child support. A court ordering child support must follow them. It can order a different amount only in limited cases, such as when special provisions already benefit the child and the guidelines amount would be inequitable given those provisions, or when both parents consent and reasonable arrangements are in place. Either Ontario's guidelines or the Federal Child Support Guidelines apply, depending on the case.
```

### `glossary:claim`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / glossary
- **Appears in:** Glossary, "claim"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/02l24

```
What you are asking the court to give you, and the reasons. It is also the name of the document that starts an action (lawsuit). For time limits, a claim is a claim to fix an injury, loss or damage caused by something someone did or failed to do, and you usually have two years from when you discovered it to start a lawsuit.
```

```

- **Appears in:** Glossary, "claim" (in civil cases in the superior court)

An action (lawsuit) usually starts with a statement of claim. A defendant's claim against the plaintiff is a counterclaim.
```

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / glossary
- **Appears in:** Glossary, "claim" (in family court)

```

A court staff person who accepts documents for filing, issues documents and keeps the court file. Clerks can also do some things a judge would otherwise do, such as signing certain orders or judgments. A registrar does the same kind of work.

The clerk can make some orders when all parties consent (clerk's orders), and in some cases signs judgment.

- **Status:** draft

The rules usually say registrar, for example when you ask the registrar to note a defendant in default.

### `glossary:cohabit`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / glossary
- **Appears in:** Glossary, "cohabit"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90f03

```
To live together as a couple, married or not. It matters for spousal support: two people who are not married count as spouses for support if they cohabited continuously for at least three years, or were in a relationship of some permanence and are parents of a child together.
```

### `glossary:consent`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / glossary
- **Appears in:** Glossary, "consent"
- **Source:** https://www.ontariocourts.ca/scj/areas-of-law/small-claims-court/default-proceedings/

```
Written agreement by a party to a step or an order. Many steps that would otherwise need a judge's decision can happen when everyone consents, such as amending a document, adjourning, or setting aside a noting in default. A consent order is an order the court makes because the parties agree on it, often without anyone having to attend court. A consent motion is a motion all parties agree to.
```

### `glossary:consent:small-claims`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / glossary
- **Appears in:** Glossary, "consent" (in small claims court)

```
For a short list of steps, such as setting aside a noting in default or dismissing an action, the clerk can make an order on a Request for Clerk's Order on Consent (Form 11.2A) signed by all parties, with no hearing.
```

### `glossary:consent:civil`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / glossary
- **Appears in:** Glossary, "consent" (in civil cases in the superior court)
- **Source:** https://www.ontariocourts.ca/scj/areas-of-law/small-claims-court/default-proceedings/

```
Many steps, such as amending a pleading, can be taken by filing the consent of all parties.
```

### `glossary:consent:family`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / glossary

- **Source:** https://www.ontariocourts.ca/scj/areas-of-law/small-claims-court/default-proceedings/

```
A consent order can be made without anyone coming to court. Consent motions can use the shorter motion form (Form 14B); a motion to change a final order on consent uses Form 15C.
```

### `glossary:contempt-of-court`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / glossary
- **Appears in:** Glossary, "contempt of court"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
When a court finds that someone disobeyed a court order. A contempt motion asks the court to make that finding; a contempt order is the finding. In civil and family cases, a contempt motion is used to enforce orders other than orders to pay money. Penalties can include a fine, imprisonment, costs, or an order to do or stop doing something.
```

### `glossary:contempt-of-court:small-claims`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / glossary
- **Appears in:** Glossary, "contempt of court" (in small claims court)
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
Contempt comes up when someone served with a notice of examination does not attend, or attends but refuses to answer or produce documents. The court can order them to a contempt hearing.
```

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / glossary
- **Appears in:** Glossary, "contempt of court" (in civil cases in the superior court)
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
The motion is made to a judge in the case where the order was made, and is served personally unless the court orders otherwise.
```

### `glossary:contempt-of-court:family`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / glossary
- **Appears in:** Glossary, "contempt of court" (in family court)
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
The notice of contempt motion (Form 31) is served with a supporting affidavit by special service.
```

### `glossary:continuing-record`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / glossary
- **Appears in:** Glossary, "continuing record"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
A family court term for the court's permanent file of the case, kept as one record that grows as documents are filed. The person who starts the case prepares it, serves it on the other parties and files it with proof of service. If a support order is filed with the Family Responsibility Office, it is called the support enforcement continuing record.
```

### `glossary:costs`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / glossary
- **Appears in:** Glossary, "costs"
- **Source:** https://www.ontariocourts.ca/scj/guides-and-service-resources/guide-to-representing-yourself/civil-resources-to-help-self-represented-litigants/steps-to-civil-case/

```
Money a judge orders one party to pay another toward what the other spent on the case, usually the losing side paying the winning side. It can cover court fees, disbursements and legal fees. Costs can be ordered after a motion, a trial, or a missed court date, and the judge decides whether to award them and how much. Costs are separate from the amount claimed.
```

### `glossary:costs:small-claims`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / glossary
- **Appears in:** Glossary, "costs" (in small claims court)

```
Costs other than disbursements are capped at 15 per cent of the amount claimed (or the value of property sought), unless the court penalizes unreasonable behaviour. A self-represented winner can get up to $500 for inconvenience and expense.
```

### `glossary:costs:civil`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / glossary
- **Appears in:** Glossary, "costs" (in civil cases in the superior court)
- **Source:** https://www.ontariocourts.ca/scj/guides-and-service-resources/guide-to-representing-yourself/civil-resources-to-help-self-represented-litigants/steps-to-civil-case/

```
Costs are in the court's discretion. The judge can weigh the result, any written offer to settle, and other listed factors.
```

### `glossary:costs:family`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / glossary
- **Appears in:** Glossary, "costs" (in family court)
- **Source:** https://www.ontariocourts.ca/scj/guides-and-service-resources/guide-to-representing-yourself/civil-resources-to-help-self-represented-litigants/steps-to-civil-case/

```
A successful party is presumed to be entitled to the costs of each step. The court deals with costs promptly after each step. The presumption does not apply in a child protection case.
```

### `glossary:counterclaim`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / glossary
- **Appears in:** Glossary, "counterclaim"
- **Source:** https://www.ontariocourts.ca/scj/guides-and-service-resources/guide-to-representing-yourself/civil-resources-to-help-self-represented-litigants/steps-to-civil-case/

```
A claim a defendant makes back against the plaintiff (and sometimes others) in the same case, for example because the defendant says the plaintiff owes them money. It works like a claim of its own, and the plaintiff can file a defence to it. The term is used in the Superior Court; Small Claims Court uses a defendant's claim, and in family court the respondent puts claims in the answer.
```

### `glossary:counterclaim:small-claims`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / glossary
- **Appears in:** Glossary, "counterclaim" (in small claims court)
- **Source:** https://www.ontariocourts.ca/scj/guides-and-service-resources/guide-to-representing-yourself/civil-resources-to-help-self-represented-litigants/steps-to-civil-case/

```
Called a defendant's claim (Form 10A).
```

### `glossary:counterclaim:civil`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / glossary
- **Appears in:** Glossary, "counterclaim" (in civil cases in the superior court)
- **Source:** https://www.ontariocourts.ca/scj/guides-and-service-resources/guide-to-representing-yourself/civil-resources-to-help-self-represented-litigants/steps-to-civil-case/

```
Counterclaim (Form 27A or 27B); the plaintiff answers with a defence to counterclaim (Form 27C). A claim against a co-defendant is a crossclaim.
```

### `glossary:counterclaim:family`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / glossary
- **Appears in:** Glossary, "counterclaim" (in family court)
- **Source:** https://www.ontariocourts.ca/scj/guides-and-service-resources/guide-to-representing-yourself/civil-resources-to-help-self-represented-litigants/steps-to-civil-case/

```
No separate document: the respondent includes claims against the applicant, or against someone else, in the answer.
```

### `glossary:court`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / glossary
- **Appears in:** Glossary, "court"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
The court where your case is being heard, including the judge (or other judicial officer) deciding it. Small Claims Court and the Family Court are both branches of the Superior Court of Justice.
```

### `glossary:court:small-claims`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / glossary
- **Appears in:** Glossary, "court" (in small claims court)
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
Court means the Small Claims Court.
```

### `glossary:court:civil`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / glossary
- **Appears in:** Glossary, "court" (in civil cases in the superior court)
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
Court includes an associate judge, who can hear some steps in a Superior Court case.
```

### `glossary:court:family`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / glossary
- **Appears in:** Glossary, "court" (in family court)
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
Family cases can be in the Ontario Court of Justice, the Family Court of the Superior Court of Justice, or the Superior Court of Justice. Property division and matrimonial home claims cannot be decided by the Ontario Court of Justice.
```

### `glossary:cross-examination`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / glossary
- **Appears in:** Glossary, "cross-examination"
- **Source:** https://www.ontariocourts.ca/scj/guides-and-service-resources/guide-to-representing-yourself/civil-resources-to-help-self-represented-litigants/steps-to-civil-case/

```
Questioning of a witness by the party who did not call that witness. It comes after the other side's questions (examination in chief) and is meant to test whether the witness is accurate and truthful, or to bring out helpful facts. Leading questions, which suggest the answer, are allowed. If you testify in your own case, you can be cross-examined too.
```

### `glossary:damages`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / glossary
- **Appears in:** Glossary, "damages"
- **Source:** https://www.ontariocourts.ca/scj/guides-and-service-resources/guide-to-representing-yourself/civil-resources-to-help-self-represented-litigants/steps-to-civil-case/

```
Money a court orders one party to pay another as compensation for harm, such as financial loss, property loss, emotional or physical injury, lost earnings and costs of care. When the amount is not fixed by a clear agreement (for example, property damage or personal injury), a judge has to assess it. Prejudgment interest is not added to punitive damages.
```

### `glossary:damages:small-claims`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / glossary
- **Appears in:** Glossary, "damages" (in small claims court)
- **Source:** https://www.ontariocourts.ca/scj/guides-and-service-resources/guide-to-representing-yourself/civil-resources-to-help-self-represented-litigants/steps-to-civil-case/

```
A claim for an amount that is not fixed (a non-liquidated claim) needs an assessment of damages by a judge, by a motion in writing or an assessment hearing, if the defendant is noted in default.
```

### `glossary:decision-making-responsibility`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / glossary
- **Appears in:** Glossary, "decision-making responsibility"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c12

```
The responsibility for making significant decisions about a child's well-being, including health, education, culture, language, religion and spirituality, and significant extra-curricular activities. The court can give it to one person, to several people, or split parts of it. It replaced the older idea of "custody". Day-to-day decisions during a parent's own time are made by that parent unless the court orders otherwise.
```

### `glossary:default-hearing`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / glossary
- **Appears in:** Glossary, "default hearing"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
A family court hearing where a person who has not paid support as ordered (the payor) has to come to court and explain why. It is started by the person owed support or by the Family Responsibility Office. After being served with the notice, the payor has 10 days to serve and file a financial statement and a default dispute.
```

### `glossary:default-judgment`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / glossary
- **Appears in:** Glossary, "default judgment"
- **Source:** https://www.ontariocourts.ca/scj/guides-and-service-resources/guide-to-representing-yourself/civil-resources-to-help-self-represented-litigants/steps-to-civil-case/

```
A judgment against a defendant who was noted in default for not filing a defence in time, made without the defendant taking part. For a clear, fixed amount (such as an unpaid invoice), the court office can sign it. When the amount must be worked out, a judge decides it. It can be enforced like any judgment, and the defendant can ask to have it set aside.
```

### `glossary:default-judgment:small-claims`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / glossary
- **Appears in:** Glossary, "default judgment" (in small claims court)
- **Source:** https://www.ontariocourts.ca/scj/guides-and-service-resources/guide-to-representing-yourself/civil-resources-to-help-self-represented-litigants/steps-to-civil-case/

```
For a debt or other fixed amount, the clerk can sign a Default Judgment (Form 11B). For other amounts, if all defendants are noted in default, ask for a motion in writing for an assessment of damages or an assessment hearing. If another defendant has filed a defence, the case goes to a settlement conference and, if necessary, trial.
```

### `glossary:default-judgment:civil`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / glossary
- **Appears in:** Glossary, "default judgment" (in civil cases in the superior court)
- **Source:** https://www.ontariocourts.ca/scj/guides-and-service-resources/guide-to-representing-yourself/civil-resources-to-help-self-represented-litigants/steps-to-civil-case/

```
For a fixed amount, the registrar can sign it on a Requisition for Default Judgment (Form 19D). Otherwise you bring a motion to a judge.
```

### `glossary:default-judgment:family`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / glossary
- **Appears in:** Glossary, "default judgment" (in family court)
- **Source:** https://www.ontariocourts.ca/scj/guides-and-service-resources/guide-to-representing-yourself/civil-resources-to-help-self-represented-litigants/steps-to-civil-case/

```
Family rules do not use this term. When no answer is filed, the case can go ahead in the respondent's absence, for example at an uncontested trial.
```

### `glossary:defence`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / glossary
- **Appears in:** Glossary, "defence"
- **Source:** https://www.ontariocourts.ca/scj/guides-and-service-resources/guide-to-representing-yourself/civil-resources-to-help-self-represented-litigants/steps-to-civil-case/

```
The document a defendant files to answer a claim. It tells the court and the plaintiff which facts and claims you agree with and which you dispute, and why. You serve it on every other party and file it with proof of service, within a set time. If you miss the deadline you can be noted in default. Family court calls this document an answer.
```

### `glossary:defence:small-claims`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / glossary
- **Appears in:** Glossary, "defence" (in small claims court)
- **Source:** https://www.ontariocourts.ca/scj/guides-and-service-resources/guide-to-representing-yourself/civil-resources-to-help-self-represented-litigants/steps-to-civil-case/

```
Defence (Form 9A), served and filed within 20 calendar days after you were served. If you agree you owe money, you can propose "terms of payment" in it.
```

Statement of Defence (Form 18A). If served in Ontario, generally within twenty days. A Notice of Intent to Defend (Form 18B) gives ten more days.
```

The response to an application is called an answer.
```

The person, business or organization being sued in an action. The person suing is the plaintiff.
```

- **Pathway / stage:** all / glossary

```
A defendant who disputes the claim files a Defence (Form 9A), and can make their own claim with a Defendant's Claim (Form 10A).
```

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / glossary
- **Appears in:** Glossary, "defendant" (in civil cases in the superior court)

A defendant who disputes the claim serves and files a Statement of Defence (Form 18A).
```

### `glossary:defendant:family`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / glossary
- **Appears in:** Glossary, "defendant" (in family court)
- **Source:** https://www.ontariocourts.ca/scj/guides-and-service-resources/guide-to-representing-yourself/civil-resources-to-help-self-represented-litigants/steps-to-civil-case/
