### `guide:starting-a-civil-action:intro`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Starting a civil action
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
This guide explains what the Rules of Civil Procedure and the Courts of Justice Act say about starting a case in the Superior Court of Justice, serving it, the time to defend, and what pleadings contain. It also describes the ontario.ca information on filing civil documents online.
```

### `guide:starting-a-civil-action:1:heading`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Starting a civil action
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
How a civil proceeding starts
```

### `guide:starting-a-civil-action:1.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Starting a civil action, "How a civil proceeding starts"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
Under the rules, “A proceeding shall be commenced by the issuing of an originating process.” The rules also say “Every proceeding in the court shall be by action, except where a statute or these rules provide otherwise.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 14.01 (1), 14.02)
```

### `guide:starting-a-civil-action:1.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Starting a civil action, "How a civil proceeding starts"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
For an action, the originating process is usually “a statement of claim (Form 14A (general) or 14B (mortgage actions))”. An originating process is issued “by the registrar's act of dating, signing and sealing it with the seal of the court and assigning to it a court file number.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 14.03 (1), 14.07 (1))
```

### `guide:starting-a-civil-action:1.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Starting a civil action, "How a civil proceeding starts"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
The title of the proceeding in an action “shall name the party commencing the action as the plaintiff and the opposite party as the defendant.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 14.06 (2))
```

### `guide:starting-a-civil-action:2:heading`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Starting a civil action
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
Notice of action and the time to serve a claim
```

### `guide:starting-a-civil-action:2.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Starting a civil action, "Notice of action and the time to serve a claim"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
“Where there is insufficient time to prepare a statement of claim, an action may be commenced by the issuing of a notice of action (Form 14C) that contains a short statement of the nature of the claim.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 14.03 (2))
```

### `guide:starting-a-civil-action:2.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Starting a civil action, "Notice of action and the time to serve a claim"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
Where a notice of action is used, the plaintiff “shall file a statement of claim (Form 14D) within thirty days after the notice of action is issued”. After that, a statement of claim may be filed only with the defendant's written consent or with leave of the court “obtained on notice to the defendant.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 14.03 (3))
```

### `guide:starting-a-civil-action:2.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Starting a civil action, "Notice of action and the time to serve a claim"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
“The notice of action shall not be served separately from the statement of claim.” A statement of claim “shall be served within six months after it is issued.” Where the action started with a notice of action, the notice and the statement of claim “shall be served together within six months after the notice of action is issued.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 14.03 (4), 14.08 (1), (2))
```

### `guide:starting-a-civil-action:3:heading`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Starting a civil action
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
When an application may be used
```

### `guide:starting-a-civil-action:3.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Starting a civil action, "When an application may be used"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
Some proceedings start with a notice of application instead of a statement of claim. “A proceeding may be commenced by an application to the Superior Court of Justice or to a judge of that court, if a statute so authorizes.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 14.05 (1), (2))
```

### `guide:starting-a-civil-action:3.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Starting a civil action, "When an application may be used"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
The rules also allow an application where the rules authorize it or where the relief claimed is one of a listed set. The list includes “the determination of rights that depend on the interpretation of a deed, will, contract or other instrument”, a remedy under the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, and any matter “where it is unlikely that there will be any material facts in dispute requiring a trial.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 14.05 (3))
```

### `guide:starting-a-civil-action:3.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Starting a civil action, "When an application may be used"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
In an application, the title names the party starting it “as the applicant and the opposite party, if any, as the respondent and the notice of application shall state the statutory provision or rule, if any, under which the application is made.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 14.06 (3))
```

### `guide:starting-a-civil-action:4:heading`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Starting a civil action
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
Claims within the Small Claims Court's limit
```

### `guide:starting-a-civil-action:4.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Starting a civil action, "Claims within the Small Claims Court's limit"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
The Courts of Justice Act says: “An action that is within the Small Claims Court's jurisdiction shall not, despite subsection 11 (2), be commenced in the Superior Court of Justice except with leave of the Superior Court of Justice as provided in the rules of court.” This does not apply to a counterclaim, crossclaim or third or subsequent party claim where the main action was started in the Superior Court of Justice. (Courts of Justice Act, s. 23 (1.1), (1.2))
```

### `guide:starting-a-civil-action:4.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Starting a civil action, "Claims within the Small Claims Court's limit"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
Under the rules, where leave to commence a proceeding is required, “it shall be obtained by motion except where a statute or these rules provide otherwise.” A motion for leave under subsection 23 (1.1) “may be made without notice, unless the court orders otherwise.” The court “may grant leave under subsection 23 (1.1) of the Courts of Justice Act only if it is in the interest of justice.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 14.01.1 (1)-(3))
```

### `guide:starting-a-civil-action:5:heading`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Starting a civil action
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
Serving the claim
```

### `guide:starting-a-civil-action:5.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Starting a civil action, "Serving the claim"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
“An originating process shall be served personally as provided in rule 16.02 or by an alternative to personal service as provided in rule 16.03.” Personal service on an individual, other than a person under disability, is made “by leaving a copy of the document with the individual”. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 16.01 (1), 16.02 (1) (a))
```

### `guide:starting-a-civil-action:5.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Starting a civil action, "Serving the claim"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
Personal service on a corporation other than a municipal corporation is made by leaving a copy with “an officer, director or agent of the corporation”, or with a person at any place of business of the corporation who appears to be in control or management of it. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 16.02 (1) (c))
```

### `guide:starting-a-civil-action:5.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Starting a civil action, "Serving the claim"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
Alternatives to personal service include mail with an acknowledgment of receipt card, which is “only effective as of the date the sender receives the card.” If personal service at a residence fails, a copy may be left in a sealed envelope with “anyone who appears to be an adult member of the same household”, with another copy mailed the same or next day. That service “is effective on the fifth day after the document is mailed.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 16.03 (4), (5))
```

### `guide:starting-a-civil-action:5.4`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Starting a civil action, "Serving the claim"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
Where prompt service is impractical, “the court may make an order for substituted service or, where necessary in the interest of justice, may dispense with service.” The court may also validate service made in an unauthorized way if the document came to the person's notice, or would have except for the person's “own attempts to evade service.” Service may be proved “by an affidavit of the person who served it (Form 16B).” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 16.04 (1), 16.08, 16.09 (1))
```

### `guide:starting-a-civil-action:6:heading`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Starting a civil action
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
Time to defend
```

### `guide:starting-a-civil-action:6.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Starting a civil action, "Time to defend"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
Except as provided in rule 18.02 and certain other rules (late delivery of a defence, and a counterclaim against the plaintiff and a non-party), a statement of defence (Form 18A) is delivered “within twenty days after service of the statement of claim, where the defendant is served in Ontario”; within forty days if served elsewhere in Canada or in the United States of America; and within sixty days if served anywhere else. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 18.01)
```

### `guide:starting-a-civil-action:6.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Starting a civil action, "Time to defend"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
A defendant who intends to defend “may deliver a notice of intent to defend (Form 18B) within the time prescribed for delivery of a statement of defence.” A defendant who does so “is entitled to ten days, in addition to the time prescribed by rule 18.01, within which to deliver a statement of defence.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 18.02 (1), (2))
```

### `guide:starting-a-civil-action:7:heading`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Starting a civil action
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
What a pleading contains
```

### `guide:starting-a-civil-action:7.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Starting a civil action, "What a pleading contains"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
In an action, pleadings “shall consist of the statement of claim (Form 14A, 14B or 14D), statement of defence (Form 18A) and reply (Form 25A), if any.” Pleadings “shall be divided into paragraphs numbered consecutively”. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 25.01 (1), 25.02)
```

### `guide:starting-a-civil-action:7.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Starting a civil action, "What a pleading contains"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
“Every pleading shall contain a concise statement of the material facts on which the party relies for the claim or defence, but not the evidence by which those facts are to be proved.” A party may raise a point of law, “but conclusions of law may be pleaded only if the material facts supporting them are pleaded.” Where damages are claimed, “the amount claimed for each claimant in respect of each claim shall be stated”. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 25.06 (1), (2), (9))
```

### `guide:starting-a-civil-action:7.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Starting a civil action, "What a pleading contains"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
In a defence, a party “shall admit every allegation of fact in the opposite party's pleading that the party does not dispute.” Allegations of fact not denied “shall be deemed to be admitted unless the party pleads having no knowledge in respect of the fact.” But “In an action for damages, the amount of damages shall be deemed to be in issue unless specifically admitted.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 25.07 (1), (2), (6))
```

### `guide:starting-a-civil-action:7.4`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Starting a civil action, "What a pleading contains"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
Where a party intends to prove a version of the facts different from that pleaded by the opposite party, “a denial of the version so pleaded is not sufficient, but the party shall plead the party's own version of the facts in the defence.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 25.07 (3))
```

### `guide:starting-a-civil-action:8:heading`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Starting a civil action
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
Reply and close of pleadings
```

### `guide:starting-a-civil-action:8.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Starting a civil action, "Reply and close of pleadings"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
A party who intends to prove a different version of the facts from the defence “shall deliver a reply setting out the different version, unless it has already been pleaded in the claim.” But “A party shall not deliver a reply except where required to do so by subrule (1) or (2).” A party who does not deliver a reply within the prescribed time is “deemed to deny the allegations of fact made in the defence of the opposite party.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 25.08 (1), (3), (4))
```

### `guide:starting-a-civil-action:8.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Starting a civil action, "Reply and close of pleadings"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
A reply “shall be delivered within ten days after service of the statement of defence”, or within twenty days where the defendant counterclaims. Pleadings are closed when the plaintiff has delivered a reply to every defence or the time for a reply has expired, and every defendant in default has been noted in default. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 25.04 (3), 25.05)
```

### `guide:starting-a-civil-action:9:heading`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Starting a civil action
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
Filing civil documents online
```

### `guide:starting-a-civil-action:9.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Starting a civil action, "Filing civil documents online"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
Ontario.ca says that starting October 14, 2025, “all online filings for the Toronto region must be submitted using the Ontario Courts Public Portal.” Outside Toronto, the Civil Claims Online and Civil Submissions Online portals remain available. Documents cannot be submitted online “to request an urgent court hearing” or for a court date or deadline 3 business days or fewer away. (ontario.ca, File civil or Divisional Court documents online)
```

### `guide:starting-a-civil-action:9.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Starting a civil action, "Filing civil documents online"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
The page says a person filing online needs “an online Ontario.ca Login” and a payment card if filing fees apply. For filings outside Toronto, a person with a fee waiver, or applying for one, “must use the Civil Submissions Online portal”, because the Civil Claims Online portal “will not apply the relevant fee exemptions.” It also says “Once you file a document, online or at a courthouse, you cannot change it.” (ontario.ca, File civil or Divisional Court documents online)
```

### `guide:starting-a-civil-action:9.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Starting a civil action, "Filing civil documents online"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
Through Civil Claims Online, a document filed on a weekday between 8:30 a.m. and 5:00 p.m. (excluding holidays) “will be considered filed at that time”; outside those hours “it will be considered filed on the next business day.” Through Civil Submissions Online, “Court staff will review your documents within 3 business days to determine if they are accepted for filing or issuance.” (ontario.ca, File civil or Divisional Court documents online)
```

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, When a defendant or respondent does not respond

This guide explains what the court rules say happens when a person who is sued, or who is named as a respondent, does not file a defence or answer in time, and how the rules deal with setting that aside. It covers Small Claims Court briefly and the Rules of Civil Procedure (Superior Court civil actions) and the Family Law Rules in more detail.

Small Claims Court: a short summary
```

### `guide:default-proceedings:1.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, When a defendant or respondent does not respond, "Small Claims Court: a short summary"

```
“A defendant generally has 20 calendar days to serve and file a defence to a claim.” “If a defendant does not file a defence in time, then the plaintiff may ask the Court to note the defendant in default.” The request to note a defendant in default “may be made in Form 9B”. (ontariocourts.ca, Small Claims Court — Default Proceedings; Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 11.01 (1))
```

A defendant who has been noted in default “shall not file a defence or take any other step in the proceeding, except making a motion under rule 11.06, without leave of the court or the plaintiff's consent.” (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 11.05 (1))
```

If a defendant has been noted in default, the clerk may sign default judgment (Form 11B) for the claim, or any part of the claim to which the default applies, that is “for a debt or liquidated demand in money, including interest if claimed”. (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 11.02 (1))
```

- **Appears in:** Guides, When a defendant or respondent does not respond, "Small Claims Court: a short summary"

If all defendants are noted in default, the plaintiff may seek judgment on the rest of the claim by a motion in writing for an assessment of damages or at an assessment hearing, where the plaintiff “is not required to prove liability against a defendant noted in default, but is required to prove the amount of the claim.” (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 11.03 (1), (2), (5))
```

```

### `guide:default-proceedings:2.1`

- **Appears in:** Guides, When a defendant or respondent does not respond, "Civil actions: time to defend and being noted in default"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/980258

```
In a Superior Court civil action, a statement of defence is delivered “within twenty days after service of the statement of claim, where the defendant is served in Ontario”. The time is forty days if the defendant is served elsewhere in Canada or in the United States, and sixty days if served anywhere else. These times are subject to listed exceptions, including rule 18.02 (notice of intent to defend). (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 18.01)
```

### `guide:default-proceedings:2.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, When a defendant or respondent does not respond, "Civil actions: time to defend and being noted in default"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/980258

```
If a defendant does not deliver a statement of defence in time, the plaintiff may, on filing proof of service of the statement of claim, “require the registrar to note the defendant in default.” The plaintiff may also, on filing a copy of the order, have the defendant noted in default where the defence was struck out without leave to deliver another, or with leave and no other was delivered within the time allowed. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 19.01 (1), (2))
```

```
“A defendant may deliver a statement of defence at any time before being noted in default under this rule.” A party under disability “may be noted in default only with leave of a judge”. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 19.01 (4), (5))
```

A defendant who has been noted in default “is deemed to admit the truth of all allegations of fact made in the statement of claim”. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 19.02 (1) (a))
```

- **Appears in:** Guides, When a defendant or respondent does not respond, "Civil actions: what being noted in default means"

That defendant also “shall not deliver a statement of defence or take any other step in the action, other than a motion to set aside the noting of default or any judgment obtained by reason of the default, except with leave of the court or the consent of the plaintiff.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 19.02 (1) (b))
```

### `guide:default-proceedings:3.3`

- **Appears in:** Guides, When a defendant or respondent does not respond, "Civil actions: what being noted in default means"

```
A defendant noted in default “is not entitled to notice of any step in the action and need not be served with any document in the action”, except where the court orders otherwise, where a party requires the defendant's personal attendance, and for certain listed documents, such as an amended pleading or a counterclaim. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 19.02 (3))

- **Appears in:** Guides, When a defendant or respondent does not respond, "Civil actions: default judgment"

```
Once a defendant is noted in default, the plaintiff may require the registrar to sign judgment for certain claims, including “a debt or liquidated demand in money, including interest if claimed in the statement of claim (Form 19A)”, recovery of possession of land, and recovery of possession of personal property. The plaintiff first files a requisition for default judgment (Form 19D). (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 19.04 (1), (2))
```

### `guide:default-proceedings:4.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, When a defendant or respondent does not respond, "Civil actions: default judgment"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/980258

```
The registrar may decline to sign default judgment if uncertain whether the claim fits the class of cases allowed, or about the interest properly recoverable. The plaintiff may then move before a judge for judgment under rule 19.05 or, for a claim listed in subrule 19.04 (1), make a motion to the court for default judgment. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 19.04 (3), (3.1))
```

### `guide:default-proceedings:4.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, When a defendant or respondent does not respond, "Civil actions: default judgment"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/980258

```
Where a defendant has been noted in default, the plaintiff may move before a judge for judgment on the statement of claim for any claim for which default judgment has not been signed. The motion “shall be supported by evidence given by affidavit if the claim is for unliquidated damages.” The judge “may grant judgment, dismiss the action or order that the action proceed to trial”. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 19.05 (1), (2), (3))
```

“The noting of default may be set aside by the court on such terms as are just.” If the defendant delivers a statement of defence with the plaintiff's consent, the noting of default “shall be deemed to have been set aside.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 19.03 (1), (2))
```

A default judgment signed by the registrar or granted on motion under rule 19.04 “may be set aside or varied by the court on such terms as are just.” A judgment obtained on a motion for judgment or after trial may be set aside or varied by a judge. When setting aside a judgment, the court or judge may also set aside the noting of default. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 19.08 (1), (2), (3))
```

```
“If an application is served outside Canada or the United States of America, the time for serving and filing an answer is 60 days.” A respondent added through a claim in an answer has 14 days, or 30 days if served outside Canada or the United States. Different times apply to an application to dispense with a parent's consent before adoption placement. (Family Law Rules, r. 10 (2), (2.1), (4))
```

(Family Law Rules, r. 3 (5), (6))
```

The Family Law Rules do not use the phrase noted in default for this step. Instead, the consequences in paragraphs 1 to 4 of subrule 1 (8.4) “apply, with necessary changes, if a respondent does not serve and file an answer.” (Family Law Rules, r. 10 (5))

Those consequences are: “The party is not entitled to any further notice of steps in the case, except as provided by subrule 25 (13) (service of order).” “The party is not entitled to participate in the case in any way.” “The court may deal with the case in the party’s absence.” “A date may be set for an uncontested trial of the case.” (Family Law Rules, r. 1 (8.4))
```

An “uncontested trial” means “a trial at which only the party making the claim provides evidence and submissions.” If no answer is filed, the clerk “shall, on request, schedule a case conference or set a date for an uncontested trial or, in an uncontested divorce case, prepare the documents for a judge”. (Family Law Rules, r. 2 (1), r. 17 (2))
```

At an uncontested trial, evidence by affidavit in Form 14A or Form 23C and, if applicable, Forms 35.1 and 35.1A may be used “unless the court directs that oral evidence must be given.” Unless the court orders otherwise, the person who prepared an order serves it on every other party, including a party to whom the no-notice consequence applies. (Family Law Rules, r. 23 (22), r. 25 (13))
```

A motion is how a party asks a judge to make an order while a case is under way. This guide sets out what the rules say about motions in Small Claims Court, in civil cases in the Superior Court of Justice, and in family cases, with each rule cited.
```

### `guide:motions:1:heading`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case

What a motion is in Small Claims Court
```

### `guide:motions:1.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "What a motion is in Small Claims Court"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/980258

```
The ontario.ca guide describes a motion as “a process for requesting that a judge make an order.” It says a party generally makes a motion “to have a matter addressed before judgment, or in some circumstances after judgment or to support an enforcement process.” The guide adds that, usually, a motion is a hearing in court before a judge. There is a fee to file a motion. (ontario.ca, Guide to Procedures in Small Claims Court: Motions and clerk's orders)
```

### `guide:motions:1.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "What a motion is in Small Claims Court"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/980258

```
The guide says anyone who is a party in the case can make a motion. The person who makes it is called the “moving party.” The person who responds is called the “responding party.” In special circumstances, a judge may allow a person who is not a party to make a motion, because the outcome would affect that person. (ontario.ca, Guide to Procedures in Small Claims Court: Motions and clerk's orders)
```

### `guide:motions:1.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "What a motion is in Small Claims Court"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/980258

```
Under the Small Claims Court rules, “A motion shall be made by a notice of motion and supporting affidavit (Form 15A).” The supporting affidavit is where the moving party states the order asked for and the facts behind the request. The guide explains that the statements must be sworn or affirmed as true and signed in front of a commissioner for taking affidavits. (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 15.01 (1); ontario.ca, Guide to Procedures in Small Claims Court: Motions and clerk's orders)
```

### `guide:motions:2:heading`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / guide

### `guide:motions:2.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Small Claims Court: dates, service and responding"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/980258

```
The moving party “shall obtain a hearing date from the clerk before serving the notice of motion and supporting affidavit”. The notice of motion and supporting affidavit “shall be served on every party who has filed a claim and any defendant who has not been noted in default, at least seven days before the hearing date”. They must be filed, with proof of service, “at least three days before the hearing date”. (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 15.01 (2), (3))
```

### `guide:motions:2.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Small Claims Court: dates, service and responding"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/980258

```
A party who prepares an affidavit (Form 15B) in response must serve it on every party who has filed a claim or defence and file it, with proof of service, “at least two days before the hearing date.” The moving party may serve and file a supplementary affidavit, also at least two days before the hearing date. A motion made after judgment has been signed must be served on all parties, including those noted in default. (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 15.01 (4), (5), (6))
```

### `guide:motions:2.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Small Claims Court: dates, service and responding"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/980258

```
A motion may be conducted with the parties attending by a method determined under rule 1.07. It may instead be in writing if the rules provide for that, or “if the judge determines that it is fair and reasonable for the motion to be in writing.” (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 15.02)
```

### `guide:motions:2.4`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Small Claims Court: dates, service and responding"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/980258

```
A motion “shall not be adjourned at a party's request before the hearing date unless the written consent of all parties is filed when the request is made, unless the court orders otherwise.” A motion cannot be withdrawn without the written consent of all the parties or leave of the court. The costs of a motion, other than disbursements, “shall not exceed $100 unless the court orders otherwise because there are special circumstances.” (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 15.05, 15.06, 15.07)
```

- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/980258

```
A motion may be made without notice “if the nature or circumstances of the motion make notice unnecessary or not reasonably possible.” A party who gets an order this way must serve it on every affected party, with the notice of motion and supporting affidavit, “within five days after the order is signed.” An affected party may move to set aside or vary the order “within 30 days after being served with the order.” (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 15.03)
```

### `guide:motions:3.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Small Claims Court: motions without notice, motions in writing and clerk's orders"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/980258

```
The guide describes a “motion in writing for assessment of damages”. A plaintiff can make it when the claim is an “unliquidated” claim and all defendants have been served with the claim, none has filed a defence, and all have been noted in default. For this motion, “the plaintiff does not have to attend court for a hearing.” The judge reviews the papers and may grant judgment, ask for another affidavit, or order an assessment hearing. (ontario.ca, Guide to Procedures in Small Claims Court: Motions and clerk's orders)
```

### `guide:motions:3.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Small Claims Court: motions without notice, motions in writing and clerk's orders"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/980258

```
The guide also explains clerk’s orders. The clerk can make certain orders listed in Rule 11.2. The guide says “These orders can only be made if the written consent of all parties has been provided to the clerk.” The request uses Form 11.2A, and “No hearing is required.” If a party does not consent, a motion to a judge is the route the guide describes. (ontario.ca, Guide to Procedures in Small Claims Court: Motions and clerk's orders)
```

### `guide:motions:3.4`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Small Claims Court: motions without notice, motions in writing and clerk's orders"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/980258

```
If the court is satisfied that a party has tried to delay the action, add to its costs or otherwise abuse the court’s process “by making numerous motions without merit”, the court may, on motion, order that the party make no further motions in the action without leave of the court. (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 15.04)
```

### `guide:motions:4:heading`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/980258

Civil cases: bringing a motion under Rule 37
```

### `guide:motions:4.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Civil cases: bringing a motion under Rule 37"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/980258

```
In the Superior Court of Justice, a motion is made by a notice of motion in Form 37A “unless the nature of the motion or the circumstances make a notice of motion unnecessary or these rules provide otherwise.” Every notice of motion must “state the precise relief sought”, state the grounds to be argued, and “list the documentary evidence to be used at the hearing of the motion.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 37.01, 37.06)
```

### `guide:motions:4.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Civil cases: bringing a motion under Rule 37"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/980258

```
“A judge has jurisdiction to hear any motion in a proceeding.” An associate judge can hear most motions, except those listed in the rule. On a motion for an order on consent, the registrar makes the order if all parties consent, the consent states no affected party is under disability, and the order is one of the kinds listed, such as setting aside the noting of a party in default. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 37.02)
```

### `guide:motions:4.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Civil cases: bringing a motion under Rule 37"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/980258

```
The notice of motion is served on any party or other person who will be affected by the order sought, unless the rules provide otherwise. Where a motion is made on notice, it “shall be served at least seven days before the date on which the motion is to be heard.” It must also be filed with proof of service at least seven days before the hearing date, in the court office where the motion is to be heard. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 37.07 (1), (6), 37.08 (1))
```

### `guide:motions:4.4`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Civil cases: bringing a motion under Rule 37"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/980258

```
Where a motion is made on notice, the moving party serves and files a motion record at least seven days before the hearing, unless the court orders otherwise. It contains a table of contents, the notice of motion, the affidavits and other material served, and other listed items. A responding party who considers it incomplete may serve and file a responding party’s motion record at least four days before the hearing. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 37.10 (1)-(3))
```

### `guide:motions:4.5`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Civil cases: bringing a motion under Rule 37"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/980258

```
A party “may serve on every other party a factum”. A factum required by the rules is “a concise argument stating the facts and law relied on”. If served, the moving party’s factum is served and filed at least seven days before the hearing and the responding party’s at least four days before. On an opposed motion proposed for a hearing in writing, the moving party must serve and file a factum (see below). (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 4.06.1 (1), 37.10 (6)-(8), 37.12.1 (4))
```

### `guide:motions:4.6`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Civil cases: bringing a motion under Rule 37"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/980258

```
A party who makes a motion on notice must confer or attempt to confer with the other party and, “not later than 2 p.m. five days before the hearing date”, give the registrar a confirmation of motion (Form 37B) and send a copy of it to the other party by email. If no confirmation is given, “the motion shall not be heard and is deemed to have been abandoned, unless the court orders otherwise.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 37.10.1 (1), (4))
```

### `guide:motions:4.7`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Civil cases: bringing a motion under Rule 37"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/980258

```
On the hearing, the judge or officer “may grant the relief sought or dismiss or adjourn the motion, in whole or in part and with or without terms”. On a motion by any party, a judge or associate judge may also prohibit another party from making further motions without leave where that party is attempting to delay or add to costs “by a multiplicity of frivolous or vexatious motions.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 37.13 (1), 37.16)
```

### `guide:motions:5:heading`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/980258

Civil cases: urgent motions, motions without notice and motions in writing
```

### `guide:motions:5.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Civil cases: urgent motions, motions without notice and motions in writing"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/980258

```
Where serving the notice is impracticable or unnecessary, the court may make an order without notice. “Where the delay necessary to effect service might entail serious consequences, the court may make an interim order without notice.” On a motion without notice, the moving party must “make full and fair disclosure of all material facts”, and failing to do so is itself enough to set the order aside. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 37.07 (2), (3), 39.01 (6))
```

### `guide:motions:5.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Civil cases: urgent motions, motions without notice and motions in writing"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/980258

```
A person affected by an order made without notice, or who missed a motion “through accident, mistake or insufficient notice”, may move to set aside or vary it. That notice of motion is served right after the order comes to the person’s attention. It names the first available hearing date at least three days after service. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 37.14 (1))
```

### `guide:motions:5.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Civil cases: urgent motions, motions without notice and motions in writing"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/980258

```
Rule 37.05 sets hearing dates where no practice direction on scheduling motions is in effect. There, an urgent motion may be set down on any day a judge or associate judge is scheduled to hear motions, even if it is expected to take more than two hours. “In an urgent case, a motion may be made before the commencement of a proceeding on the moving party's undertaking to commence the proceeding forthwith.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 37.05 (1), (3), 37.17)
```

### `guide:motions:5.4`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Civil cases: urgent motions, motions without notice and motions in writing"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/980258

```
A motion on consent, unopposed, or made without notice under rule 37.07 (2) “may be heard in writing without the attendance of the parties, unless the court orders otherwise.” An opposed motion can also be proposed for a hearing in writing. In that case, it “shall be made on at least fourteen days notice” and the moving party files a motion record, a draft order and a factum. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 37.12.1)
```

### `guide:motions:6:heading`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/980258

Civil cases: evidence on a motion (Rule 39)
```

### `guide:motions:6.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Civil cases: evidence on a motion (Rule 39)"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/980258

```
“Evidence on a motion or application may be given by affidavit unless a statute or these rules provide otherwise.” Where a motion is made on notice, the moving party’s affidavits are served with the notice of motion and filed at least seven days before the hearing. Affidavits in opposition or in reply are served and filed “at least four days before the hearing.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 39.01 (1), (2), (3))
```

### `guide:motions:6.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Civil cases: evidence on a motion (Rule 39)"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/980258

```
An affidavit for a motion may include what the person signing it was told and believes, “if the source of the information and the fact of the belief are specified in the affidavit.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 39.01 (4))
```

### `guide:motions:6.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Civil cases: evidence on a motion (Rule 39)"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/980258

```
A party who has served every affidavit it relies on and completed all examinations under rule 39.03 may cross-examine anyone who swore an affidavit for an adverse party (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 39.02 (1))
```

### `guide:motions:6.4`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Civil cases: evidence on a motion (Rule 39)"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/980258

```
On a motion other than for summary judgment or a contempt order, the cross-examining party is liable for the adverse party’s partial indemnity costs of the cross-examination, “regardless of the outcome of the proceeding, unless the court orders otherwise.” With leave, a person may be examined at the hearing “in the same manner as at a trial.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 39.02 (4), 39.03 (4))
```

### `guide:motions:7:heading`

- **Status:** draft

- **Appears in:** Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case

Family cases: motions for temporary orders (rule 14)
```

### `guide:motions:7.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Family cases: motions for temporary orders (rule 14)"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/980258

```
Under the Family Law Rules, a person may make a motion for “A temporary order for a claim made in an application”, for “Directions on how to carry on the case”, or for “A change in a temporary order.” A motion may be made “by a party to the case or by a person with an interest in the case.” (Family Law Rules, r. 14 (1), (2))
```

### `guide:motions:7.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Family cases: motions for temporary orders (rule 14)"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/980258

```
A motion “requires a notice of motion (Form 14) and an affidavit (Form 14A)” and may be supported by more evidence. If a motion is limited to “procedural, uncomplicated or unopposed matters”, the party may use a motion form (Form 14B) instead. (Family Law Rules, r. 14 (9), (10))
```

### `guide:motions:7.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Family cases: motions for temporary orders (rule 14)"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/980258

```
As a general rule, “No notice of motion or supporting evidence may be served and no motion may be heard before a conference dealing with the substantive issues in the case has been completed.” This does not apply “if the court is of the opinion that there is a situation of urgency or hardship or that a case conference is not required for some other reason in the interest of justice.” (Family Law Rules, r. 14 (4), (4.2))
```

### `guide:motions:7.4`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Family cases: motions for temporary orders (rule 14)"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/980258

```
The rule also lists motions that may go ahead before that conference. They include a motion for summary judgment under rule 16, a motion in a child protection case, and a motion “made without notice, made on consent, that is unopposed or that is limited to procedural, uncomplicated or unopposed matters (Form 14B)”. (Family Law Rules, r. 14 (6))
```

### `guide:motions:8:heading`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/980258

Family cases: service, confirmation and responding
```

### `guide:motions:8.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Family cases: service, confirmation and responding"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/980258

```
A party making a motion with notice serves the documents on all other parties “not later than six days before the motion date”. The party files them as soon as possible after service, “but not later than four days before the motion date”. The party must also “confer or make best efforts to confer orally or in writing with every other party” about the issues in dispute, subject to the exceptions the rule lists. (Family Law Rules, r. 14 (11) (a)-(c))
```

### `guide:motions:8.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Family cases: service, confirmation and responding"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/980258

```
The party gives the clerk a confirmation of motion (Form 14C) “not later than 2 p.m. three days before the motion date”, after giving a copy to every other party (the rule excepts child protection cases, other than applications under sections 53.1 to 53.5 of O. Reg. 155/18, from giving that copy). Unless the court orders otherwise, “a motion shall not be heard if confirmation of the motion is not given to the clerk” as required. (Family Law Rules, r. 14 (11) (d), (e), (11.0.1), (11.1))
```

### `guide:motions:8.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Family cases: service, confirmation and responding"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/980258

```
A response to a notice of motion (Form 14) is served and filed “not later than four days before the motion date.” A response to a motion form (Form 14B) is served and filed not later than seven days after the motion form is served. The party who used Form 14 may reply “not later than 2 p.m. three days before the motion date.” No reply is allowed to a response to Form 14B. (Family Law Rules, r. 14 (11.3)-(11.6))
```

### `guide:motions:9:heading`

- **Status:** draft

- **Appears in:** Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/980258

Family cases: urgent motions without notice, and evidence
```

### `guide:motions:9.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Family cases: urgent motions without notice, and evidence"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/980258

```
A motion may be made without notice if notice is unnecessary or not reasonably possible, if service “would probably have serious consequences”, or where there is an immediate danger of a child being removed from Ontario, or to the health or safety of a child or of the party making the motion, and the delay of serving notice would probably have serious consequences. (Family Law Rules, r. 14 (12))
```

### `guide:motions:9.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Family cases: urgent motions without notice, and evidence"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/980258

```
An order made without notice (Form 14D) “shall require the matter to come back to the court and, if possible, to the same judge, within 14 days or on a date chosen by the court.” It must be served immediately on all parties affected, together with all documents used on the motion, unless the court orders otherwise. (Family Law Rules, r. 14 (14), (15))
```

### `guide:motions:9.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Family cases: urgent motions without notice, and evidence"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/980258

```
Evidence on a motion may be given by affidavit or other admissible evidence in writing, by a transcript of questioning under rule 20, or, with the court’s permission, orally (Family Law Rules, r. 14 (17))
```

### `guide:motions:9.4`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Family cases: urgent motions without notice, and evidence"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/980258

```
An affidavit “shall, as much as possible, contain only information within the personal knowledge of the person signing the affidavit.” Information from someone else is allowed only if the source is named and the affidavit states the person believes it is true; on a contempt motion under rule 31, it must also be unlikely to be disputed. (Family Law Rules, r. 14 (18), (19))
```

### `guide:motions:9.5`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Motions: asking the court for an order during a case, "Family cases: urgent motions without notice, and evidence"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/980258

```
Unless the court orders otherwise, the moving party serves all supporting evidence with the notice of motion, the responding party then serves its evidence, and the moving party may reply only to new matters. “No other evidence may be used.” A party who makes “numerous motions without merit” to delay the case or add to its costs may be ordered not to make other motions without the court’s permission. (Family Law Rules, r. 14 (20), (21))
```

### `guide:discovery:intro`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Discovery in a civil action
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
This guide explains what the Rules of Civil Procedure say about discovery in a Superior Court of Justice action: the discovery plan, proportionality, sharing documents, and examinations for discovery, whether oral or by written questions.
```

### `guide:discovery:1:heading`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Discovery in a civil action
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
The discovery plan
```

### `guide:discovery:1.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Discovery in a civil action, "The discovery plan"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
Where a party intends to obtain evidence under the discovery rules, including Rule 30 (Discovery of Documents), Rule 31 (Examination for Discovery) and Rule 35 (Examination for Discovery by Written Questions), “the parties to the action shall agree to a discovery plan”. The plan is agreed before the earlier of “60 days after the close of pleadings or such longer period as the parties may agree to” and attempting to obtain the evidence. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 29.1.03 (1), (2))
```

### `guide:discovery:1.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Discovery in a civil action, "The discovery plan"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
“The discovery plan shall be in writing”. It includes the intended scope of documentary discovery, dates for serving each party's affidavit of documents, information on the timing, costs and manner of producing documents, and “the names of persons intended to be produced for oral examination for discovery under Rule 31 and information respecting the timing and length of the examinations”. The parties “shall ensure that the discovery plan is updated”. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 29.1.03 (3), 29.1.04)
```

### `guide:discovery:1.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Discovery in a civil action, "The discovery plan"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
On a discovery motion, “the court may refuse to grant any relief or to award any costs if the parties have failed to agree to or update a discovery plan”. If the parties fail to agree, the court may order examinations “in accordance with a discovery plan established by the court”. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 29.1.05 (1), (2))
```

### `guide:discovery:2:heading`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Discovery in a civil action
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
Proportionality
```

### `guide:discovery:2.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Discovery in a civil action, "Proportionality"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
When deciding whether a party or other person must answer a question or produce a document, the court shall consider whether the time required “would be unreasonable”, whether the expense “would be unjustified”, whether it “would cause him or her undue prejudice”, whether it “would unduly interfere with the orderly progress of the action”, and whether the information or document “is readily available to the party requesting it from another source.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 29.2.03 (1))
```

### `guide:discovery:2.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Discovery in a civil action, "Proportionality"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
For documents, the court also considers “whether such an order would result in an excessive volume of documents required to be produced by the party or other person.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 29.2.03 (2))
```

### `guide:discovery:3:heading`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Discovery in a civil action
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194
