### `guide:appeals:3.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Appealing a decision, "Leave to appeal"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
Some appeals can only go ahead with “leave” of the appeal court. The Courts of Justice Act says “No appeal lies without leave of the court to which the appeal is to be taken,” from “an order made with the consent of the parties” or “where the appeal is only as to costs that are in the discretion of the court that made the order for costs.” (Courts of Justice Act, s. 133)
```

### `guide:appeals:3.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Appealing a decision, "Leave to appeal"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
Leave to appeal to the Divisional Court from “An interlocutory order of a judge of the Superior Court of Justice” is obtained from a panel of that court. The motion for leave “shall be heard in writing, without the attendance of parties or lawyers.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 62.02 (1), (2))
```

### `guide:appeals:3.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Appealing a decision, "Leave to appeal"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
Leave to appeal from an interlocutory order “shall not be granted unless” there is “a conflicting decision by another judge or court in Ontario or elsewhere on the matter involved in the proposed appeal” and the panel considers leave desirable, or there appears to the panel “good reason to doubt the correctness of the order in question” and the proposed appeal “involves matters of such importance that, in the panel's opinion, leave to appeal should be granted”. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 62.02 (4))
```

### `guide:appeals:3.4`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Appealing a decision, "Leave to appeal"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
A notice of motion for leave to appeal to the Divisional Court is to be served “within 15 days after the making of the order or decision from which leave to appeal is sought, unless a statute provides otherwise”, and filed with proof of service “within five days after service”. The same 15-day and five-day times apply to a motion for leave from an interlocutory order under rule 62.02. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 61.03 (1), r. 61.03.1 (3), r. 62.02 (3))
```

### `guide:appeals:3.5`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Appealing a decision, "Leave to appeal"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
Where the Court of Appeal's leave is required, the motion “shall be heard in writing, without the attendance of parties or lawyers”, and the notice of motion has the same 15-day service and five-day filing times. If the court decides an oral hearing is warranted, it orders one. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 61.03.1 (1), (3), (15))
```

### `guide:appeals:3.6`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Appealing a decision, "Leave to appeal"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
In both courts, “Where leave is granted, the notice of appeal shall be delivered within seven days after the granting of leave.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 61.03 (6), r. 61.03.1 (16), r. 62.02 (8))
```

### `guide:appeals:4:heading`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Appealing a decision
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
Starting an appeal in a civil case
```

### `guide:appeals:4.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Appealing a decision, "Starting an appeal in a civil case"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
An appeal to the Court of Appeal or the Divisional Court starts by serving a notice of appeal in Form 61A.2 (Court of Appeal) or 61A.3 (Divisional Court), with a certificate respecting evidence, “within 30 days after the making of the order appealed from, unless a statute or these rules provide otherwise”. It is served on “every party whose interest may be affected by the appeal” and on “any person entitled by statute to be heard on the appeal”. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 61.04 (1))
```

### `guide:appeals:4.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Appealing a decision, "Starting an appeal in a civil case"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
It need not be served on a defendant who was noted in default, or on a respondent who has not delivered a notice of appearance unless that respondent was heard at the hearing with leave. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 61.04 (1.1))
```

### `guide:appeals:4.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Appealing a decision, "Starting an appeal in a civil case"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
The notice of appeal states “the relief sought”, “the grounds of appeal”, and the basis for the appeal court's jurisdiction, including whether the order is final or interlocutory and whether leave is needed. It is filed with proof of service “within ten days after service”. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 61.04 (3), (4))
```

### `guide:appeals:4.4`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Appealing a decision, "Starting an appeal in a civil case"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
With the notice of appeal, the appellant serves and files a certificate (Form 61C) “setting out only the portions of the evidence that, in the appellant's opinion, are required for the appeal.” Instead, the parties may, within thirty days after service of the notice of appeal, make an agreement about the documents and transcript required for the appeal. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 61.05 (1), (4))
```

### `guide:appeals:4.5`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Appealing a decision, "Starting an appeal in a civil case"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
Within thirty days after filing the notice of appeal, the appellant files proof of having ordered a transcript of all oral evidence that the parties have not agreed to omit. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 61.05 (5))
```

### `guide:appeals:4.6`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Appealing a decision, "Starting an appeal in a civil case"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
The appellant “perfects” the appeal by serving and filing the appeal book and compendium, exhibit book, any transcript and a factum. This is due “within thirty days after filing the notice of appeal” if no transcript is needed, or “within 60 days after receiving notice that the evidence has been transcribed” if one is. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 61.09 (1), (3))
```

### `guide:appeals:4.7`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Appealing a decision, "Starting an appeal in a civil case"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
“No grounds other than those stated in the notice of appeal or cross-appeal or supplementary notice may be relied on at the hearing, except with leave of the court hearing the appeal.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 61.08 (2))
```

### `guide:appeals:4.8`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Appealing a decision, "Starting an appeal in a civil case"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
A different procedure, in rule 62.01, applies to an appeal made to a judge, such as an appeal to the Superior Court of Justice from “an interlocutory order of a master, case management master or associate judge”. That appeal starts by serving a notice of appeal (Form 62A) “within seven days after the making of the order or certificate appealed from.” (Courts of Justice Act, s. 17; Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 62.01 (1), (2))
```

### `guide:appeals:5:heading`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Appealing a decision
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
What happens to the order during an appeal
```

### `guide:appeals:5.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Appealing a decision, "What happens to the order during an appeal"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
Delivering a notice of appeal “stays, until the disposition of the appeal, any provision of the order for the payment of money, except a provision that awards support or enforces a support order.” When an order is stayed, “no steps may be taken under the order or for its enforcement,” except by order of a judge of the appeal court or as the rules otherwise provide. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 63.01 (1), r. 63.03 (1))
```

### `guide:appeals:5.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Appealing a decision, "What happens to the order during an appeal"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
An appeal from an order refusing to set aside a default judgment “does not stay the default judgment”, but it may be stayed by order. A judge of the appeal court may also order that the automatic stay does not apply. An order may be stayed “on such terms as are just” by the court that made it or by a judge of the appeal court. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 63.01 (2), (5), r. 63.02 (1))
```

### `guide:appeals:6:heading`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Appealing a decision
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
Family cases: which court and which rules
```

### `guide:appeals:6.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Appealing a decision, "Family cases: which court and which rules"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
An appeal lies to the Divisional Court from “a final order of a judge of the Family Court made only under a provision of an Act or regulation of Ontario”. (Courts of Justice Act, s. 19 (1) (a.1))
```

### `guide:appeals:6.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Appealing a decision, "Family cases: which court and which rules"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
For family appeals to the Divisional Court or the Court of Appeal, including where leave is required, “Rules 61, 62 and 63 of the Rules of Civil Procedure apply with necessary changes”, including changes the rule sets out, such as different time periods in an appeal in a case under the Child, Youth and Family Services Act, 2017. (Family Law Rules, r. 38 (1), (2))
```

### `guide:appeals:6.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Appealing a decision, "Family cases: which court and which rules"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
Rule 38 of the Family Law Rules sets out its own steps for appeals from an order of the Ontario Court of Justice to the Superior Court of Justice under provisions such as section 48 of the Family Law Act and section 73 of the Children's Law Reform Act. (Family Law Rules, r. 38 (4))
```

### `guide:appeals:6.4`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Appealing a decision, "Family cases: which court and which rules"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
A final order of a Superior Court judge made on a first appeal from certain Ontario Court of Justice orders (under the Change of Name Act, the Children's Law Reform Act except sections 59 and 60, or section 6 of the Marriage Act) “may be appealed to the Court of Appeal only with leave from the Court of Appeal, as provided in the rules of court.” (Courts of Justice Act, s. 6 (1.1), (1.2))
```

### `guide:appeals:7:heading`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Appealing a decision
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
Starting a family appeal from the Ontario Court of Justice
```

### `guide:appeals:7.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Appealing a decision, "Starting a family appeal from the Ontario Court of Justice"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
To appeal a final order of the Ontario Court of Justice to the Superior Court of Justice under a provision listed in rule 38 (4), a party serves a notice of appeal (Form 38) “within 30 days after the date of the order or decision being appealed from”. It goes to every other party affected by or entitled to appeal, the clerk of the court that made the order and, in some child protection appeals, certain other persons. (Family Law Rules, r. 38 (4), (5))
```

### `guide:appeals:7.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Appealing a decision, "Starting a family appeal from the Ontario Court of Justice"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
The notice of appeal is filed “within 10 days after serving the notice of appeal”. (Family Law Rules, r. 38 (5))
```

### `guide:appeals:7.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Appealing a decision, "Starting a family appeal from the Ontario Court of Justice"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
For a temporary order, the notice of appeal is served “within seven days after the date of the temporary order.” In a case under the Child, Youth and Family Services Act, 2017, the time for appealing a temporary order is 30 days. (Family Law Rules, r. 38 (6), (7))
```

### `guide:appeals:7.4`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Appealing a decision, "Starting a family appeal from the Ontario Court of Justice"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
The notice of appeal states “the order that the appellant wants the appeal court to make and the legal grounds for the appeal.” At the hearing, “no grounds other than the ones stated in the notice of appeal may be argued unless the court gives permission.” (Family Law Rules, r. 38 (10), (11))
```

### `guide:appeals:7.5`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Appealing a decision, "Starting a family appeal from the Ontario Court of Justice"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
If a transcript is needed, the appellant files proof it was ordered “within 30 days after filing the notice of appeal”. Outside child protection cases, the appellant's appeal record and factum are due within 60 days after notice that the evidence was transcribed, or within 30 days of filing the notice of appeal if no transcript is needed. (Family Law Rules, r. 38 (12), (21))
```

- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/page/fees-small-claims-court

```
This guide lists the fees the Ontario government charges for the main steps in Small Claims Court, civil proceedings in the Superior Court of Justice, and family proceedings. Fees as published on ontario.ca and in the regulations on e-Laws, read 2026-09-30 (the fee waiver page was read 2026-09-27).
```

### `guide:court-fees:1:heading`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, What court steps cost
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/page/fees-small-claims-court

How court fees are set and paid
```

### `guide:court-fees:1.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, What court steps cost, "How court fees are set and paid"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/page/fees-small-claims-court

```
The ontario.ca pages say “You must pay a fee for most steps in a Small Claims Court proceeding” and “You must pay a fee for most steps in a civil court proceeding”. The Small Claims page says “Court fees are set out in regulations made under the Administration of Justice Act”; the civil page says they are “primarily set out” in those regulations. The Small Claims tables are described as “an unofficial presentation of the fees prescribed by an Ontario regulation.” (ontario.ca, Fees: Small Claims Court; ontario.ca, Civil court fees)
```

### `guide:court-fees:1.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, What court steps cost, "How court fees are set and paid"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/page/fees-small-claims-court

```
In Small Claims Court, fees are payable in Canadian funds by cash at the court or enforcement office counter, by “cheque or money order, payable to the Minister of Finance”, or by debit or credit card “in certain locations, and when filing Small Claims Court documents online”. (ontario.ca, Fees: Small Claims Court)
```

### `guide:court-fees:1.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, What court steps cost, "How court fees are set and paid"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/page/fees-small-claims-court

```
For civil and family proceedings, the pages list cash, cheque or money order payable to the Minister of Finance, debit card in person and when filing online, and credit card “in person, over the phone and when filing civil court documents online” (the family page says the same for family court documents). (ontario.ca, Civil court fees; ontario.ca, Family court fees)
```

### `guide:court-fees:1.4`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, What court steps cost, "How court fees are set and paid"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/page/fees-small-claims-court

```
“Starting October 14, 2025, there are different online portals to file court documents online depending on the region you are filing in.” “Use the Ontario Courts Public Portal for matters in the Toronto region.” “Use the Justice Services Online portal for matters outside of Toronto.” For the Court of Appeal, the civil page says “Use the Ontario Court of Appeal Public Portal for matters at the Court of Appeal.” (ontario.ca, Fees: Small Claims Court; ontario.ca, Civil court fees)
```

### `guide:court-fees:1.5`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, What court steps cost, "How court fees are set and paid"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/page/fees-small-claims-court

```
The Small Claims Court page says “If there is a fee associated with your submission, you can pay online through these portals or request a fee waiver”. (ontario.ca, Fees: Small Claims Court)
```

### `guide:court-fees:1.6`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, What court steps cost, "How court fees are set and paid"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/page/fees-small-claims-court

```
Both regulations say: “If the applicable filing fee is paid on the filing of a document electronically in accordance with the rules of court, the fee is not payable again on the subsequent filing of a paper copy of the document.” (O. Reg. 332/16, s. 1 (4); O. Reg. 293/92, s. 7)
```

### `guide:court-fees:1.7`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, What court steps cost, "How court fees are set and paid"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/page/fees-small-claims-court

```
The amounts can change. Both regulations say that “Beginning on January 1, 2027, and on every third January 1 that follows, the fees payable under this Regulation shall be adjusted” using the Ontario Consumer Price Index. If the change “results in a negative amount, the fees shall not be increased.” (O. Reg. 332/16, s. 4 (1); O. Reg. 293/92, s. 6 (1))
```

### `guide:court-fees:1.8`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, What court steps cost, "How court fees are set and paid"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/page/fees-small-claims-court

```
A fee is not adjusted if, before the adjustment would take effect, the Minister determines that the adjusted fee “would exceed full cost recovery” and publishes notice confirming the amount of the fee on a Government of Ontario website. (O. Reg. 332/16, s. 4 (3); O. Reg. 293/92, s. 6 (3))
```

### `guide:court-fees:1.9`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, What court steps cost, "How court fees are set and paid"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/page/fees-small-claims-court

```
A person who cannot afford court fees “may request a fee waiver”; the court decides “whether you meet the requirements to qualify.” “If you are granted a fee waiver, it will apply to most fees in your court proceeding from that point forward.” “There is no cost to apply for a fee waiver.” Some fees “cannot be waived”, including fees paid “to someone who is not part of the court”. The site’s fee waiver guide covers this in full. (ontario.ca, Civil court fees; ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)
```

### `guide:court-fees:2.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, What court steps cost, "Small Claims Court: starting and answering a claim"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/page/fees-small-claims-court

```
Some Small Claims Court fees depend on whether the person filing is a frequent or infrequent claimant. A “frequent claimant” “means a claimant who files a claim in a Small Claims Court office on or after January 1 in any calendar year and who has already filed 10 or more claims in the same office in that calendar year”. An “infrequent claimant” “means a claimant who is not a frequent claimant.” (O. Reg. 332/16, s. 1 (1))
```

### `guide:court-fees:2.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, What court steps cost, "Small Claims Court: starting and answering a claim"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/page/fees-small-claims-court

```
A “claimant” “includes an individual, a sole proprietorship, a partnership, an unincorporated organization and a corporation”. For these fees, a claim does not include a defendant’s claim. (O. Reg. 332/16, s. 1 (1))
```

### `guide:court-fees:2.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, What court steps cost, "Small Claims Court: starting and answering a claim"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/page/fees-small-claims-court

```
The fees to start a claim are: “On the filing of a claim by an infrequent claimant, $108.” “On the filing of a claim by a frequent claimant, $228.” “On the filing of a defendant’s claim, $108.” (O. Reg. 332/16, s. 1 (2), paras. 1-3)
```

### `guide:court-fees:2.4`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, What court steps cost, "Small Claims Court: starting and answering a claim"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/page/fees-small-claims-court

```
The fee to answer a claim is: “On the filing of a defence, $77.” (O. Reg. 332/16, s. 1 (2), para. 5)
```

For a motion: “On the filing of a notice of motion served on another party, a notice of motion without notice or a notice of motion for a consent order (except a notice of motion under the Wages Act), $127.” (O. Reg. 332/16, s. 1 (2), para. 4)
```

```

```
For a trial date: “For the fixing of a date for a trial or an assessment hearing by an infrequent claimant, $308.” “For the fixing of a date for a trial or an assessment hearing by a frequent claimant, $403.” (O. Reg. 332/16, s. 1 (2), paras. 6-7)
```

- **Status:** draft

- **Appears in:** Guides, What court steps cost, "Small Claims Court: motions, default judgment and trial"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/page/fees-small-claims-court

```
The page says “If you summons a witness to attend your trial, you must pay attendance money to the witness at the time you personally serve them.” (ontario.ca, Fees: Small Claims Court)
```

### `guide:court-fees:3.6`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, What court steps cost, "Small Claims Court: motions, default judgment and trial"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/page/fees-small-claims-court

```

(O. Reg. 332/16, s. 3)
```

### `guide:fee-waivers:intro`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Having court fees waived
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/page/have-your-court-fees-waived

```
This guide explains what the Ontario government says about fee waivers in Small Claims Court, the Superior Court of Justice and family court: who can ask, who may qualify, how to apply, what is not covered and when a waiver applies.
```

### `guide:fee-waivers:1:heading`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Having court fees waived
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/page/have-your-court-fees-waived

```
What a fee waiver is
```

### `guide:fee-waivers:1.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Having court fees waived, "What a fee waiver is"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/page/have-your-court-fees-waived

```
“You might need to pay fees if you go to court in Ontario. If you cannot afford to pay the fees, you can ask the court to waive them.” The court “will consider your financial situation and decide whether you meet the requirements to qualify.” (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)
```

### `guide:fee-waivers:1.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Having court fees waived, "What a fee waiver is"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/page/have-your-court-fees-waived

```
If the person meets the requirements “and the court agrees to waive the fees”, they get “a certificate called a fee waiver.” The page says to “Show this certificate to court staff if they ask you to pay a fee.” (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)
```

### `guide:fee-waivers:1.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Having court fees waived, "What a fee waiver is"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/page/have-your-court-fees-waived

```
“There is no cost to apply for a fee waiver.” “You need to apply for a separate fee waiver for each case or proceeding you are involved in. A fee waiver will not apply to any fees you have already paid.” (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)
```

### `guide:fee-waivers:1.4`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Having court fees waived, "What a fee waiver is"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/page/have-your-court-fees-waived

```
“Each request is reviewed based on the form and documents you submit. The decision of staff or a judge is final. If your financial situation changes, you can request a fee waiver again.” (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)
```

### `guide:fee-waivers:2:heading`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Having court fees waived
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/page/have-your-court-fees-waived

Who can ask, and who may qualify
```

### `guide:fee-waivers:2.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Having court fees waived, "Who can ask, and who may qualify"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/page/have-your-court-fees-waived

```
A person can ask for a fee waiver if they “are or will be involved in a family, civil or small claims court matter”, “are not acting on behalf of a business or organization”, and their fees “are not being paid by a lawyer under a contingency fee agreement”. (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)
```

### `guide:fee-waivers:2.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Having court fees waived, "Who can ask, and who may qualify"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/page/have-your-court-fees-waived

```
The court may approve the request if the main source of household income is from Ontario Works, the Ontario Disability Support Program, the Old Age Security Pension and the Guaranteed Income Supplement, the War Veterans Allowance, or Canada Pension Plan benefits. It may also approve it if “your lawyer is being paid by a Legal Aid Certificate”. (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)
```

### `guide:fee-waivers:2.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Having court fees waived, "Who can ask, and who may qualify"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/page/have-your-court-fees-waived

```
The financial requirements refer to “gross annual household income”, meaning what everyone in the household earns in a year before taxes or deductions. The page says it must be below $33,100 for one person, $49,600 for two people, $57,300 for three people, $68,700 for four people, and $80,200 for five or more people. It also lists household liquid assets of less than $2,800 and household net worth of less than $11,100. (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)
```

### `guide:fee-waivers:2.4`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Having court fees waived, "Who can ask, and who may qualify"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/page/have-your-court-fees-waived

```
Listed with the income limits, as part of the same financial eligibility requirements, are “your household liquid assets are less than $2,800” and “your household net worth is less than $11,100”. Net worth is “the value of all assets owned by the members of your household, minus their debts and other financial liabilities”. (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)
```

### `guide:fee-waivers:2.5`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Having court fees waived, "Who can ask, and who may qualify"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/page/have-your-court-fees-waived

```
A person who does not meet the requirements but does not believe they can afford the fees “can make a request directly to the court to have your financial situation evaluated by a judge.” (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)
```

(ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)

- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/page/have-your-court-fees-waived

```
Also excluded are disbursements paid to the sheriff or small claims court bailiff to enforce an order (with one exception for orders under subsection 31(3) of the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006), and fees prescribed for bankruptcy proceedings. “A fee waiver does not apply to any costs a court has ordered you to pay to another party.” (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)
```

```
A person who thinks they meet the financial requirements uses the Fee Waiver Request to Registrar, Clerk or Sheriff (form FW-A-3). A person who does not think they meet them uses the Fee Waiver Request to Court (form FW-A 4). Forms FW-A 6 and FW-A 7 are the versions for a litigation guardian or special party representative. (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)
```

(ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)

With Exhibit C, they provide the first document filed in the case showing their position, or “a copy of the order you wish to enforce or continue enforcing”. (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)

If they determine that you do not meet the requirements, your request will be presented to a judge for review.” (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)

### `guide:getting-help:intro`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
This guide sets out who may represent a party in Small Claims Court, the Superior Court of Justice and family court, where the sources on this site say legal help and information can be found, and what they say about language rights and interpreters.
```

### `guide:getting-help:1:heading`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
Who can represent a party in Small Claims Court
```

### `guide:getting-help:1.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters, "Who can represent a party in Small Claims Court"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
The Courts of Justice Act says “A party may be represented in a proceeding in the Small Claims Court by a person authorized under the Law Society Act to represent the party”. (Courts of Justice Act, s. 26)
```

### `guide:getting-help:1.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters, "Who can represent a party in Small Claims Court"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
The same section lets the court exclude a representative from a hearing. The court may exclude “anyone, other than a person licensed under the Law Society Act, appearing on behalf of the party if it finds that such person is not competent properly to represent the party, or does not understand and comply at the hearing with the duties and responsibilities of an advocate.” (Courts of Justice Act, s. 26)
```

### `guide:getting-help:1.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters, "Who can represent a party in Small Claims Court"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
Steps to Justice says “You do not have to hire a lawyer or paralegal when you go to Small Claims Court.” It also says “both lawyers and paralegals can represent you in Small Claims Court. However, only a lawyer can represent you in Superior Court, or the Court of Appeal.” (Steps to Justice, Where can I get legal help and information about my Small Claims issue?)
```

### `guide:getting-help:1.4`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters, "Who can represent a party in Small Claims Court"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
That page was last reviewed on February 23, 2017; the family court section below sets out what the Family Law Rules now say about family legal services providers. (Steps to Justice, Where can I get legal help and information about my Small Claims issue?)
```

### `guide:getting-help:2:heading`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
Who can represent a party in the Superior Court of Justice
```

### `guide:getting-help:2.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters, "Who can represent a party in the Superior Court of Justice"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
Under the Rules of Civil Procedure, “A party to a proceeding who is under disability or acts in a representative capacity shall be represented by a lawyer.” A party that is a corporation “shall be represented by a lawyer, except with leave of the court.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 15.01 (1), (2))
```

### `guide:getting-help:2.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters, "Who can represent a party in the Superior Court of Justice"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
Every other party has a choice: “Any other party to a proceeding may act in person or be represented by a lawyer.” This includes a lawyer “acting under a limited scope retainer”, but such a retainer “does not, in itself, make a lawyer the lawyer of record for the party.” (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 15.01 (3), (4))
```

### `guide:getting-help:2.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters, "Who can represent a party in the Superior Court of Justice"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
When a party acts in person, “anything these rules require or permit a lawyer to do shall be done by the party.” A party acting in person may appoint a lawyer of record by serving and filing a notice of appointment of lawyer (Form 15B) (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 15.01.1 (1), 15.03 (2))
```

### `guide:getting-help:2.4`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** civil / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters, "Who can represent a party in the Superior Court of Justice"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
Subject to the rules that require some parties to have a lawyer, a party with a lawyer of record may elect to act in person by serving and filing a notice of intention to act in person (Form 15C). (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 15.01 (1), (2), 15.03 (3))
```

### `guide:getting-help:3:heading`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
Who can represent a party in family court
```

### `guide:getting-help:3.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters, "Who can represent a party in family court"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
Under the Family Law Rules, a party may “act in person”, “be represented by a lawyer”, be represented by a family legal services provider in certain listed cases (such as some uncontested divorces, some child support motions and some support enforcement) unless the court decides that is inappropriate, or, “if the court gives permission in advance, be represented by any other person, on terms set out by the court.” (Family Law Rules, r. 4 (1), (1.2))
```

### `guide:getting-help:3.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters, "Who can represent a party in family court"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
A party may also be represented by a “family legal services provider” in a limited list of cases and matters “as authorized under the Law Society Act”. The list includes an uncontested divorce or one started by a joint application where the only claim is for divorce, filing a domestic contract, a change of name application, some motions under rule 15 to change child support, and some enforcement of support. Each item has its own conditions, set out in the rule. (Family Law Rules, r. 4 (1) (c))
```

### `guide:getting-help:3.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters, "Who can represent a party in family court"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
This does not apply “if the court determines that representation by a family legal services provider is inappropriate in the circumstances” (Family Law Rules, r. 4 (1.2))
```

### `guide:getting-help:3.4`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters, "Who can represent a party in family court"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
A lawyer or family legal services provider may act under a limited scope retainer, which the rules define, for a lawyer, as legal services for “part, but not all, of a party’s case, by agreement” and, for a family legal services provider, as “some, but not all, of the services that a family legal services provider is authorized to provide in a party’s case or matter”. (Family Law Rules, r. 4 (0.1), (1.2), (1.4), (1.5))
```

### `guide:getting-help:3.5`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters, "Who can represent a party in family court"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
A party acting in person may choose a licensed representative “by serving on every other party and filing a notice of change in representation (Form 4) containing the consent of the licensed representative to act.” This is not needed for a limited scope representative who is not the representative of record (Family Law Rules, r. 4 (9), (9.1))
```

### `guide:getting-help:3.6`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters, "Who can represent a party in family court"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
A represented party may use Form 4 to change representatives or act in person, but in a child protection case scheduled for trial or on a trial list, acting in person needs the court’s permission in advance. (Family Law Rules, r. 4 (10), (10.1))
```

### `guide:getting-help:4:heading`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

Lawyers, paralegals and the Law Society of Ontario
```

### `guide:getting-help:4.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters, "Lawyers, paralegals and the Law Society of Ontario"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
Steps to Justice explains that “Lawyers can give legal advice. This means they can explain what the law says and how it applies to your situation.” A paralegal “is another kind of legal professional that can give legal advice about Small Claims Court.” It says “a paralegal is not allowed to work in all the legal areas that a lawyer can.” That page was last reviewed on February 23, 2017. (Steps to Justice, Where can I get legal help and information about my Small Claims issue?)
```

### `guide:getting-help:4.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters, "Lawyers, paralegals and the Law Society of Ontario"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
“The Law Society of Ontario regulates lawyers and paralegals in Ontario.” It has rules about who can become a lawyer or paralegal and how they must behave, and it deals with complaints. That page was last reviewed on February 23, 2017. (Steps to Justice, Where can I get legal help and information about my Small Claims issue?)
```

### `guide:getting-help:4.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters, "Lawyers, paralegals and the Law Society of Ontario"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
The Law Society Referral Service “can provide you with the name of a lawyer or paralegal in your area, who will provide a free initial consultation of up to 30 minutes to help determine your rights and options.” A request can be made through the online form at www.lawsocietyreferralservice.ca. (ontario.ca, Guide to Procedures in Small Claims Court: After judgment)
```

### `guide:getting-help:4.4`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters, "Lawyers, paralegals and the Law Society of Ontario"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
For people unable to use the online service, “A crisis line is available Monday to Friday, 9:00 am to 5:00 pm.” The number given is 416-947-5255 (toll free 1-855-947-5255). The Law Society also has a Lawyer and Paralegal Directory at www.lawyerandparalegal.directory. (ontario.ca, Guide to Procedures in Small Claims Court: After judgment)
```

### `guide:getting-help:4.5`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters, "Lawyers, paralegals and the Law Society of Ontario"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
Some lawyers offer “unbundled services” or “limited scope retainer” services: “This means you pay them to help you with part of your case.” Examples given are summary advice, preparing documents, appearances, and coaching on the court process. Steps to Justice says “Some lawyers and paralegals do not charge for the first meeting.” (Steps to Justice, How do I prepare for my meeting with a lawyer or paralegal?)
```

### `guide:getting-help:4.6`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters, "Lawyers, paralegals and the Law Society of Ontario"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
A complaint can be made to the Law Society only if a lawyer or paralegal “did not do their job properly, or behaved unprofessionally.” The Law Society does not deal with legal fees. A complaint must be made “within 3 years of when the problem happened or when you became aware of it.” The page adds that there is no time limit for a complaint about sexual abuse. (Steps to Justice, How do I complain to the Law Society of Ontario about a lawyer or paralegal?)
```

### `guide:getting-help:7.1`

- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
“The official languages of the courts of Ontario are English and French.” Unless French-language rules apply, hearings are in English and “evidence adduced in a language other than English shall be interpreted into the English language”. Documents filed must be in English or come with a translation “certified by affidavit of the translator.” (Courts of Justice Act, s. 125)
```

### `guide:getting-help:7.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Getting help: representation, legal help and interpreters, "English, French and interpreters"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
Pleadings and other documents filed by a party may be written in French. “A party to a proceeding who speaks French has the right to require that it be conducted as a bilingual proceeding”. The hearings the party specifies are then “presided over by a judge or officer who speaks English and French.” (Courts of Justice Act, s. 126 (1), (4))
```

```
The Ontario government says “You have the right to use a court interpreter if you or a witness are deaf or do not understand the language of the proceeding.” A person with a fee waiver “can request the help of a court interpreter for free for any language other than English or French”, using form FW-A 5. (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)
```

Without a fee waiver, “you are responsible for booking and paying for interpreter services for yourself or for your witness.” A fee waiver is not needed for an English-French or French-English interpreter in a civil, family or small claims court matter. (ontario.ca, Have your court fees waived)
```

Superior Court: where a witness at the trial of an action does not understand the language of the examination or is deaf or mute, “the party calling the witness shall provide the interpreter, unless the interpretation is to be from English to French or from French to English and an interpreter is provided by the Ministry of the Attorney General.” A similar rule applies at oral examinations. (Rules of Civil Procedure, r. 53.01 (1), (5), (6), 34.09)

### `guide:divorce:title`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Getting a divorce
- **Source:** https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/D-3.4/FullText.html

```
Getting a divorce
```

### `guide:divorce:intro`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Getting a divorce
- **Source:** https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/D-3.4/FullText.html

```
This guide describes, in general terms, what the Divorce Act and rule 36 of Ontario's Family Law Rules say about getting a divorce: which court hears it, the ground for divorce, and how a divorce takes effect. It explains what the law and rules say; it does not say whether any particular person can get a divorce.
```

### `guide:divorce:1:heading`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Getting a divorce
- **Source:** https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/D-3.4/FullText.html

```
Which court and who can apply
```

### `guide:divorce:1.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Getting a divorce, "Which court and who can apply"
- **Source:** https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/D-3.4/FullText.html

```
The Divorce Act defines a “divorce proceeding” as “a proceeding in a court in which either or both spouses seek a divorce alone or together with a child support order, a spousal support order or a parenting order”. (Divorce Act, s. 2 (1))
```

### `guide:divorce:1.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Getting a divorce, "Which court and who can apply"
- **Source:** https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/D-3.4/FullText.html

```
For Ontario, the Act names the court as “the Superior Court of Justice”. The definition also includes any other court in the province whose judges are appointed by the Governor General and that the province designates as a court for the purposes of the Act. (Divorce Act, s. 2 (1))
```

### `guide:divorce:1.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Getting a divorce, "Which court and who can apply"
- **Source:** https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/D-3.4/FullText.html

```
“A court in a province has jurisdiction to hear and determine a divorce proceeding if either spouse has been habitually resident in the province for at least one year immediately preceding the commencement of the proceeding.” If divorce proceedings between the same spouses are pending in two courts with jurisdiction, started on different days, and the first one “is not discontinued”, the court where the proceeding was started first has exclusive jurisdiction, and the second proceeding “is deemed to be discontinued.” (Divorce Act, s. 3 (1), (2))
```

### `guide:divorce:1.4`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Getting a divorce, "Which court and who can apply"
- **Source:** https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/D-3.4/FullText.html

```
“A court of competent jurisdiction may, on application by either or both spouses, grant a divorce to the spouse or spouses on the ground that there has been a breakdown of their marriage.” The power to grant a divorce “shall be exercised only by a judge of the court without a jury.” (Divorce Act, ss. 7, 8 (1))
```

### `guide:divorce:2:heading`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Getting a divorce
- **Source:** https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/D-3.4/FullText.html

```
The ground: breakdown of the marriage
```

### `guide:divorce:2.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Getting a divorce, "The ground: breakdown of the marriage"
- **Source:** https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/D-3.4/FullText.html

```
Under the Divorce Act, “Breakdown of a marriage is established only if” one of the situations in subsection 8 (2) applies. The first is that “the spouses have lived separate and apart for at least one year immediately preceding the determination of the divorce proceeding and were living separate and apart at the commencement of the proceeding”. (Divorce Act, s. 8 (2) (a))
```

### `guide:divorce:2.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Getting a divorce, "The ground: breakdown of the marriage"
- **Source:** https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/D-3.4/FullText.html

```
The other situations are that the spouse against whom the proceeding is brought has, since the marriage, “committed adultery”, or “treated the other spouse with physical or mental cruelty of such a kind as to render intolerable the continued cohabitation of the spouses.” (Divorce Act, s. 8 (2) (b))
```

### `guide:divorce:2.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Getting a divorce, "The ground: breakdown of the marriage"
- **Source:** https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/D-3.4/FullText.html

```
For the one-year separation in paragraph 8 (2) (a), spouses are deemed to have lived separate and apart “for any period during which they lived apart and either of them had the intention to live separate and apart from the other”. A period of separation is not interrupted or ended “by reason only that the spouses have resumed cohabitation during a period of, or periods totalling, not more than ninety days with reconciliation as its primary purpose.” (Divorce Act, s. 8 (3))
```

### `guide:divorce:2.4`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Getting a divorce, "The ground: breakdown of the marriage"
- **Source:** https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/D-3.4/FullText.html

```
A period of separation is also not interrupted by reason only that a spouse has become incapable of forming or having an intention to continue to live separate and apart, or of doing so of their own volition, “if it appears to the court that the separation would probably have continued if the spouse had not become so incapable”. (Divorce Act, s. 8 (3) (b) (i))
```

### `guide:divorce:3:heading`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Getting a divorce
- **Source:** https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/D-3.4/FullText.html

```
Reconciliation and the bars to divorce
```

### `guide:divorce:3.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Getting a divorce, "Reconciliation and the bars to divorce"
- **Source:** https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/D-3.4/FullText.html

```
In a divorce proceeding, the court has a duty, before considering the evidence, “to satisfy itself that there is no possibility of the reconciliation of the spouses, unless the circumstances of the case are of such a nature that it would clearly not be appropriate to do so.” (Divorce Act, s. 10 (1))
```

### `guide:divorce:3.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Getting a divorce, "Reconciliation and the bars to divorce"
- **Source:** https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/D-3.4/FullText.html

```
If it appears to the court at any stage that reconciliation is possible, the court shall adjourn the proceeding “to afford the spouses an opportunity to achieve a reconciliation” and, “with the consent of the spouses or in the discretion of the court”, nominate a person with experience or training in marriage counselling or guidance (or, in special circumstances, some other suitable person) to assist. Once fourteen days have passed, the court shall resume the proceeding on the application of either or both spouses. (Divorce Act, s. 10 (2), (3))
```

### `guide:divorce:3.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Getting a divorce, "Reconciliation and the bars to divorce"
- **Source:** https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/D-3.4/FullText.html

```
The court must also “satisfy itself that there has been no collusion in relation to the application for a divorce and to dismiss the application if it finds that there was collusion in presenting it”. (Divorce Act, s. 11 (1) (a))
```

### `guide:divorce:3.4`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Getting a divorce, "Reconciliation and the bars to divorce"
- **Source:** https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/D-3.4/FullText.html

```
Under section 11, collusion is an agreement or conspiracy, to which an applicant for a divorce is directly or indirectly a party, “for the purpose of subverting the administration of justice”, including to “fabricate or suppress evidence or to deceive the court”. It excludes an agreement to the extent it provides for separation, financial support, division of property or “the exercise of parenting time or decision-making responsibility.” (Divorce Act, s. 11 (4))
```

### `guide:divorce:3.5`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Getting a divorce, "Reconciliation and the bars to divorce"
- **Source:** https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/D-3.4/FullText.html

```
The court must “satisfy itself that reasonable arrangements have been made for the support of any children of the marriage, having regard to the applicable guidelines”. If such arrangements have not been made, the court is “to stay the granting of the divorce until such arrangements are made”. (Divorce Act, s. 11 (1) (b))
```

### `guide:divorce:3.6`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Getting a divorce, "Reconciliation and the bars to divorce"
- **Source:** https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/D-3.4/FullText.html

```
Where divorce is sought for adultery or cruelty, the court must satisfy itself that there has been no condonation or connivance by the spouse bringing the proceeding. It dismisses the application if there was, “unless, in the opinion of the court, the public interest would be better served by granting the divorce.” Continuing or resuming cohabitation “during a period of, or periods totalling, not more than ninety days with reconciliation as its primary purpose” is not condonation. (Divorce Act, s. 11 (1) (c), (3))
```

### `guide:divorce:4:heading`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Getting a divorce
- **Source:** https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/D-3.4/FullText.html

```
Duties of the parties and legal advisers
```

### `guide:divorce:4.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Getting a divorce, "Duties of the parties and legal advisers"
- **Source:** https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/D-3.4/FullText.html

```
The Divorce Act sets out duties for parties. “A party to a proceeding under this Act shall, to the best of their ability, protect any child of the marriage from conflict arising from the proceeding.” “To the extent that it is appropriate to do so, the parties to a proceeding shall try to resolve the matters that may be the subject of an order under this Act through a family dispute resolution process.” (Divorce Act, ss. 7.2, 7.3)
```

### `guide:divorce:4.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Getting a divorce, "Duties of the parties and legal advisers"
- **Source:** https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/D-3.4/FullText.html

```
A “family dispute resolution process” means “a process outside of court that is used by parties to a family law dispute to attempt to resolve any matters in dispute, including negotiation, mediation and collaborative law”. (Divorce Act, s. 2 (1))
```

### `guide:divorce:4.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Getting a divorce, "Duties of the parties and legal advisers"
- **Source:** https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/D-3.4/FullText.html

```
A party or a person subject to an order “shall provide complete, accurate and up-to-date information if required to do so under this Act.” A person subject to an order “shall comply with the order until it is no longer in effect.” A person with parenting time or decision-making responsibility for a child of the marriage, or contact under a contact order, exercises it “in a manner that is consistent with the best interests of the child.” (Divorce Act, ss. 7.1, 7.4, 7.5)
```

### `guide:divorce:4.4`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Getting a divorce, "Duties of the parties and legal advisers"
- **Source:** https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/D-3.4/FullText.html

```
Every document that formally starts or responds to a proceeding under the Act and is filed by a party “shall contain a statement by the party certifying that they are aware of their duties under sections 7.1 to 7.5.” (Divorce Act, s. 7.6)
```

### `guide:divorce:4.5`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Getting a divorce, "Duties of the parties and legal advisers"
- **Source:** https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/D-3.4/FullText.html

```
A legal adviser acting for a spouse in a divorce proceeding has duties, unless it “would clearly not be appropriate”: to draw the spouse's attention to the Act's provisions aimed at reconciliation, to discuss the possibility of reconciliation, and to inform the spouse of known marriage counselling or guidance facilities that might help the spouses reconcile. (Divorce Act, s. 7.7 (1))
```

### `guide:divorce:4.6`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Getting a divorce, "Duties of the parties and legal advisers"
- **Source:** https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/D-3.4/FullText.html

```
In any proceeding under the Act, a legal adviser must also encourage the person to use a family dispute resolution process unless that would clearly not be appropriate, inform the person of known family justice services, and inform them “of the parties’ duties under this Act.” (Divorce Act, s. 7.7 (2))
```

### `guide:divorce:4.7`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Getting a divorce, "Duties of the parties and legal advisers"
- **Source:** https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/D-3.4/FullText.html

```
A document filed by a legal adviser that starts or responds to a proceeding “shall contain a statement by the legal adviser certifying that they have complied with this section.” (Divorce Act, s. 7.7 (3))
```

### `guide:divorce:5:heading`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Getting a divorce
- **Source:** https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/D-3.4/FullText.html

```
Starting a divorce case in Ontario
```

### `guide:divorce:5.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Getting a divorce, "Starting a divorce case in Ontario"
- **Source:** https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/D-3.4/FullText.html

```
Under the Family Law Rules, “Either spouse may start a divorce case by,” “filing an application naming the other spouse as a respondent” or “filing a joint application with no respondent.” In a joint application, “the divorce and any other order sought shall be made only with the consent of both spouses.” (Family Law Rules, r. 36 (1), (2))
```

### `guide:divorce:5.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Getting a divorce, "Starting a divorce case in Ontario"
- **Source:** https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/D-3.4/FullText.html

```
To start a case, a person files an application in one of the forms listed in rule 8 (1). The rules' table of forms lists Form 8A as “APPLICATION (DIVORCE)”. (Family Law Rules, r. 8 (1); Table of Forms)
```

### `guide:divorce:5.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide

It confirms the information in the application, gives proof of the marriage if no certificate was filed, and includes the information about arrangements for support of any children required by paragraph 11 (1) (b) of the Divorce Act, among other things. (Family Law Rules, r. 36 (5), (5.1))

With the affidavit, the applicant files “three copies of a draft divorce order (Form 25A)”, “a stamped envelope addressed to each party”, and, if the divorce order is to contain a support order, an extra copy of the draft order and two copies of a draft support deduction order. (Family Law Rules, r. 36 (6))

The judge may grant the divorce as set out in the draft order, have the documents returned for corrections, or change or refuse the order “after giving the applicant a chance to file an additional affidavit or come to court to explain why the order should be made without change.” (Family Law Rules, r. 36 (7))

```
“Subject to this section, a divorce takes effect on the thirty-first day after the day on which the judgment granting the divorce is rendered.” (Divorce Act, s. 12 (1))
```

### `guide:divorce:7.2`

```
The court may order that a divorce take effect earlier if it is of the opinion that “by reason of special circumstances the divorce should take effect earlier”, and “the spouses agree and undertake that no appeal from the judgment will be taken, or any appeal from the judgment that was taken has been abandoned”. (Divorce Act, s. 12 (2))
```

```
If an appeal is pending at the end of the period referred to in subsection 12 (1), the divorce, unless voided on appeal, takes effect when the time for appealing the appeal decision expires without a further appeal. If an appeal goes to the Supreme Court of Canada, the divorce, unless voided, “takes effect on the day on which the judgment on the appeal is rendered.” (Divorce Act, s. 12 (3), (6))
```
