```
Who Part I applies to
```

### `guide:property-division:1.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends, "Who Part I applies to"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90f03

```
Part I (Family Property) uses the Act’s general definition of “spouse”: either of two persons who “are married to each other”, or who “have together entered into a marriage that is voidable or void, in good faith on the part of a person relying on this clause to assert any right.” (Family Law Act, s. 1 (1))
```

### `guide:property-division:1.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends, "Who Part I applies to"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90f03

```
Part I’s own definitions do not add unmarried partners. By contrast, the wider definition in Part III (Support Obligations), stated to apply “In this Part”, adds two persons “who are not married to each other and have cohabited,” either “continuously for a period of not less than three years” or “in a relationship of some permanence, if they are the parents of a child as set out in section 4 of the Children’s Law Reform Act.” (Family Law Act, ss. 4 (1), 29)
```

### `guide:property-division:1.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends, "Who Part I applies to"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90f03

```
For Part I, “court” means a court as defined in subsection 1 (1), “but does not include the Ontario Court of Justice”. (Family Law Act, s. 4 (1))
```

- **Status:** draft

### `guide:property-division:2.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends, "Net family property and the valuation date"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90f03

```
“Net family property” means “the value of all the property, except property described in subsection (2), that a spouse owns on the valuation date”, after deducting the spouse’s debts and other liabilities, and the value of property, “other than a matrimonial home”, that the spouse owned on the date of the marriage. That date-of-marriage value is net of the spouse’s debts and liabilities at that date, “other than debts or liabilities related directly to the acquisition or significant improvement of a matrimonial home”. (Family Law Act, s. 4 (1))
```

### `guide:property-division:2.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends, "Net family property and the valuation date"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90f03

```
The liabilities deducted in calculating net family property “include any applicable contingent tax liabilities in respect of the property.” (Family Law Act, s. 4 (1.1))
```

### `guide:property-division:2.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends, "Net family property and the valuation date"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90f03

```
The “valuation date” is “the earliest of” these dates: “The date the spouses separate and there is no reasonable prospect that they will resume cohabitation”; “The date a divorce is granted”; “The date the marriage is declared a nullity”; the date an application for improvident depletion is started that is later granted; and “The date before the date on which one of the spouses dies leaving the other spouse surviving.” (Family Law Act, s. 4 (1))
```

### `guide:property-division:2.4`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends, "Net family property and the valuation date"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90f03

```
“Property” is defined broadly as “any interest, present or future, vested or contingent, in real or personal property”. For a pension plan, it includes the “imputed value, for family law purposes, of the spouse’s interest in the plan”, for the period from the date of marriage to the valuation date. (Family Law Act, s. 4 (1))
```

### `guide:property-division:2.5`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends, "Net family property and the valuation date"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90f03

```
When section 4 requires a value to be calculated as of a given date, it “shall be calculated as of close of business on that date.” If a spouse’s net family property as calculated under subsections (1), (2) and (4) is less than zero, “it shall be deemed to be equal to zero.” (Family Law Act, s. 4 (4), (5))
```

### `guide:property-division:3:heading`

- **Status:** draft

- **Appears in:** Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends

```
Excluded property
```

### `guide:property-division:3.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends, "Excluded property"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90f03

```
Some property a spouse owns on the valuation date “does not form part of the spouse’s net family property”. The list includes property, “other than a matrimonial home, that was acquired by gift or inheritance from a third person after the date of the marriage”, and income from that property if the donor or testator “has expressly stated that it is to be excluded”. (Family Law Act, s. 4 (2), paras. 1, 2)
```

### `guide:property-division:3.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends, "Excluded property"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90f03

```
The list also includes damages, or a right to damages, for personal injuries, nervous shock, mental distress or loss of guidance, care and companionship, or the part of a settlement that represents those damages. (Family Law Act, s. 4 (2), para. 3)
```

### `guide:property-division:3.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends, "Excluded property"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90f03

```
The list also includes certain life insurance proceeds payable on death; property, other than a matrimonial home, into which property described in paragraphs 1 to 4 “can be traced”; “Property that the spouses have agreed by a domestic contract is not to be included in the spouse’s net family property”; and “Unadjusted pensionable earnings under the Canada Pension Plan.” (Family Law Act, s. 4 (2), paras. 4-7)
```

### `guide:property-division:3.4`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends, "Excluded property"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90f03

```
The Act places the onus of proving a deduction from net family property, or an exclusion under subsection 4 (2), on the person claiming it: the onus “is on the person claiming it.” (Family Law Act, s. 4 (3))
```

### `guide:property-division:4:heading`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends

### `guide:property-division:4.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends, "Equalization and unequal shares"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90f03

```
When a divorce is granted, a marriage is declared a nullity, or the spouses are separated with no reasonable prospect of resuming cohabitation, “the spouse whose net family property is the lesser of the two net family properties is entitled to one-half the difference between them.” (Family Law Act, s. 5 (1))
```

### `guide:property-division:4.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends, "Equalization and unequal shares"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90f03

```
When a spouse dies, the surviving spouse is entitled to one-half the difference only “if the net family property of the deceased spouse exceeds the net family property of the surviving spouse”. (Family Law Act, s. 5 (2))
```

### `guide:property-division:4.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends, "Equalization and unequal shares"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90f03

```
While spouses are cohabiting, “if there is a serious danger that one spouse may improvidently deplete his or her net family property”, the other spouse may apply under section 7 to have the difference divided as if they had separated. After such an order, “neither spouse may make a further application under section 7 in respect of their marriage.” (Family Law Act, s. 5 (3), (4))
```

### `guide:property-division:4.4`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends, "Equalization and unequal shares"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90f03

```
The Act states the purpose of section 5: to recognize that “child care, household management and financial provision are the joint responsibilities of the spouses” and that “inherent in the marital relationship there is equal contribution, whether financial or otherwise, by the spouses to the assumption of these responsibilities, entitling each spouse to the equalization of the net family properties, subject only to the equitable considerations set out in subsection (6).” (Family Law Act, s. 5 (7))
```

### `guide:property-division:4.5`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends, "Equalization and unequal shares"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90f03

```
The court “may award a spouse an amount that is more or less than half the difference between the net family properties if the court is of the opinion that equalizing the net family properties would be unconscionable”. The circumstances it has regard to include failure to disclose debts existing at marriage, debts “incurred recklessly or in bad faith”, gifts from the other spouse, and “a spouse’s intentional or reckless depletion of his or her net family property”. (Family Law Act, s. 5 (6) (a)-(d))
```

### `guide:property-division:4.6`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends, "Equalization and unequal shares"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90f03

```
The other listed circumstances are an amount “disproportionately large in relation to a period of cohabitation that is less than five years”; one spouse incurring “a disproportionately larger amount of debts or other liabilities than the other spouse for the support of the family”; “a written agreement between the spouses that is not a domestic contract”; and “any other circumstance relating to the acquisition, disposition, preservation, maintenance or improvement of property.” (Family Law Act, s. 5 (6) (e)-(h))
```

- **Appears in:** Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends, "Applying to the court and the time limits"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90f03

```
“The court may, on the application of a spouse, former spouse or deceased spouse’s personal representative, determine any matter respecting the spouses’ entitlement under section 5.” (Family Law Act, s. 7 (1))
```

### `guide:property-division:5.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends, "Applying to the court and the time limits"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90f03

```
An application based on subsection 5 (1) or (2) “shall not be brought after the earliest of,” (a) “two years after the day the marriage is terminated by divorce or judgment of nullity”; (b) “six years after the day the spouses separate and there is no reasonable prospect that they will resume cohabitation”; (c) “six months after the first spouse’s death.” (Family Law Act, s. 7 (3))
```

### `guide:property-division:5.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends, "Applying to the court and the time limits"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90f03

```
Separately, the Act says the court “may, on motion, extend a time prescribed by this Act” if it is satisfied that “there are apparent grounds for relief”, that “relief is unavailable because of delay that has been incurred in good faith”, and that “no person will suffer substantial prejudice by reason of the delay.” (Family Law Act, s. 2 (8))
```

### `guide:property-division:6:heading`

- **Status:** draft

### `guide:property-division:6.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends, "What the court can order"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90f03

```
In an application under section 7, the court may order one spouse to pay the other the amount the court finds that spouse is entitled to, and that security be given. If “necessary to avoid hardship”, payment may be made in instalments or delayed for “a period not exceeding ten years”. If appropriate to satisfy an obligation imposed by the order, property may be transferred to a spouse, or “partitioned or sold”. (Family Law Act, s. 9 (1))
```

### `guide:property-division:6.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends, "What the court can order"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90f03

```
An order made under section 9 or 10 “shall not be made so as to require or result in the sale of an operating business or farm or so as to seriously impair its operation, unless there is no reasonable alternative method of satisfying the award.” (Family Law Act, s. 11 (1))
```

### `guide:property-division:6.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends, "What the court can order"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90f03

```
In an application under section 7 or 10, if the court “considers it necessary for the protection of the other spouse’s interests under this Part”, it may make an interim or final order “restraining the depletion of a spouse’s property” and for its “possession, delivering up, safekeeping and preservation”. (Family Law Act, s. 12)
```

### `guide:property-division:6.4`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends, "What the court can order"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90f03

```
Separately, a person may apply for a determination of a question with a spouse or former spouse “as to the ownership or right to possession of particular property, other than a question arising out of an equalization of net family properties under section 5”. (Family Law Act, s. 10 (1))
```

### `guide:property-division:7:heading`

- **Status:** draft

### `guide:property-division:7.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends, "Financial disclosure"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90f03

```
In an application under section 7, each party must serve and file a sworn or declared statement “disclosing particulars of” the party’s property, debts and other liabilities as of the date of marriage, the valuation date and the date of the statement; the deductions and exclusions claimed; and property disposed of “during the two years immediately preceding the making of the statement, or during the marriage, whichever period is shorter.” (Family Law Act, s. 8)
```

### `guide:property-division:7.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends, "Financial disclosure"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90f03

```
Under the Family Law Rules, when an application, answer or motion contains “a property claim”, the party making the claim “shall serve and file a financial statement (Form 13 or 13.1)” with it, and the other party must do so within the time for responding. If there is a property claim, the financial statement “shall be in Form 13.1, whether a claim for support is also included or not.” (Family Law Rules, r. 13 (1), (1.2))
```

### `guide:property-division:7.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends, "Financial disclosure"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90f03

```
For a Part I claim, unless the court orders otherwise, a party must, “no later than 30 days after the day by which the financial statement is required to be served”, serve further documents. These include statements closest to the valuation date for accounts, savings and investments; any pension valuation request made; property assessments; life insurance statements; and business, partnership, corporation and trust records. (Family Law Rules, r. 13 (3.3), paras. 1-9)
```

### `guide:property-division:7.4`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends, "Financial disclosure"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90f03

```
They also include documentation of the valuation-date value of any other property; “Documentation that supports a claim, if any, for an exclusion under subsection 4 (2) of the Family Law Act”; statements for debts owed on the valuation date; and “Any available documentation showing the value, on the date of marriage,” of property and debts. (Family Law Rules, r. 13 (3.3), paras. 10-13)
```

### `guide:property-division:7.5`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends, "Financial disclosure"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90f03

```
A party serving these documents confirms service with “a certificate of financial disclosure (Form 13A)”. If a party thinks the other’s disclosure is not enough, “the party shall make a request in writing to the other party for the necessary additional information”, and if it is not given “within seven days of the request”, the court may order it. (Family Law Rules, r. 13 (5.0.2), (11))
```

- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90f03

```
Marriage contracts, cohabitation agreements and separation agreements may each deal with “ownership in or division of property”. A domestic contract is “unenforceable unless made in writing, signed by the parties and witnessed.” (Family Law Act, ss. 52 (1) (a), 53 (1) (a), 54 (a), 55 (1))
```

### `guide:property-division:8.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends, "Agreements about property"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90f03

```
“A domestic contract dealing with a matter that is also dealt with in this Act prevails unless this Act provides otherwise.” Property the spouses have agreed by domestic contract is not to be included is excluded property. (Family Law Act, ss. 2 (10), 4 (2), para. 6)
```

### `guide:property-division:8.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Dividing property when a marriage ends, "Agreements about property"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90f03

```
A court may, on application, set aside a domestic contract or a provision in it “if a party failed to disclose to the other significant assets, or significant debts or other liabilities, existing when the domestic contract was made”, “if a party did not understand the nature or consequences of the domestic contract”, or “otherwise in accordance with the law of contract.” (Family Law Act, s. 56 (4))
```

### `guide:matrimonial-home:title`

```
The matrimonial home
```

### `guide:matrimonial-home:intro`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, The matrimonial home
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90f03

```
This guide describes, in general terms, what Part II of Ontario's Family Law Act says about the matrimonial home: what it is, who may live in it, and the orders a court may make about it. It explains what the law says; it does not say how the law applies to any particular home or family.
```

### `guide:matrimonial-home:1:heading`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, The matrimonial home
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90f03

```
What counts as a matrimonial home
```

### `guide:matrimonial-home:1.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, The matrimonial home, "What counts as a matrimonial home"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90f03

```
Part II of the Family Law Act deals with the matrimonial home. It says: “Every property in which a person has an interest and that is or, if the spouses have separated, was at the time of separation ordinarily occupied by the person and his or her spouse as their family residence is their matrimonial home.” In Part II, “property” means “real or personal property.” (Family Law Act, ss. 17, 18 (1))
```

### `guide:matrimonial-home:1.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, The matrimonial home, "What counts as a matrimonial home"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90f03

```
Part II does not give its own definition of “spouse”. The Act's general definition says “spouse” means either of two persons who “are married to each other”, or who “have together entered into a marriage that is voidable or void, in good faith on the part of a person relying on this clause to assert any right.” (Family Law Act, s. 1 (1))
```

### `guide:matrimonial-home:1.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, The matrimonial home, "What counts as a matrimonial home"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90f03

```
Owning shares in a corporation that entitle the owner “to occupy a housing unit owned by the corporation” is treated as an interest in the unit. If property that includes a matrimonial home “is normally used for a purpose other than residential”, the matrimonial home is only the part “that may reasonably be regarded as necessary to the use and enjoyment of the residence.” (Family Law Act, s. 18 (2), (3))
```

### `guide:matrimonial-home:1.4`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, The matrimonial home, "What counts as a matrimonial home"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90f03

```
Part II “applies to matrimonial homes that are situated in Ontario.” It applies whether the spouses were married before or after March 1, 1986, and whether the home was acquired before or after that day. (Family Law Act, s. 28)
```

### `guide:matrimonial-home:1.5`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, The matrimonial home, "What counts as a matrimonial home"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90f03

```
The Act defines “court” as “the Ontario Court of Justice, the Family Court of the Superior Court of Justice or the Superior Court of Justice”. For Part II, “court” means a court as defined in subsection 1 (1) “but does not include the Ontario Court of Justice”. (Family Law Act, ss. 1 (1), 17)
```

### `guide:matrimonial-home:2:heading`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, The matrimonial home
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90f03

```
The right to live in the home
```

### `guide:matrimonial-home:2.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, The matrimonial home, "The right to live in the home"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90f03

```
The Act says: “Both spouses have an equal right to possession of a matrimonial home.” (Family Law Act, s. 19 (1))
```

### `guide:matrimonial-home:2.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, The matrimonial home, "The right to live in the home"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90f03

```
When only one spouse has an interest in the home, the other spouse's right of possession “is personal as against the first spouse” and “ends when they cease to be spouses, unless a separation agreement or court order provides otherwise.” (Family Law Act, s. 19 (2))
```

### `guide:matrimonial-home:2.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, The matrimonial home, "The right to live in the home"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90f03

```
A spouse who has no interest in a matrimonial home but is occupying it when the other spouse dies, “whether under an order for exclusive possession or otherwise, is entitled to retain possession against the spouse’s estate, rent free, for sixty days after the spouse’s death.” (Family Law Act, s. 26 (2))
```

### `guide:matrimonial-home:2.4`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, The matrimonial home, "The right to live in the home"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90f03

```
If a spouse dies owning an interest in a matrimonial home as a joint tenant with a third person, and not with the other spouse, “the joint tenancy shall be deemed to have been severed immediately before the time of death.” (Family Law Act, s. 26 (1))
```

### `guide:matrimonial-home:3:heading`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, The matrimonial home
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90f03

```
Designating a matrimonial home
```

### `guide:matrimonial-home:3.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, The matrimonial home, "Designating a matrimonial home"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90f03

```
“One or both spouses may designate property owned by one or both of them as a matrimonial home, in the form prescribed by the regulations.” The designation may include property described in it that is contiguous to the matrimonial home, and it “may be registered in the proper land registry office.” (Family Law Act, s. 20 (1)-(3))
```

### `guide:matrimonial-home:3.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, The matrimonial home, "Designating a matrimonial home"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90f03

```
When a designation made by both spouses is registered, any other property that is a matrimonial home under section 18 but is not designated by both spouses “ceases to be a matrimonial home.” When a designation made by one spouse only is registered, any other matrimonial home under section 18 “remains a matrimonial home.” (Family Law Act, s. 20 (4), (5))
```

### `guide:matrimonial-home:3.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, The matrimonial home, "Designating a matrimonial home"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90f03

```
A designation is cancelled, and the property stops being a matrimonial home, on the registration or deposit of a cancellation in the prescribed form signed by the person or persons who made it, “a decree absolute of divorce or judgment of nullity”, an order under clause 23 (e) cancelling it, or “proof of death of one of the spouses.” When a designation by both spouses is cancelled, section 18 applies again to other property that is a matrimonial home. (Family Law Act, s. 20 (6), (7))
```

### `guide:matrimonial-home:4:heading`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, The matrimonial home
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90f03

```
Disposing of or encumbering the home
```

### `guide:matrimonial-home:4.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, The matrimonial home, "Disposing of or encumbering the home"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90f03

```
“No spouse shall dispose of or encumber an interest in a matrimonial home unless,” “the other spouse joins in the instrument or consents to the transaction”; the other spouse “has released all rights under this Part by a separation agreement”; “a court order has authorized the transaction or has released the property from the application of this Part”; or the property is not designated by both spouses and a designation of another property by both spouses is registered and not cancelled. (Family Law Act, s. 21 (1))
```

### `guide:matrimonial-home:4.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, The matrimonial home, "Disposing of or encumbering the home"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90f03

```
A transaction made contrary to subsection 21 (1) “may be set aside on an application under section 23”. That does not apply if the person holding the interest or encumbrance at the time of the application “acquired it for value, in good faith and without notice”, when acquiring it or agreeing to acquire it, that the property was a matrimonial home. (Family Law Act, s. 21 (2))
```

### `guide:matrimonial-home:4.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, The matrimonial home, "Disposing of or encumbering the home"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90f03

```
A statement by the person making the disposition or encumbrance, verifying one of the matters listed in subsection 21 (3) (for example, that the person “is not, or was not, a spouse at the time of the disposition or encumbrance”), is deemed to be “sufficient proof that the property is not a matrimonial home”, unless the person receiving it “had notice to the contrary”. (Family Law Act, s. 21 (3))
```

### `guide:matrimonial-home:4.4`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, The matrimonial home, "Disposing of or encumbering the home"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90f03

```
On the application of a spouse or a person having an interest in property, the court may, among other things, “determine whether or not the property is a matrimonial home and, if so, its extent”, set aside a transaction made contrary to subsection 21 (1), or cancel a designation if the property is not a matrimonial home. (Family Law Act, s. 23 (a), (d), (e))
```

### `guide:matrimonial-home:4.5`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, The matrimonial home, "Disposing of or encumbering the home"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90f03

```
The court may also authorize a disposition or encumbrance of the home if it finds that the spouse whose consent is required “cannot be found or is not available”, “is not capable of giving or withholding consent”, or “is unreasonably withholding consent”, subject to any conditions the court considers appropriate, “including provision of other comparable accommodation or payment in place of it”. (Family Law Act, s. 23 (b))
```

### `guide:matrimonial-home:4.6`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, The matrimonial home, "Disposing of or encumbering the home"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90f03

```
When someone enforces a lien, encumbrance or execution, or exercises a forfeiture, against a matrimonial home, the spouse who has a right of possession under section 19 “has the same right of redemption or relief against forfeiture as the other spouse and is entitled to the same notice respecting the claim and its enforcement or realization.” For a power of sale, sections 33 and 34 of the Mortgages Act apply. (Family Law Act, s. 22 (1), (3))
```

### `guide:matrimonial-home:5:heading`

### `guide:matrimonial-home:5.1`

- **Status:** draft

- **Appears in:** Guides, The matrimonial home, "Orders about possession of the home"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90f03

```
“Regardless of the ownership of a matrimonial home and its contents, and despite section 19 (spouse’s right of possession), the court may on application, by order,” among other things, “direct that one spouse be given exclusive possession of the matrimonial home or part of it for the period that the court directs”, and direct the spouse given exclusive possession “to make periodic payments to the other spouse”. (Family Law Act, s. 24 (1) (b), (c))
```

### `guide:matrimonial-home:5.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, The matrimonial home, "Orders about possession of the home"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90f03

```
Other orders listed in subsection 24 (1) include providing for “the delivering up, safekeeping and preservation of the matrimonial home and its contents”, directing that contents stay in the home or be removed “for the use of a spouse or child”, ordering a spouse to pay for “all or part of the repair and maintenance of the matrimonial home”, and authorizing a disposition or encumbrance of a spouse’s interest “subject to the other spouse’s right of exclusive possession as ordered”. (Family Law Act, s. 24 (1) (a), (d), (e), (f))
```

### `guide:matrimonial-home:5.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, The matrimonial home, "Orders about possession of the home"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90f03

```
“The court may, on motion, make a temporary or interim order under clause (1) (a), (b), (c), (d) or (e).” (Family Law Act, s. 24 (2))
```

### `guide:matrimonial-home:5.4`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, The matrimonial home, "Orders about possession of the home"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90f03

```
In deciding whether to make an order for exclusive possession, “the court shall consider,” “the best interests of the children affected”; “any existing orders under Part I (Family Property) and any existing support orders or other enforceable support obligations”; “the financial position of both spouses”; “any written agreement between the parties”; “the availability of other suitable and affordable accommodation”; and “any violence committed by a spouse against the other spouse or the children.” (Family Law Act, s. 24 (3))
```

### `guide:matrimonial-home:5.5`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, The matrimonial home, "Orders about possession of the home"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90f03

```
In determining the best interests of a child, the court shall consider “the possible disruptive effects on the child of a move to other accommodation” and “the child’s views and preferences, if they can reasonably be ascertained.” (Family Law Act, s. 24 (4))
```

### `guide:matrimonial-home:5.6`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, The matrimonial home, "Orders about possession of the home"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90f03

```
In making any order under Part II, the court may also make an interim order prohibiting a party “from directly or indirectly contacting or communicating with another party”, if it determines that the order “is necessary to ensure that an application under this Part is dealt with justly.” (Family Law Act, s. 25.1)
```

```
“A person who contravenes an order for exclusive possession is guilty of an offence”. On conviction, for a first offence the Act sets a fine of not more than $5,000 or imprisonment of not more than three months, or both; for a second or subsequent offence, a fine of not more than $10,000 or imprisonment of not more than two years, or both. (Family Law Act, s. 24 (5))
```

### `guide:matrimonial-home:6.2`

- **Status:** draft

```
“A police officer may arrest without warrant a person the police officer believes on reasonable and probable grounds to have contravened an order for exclusive possession.” (Family Law Act, s. 24 (6))
```

- **Status:** draft

- **Appears in:** Guides, The matrimonial home, "Contravening, changing and registering orders"

```
A person named in an order under clause 24 (1) (a), (b), (c), (d) or (e), or their personal representative, may apply, and “if the court is satisfied that there has been a material change in circumstances, the court may discharge, vary or suspend the order.” Conditions imposed under clause 23 (b) or (d) or 24 (1) (g) may be discharged, varied or suspended on motion if the court is satisfied they “are no longer appropriate”. (Family Law Act, s. 25 (1), (2))
```

```
This guide describes, in general terms, the restraining orders available under section 46 of Ontario's Family Law Act and section 35 of the Children's Law Reform Act: who may apply, against whom, and what an order may contain. It explains what the law says; it does not say whether an order is available in any particular situation.
```

- **Appears in:** Guides, Restraining orders in family cases, "Two laws that provide restraining orders"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90f03

```
Two Ontario laws let a family court make a restraining order: section 46 of the Family Law Act and section 35 of the Children's Law Reform Act. Under both, the court may make “an interim or final restraining order”. (Family Law Act, s. 46 (1); Children's Law Reform Act, s. 35 (1))
```

### `guide:restraining-orders:1.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / guide

```
In the Family Law Act, “court” means “the Ontario Court of Justice, the Family Court of the Superior Court of Justice or the Superior Court of Justice”. In Part III of the Children's Law Reform Act, where section 35 appears, “court” means “the Ontario Court of Justice, the Family Court or the Superior Court of Justice”. (Family Law Act, s. 1 (1); Children's Law Reform Act, s. 18 (1))
```

```
The wording of section 46 now in force says: “On application, the court may make an interim or final restraining order against a person described in subsection (2) if the applicant has reasonable grounds to fear for his or her own safety or for the safety of any child in his or her lawful custody.” (Family Law Act, s. 46 (1))
```

```
Under the wording now in force, the order may be made against “a spouse or former spouse of the applicant”, or against a person other than a spouse or former spouse of the applicant, “if the person is cohabiting with the applicant or has cohabited with the applicant for any period of time.” (Family Law Act, s. 46 (2))
```

```
Section 46 is in Part III of the Act, where “spouse” means a spouse as defined in subsection 1 (1) and also includes either of two persons who are not married to each other and have cohabited “continuously for a period of not less than three years”, or “in a relationship of some permanence, if they are the parents of a child as set out in section 4 of the Children’s Law Reform Act.” (Family Law Act, s. 29)
```

### `guide:tenant-and-landlord:intro`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Renting a home: tenants, landlords and the Landlord and Tenant Board
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/06r17

```
This guide explains what Ontario's Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 says about who it covers, the role of the Landlord and Tenant Board, repairs, rent deposits, ending a tenancy and applications to the Board. It describes the Act generally and does not say how it applies to any particular tenancy.
```

### `guide:tenant-and-landlord:1:heading`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Renting a home: tenants, landlords and the Landlord and Tenant Board

```
What the Act covers
```

### `guide:tenant-and-landlord:1.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Renting a home: tenants, landlords and the Landlord and Tenant Board, "What the Act covers"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/06r17

```
Except for Part V.1, the Act says it “applies with respect to rental units in residential complexes, despite any other Act and despite any agreement or waiver to the contrary.” A “rental unit” means “any living accommodation used or intended for use as rented residential premises”. It includes “a room in a boarding house, rooming house or lodging house and a unit in a care home”. (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, ss. 2 (1), 3 (1))
```

### `guide:tenant-and-landlord:1.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Renting a home: tenants, landlords and the Landlord and Tenant Board, "What the Act covers"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/06r17

```
A “tenancy agreement” means “a written, oral or implied agreement between a tenant and a landlord for occupancy of a rental unit and includes a licence to occupy a rental unit”. Subject to subsection 12.1 (11) and section 194, “a provision in a tenancy agreement that is inconsistent with this Act or the regulations is void”. (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, ss. 2 (1), 4 (1))
```

### `guide:tenant-and-landlord:1.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Renting a home: tenants, landlords and the Landlord and Tenant Board, "What the Act covers"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/06r17

```
If the Act conflicts with another Act, the Act applies, with one exception: “other than the Human Rights Code”. (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, s. 3 (4))
```

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide

- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/06r17

```
Section 5 lists kinds of living accommodation the Act “does not apply with respect to”. Examples include accommodation for “the travelling or vacationing public” in places such as hotels, motels and campgrounds, and “short-term living accommodation provided as emergency shelter”. (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, s. 5 (a), (f))
```

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Renting a home: tenants, landlords and the Landlord and Tenant Board, "Housing the Act does not cover"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/06r17

```
Another listed exemption is accommodation where the occupant is “required to share a bathroom or kitchen facility with the owner, the owner's spouse, child or parent or the spouse's child or parent”, and that person “lives in the building in which the living accommodation is located”. The full list in section 5 has more categories, such as certain student housing and farm-employment housing. (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, s. 5 (b), (g), (i))
```

```
A separate statute, the Commercial Tenancies Act, says: “This Act does not apply to tenancies and tenancy agreements to which the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006 applies.” (Commercial Tenancies Act, s. 2)
```

```
The Act continues the former tribunal “under the name Landlord and Tenant Board”. It says: “The Board has exclusive jurisdiction to determine all applications under this Act and with respect to all matters in which jurisdiction is conferred on it by this Act.” (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, s. 168 (1), (2))
```

- **Status:** draft

- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/06r17

```
The Board “has authority to hear and determine all questions of law and fact with respect to all matters within its jurisdiction under this Act.” (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, s. 174)
```

```
Tribunals Ontario describes the Board as the place to “Resolve a dispute with a landlord or tenant, and/or end a tenancy or co-op member’s occupancy”. Its page says the Tribunals Ontario Portal can be used to “submit applications, check file status, upload evidence and use the dispute resolution tool to try and reach an agreement.” (Tribunals Ontario, Landlord and Tenant Board)
```

```
Where it otherwise has the jurisdiction, the Board may order payment “of an amount of money up to the greater of $10,000 and the monetary jurisdiction of the Small Claims Court.” (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, s. 207 (1))
```

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Renting a home: tenants, landlords and the Landlord and Tenant Board, "Money limits and going to court"

```
A person entitled to apply under the Act “but whose claim exceeds the Board's monetary jurisdiction may commence a proceeding in any court of competent jurisdiction”. The court may then exercise any powers the Board could have exercised. (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, s. 207 (2))
```

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide

```
If a party claims an amount at or below the Board's limit, “all rights of the party in excess of the Board's monetary jurisdiction are extinguished once the Board issues its order.” (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, s. 207 (3))
```

### `guide:tenant-and-landlord:5.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Renting a home: tenants, landlords and the Landlord and Tenant Board, "Repairs and maintenance"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/06r17

```
Under the Act, “A landlord is responsible for providing and maintaining a residential complex, including the rental units in it, in a good state of repair and fit for habitation and for complying with health, safety, housing and maintenance standards.” This applies even if the tenant was aware of a state of non-repair, or of “a contravention of a standard before entering into the tenancy agreement.” (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, s. 20 (1), (2))
```

### `guide:tenant-and-landlord:5.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Renting a home: tenants, landlords and the Landlord and Tenant Board, "Repairs and maintenance"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/06r17

```
If the Board determines on a tenant's application that a landlord breached this obligation, the orders it may make include to “Terminate the tenancy”, “Order an abatement of rent”, and “Order the landlord to do specified repairs or replacements or other work within a specified time.” The full list is in section 30. (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, s. 30 (1))
```

```
The Act says: “The only security deposit that a landlord may collect is a rent deposit collected in accordance with section 106.” A landlord may require a rent deposit “if the landlord does so on or before entering into the tenancy agreement.” (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, ss. 105 (1), 106 (1))
```

### `guide:tenant-and-landlord:6.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Renting a home: tenants, landlords and the Landlord and Tenant Board, "Rent deposits"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/06r17

```
The deposit “shall not be more than the lesser of the amount of rent for one rent period and the amount of rent for one month.” The landlord “shall pay interest to the tenant annually” on the deposit at the rent increase guideline rate. (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, s. 106 (2), (6))
```

### `guide:tenant-and-landlord:6.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide

```
A landlord “shall apply a rent deposit that a tenant has paid to the landlord or to a former landlord in payment of the rent for the last rent period before the tenancy terminates.” (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, s. 106 (10))
```

### `guide:tenant-and-landlord:7.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Renting a home: tenants, landlords and the Landlord and Tenant Board, "Ending a tenancy: notices and grounds"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/06r17

```
The Act says: “A tenancy may be terminated only in accordance with this Act.” A notice of termination must be in a form approved by the Board (or a prescribed form), and must identify the rental unit, state the termination date, and be signed by the person giving it or that person's agent. A landlord's notice must also “set out the reasons and details respecting the termination”. (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, ss. 37 (1), 43)
```

### `guide:tenant-and-landlord:7.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Renting a home: tenants, landlords and the Landlord and Tenant Board, "Ending a tenancy: notices and grounds"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/06r17

```
A landlord's notice must tell the tenant that if the tenant does not move out, “the landlord may apply to the Board for an order terminating the tenancy and evicting the tenant”, and that “the tenant is entitled to dispute the application.” A tenant may end a tenancy at the end of a period or term by giving notice under section 44. (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, ss. 43 (2), 47)
```

### `guide:tenant-and-landlord:7.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Renting a home: tenants, landlords and the Landlord and Tenant Board, "Ending a tenancy: notices and grounds"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/06r17

```
Grounds on which the Act lets a landlord give notice include: non-payment of rent; persistent late payment; an illegal act; undue damage; substantial interference with reasonable enjoyment; an act that seriously impairs safety; and more people living in the unit than health, safety or housing standards allow. (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, ss. 58 to 67)
```

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Renting a home: tenants, landlords and the Landlord and Tenant Board, "Ending a tenancy: notices and grounds"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/06r17

```
Other grounds include the landlord or a purchaser requiring the unit in good faith for residential occupation by listed people (such as the landlord or purchaser, their spouse, or a child or parent). Each ground has its own conditions in the section that sets it out. (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, ss. 48, 49)
```

- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/06r17


- **Status:** draft
