- **Appears in:** Guides, Renting a home: tenants, landlords and the Landlord and Tenant Board, "Applications to the Board and their time limits"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/06r17

```
A tenant or former tenant may apply to the Board for the orders listed in section 29, about: the landlord's repair obligation; withholding or deliberately interfering with the reasonable supply of a vital service, care service or food; substantial interference with reasonable enjoyment; harassment, obstruction, coercion, threats or interference by the landlord, superintendent or agent; altering the locking system without giving replacement keys; and illegal entry. (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, s. 29 (1))
```

### `guide:tenant-and-landlord:8.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Renting a home: tenants, landlords and the Landlord and Tenant Board, "Applications to the Board and their time limits"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/06r17

```
For these tenant applications, “No application may be made under subsection (1) more than one year after the day the alleged conduct giving rise to the application occurred.” (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, s. 29 (2))
```

### `guide:tenant-and-landlord:8.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Renting a home: tenants, landlords and the Landlord and Tenant Board, "Applications to the Board and their time limits"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/06r17

```
A landlord who has given notice may apply for “an order terminating a tenancy and evicting the tenant”. That application “may not be made later than 30 days after the termination date specified in the notice”, but this does not apply to an application based on failure to pay rent. (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, s. 69 (1), (2), (3))
```

### `guide:tenant-and-landlord:8.4`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Renting a home: tenants, landlords and the Landlord and Tenant Board, "Applications to the Board and their time limits"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/06r17

```
A landlord may also apply for an order that a tenant or former tenant pay arrears of rent, or pay reasonable repair or replacement costs where the tenant, another occupant or a person the tenant permitted there wilfully or negligently caused undue damage. Each may be made “while the tenant is in possession of the rental unit” or “no later than one year after the tenant or former tenant ceased to be in possession of the rental unit.” (Residential Tenancies Act, 2006, ss. 87 (1), (1.1), 89 (1), (1.1))
```

### `guide:human-rights:title`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90h19

```
Human rights and discrimination in Ontario
```

### `guide:human-rights:intro`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90h19

```
This guide explains what Ontario's Human Rights Code says about equal treatment and harassment, how an application to the Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario works, what the Tribunal can order, and when a court can deal with a human rights claim. It describes the law generally and does not say how it applies to anyone's situation.
```

### `guide:human-rights:1:heading`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90h19

```
Where the Code gives a right to equal treatment
```

### `guide:human-rights:1.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario, "Where the Code gives a right to equal treatment"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90h19

```
Part I of the Code is headed Freedom from Discrimination. It gives every person a right to equal treatment “with respect to services, goods and facilities” and “with respect to the occupancy of accommodation”. (Human Rights Code, ss. 1, 2 (1))
```

### `guide:human-rights:1.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario, "Where the Code gives a right to equal treatment"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90h19

```
Part I also covers contracts, employment and vocational associations. Every person having legal capacity “has a right to contract on equal terms”. Every person has a right to equal treatment “with respect to employment”, and with respect to “membership in any trade union, trade or occupational association or self-governing profession”. (Human Rights Code, ss. 3, 5 (1), 6)
```

### `guide:human-rights:1.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario, "Where the Code gives a right to equal treatment"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90h19

```
The Code also says: “No person shall infringe or do, directly or indirectly, anything that infringes a right under this Part.” Part II then sets out cases in which a right under Part I “is not infringed”, for example by “the implementation of a special program” of the kind section 14 describes. (Human Rights Code, ss. 9, 14 (1), 17 (1), 18)
```

### `guide:human-rights:2:heading`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90h19

```
The protected grounds
```

### `guide:human-rights:2.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario, "The protected grounds"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90h19

```
For services, the listed grounds are “race, ancestry, place of origin, colour, ethnic origin, citizenship, creed, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression, age, marital status, family status or disability.” The same list applies to contracts and to vocational associations. (Human Rights Code, ss. 1, 3, 6)
```

### `guide:human-rights:2.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario, "The protected grounds"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90h19

```
For housing, the list adds “the receipt of public assistance”. For employment, the list adds “record of offences”. (Human Rights Code, ss. 2 (1), 5 (1))
```

### `guide:human-rights:2.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario, "The protected grounds"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90h19

```
The Code defines some grounds. For example, “age” means “an age that is 18 years or more”. Section 10 has the other definitions, including “disability” and “marital status”. (Human Rights Code, s. 10 (1))
```

### `guide:human-rights:2.4`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario, "The protected grounds"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90h19

```
Community Legal Education Ontario describes the same protections in plain words: the Code “says that everyone has the right to be treated equally and not be discriminated against” at work, in housing, in a union or professional group, and by a service provider. (CLEO, Steps to Justice: How do I make a claim to the Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario?, last reviewed June 12, 2025)
```

### `guide:human-rights:3:heading`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90h19

```
Harassment and reprisal
```

### `guide:human-rights:3.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario, "Harassment and reprisal"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90h19

```
The Code defines “harassment” as “engaging in a course of vexatious comment or conduct that is known or ought reasonably to be known to be unwelcome”. (Human Rights Code, s. 10 (1))
```

### `guide:human-rights:3.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario, "Harassment and reprisal"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90h19

```
A person who occupies accommodation has a right to freedom from harassment “by the landlord or agent of the landlord or by an occupant of the same building” because of listed grounds. An employee has a right to freedom from harassment “in the workplace by the employer or agent of the employer or by another employee” because of listed grounds. (Human Rights Code, ss. 2 (2), 5 (2))
```

### `guide:human-rights:3.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario, "Harassment and reprisal"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90h19

```
Section 7 deals with harassment “because of sex, sexual orientation, gender identity or gender expression” in housing and at work. It also gives a right to be free from a sexual solicitation or advance by “a person in a position to confer, grant or deny a benefit or advancement” where that person “knows or ought reasonably to know that it is unwelcome”, and from a reprisal or threat of reprisal by such a person for rejecting one. (Human Rights Code, s. 7)
```

### `guide:human-rights:3.4`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario, "Harassment and reprisal"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90h19

```
Every person has a right “to claim and enforce his or her rights under this Act, to institute and participate in proceedings under this Act and to refuse to infringe a right of another person under this Act, without reprisal or threat of reprisal for so doing.” (Human Rights Code, s. 8)
```

### `guide:human-rights:4:heading`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90h19

```
Disability and the duty to accommodate
```

### `guide:human-rights:4.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario, "Disability and the duty to accommodate"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90h19

```
A right under the Code is not infringed “for the reason only that the person is incapable of performing or fulfilling the essential duties or requirements attending the exercise of the right because of disability.” (Human Rights Code, s. 17 (1))
```

### `guide:human-rights:4.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario, "Disability and the duty to accommodate"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90h19

```
But no tribunal or court “shall find a person incapable unless it is satisfied that the needs of the person cannot be accommodated without undue hardship on the person responsible for accommodating those needs, considering the cost, outside sources of funding, if any, and health and safety requirements, if any.” In deciding whether there would be undue hardship, a tribunal or court “shall consider any standards prescribed by the regulations.” (Human Rights Code, s. 17 (2), (3))
```

### `guide:human-rights:4.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario, "Disability and the duty to accommodate"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90h19

```
CLEO explains that for a tenant with a disability, a landlord “must make adjustments so that you can use and access your apartment and your building”, unless this would cause undue hardship. It adds that where a landlord and tenant cannot agree, “the Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario might have to decide. In some situations, the Landlord and Tenant Board may also decide.” (CLEO, Steps to Justice: I have mobility issues. Does my landlord have to make adjustments to the rental unit for me?, last reviewed March 4, 2021)
```

### `guide:human-rights:5:heading`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90h19

```
Applying to the Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario
```

### `guide:human-rights:5.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario, "Applying to the Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90h19

```
Tribunals Ontario says the Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario (HRTO) “resolves claims of discrimination and harassment under the Human Rights Code”. (Tribunals Ontario, Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario)
```

### `guide:human-rights:5.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario, "Applying to the Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90h19

```
A person who believes their Part I rights were infringed may apply to the Tribunal “within one year after the incident to which the application relates” or, “if there was a series of incidents, within one year after the last incident in the series.” The application “shall be in a form approved by the Tribunal.” (Human Rights Code, s. 34 (1), (3))
```

### `guide:human-rights:5.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario, "Applying to the Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90h19

```
A person may apply after the one-year limit “if the Tribunal is satisfied that the delay was incurred in good faith and no substantial prejudice will result to any person affected by the delay.” (Human Rights Code, s. 34 (2))
```

### `guide:human-rights:5.4`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario, "Applying to the Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90h19

```
A person or organization, other than the Commission, may apply on behalf of another person if that person would have been entitled to apply and “consents to the application.” Two or more people entitled to apply may file jointly, subject to any Tribunal rule that lets the Tribunal direct that an application be considered in a separate proceeding. (Human Rights Code, s. 34 (4), (5))
```

### `guide:human-rights:6:heading`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90h19

```
Mediation and hearings at the Tribunal
```

### `guide:human-rights:6.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario, "Mediation and hearings at the Tribunal"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90h19

```
CLEO explains that “Mediation is when you, the Respondent, and an HRTO member try to resolve your case before it goes to a hearing.” The HRTO member “will not make any decisions” at mediation. (CLEO, Steps to Justice: What happens at mediation at the Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario?, last reviewed June 12, 2025)
```

### `guide:human-rights:6.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario, "Mediation and hearings at the Tribunal"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90h19

```
CLEO says that for applications filed after June 1, 2025, “you will have to do mediation first to try and resolve your issue.” For applications filed before June 1, 2025, it says the HRTO will ask the parties to try mediation, but it is not required. (CLEO, Steps to Justice: What happens at mediation at the Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario?, last reviewed June 12, 2025)
```

### `guide:human-rights:6.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario, "Mediation and hearings at the Tribunal"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90h19

```
If the parties agree, they sign a document “usually called a settlement agreement”, and the HRTO then closes the case. If they cannot agree, there is a hearing on another date with a different HRTO member. (CLEO, Steps to Justice: What happens at mediation at the Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario?, last reviewed June 12, 2025)
```

### `guide:human-rights:6.4`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario, "Mediation and hearings at the Tribunal"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90h19

```
At a hearing, both sides present their case to an HRTO member. The member listens to both sides and any witnesses, looks at the evidence, and then decides. CLEO notes: “The HRTO member usually does not give a decision at the hearing. They will send you one later.” (CLEO, Steps to Justice: What happens at a Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario hearing?, last reviewed June 12, 2025)
```

### `guide:human-rights:6.5`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario, "Mediation and hearings at the Tribunal"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90h19

```
The CLEO pages on mediation and hearings were last reviewed on June 12, 2025. Tribunals Ontario's HRTO page says that effective August 17, 2026, the HRTO “is introducing updates to its Rules of Procedure and Practice Directions along with process improvements”. (Tribunals Ontario, Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario)
```

### `guide:human-rights:7:heading`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90h19

```
What the Tribunal can order
```

### `guide:human-rights:7.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario, "What the Tribunal can order"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90h19

```
If the Tribunal determines that a party infringed another party's Part I right, it may order the party who infringed the right “to pay monetary compensation to the party whose right was infringed for loss arising out of the infringement, including compensation for injury to dignity, feelings and self-respect.” It may also order restitution other than money. (Human Rights Code, s. 45.2 (1), paras. 1, 2)
```

### `guide:human-rights:7.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario, "What the Tribunal can order"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90h19

```
The Tribunal may also order any party “to do anything that, in the opinion of the Tribunal, the party ought to do to promote compliance with this Act.” Such an order “may direct a person to do anything with respect to future practices” and “may be made even if no order under that paragraph was requested.” (Human Rights Code, s. 45.2 (1), para. 3, (2))
```

### `guide:human-rights:8:heading`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90h19

```
Human rights claims in a court case
```

### `guide:human-rights:8.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario, "Human rights claims in a court case"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90h19

```
If, “in a civil proceeding in a court, the court finds that a party to the proceeding has infringed a right under Part I of another party”, the court may order monetary compensation, restitution, or both. But this “does not permit a person to commence an action based solely on an infringement of a right under Part I.” (Human Rights Code, s. 46.1 (1), (2))
```

### `guide:human-rights:8.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Human rights and discrimination in Ontario, "Human rights claims in a court case"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90h19

```
A person may not apply to the Tribunal about a right if a civil proceeding seeking an order under section 46.1 about the same alleged infringement “has not been finally determined or withdrawn”, or if “a court has finally determined the issue of whether the right has been infringed or the matter has been settled.” (Human Rights Code, s. 34 (11))
```

### `guide:employment-standards:title`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Employment standards
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/00e41

```
Employment standards
```

### `guide:employment-standards:intro`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Employment standards
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/00e41

```
This guide describes, in general terms, what Ontario's Employment Standards Act, 2000 says about who it covers, some of the standards it sets, and how a complaint or a court case about those standards is started. It explains what the Act says; it does not say whether any standard applies to a particular job.
```

### `guide:employment-standards:1:heading`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Employment standards
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/00e41

```
Who the Act covers
```

### `guide:employment-standards:1.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Employment standards, "Who the Act covers"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/00e41

```
Subject to the exceptions in subsections (2) to (5), the employment standards in the Act apply to an employee and employer if “the employee's work is to be performed in Ontario”, or if the work is performed in Ontario and outside Ontario but “the work performed outside Ontario is a continuation of work performed in Ontario”. (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 3 (1))
```

### `guide:employment-standards:1.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Employment standards, "Who the Act covers"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/00e41

```
The Act “does not apply with respect to an employee and his or her employer if their employment relationship is within the legislative jurisdiction of the Parliament of Canada.” It also lists other people it does not apply to, such as “A secondary school student who performs work under a work experience program authorized by the school board”, “A holder of political, religious or judicial office” and “Any prescribed individuals.” (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 3 (2), (5))
```

### `guide:employment-standards:1.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Employment standards, "Who the Act covers"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/00e41

```
The Act also says “An employer shall not treat, for the purposes of this Act, a person who is an employee of the employer as if the person were not an employee under this Act.” (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 5.1 (1))
```

### `guide:employment-standards:2:heading`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Employment standards
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/00e41

```
Standards cannot be signed away
```

### `guide:employment-standards:2.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Employment standards, "Standards cannot be signed away"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/00e41

```
Section 5 is headed “No contracting out”. It says “no employer or agent of an employer and no employee or agent of an employee shall contract out of or waive an employment standard and any such contracting out or waiver is void.” (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 5 (1))
```

### `guide:employment-standards:2.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Employment standards, "Standards cannot be signed away"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/00e41

```
There is one exception. If one or more provisions in an employment contract or in another Act “that directly relate to the same subject matter as an employment standard provide a greater benefit to an employee than the employment standard”, then “the provision or provisions in the contract or Act apply and the employment standard does not apply.” (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 5 (2))
```

### `guide:employment-standards:3:heading`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Employment standards
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/00e41

```
Getting paid
```

### `guide:employment-standards:3.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Employment standards, "Getting paid"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/00e41

```
“An employer shall establish a recurring pay period and a recurring pay day and shall pay all wages earned during each pay period, other than accruing vacation pay, no later than the pay day for that period.” (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 11 (1))
```

### `guide:employment-standards:3.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Employment standards, "Getting paid"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/00e41

```
When employment ends, the employer must pay any wages owing no later than the later of “seven days after the employment ends” and “the day that would have been the employee's next pay day.” (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 11 (5))
```

### `guide:employment-standards:3.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Employment standards, "Getting paid"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/00e41

```
The Act says “An employer shall pay employees at least the minimum wage.” Minimum wages are adjusted each October 1 by a formula using the Consumer Price Index, with no adjustment if it would result in a decrease. “The Minister shall, not later than April 1 of every year after 2021, publish on a website of the Government of Ontario the minimum wages that are to apply starting on October 1 of that year.” (Employment Standards Act, 2000, ss. 23 (1), 23.1 (4), (6), (7))
```

### `guide:employment-standards:3.4`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Employment standards, "Getting paid"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/00e41

```
This guide does not state current minimum wage amounts. The Act sets separate minimum wage classes, such as students under 18 and homeworkers, and allows a class and its minimum wage to be prescribed by regulation. The current rates are published by the Minister; the site does not yet hold a source for those rates or any such regulation. (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 23.1 (1), (2), (7))
```

### `guide:employment-standards:4:heading`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Employment standards
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/00e41

```
Hours of work, overtime and public holidays
```

### `guide:employment-standards:4.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Employment standards, "Hours of work, overtime and public holidays"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/00e41

```
No employer shall require or permit an employee to work more than “eight hours in a day” (or the employee's regular work day, if the employer set one longer than eight hours) and “48 hours in a work week”. The limits may be exceeded where the employee “has made an agreement with the employer”, and the Act sets conditions for such an agreement to be valid. (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 17 (1)-(5))
```

### `guide:employment-standards:4.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Employment standards, "Hours of work, overtime and public holidays"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/00e41

```
An employer “shall pay an employee overtime pay of at least one and one-half times his or her regular rate for each hour of work in excess of 44 hours in each work week or, if another threshold is prescribed, that prescribed threshold.” (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 22 (1))
```

### `guide:employment-standards:4.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Employment standards, "Hours of work, overtime and public holidays"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/00e41

```
The Act lists the public holidays: New Year's Day, Family Day, Good Friday, Victoria Day, Canada Day, Labour Day, Thanksgiving Day, Christmas Day, December 26, and “Any day prescribed as a public holiday”. (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 1 (1), “public holiday”)
```

### `guide:employment-standards:4.4`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Employment standards, "Hours of work, overtime and public holidays"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/00e41

```
If a public holiday falls on a day that would ordinarily be a working day and the employee is not on vacation, “the employer shall give the employee the day off work and pay him or her public holiday pay for that day.” The Act sets out exceptions and rules for agreeing to work on the holiday. (Employment Standards Act, 2000, ss. 26, 27)
```

### `guide:employment-standards:5:heading`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Employment standards
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/00e41

```
Vacation and vacation pay
```

### `guide:employment-standards:5.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Employment standards, "Vacation and vacation pay"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/00e41

```
An employer shall give an employee a vacation of “at least two weeks after each vacation entitlement year that the employee completes, if the employee's period of employment is less than five years”, or “at least three weeks” if the period of employment is five years or more. (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 33 (1))
```

### `guide:employment-standards:5.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Employment standards, "Vacation and vacation pay"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/00e41

```
Vacation pay must equal at least “4 per cent of the wages, excluding vacation pay, that the employee earned during the period for which the vacation is given, if the employee's period of employment is less than five years”, or “6 per cent” if it is five years or more. (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 35.2)
```

### `guide:employment-standards:6:heading`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Employment standards
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/00e41

```
Notice of termination or termination pay
```

### `guide:employment-standards:6.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Employment standards, "Notice of termination or termination pay"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/00e41

```
“No employer shall terminate the employment of an employee who has been continuously employed for three months or more” unless the employer has given written notice under section 57 or 58 and the notice has expired, or has complied with section 61. The Act also says: “Prescribed employees are not entitled to notice of termination or termination pay under this Part.” (Employment Standards Act, 2000, ss. 54, 55)
```

### `guide:employment-standards:6.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Employment standards, "Notice of termination or termination pay"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/00e41

```
Under the Act, an employer terminates employment if it “dismisses the employee or otherwise refuses or is unable to continue employing him or her”, if it “constructively dismisses the employee and the employee resigns from his or her employment in response to that within a reasonable period”, or if it lays the employee off for longer than a temporary lay-off. (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 56 (1))
```

### `guide:employment-standards:6.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Employment standards, "Notice of termination or termination pay"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/00e41

```
The notice period depends on the period of employment: “at least one week before the termination, if the employee's period of employment is less than one year”, rising by steps to “at least eight weeks before the termination, if the employee's period of employment is eight years or more.” Different rules apply when an employer terminates 50 or more employees at the employer's establishment in the same four-week period. (Employment Standards Act, 2000, ss. 57, 58 (1))
```

### `guide:employment-standards:6.4`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Employment standards, "Notice of termination or termination pay"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/00e41

```
Instead of notice, an employer may pay “termination pay in a lump sum equal to the amount the employee would have been entitled to receive under section 60 had notice been given”, and must continue benefit plan contributions for the notice period. (Employment Standards Act, 2000, ss. 60 (1), 61 (1))
```

### `guide:employment-standards:7:heading`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Employment standards
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/00e41

```
Severance pay
```

### `guide:employment-standards:7.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Employment standards, "Severance pay"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/00e41

```
An employer who severs an employment relationship must pay severance pay “if the employee was employed by the employer for five years or more” and one of two conditions is met. The first is that the severance came from a permanent discontinuance of all or part of the business at an establishment and the employee “is one of 50 or more employees who have their employment relationship severed within a six-month period as a result”. (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 64 (1))
```

### `guide:employment-standards:7.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Employment standards, "Severance pay"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/00e41

```
The second is that “the employer has a payroll of $2.5 million or more”, measured as set out in subsection 64 (2). The Act also says: “Prescribed employees are not entitled to severance pay under this section.” (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 64 (1), (2), (3))
```

### `guide:employment-standards:7.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Employment standards, "Severance pay"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/00e41

```
Severance pay is calculated by multiplying “the employee's regular wages for a regular work week” by the completed years of employment plus completed extra months divided by 12. It “shall not exceed an amount equal to the employee's regular wages for a regular work week for 26 weeks.” (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 65 (1), (5))
```

### `guide:employment-standards:7.4`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Employment standards, "Severance pay"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/00e41

```
Severance pay under section 65 is “in addition to any other amount to which an employee is entitled under this Act or his or her employment contract”, subject to the set-offs and deductions listed in subsection 65 (8). (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 65 (7), (8))
```

### `guide:employment-standards:8:heading`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Employment standards
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/00e41

```
Filing a complaint and its time limit
```

### `guide:employment-standards:8.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Employment standards, "Filing a complaint and its time limit"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/00e41

```
“A person alleging that this Act has been or is being contravened may file a complaint with the Ministry in a written or electronic form approved by the Director.” A complaint not filed in an approved form “shall be deemed not to have been filed.” (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 96 (1), (2))
```

### `guide:employment-standards:8.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Employment standards, "Filing a complaint and its time limit"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/00e41

```
Where an employer is or has been bound by a collective agreement, subsection 99 (1) makes the Act “enforceable against the employer as if it were part of the collective agreement” for contraventions in the periods it lists. (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 99 (1))
```

### `guide:employment-standards:8.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Employment standards, "Filing a complaint and its time limit"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/00e41

```
An employee represented by a trade union that is or was a party to a collective agreement “may not file a complaint alleging a contravention of this Act that is enforceable under subsection (1) or have such a complaint investigated.” However, the Director “may permit an employee to file a complaint” despite this “if the Director considers it appropriate in the circumstances.” (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 99 (1), (2), (6))
```

### `guide:employment-standards:8.4`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Employment standards, "Filing a complaint and its time limit"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/00e41

```
The Act sets a time limit: “A complaint regarding a contravention that occurred more than two years before the day on which the complaint was filed shall be deemed not to have been filed.” (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 96 (3))
```

### `guide:employment-standards:8.5`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Employment standards, "Filing a complaint and its time limit"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/00e41

```
An employment standards officer investigating a complaint “may not issue an order for wages that became due to the employee” if “the wages became due more than two years before the complaint was filed.” (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 111 (1))
```

### `guide:employment-standards:9:heading`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Employment standards
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/00e41

A complaint or a court case
```

### `guide:employment-standards:9.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Employment standards, "A complaint or a court case"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/00e41

```
The Act says “Subject to section 97, no civil remedy of an employee against his or her employer is affected by this Act.” An employee who starts a civil proceeding against the employer under the Act must serve notice on the Director, on a form approved by the Director, “on or before the date the civil proceeding is set down for trial.” (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 8 (1), (2))
```

### `guide:employment-standards:9.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Employment standards, "A complaint or a court case"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/00e41

```
An employee who files a complaint about unpaid wages or benefit plans “may not commence a civil proceeding with respect to the same matter.” An employee who files a complaint claiming termination or severance pay “may not commence a civil proceeding for wrongful dismissal if the complaint and the proceeding would relate to the same termination or severance of employment.” (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 97 (1), (2))
```

### `guide:employment-standards:9.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Employment standards, "A complaint or a court case"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/00e41

```
There is a withdrawal window: an employee who has filed a complaint may start a civil proceeding on those matters “if he or she withdraws the complaint within two weeks after it is filed.” (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 97 (4))
```

### `guide:employment-standards:9.4`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Employment standards, "A complaint or a court case"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/00e41

```
It works the other way too. An employee who starts a civil proceeding about unpaid wages or benefit plans “may not file a complaint with respect to the same matter”, and one who starts a proceeding for wrongful dismissal may not file a complaint for termination or severance pay about the same termination or severance. (Employment Standards Act, 2000, s. 98 (1), (2))
```

### `guide:employment-standards:9.5`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Employment standards, "A complaint or a court case"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/00e41

```
CLEO's Steps to Justice has plain-language questions on these subjects, grouped under headings including “Getting paid”, “Getting fired or laid off” and “Claiming your rights as a worker”. (CLEO, Steps to Justice: Employment and work)
```

Debt collection and being sued for a debt
```

### `guide:debt-and-collections:intro`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c14

```
This guide describes, in general terms, the Ontario rules for collection agencies, the time limit for starting a court case, what happens when a creditor sues in Small Claims Court, and some basics about bankruptcy, consumer proposals and credit reports. It explains what the sources say; it does not say whether any particular debt is owed.
```

### `guide:debt-and-collections:1:heading`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c14

```
What a collection agency is
```

### `guide:debt-and-collections:1.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt, "What a collection agency is"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c14

```
Under the Collection and Debt Settlement Services Act, a “collection agency” includes “a person, other than a collector, who obtains or arranges for payment of money owing to another person” and “a person who purchases debts that are in arrears and collects them”. (Collection and Debt Settlement Services Act, s. 1 (1))
```

### `guide:debt-and-collections:1.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt, "What a collection agency is"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c14

```
“No person shall carry on the business of a collection agency unless the person is registered by the Registrar under this Act.” A creditor may deal with a debtor for payment only “under the name in which the debt is lawfully owing or through a registered collection agency.” (Collection and Debt Settlement Services Act, ss. 4 (1), 5)
```

### `guide:debt-and-collections:1.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt, "What a collection agency is"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c14

```
The Act does not apply to some people, including a lawyer in the regular practice of their profession (subject to the regulations), a bank, a credit union or its employees acting in the regular course of their employment, and “an isolated collection made by a person whose usual business is not collecting debts for other persons”. The Act also says “Any waiver or release of any right, benefit or protection provided by this Act or the regulations is void.” (Collection and Debt Settlement Services Act, ss. 2 (1), 22.1)
```

### `guide:debt-and-collections:2:heading`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c14

```
What collectors may not do
```

### `guide:debt-and-collections:2.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt, "What collectors may not do"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c14

```
No collection agency or collector shall “collect or attempt to collect, on its own behalf or for a person for whom it acts, any money in addition to the amount owing by the debtor”, or “deal with a debtor in a name other than that authorized by the registration”, or “engage in any prohibited practice or employ any prohibited method in the collection of debts”. (Collection and Debt Settlement Services Act, s. 22)
```

### `guide:debt-and-collections:2.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt, "What collectors may not do"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c14

```
The detailed rules are in a regulation that the site does not yet hold. Ontario's guide for collection agencies summarizes them. Before contacting a debtor to demand payment, an agency “must send a written notice to the debtor”, and must “wait six calendar days after sending a written notice” before contacting the debtor or demanding payment. (ontario.ca, A guide for collection agencies)
```

### `guide:debt-and-collections:2.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt, "What collectors may not do"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c14

```
The guide says an agency cannot contact anyone about a debt “between 9 p.m. and 7 a.m. (debtor's local time) from Monday to Saturday”, “on a Sunday, except between 1 p.m. and 5 p.m. (debtor's local time)”, or “on a public holiday”. (ontario.ca, A guide for collection agencies)
```

### `guide:debt-and-collections:2.4`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt, "What collectors may not do"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c14

```
It also says “you can contact a debtor up to three times within a seven-day period on behalf of the same creditor”, and not more often “unless additional contact was agreed to, requested or initiated by the debtor, or if contact is by mail.” It adds: “This rule does not apply until you have spoken to the debtor in person or by phone.” (ontario.ca, A guide for collection agencies)
```

### `guide:debt-and-collections:2.5`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt, "What collectors may not do"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c14

```
When dealing with a debtor, the guide says an agency cannot “use threatening, profane, intimidating or coercive language”, “use excessive or unreasonable pressure”, “give false or misleading information”, or “threaten legal action without the creditor's written authority to commence legal proceedings”. (ontario.ca, A guide for collection agencies)
```

### `guide:debt-and-collections:3:heading`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt

```

### `guide:debt-and-collections:3.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt, "Contacting other people, and disputed debts"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c14

```
The guide lists limited situations in which an agency can contact a debtor's employer, such as where “the debtor has given you written permission”, or once “to confirm that the debtor works there”. It can contact family, friends or neighbours only in listed situations, such as where that person “has guaranteed to pay the debt”. (ontario.ca, A guide for collection agencies)
```

### `guide:debt-and-collections:3.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt, "Contacting other people, and disputed debts"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c14

```
The guide says an agency cannot contact someone if “you know or reasonably should know they are not responsible for the debt”. It also says “If the debtor sends you a notice suggesting that the matter be taken to court, you cannot contact or attempt to contact the debtor”, unless the debtor consents to or requests contact. (ontario.ca, A guide for collection agencies)
```

### `guide:debt-and-collections:3.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt, "Contacting other people, and disputed debts"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c14

```
CLEO explains that when someone is contacted about a debt they do not think they owe, “Your creditor or the collection agency may have made a mistake.” (CLEO, Steps to Justice: A collection agency called about a debt I do not owe)
```

### `guide:debt-and-collections:3.4`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt, "Contacting other people, and disputed debts"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c14

```
If talking to the agency or creditor does not work, CLEO describes sending “a formal letter by registered mail to the collection agency” disputing the debt and asking that a court decide the problem, after which “the collection agency can only contact you if they plan to take you to court.” (CLEO, Steps to Justice: A collection agency called about a debt I do not owe)
```

### `guide:debt-and-collections:3.5`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt, "Contacting other people, and disputed debts"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c14

```
CLEO also says that ignoring a collection agency can have consequences: “your credit rating could drop and you might get sued in court”. (CLEO, Steps to Justice: A collection agency called me. Do I have to talk to them?)

Ontario's guide says “Consumers can submit complaints about collection agencies to the Ministry of Public and Business Service Delivery and Procurement.” When the Registrar receives a complaint and asks in writing, the collection agency “shall furnish the Registrar with such information respecting the matter complained of as the Registrar requires.” (ontario.ca, A guide for collection agencies; Collection and Debt Settlement Services Act, s. 12 (1))
```

### `guide:debt-and-collections:5.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt, "Time limits for suing on a debt"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c14

```
The Limitations Act, 2002 sets the general rule: “Unless this Act provides otherwise, a proceeding shall not be commenced in respect of a claim after the second anniversary of the day on which the claim was discovered.” Section 15 also sets an ultimate limit: no proceeding “after the 15th anniversary of the day on which the act or omission on which the claim is based took place”, subject to the exceptions in that section. (Limitations Act, 2002, ss. 4, 15 (2), (4))
```

### `guide:debt-and-collections:5.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt, "Time limits for suing on a debt"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c14

```
If a person “acknowledges liability in respect of a claim for payment of a liquidated sum”, the act or omission the claim is based on is treated as having taken place “on the day on which the acknowledgment was made.” The acknowledgment must be “in writing and signed”, and “part payment of the sum” by the person against whom the claim is made “has the same effect”. (Limitations Act, 2002, s. 13 (1), (10), (11))
```

### `guide:debt-and-collections:5.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt, "Time limits for suing on a debt"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c14

```
An acknowledgment counts only if it is made to the person with the claim, their agent, or a bankruptcy trustee or official receiver “before the expiry of the limitation period applicable to the claim.” (Limitations Act, 2002, s. 13 (9))
```

### `guide:debt-and-collections:6:heading`

- **Status:** draft

Being sued for a debt in Small Claims Court
```

### `guide:debt-and-collections:6.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt, "Being sued for a debt in Small Claims Court"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c14

```
The Small Claims Court “has jurisdiction in any action for the payment of money where the amount claimed does not exceed the prescribed amount exclusive of interest and costs”. A regulation says “The maximum amount of a claim in the Small Claims Court is $50,000.” (Courts of Justice Act, s. 23 (1); O. Reg. 626/00, s. 1 (1))
```

### `guide:debt-and-collections:6.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt, "Being sued for a debt in Small Claims Court"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c14

```
“An action that is within the Small Claims Court's jurisdiction shall not, despite subsection 11 (2), be commenced in the Superior Court of Justice except with leave of the Superior Court of Justice as provided in the rules of court.” This does not apply to a counterclaim, crossclaim or third or subsequent party claim where the main action was commenced in the Superior Court of Justice. (Courts of Justice Act, s. 23 (1.1), (1.2))
```

### `guide:debt-and-collections:6.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt, "Being sued for a debt in Small Claims Court"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c14

```
“A defendant who wishes to dispute a plaintiff's claim shall, within 20 days of being served with the claim,” serve a defence (Form 9A) on every other party, and file it with proof of service with the clerk. (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 9.01)
```

### `guide:debt-and-collections:6.4`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt, "Being sued for a debt in Small Claims Court"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c14

```
“A defendant who admits liability for all or part of the plaintiff's claim but wishes to arrange terms of payment may in the defence admit liability and propose terms of payment.” (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 9.03 (1))
```

### `guide:debt-and-collections:6.5`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt, "Being sued for a debt in Small Claims Court"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c14

```
If a defendant “fails to file a defence to all or part of the claim with the clerk within the prescribed time, the clerk may note the defendant in default” when a request to note the defendant in default and proof that the claim was served within the court's territorial division are filed. Other requirements apply if all defendants were served outside that division. (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 11.01 (1), (3))
```

### `guide:debt-and-collections:6.6`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt, "Being sued for a debt in Small Claims Court"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c14

```
The rules also say: “A person under disability may not be noted in default under subrule (1), except with leave of the court.” (Rules of the Small Claims Court, r. 11.01 (2))
```

### `guide:debt-and-collections:7.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt, "Bankruptcy and consumer proposals"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c14

```
CLEO describes options other than bankruptcy, including making “a repayment plan with your creditors” and filing “a consumer proposal with a Licensed Insolvency Trustee”. It says “Bankruptcy is a legal process that you can only start with a Licensed Insolvency Trustee”. (CLEO, Steps to Justice: Are there options other than bankruptcy if I'm in debt?, last reviewed November 30, 2021; How do I file for bankruptcy?, last reviewed November 10, 2023)
```

### `guide:debt-and-collections:7.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt, "Bankruptcy and consumer proposals"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c14

```
CLEO explains “A consumer proposal is a legal agreement between you and your creditors.” It says “A consumer proposal only helps you settle your unsecured debts” and that, for it to be accepted, “the creditors that you owe more than half of your debts to must agree to it.” (CLEO, Steps to Justice: Can a consumer proposal help me get out of debt?, last reviewed November 30, 2021)
```

### `guide:debt-and-collections:7.3`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt, "Bankruptcy and consumer proposals"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c14

```
CLEO lists debts that “survive your bankruptcy”, including “child and spousal support payments”, “fines and court penalties”, “debts that are the result of a crime”, and “government student loans, if you have been out of school for less than 7 years”. (CLEO, Steps to Justice: Can I still owe money after I have been discharged from bankruptcy?, last reviewed November 30, 2021)
```

### `guide:debt-and-collections:8.1`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt, "Credit reports"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c14

```
CLEO says the two main consumer reporting agencies in Canada are TransUnion and Equifax. A bankruptcy “will stay on your credit report for 6 or 7 years after you are discharged”, and a note about a consumer proposal stays “for 3 years after your consumer proposal is completed.” (CLEO, Steps to Justice: How do I file for bankruptcy?, last reviewed November 10, 2023; Can a consumer proposal help me get out of debt?, last reviewed November 30, 2021)
```

### `guide:debt-and-collections:8.2`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** all / guide
- **Appears in:** Guides, Debt collection and being sued for a debt, "Credit reports"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c14

```
On mistakes, CLEO describes a letter to the consumer reporting agency asking it to “correct, remove, or explain any wrong information”. It says “The agency must put that letter in your file” and “the consumer reporting agency must answer your letter and tell you what they are doing about it.” If the agency does not fix the information, a complaint can be filed “with the Ministry of Public and Business Service Delivery”. (CLEO, Steps to Justice: There's a mistake in my credit report)
```

Car accidents and insurance
