## remedy (4)

### `sc-remedy-monetary-judgment`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / readiness
- **Appears in:** Readiness gate, remedy confirmation
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/docs/000626_e.doc

```
Money judgments

Small Claims Court can order one party to pay money to another, up to $50,000 (not counting interest and costs). See the education topic on the $50,000 limit for how that cap works.
```

### `sc-remedy-return-of-property`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / readiness
- **Appears in:** Readiness gate, remedy confirmation
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/document/guide-procedures-small-claims-court/making-claim

```
Return of personal property

Alongside money, Small Claims Court can order the return of specific personal property -- for example, an item someone is holding onto that belongs to someone else. This is generally only available for personal property (belongings, not land or buildings), and is part of the same $50,000 jurisdiction that applies to money claims.
```

### `sc-remedy-outside-jurisdiction`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / readiness
- **Appears in:** Readiness gate, remedy confirmation
- **Source:** https://www.ontariocourts.ca/scj/small-claims-court/

```
What Small Claims Court generally doesn't handle

Small Claims Court's jurisdiction is generally limited to two kinds of remedies: money, and the return of personal property, each up to $50,000. Under s. 23(1) of the Courts of Justice Act, the court has jurisdiction in actions for the payment of money and for the recovery of possession of personal property, up to the prescribed amount; under s. 96(3), only the Court of Appeal and the Superior Court of Justice, exclusive of the Small Claims Court, may grant equitable relief, unless otherwise provided. If what someone is looking for doesn't fit either of those -- for example, asking a court to order someone to do or stop doing something, rather than pay money or return an item -- that generally falls outside what Small Claims Court can order, and would typically need to go to a different court instead.
```

### `sc-remedy-interest-and-costs`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / readiness
- **Appears in:** Readiness gate, remedy confirmation
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/document/guide-procedures-small-claims-court/making-claim

```
Interest and costs

Interest and costs (such as court filing fees) are generally handled separately from, and in addition to, the amount claimed -- they don't count against the $50,000 limit. Whether interest or costs are awarded, and how much, depends on the specific case; this is general information that these can be part of an order, not a specific amount for any claim. Under s. 29 of the Courts of Justice Act, an award of costs in Small Claims Court, other than disbursements, shall not exceed 15 per cent of the amount claimed or the value of the property sought to be recovered, unless the court considers it necessary in the interests of justice to penalize a party or a party's representative for unreasonable behaviour in the proceeding. Costs can go either way: Ontario's page on suing in Small Claims Court says the judge might order the defendant to pay some of the costs if the plaintiff wins, and a plaintiff who loses might have to pay their own costs and some of the defendant's costs.
```

## safety-resource (3)

### `family-violence-support-resources`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** family / all
- **Appears in:** Family intake and overview
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/page/violence-family

```
Support if family violence is part of your situation

If family violence is part of what you're dealing with, Ontario has support services separate from the court process itself. A Family Court Support Worker can help you understand and go through the family court process if you're a victim of domestic violence -- Family Court Support Workers do not give legal advice, but they can help you understand what's happening and connect you to other services. Every courthouse also has a Family Law Information Centre (FLIC) that provides information about the court process and referrals to local resources.

Ontario also names specific support organizations for family violence:
- Assaulted Women's Helpline: 1-866-863-0511 (toll-free), or 416-863-0511
- Fem'aide (French-language support): 1-877-336-2433 (toll-free)
- Victim Support Line: 1-888-579-2888 (toll-free), or 416-314-2447

The Family Court Support Worker Program and the Family Law Information Centre are delivered locally through each court location rather than through a single province-wide phone number. To find the Family Court Support Worker for your court, use Ontario's own listing of service providers by court location, which links directly to the organization delivering the program there. To reach the Family Law Information Centre, contact or visit the courthouse handling your case -- Ontario's own courthouse listing gives the address and contact information, including a phone number, for each location.
```

Other support that may help:

- Fem'aide (French-language support): 1-877-336-2433 (toll-free)
- ConnexOntario mental health, addictions, and problem gambling helpline: 1-866-531-2600 (toll-free)
- To report a child who may be in need of protection: contact your local Children's Aid Society, or call police if a child is in immediate danger. There is no single province-wide number for this -- Ontario's own guidance directs people to their local society.

## stage-answer (486)

### `answer:before-filing:deciding-whether-to-sue:whats-happening`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / before-filing:deciding-whether-to-sue
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "Can I sue over this, and is Small Claims the right court?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/000626

```
Small Claims Court can hear a claim for money or personal property of up to $50,000, not counting interest and costs. The two-year time limit counts from the day the claim was discovered, which is the earlier of two days. One is the day you first knew four things. First, that the loss happened. Second, that something done or not done caused it or helped cause it. Third, who did it. Fourth, that suing is a fitting way to try to remedy it, given the kind of loss. The other is the first day a reasonable person with your abilities and in your circumstances ought to have known them. Even within the two years, most claims can't be started more than 15 years after the act or omission. There are exceptions. For example, there is no time limit for a claim based on a sexual assault. There is also none for other sexual misconduct if, at the time, the person was a minor. The same applies if the other person had charge of them or was in a position of trust or authority over them. It also applies if the person depended on the other person in some way. There is no time limit for a claim based on an assault if, at the time, the person was a minor. The same applies if the two had an intimate relationship, or the person depended on the other person in some way.
```

> **Read this as the person at this stage.** Does every instruction apply to
> you, and could you follow it? Check whose step it is (a plaintiff asks the
> clerk to note a defendant in default with Form 9B; a defendant files the
> Defence, Form 9A), whether it speaks _to_ you or _about_ you, and who served
> whom. If it has those the wrong way round, nothing else about it matters.

### `answer:before-filing:deciding-whether-to-sue:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / before-filing:deciding-whether-to-sue
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "Can I sue over this, and is Small Claims the right court?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/000626

```
You can sue for money owed under an agreement, like an unpaid loan, or goods or services that were not paid for. You can also sue for harm done, like damage to property, an injury or a broken contract. Only the Landlord and Tenant Board can decide applications under the Residential Tenancies Act, 2006. For more than $50,000, you can go to the Superior Court of Justice, or waive the amount over $50,000 and file in Small Claims Court. A claim within that limit needs the Superior Court's leave to be started there.
```

### `answer:before-filing:deciding-whether-to-sue:your-deadline`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / before-filing:deciding-whether-to-sue
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "Can I sue over this, and is Small Claims the right court?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/000626

```
The general deadline to start a court case. You have 2 years after the day the claim was discovered. The last day is the anniversary of that day, 2 years later. If that day was February 29, the anniversary is February 28, except in a leap year. This applies unless the Limitations Act, 2002 provides otherwise. For example, a claim based on a sexual assault has no limitation period. The other side may admit in writing, and sign, that they owe a fixed sum of money. The same goes for an admission that they must return personal property. It also goes for enforcing a charge on personal property, or relief from that. Then the act or omission is treated as happening on the day of that admission. This counts only if it was made before the time ran out. It must be made to you, your agent, or an official receiver or trustee under the Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act (Canada). For a fixed sum of money, a part payment by the other side or their agent works the same way as a written, signed admission.

A deadline in an Ontario statute is counted under the Legislation Act, 2006, unless the statute shows otherwise. When a period is described as starting after a day, that day is not counted (s. 89 (5)). If the last day is a Sunday or a holiday, the deadline moves to the next day that is not a holiday (s. 89 (1)). Saturday is not a holiday under that Act, so a Saturday does not by itself move the deadline. Some deadlines are for doing something at a place, such as filing at an office. If that place is not open during its regular hours on the last day, the deadline moves to the next day it is open during its regular hours (s. 89 (2)).
```

### `answer:before-filing:deciding-whether-to-sue:what-happens-after`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / before-filing:deciding-whether-to-sue
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "Can I sue over this, and is Small Claims the right court?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/000626

```
Some injury claims need written notice much sooner: 60 days for snow or ice, to an occupier or its snow contractor. If a municipality did not keep a highway in repair, notice must go to its clerk within 10 days of the injury. A judge can still let that case go ahead if there is a reasonable excuse and the municipality is not prejudiced. Missing notice also does not stop the case if the injured person died as a result of the injury. The snow or ice notice has the same two exceptions.
```

### `answer:before-filing:notice-municipality:whats-happening`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / before-filing:notice-municipality
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I was hurt because a road or sidewalk was in bad repair — do I have to tell the city first?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/01m25

```
A municipality must keep its highways and bridges in repair. The repair must be reasonable in the circumstances. You can't sue for damages from that failure unless written notice is given first. But a municipality is not liable for an injury from snow or ice on a sidewalk, except for gross negligence.
```

### `answer:before-filing:notice-municipality:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / before-filing:notice-municipality
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I was hurt because a road or sidewalk was in bad repair — do I have to tell the city first?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/01m25

```
Before you can sue, the notice must be served on the municipal clerk or sent to the clerk by registered mail. It must describe the claim and the injury. It must give the date, time and place of the injury. If the claim is against two or more municipalities jointly responsible for the repair, it goes to the clerk of each.
```

Give written notice of the claim to the clerk of the municipality. You have 10 days after the occurrence of the injury.

The general deadline to start a court case. You have 2 years after the day the claim was discovered. The last day is the anniversary of that day, 2 years later. If that day was February 29, the anniversary is February 28, except in a leap year. This applies unless the Limitations Act, 2002 provides otherwise. For example, a claim based on a sexual assault has no limitation period. The other side may admit in writing, and sign, that they owe a fixed sum of money. The same goes for an admission that they must return personal property. It also goes for enforcing a charge on personal property, or relief from that. Then the act or omission is treated as happening on the day of that admission. This counts only if it was made before the time ran out. It must be made to you, your agent, or an official receiver or trustee under the Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act (Canada). For a fixed sum of money, a part payment by the other side or their agent works the same way as a written, signed admission.

A deadline in an Ontario statute is counted under the Legislation Act, 2006, unless the statute shows otherwise. When a period is described as starting after a day, that day is not counted (s. 89 (5)). If the last day is a Sunday or a holiday, the deadline moves to the next day that is not a holiday (s. 89 (1)). Saturday is not a holiday under that Act, so a Saturday does not by itself move the deadline. Some deadlines are for doing something at a place, such as filing at an office. If that place is not open during its regular hours on the last day, the deadline moves to the next day it is open during its regular hours (s. 89 (2)).
```

### `answer:before-filing:limitation-period-may-have-passed:whats-happening`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / before-filing:limitation-period-may-have-passed
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "This happened a long time ago — am I out of time?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/02l24

```
Unless the Limitations Act, 2002 says otherwise, you have two years from when a claim was discovered to start it. A claim is discovered on the earlier of two days. One is the day you first knew four things. First, that the loss happened. Second, that something done or not done caused it or helped cause it. Third, who did it. Fourth, that suing is a fitting way to try to remedy it, given the kind of loss. The other is the day a reasonable person as able as you, in your place, first ought to have known them.
```

### `answer:before-filing:limitation-period-may-have-passed:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / before-filing:limitation-period-may-have-passed
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "This happened a long time ago — am I out of time?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/02l24

```
The law presumes you knew them on the day of the act or omission, unless proved otherwise. For a demand obligation made since 2004, the loss happens the first day it is not met after a demand. For a fixed sum owed, the act or omission is treated as taking place on the day of a signed written admission or part payment. It must happen before time runs out, and an admission must go to you, your agent or a bankruptcy trustee. You and the other side can agree to have a neutral third party help settle the claim, and the time stops while you try.
```

### `answer:before-filing:limitation-period-may-have-passed:what-happens-after`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / before-filing:limitation-period-may-have-passed
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "This happened a long time ago — am I out of time?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/02l24

```
Most claims also can't be started more than 15 years after the act or omission. There are exceptions. For example, there is no time limit for a claim based on a sexual assault. There is also none for other sexual misconduct if, at the time, the person was a minor. The same applies if the other person had charge of them or was in a position of trust or authority over them. It also applies if the person depended on the other person in some way. There is no time limit for a claim based on an assault if, at the time, the person was a minor. The same applies if the two had an intimate relationship, or the person depended on the other person in some way. The two years stop while you have no litigation guardian and are a minor, or can't sue due to a physical, mental or psychological condition. But the law presumes you could start a case at all times, unless proved otherwise. If less than six months is left when a pause for such a condition ends, the time runs until six months after it ends. The 15 years also stop in some cases, like while the other side wilfully hides the loss, but you must prove that.
```

- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "How do I actually file my claim, and what does it cost?"

```
You can file in the territorial division where the problem happened or a defendant lives or does business, or where the court sits nearest to where a defendant lives or does business. Under the Limitations Act, 2002, a claim is discovered on the earlier of two days. One is the day you first knew certain facts; the other is the first day a reasonable person with your abilities and in your circumstances ought to have known them. There are four facts. - **Appears in:** Stage answer for "How do I actually file my claim, and what does it cost?"

```
If your claim is based on a document, attach a copy to each copy of the claim; if it is unavailable, the claim must say why. On paper, you file your Plaintiff's Claim (Form 7A) in person or by mail at the court office, with copies for you and each defendant. Online, you do not need extra copies; Toronto uses the Ontario Courts Public Portal, and other regions use the Small Claims Court Submissions Online portal. The fee is $108, or $228 if you have already filed 10 or more claims at that court office this calendar year. If you cannot afford the fees, you may ask for a fee waiver; online, you say so when you submit.
```

- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/980258

```
The general deadline to start a court case. You have 2 years after the day the claim was discovered. The last day is the anniversary of that day, 2 years later. If that day was February 29, the anniversary is February 28, except in a leap year. This applies unless the Limitations Act, 2002 provides otherwise. For example, a claim based on a sexual assault has no limitation period. The other side may admit in writing, and sign, that they owe a fixed sum of money. The same goes for an admission that they must return personal property. It also goes for enforcing a charge on personal property, or relief from that. Then the act or omission is treated as happening on the day of that admission. This counts only if it was made before the time ran out. It must be made to you, your agent, or an official receiver or trustee under the Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act (Canada). For a fixed sum of money, a part payment by the other side or their agent works the same way as a written, signed admission.

A deadline in an Ontario statute is counted under the Legislation Act, 2006, unless the statute shows otherwise. When a period is described as starting after a day, that day is not counted (s. 89 (5)). If the last day is a Sunday or a holiday, the deadline moves to the next day that is not a holiday (s. 89 (1)). Saturday is not a holiday under that Act, so a Saturday does not by itself move the deadline. Some deadlines are for doing something at a place, such as filing at an office. If that place is not open during its regular hours on the last day, the deadline moves to the next day it is open during its regular hours (s. 89 (2)).
```

Court staff review online filings within 3 business days. You cannot file online to meet a deadline that is 3 business days away or less. Instead, you can file in person at the courthouse, by mail or by email. The clerk then issues the claim and gives it a court file number. Online, you get an email once the claim is issued. On paper, the clerk returns stamped copies for you to serve on each defendant.

Once the claim is issued, a stamped copy is served on each defendant. The rules allow personal service or other set methods. To serve a person who is not under a disability, you leave a copy with them.

If you cannot serve a person at home, you can leave a copy with an adult who lives there, in a sealed envelope addressed to them. You then mail or courier another copy there that day or the next. ### `answer:plaintiff:claim-issued-not-served:your-deadline`

- **Status:** draft

- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "The court gave me back my claim — how do I get it to the defendant?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/980258

```
Serve the claim on the defendant. You have 6 months after the date the claim was issued. The court may extend the time for service, before or after the six months has passed.

Ask for an assessment of damages under rule 11.03 or request a trial date, or the clerk will dismiss the action for delay. An assessment can be asked for only once every defendant has been noted in default. You have 2 years after the commencement of the action. The last day is the anniversary of that day, 2 years later. If that day was February 29, the anniversary is February 28, except in a leap year. This does not apply if the action was already decided by an order. An order includes a judgment, such as a default judgment signed by the clerk. Nor does it apply if an offer to settle was accepted and filed, if the defence admits liability for your claim and proposes terms of payment, or if you are under disability. The court may order otherwise.
```

A claim must be served within six months after it is issued. If there is more than one defendant, all of them must be served within that time. But the court may extend the time for service, before or after the six months has passed. If you ask the court for more time, you explain in an affidavit why you could not serve the claim within the six months. The time to serve can also be lengthened by filing the parties' consent.
```

If a defence admits some or all of the claim and proposes terms of payment, you have 20 days after it is served to dispute them. To do so, you file a Request to Clerk (Form 9B) for a terms of payment hearing and serve it on the defendant. If you do not, the defendant must pay as proposed, as if it were a court order.

Once the defendant is noted in default, for a debt or set amount you can file a Default Judgment (Form 11B), which the clerk may sign; there is a fee. For other claims, once all defendants are in default, you can ask a judge to assess damages. You do this by a motion in writing (Form 15A) or a request for a hearing (Form 9B). If another defendant filed a defence, the case goes to a settlement conference instead, then a trial if needed.
```

For a debt or set amount, you can file a Default Judgment (Form 11B); the fee is $94, or $128 for a frequent claimant. This does not stop you from going ahead on the rest of the claim, or against another defendant. For other claims, you can file a Notice of Motion and Supporting Affidavit (Form 15A) for a motion in writing; it costs $127. Your affidavit gives your reasons for the motion, with any relevant documents attached. Or you can ask for a hearing with a Request to Clerk (Form 9B); setting the date costs $308, or $403 for a frequent claimant.
```

```
Ask for an assessment of damages under rule 11.03 or request a trial date, or the clerk will dismiss the action for delay. An assessment can be asked for only once every defendant has been noted in default. You have 2 years after the commencement of the action. The last day is the anniversary of that day, 2 years later. If that day was February 29, the anniversary is February 28, except in a leap year. This does not apply if the action was already decided by an order. An order includes a judgment, such as a default judgment signed by the clerk. Nor does it apply if an offer to settle was accepted and filed, if the defence admits liability for your claim and proposes terms of payment, or if you are under disability. The court may order otherwise.
```

The clerk sends you the order by mail or email; for mail, include a stamped, self-addressed envelope with the motion. If all defendants are noted in default, you can ask a judge to assess the damages. If one or more defendants filed a defence, you go to a settlement conference and, if needed, a trial instead. The clerk can sign a default judgment only for a "liquidated" claim, which is a claim for a set amount owing. You do not have to prove liability against a defendant noted in default, but you must prove the amount of the claim. You can also ask for pre-judgment interest up to the judgment date, in your motion papers or at the hearing.

### `answer:plaintiff:default-judgment-signed:whats-happening`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / plaintiff:default-judgment-signed
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I have a default judgment — how do I actually get paid?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/980258

```
A default judgment does not guarantee that you will be paid. It is up to you to start the steps to collect. You can start right away. You can use garnishment, or a writ of seizure and sale of personal property (Form 20C) or of land (Form 20D). If the debtor lives or does business in another court's area, you need a Certificate of Judgment (Form 20A) first. You need it to get a notice of garnishment or examination from that court.
```

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / plaintiff:default-judgment-signed
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I have a default judgment — how do I actually get paid?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/980258

```
To have the debtor questioned, you file a Notice of Examination (Form 20H) and an Affidavit for Enforcement Request (Form 20P). Serve the notice personally, or by an alternative to personal service, at least 30 days before the hearing. Add a blank Financial Information Form (Form 20I) if the debtor is an individual. File proof of service at least three days before the hearing. To take pay or bank money owed to the debtor, you file a Notice of Garnishment (Form 20E) and Form 20P. Serve it on the garnishee with a blank Garnishee's Statement (Form 20F), then on the debtor with Form 20P within five days. The fees are $68 for a notice of examination or a writ of seizure and sale, and $144 for a notice of garnishment.
```

Six years after the order: after that, a notice of garnishment or a writ of seizure and sale can be issued only with the court's permission (leave). That point is 6 years after the day the order was made: the anniversary of that day. If that day was February 29, the anniversary is February 28, except in a leap year. A notice of garnishment needs leave sooner if enforcing the order is subject to a condition. In these rules, an order includes a judgment.

```
If the defence admits all or part of your claim and proposes terms of payment, you can dispute the terms. Within 20 days after the defence was served, you file a Request to Clerk (Form 9B) for a terms of payment hearing, and serve it on the defendant. At least 14 days before the conference, serve each other party with any document you will rely on at trial, such as an expert report, if not attached to your claim. File them in court. By the same date, serve and file a List of Proposed Witnesses (Form 13A), which also names others who know about the matters in dispute.
```

The court holds the settlement conference within 90 days after the day the first defence was filed. This is the court's timetable, not a step you take. The clerk fixes the time, date and place and serves a notice of settlement conference on the parties. No conference is held if the defence admits all of the claim and proposes terms of payment.

Request a trial date, or the clerk will dismiss the action for delay. You have 2 years after the commencement of the action. The last day is the anniversary of that day, 2 years later. An order includes a judgment, such as a default judgment signed by the clerk. Nor does it apply if an offer to settle was accepted and filed, if the defence admits liability for your claim and proposes terms of payment, or if you are under disability. The court may order otherwise.
```

If you do not dispute a payment proposal in time, the defendant must pay as proposed, as if it were a court order. If the defendant then does not pay as proposed, you can serve a Notice of Default of Payment (Form 20L). Once 15 days have passed since you served it, you can file an Affidavit of Default of Payment (Form 20M), and the clerk signs judgment for the unpaid balance of the undisputed amount. If you do dispute the terms, the clerk fixes a time for a hearing and serves a notice of hearing on the parties. A party who got notice of the conference and does not attend may face costs or other sanctions, and another conference.
```

An order includes a judgment, such as a default judgment signed by the clerk. Nor does it apply if an offer to settle was accepted and filed, if the defence admits liability for your claim and proposes terms of payment, or if you are under disability. The court may order otherwise.
```

### `answer:plaintiff:trial-date-set:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / plaintiff:trial-date-set
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I have a trial date — what do I need to do to get ready?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/980258

```
You can serve documents and written statements on all parties who got the notice of trial, at least 30 days before trial. They are then received in evidence, unless the trial judge orders otherwise. Each must give the name, phone number and address for service of the witness or author, and for an expert, a summary of qualifications. The court can issue a Summons to Witness (Form 18A) for a fee, and you serve it personally at least 10 days before trial, with attendance money. If you summon the author of a served statement, serve a copy of the summons on every other party at the same time. If a witness you summon needs an interpreter, you must arrange for a qualified one to attend. This does not apply if the Ministry provides an English-French interpreter. If you miss either step, the other parties may ask to put off the trial, with costs.
```

Serve any documents, written statements, or audio or visual records you want received in evidence, on every party who got the notice of trial. Do this at least 30 days before the trial date. This is optional. A document served this way is received in evidence unless the trial judge orders otherwise. Earlier is fine.

If you need a witness to come, hand them a summons to witness (Form 18A) with their attendance money. Do this at least 10 days before the trial date. The summons must be served on the witness personally. Earlier is fine.

You can ask for a notice of examination [Form 20H] or garnishment [Form 20E], or a writ of seizure and sale [Form 20C or 20D]. Each is filed with an Affidavit for Enforcement Request [Form 20P]. Either notice needs a Certificate of Judgment [Form 20A] in another court's area where the debtor lives or does business. You file an issued writ at the enforcement office, which has its own fees and deposits. For an examination, you serve the notice at least 30 days before the hearing.

A debtor who is a person also gets a blank Financial Information Form [Form 20I], and you use personal service or an alternative. You file proof at least 3 days before, and the court may order payments. For garnishment, you serve the garnishee the notice and a blank Garnishee's Statement [Form 20F]. Within 5 days, you serve the debtor the notice and your affidavit, and file proof of both. The garnishee pays the clerk what it owes the debtor, up to the notice amount, within 10 days of service, or of the debt coming due if later.

- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I have been sued — what do I have to do, and by when?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/980258

```
You have been served with a claim, and the 20 days to deliver a defence have not run out. A defence is your answer to the claim. If it relies on a document, a copy goes with each copy of the defence, or the defence says why it is not attached. The first day is not counted, and if the last day is a holiday, the time ends on the next day that is not one. If you ignore a claim, the plaintiff can get judgment with no further notice, as if there had been a trial.
```

- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I have been sued — what do I have to do, and by when?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/980258

```
To dispute the claim, you can serve a Defence [Form 9A] on every other party. You then file it, with an affidavit of service for each party served, at the court office named on the claim. The fee to file a defence is $77. If you agree you owe all or part of the claim, you can admit it in the defence and propose terms of payment. You can also file a Defendant's Claim [Form 10A] against the plaintiff, or against someone else about the same events or related to the claim.
```

### `answer:defendant:served-defence-period-running:your-deadline`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / defendant:served-defence-period-running
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I have been sued — what do I have to do, and by when?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/980258

```
Serve a defence on every other party and file it with the clerk, with proof of service. You have 20 days after the day of being served with the claim. If the claim was left at your home with an adult and a copy mailed or couriered, service takes effect on the fifth day after the mailing or the courier's confirmed delivery. The same is true when a company cannot be found at its last address on record and is served by mail or courier to that address and to its directors. If the claim was sent by registered mail or courier and signed for, service takes effect on the date of the signature. The parties can lengthen the time by filing their consent, and the court can lengthen it.
```

If you dispute all or part of the claim, you attend a settlement conference. The plaintiff has 20 days after your defence is served to dispute a payment proposal by asking for a hearing. If you admit the whole claim and the plaintiff does not dispute your payment plan, no more steps are needed while you pay on time. If no defence is filed in time, the clerk may note you in default when the plaintiff files a request. If you choose to make a defendant's claim, it may be issued within 20 days after your defence is filed, or later with leave, before trial or default judgment.

The court may set the judgment aside on just terms if it finds a meritorious defence, a reasonable explanation for the default, and a motion made as soon as reasonably possible. A clerk's order can set aside only listed enforcement steps not yet done, and a copy is filed at each court where they were requested. If the judgment is set aside, you will need to file a Defence [Form 9A].
```

At least 14 days before the conference, you serve each other party and file any document for trial not attached to your defence. By then, you also serve and file a List of Proposed Witnesses [Form 13A], naming others who know about the dispute. The court may award costs against a person who attends without having filed this material. If you cannot attend on the date set, you can ask the court to adjourn it, and the court office can help. - **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I filed my defence — what happens next?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/980258

```
If you want to make a defendant's claim (Form 10A), it can be issued without the court's leave. You have 20 days after the day the defence is filed. After that, it may be issued only with leave of the court, and only before trial or default judgment.

The court holds the settlement conference within 90 days after the day the first defence was filed. This is the court's timetable, not a step you take. The clerk fixes the time, date and place and serves a notice of settlement conference on the parties. No conference is held if the defence admits all of the claim and proposes terms of payment.
```

Each party takes part in the conference, unless the court orders otherwise. A party with notice who does not come may face costs or other penalties, and the court may order another conference. If you miss the first conference and a second one you had notice of, the court may strike out your defence or make another just order. At the end, the court writes a memo of the issues left and matters agreed for the trial judge, who will be a different judge. The clerk's notice says a party must ask for a trial date and pay the fee if the case is not resolved within 30 days after the conference.
```

### `answer:defendant:considering-defendants-claim:whats-happening`

- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "They owe me money too — can I sue them back in the same case?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/980258

```
You may make a claim against the plaintiff, called a defendant's claim, or against someone else if it arises from the same events or relates to the plaintiff's claim. A defendant's claim is tried at the same trial as the main case, unless the court orders otherwise. The court may order a separate trial or a separate action if your claim may unduly complicate or delay the trial, or cause undue prejudice to a party. If the case is about a debt, a defendant may also claim in the defence to set off a debt the plaintiff owes them. To dispute the plaintiff's claim, you must still serve and file a Defence (Form 9A) within 20 days of being served with it.
```

At least 30 days before trial, you can serve documents, statements, and audio or visual records on all parties who got the notice of trial. They are then received in evidence, unless the trial judge orders otherwise, but a statement only counts for what its writer could say in court. With each one, give the writer's name, phone number and address for service, and a summary of an expert's qualifications. You can summon a witness in Ontario, such as the writer of a statement served on you, with a Summons to Witness (Form 18A). If you summon such a writer, you must serve a copy of the summons on every other party at the same time.
```

- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I lost — what happens now, and what if I cannot pay?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/980258

```
If you must pay money, you are the debtor, and the creditor can enforce right away. This can be by garnishment, or a writ of seizure and sale of your goods or land. Serving and filing a notice of appeal puts the money parts on hold until the appeal ends, unless an appeal judge lifts it. If you do not pay, the creditor can have a Notice of Examination (Form 20H) issued to you. If you are served and do not go, the court may order you to a contempt hearing.
```

If you cannot pay in full, you can contact the creditor to set up payments. On a motion (Form 15A), the court may pause enforcement on just terms, or change when and how much you pay if things change. With more than one such judgment, you can ask the court where you live for a consolidation order. When it is all paid, you can both sign and file a Request for Clerk's Order on Consent (Form 11.2A). If the creditor will not sign, you can bring a motion.

If you want to ask for a new trial, bring a motion for a new trial. You have 30 days after the day the final order was made. The court can grant one only for a purely arithmetical error in the amount of damages, or for relevant evidence that was not available at the trial and could not reasonably have been expected to be.

If you want to appeal to the Divisional Court, serve a notice of appeal (Form 61A.3) with a certificate respecting evidence (Form 61C). You have 30 days after the day the order was made. File the notice, with proof of service, within 10 days after serving it, and file the certificate with it. You can appeal only a final order to pay more than $5,000, not counting costs, or to return personal property worth more than $5,000.
```

### `answer:both:missed-trial:whats-happening`

- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I missed my trial date — is my case over?"

```
If all the parties are absent, the trial judge may strike the action off the trial list. If one party is absent, the judge may go ahead without them, or make another order that is just. The judge may strike out an absent defendant's defence and any claim of theirs, and must rule on any place of trial issue it raises. The judge may dismiss an absent plaintiff's action and let the defendant prove any claim of their own. In those two cases, the party with the claim must prove its amount, but not that the absent party is liable.

Ask the court, by making a motion, to set aside or change a judgment made when you did not attend. You have 30 days after the day you became aware of the judgment. A party may instead make a motion to extend the 30 days, and the court may extend them if satisfied that special circumstances justify it.
```

A case must be started where the problem arose or where a defendant lives or does business, or at the court nearest that home or business. The court hears only claims for money, not counting interest and costs, or to get back personal property, up to a set amount. The limit is $50,000, and a larger claim goes to the Superior Court of Justice, unless the claimant gives up the amount over $50,000. A claim may not be split into two or more actions to bring it within the court's limit. A claim within that limit cannot be started in the Superior Court of Justice without that court's leave.

### `answer:before-filing:notice-vehicle-injury:whats-happening`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / before-filing:notice-vehicle-injury
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I was hurt by a car, truck or bus — is there something I have to do before I sue?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90i08

```
This is about an injury or a death that came, directly or indirectly, from the use or operation of an automobile. The law lists six things to be done before this kind of lawsuit is started. You must always do three of them. You only have to do the other three if the person you plan to sue asks. The first two are to apply for statutory accident benefits and to serve a written notice that you plan to sue. The others are below. If you do not do one or more of these six things, you can still sue. But the court must take that into account when it decides costs.
```

### `answer:before-filing:notice-vehicle-injury:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / before-filing:notice-vehicle-injury
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I was hurt by a car, truck or bus — is there something I have to do before I sue?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90i08

```
Apply for statutory accident benefits. Also serve a written notice on the person you plan to sue, saying that you plan to sue them. You must serve this notice within 120 days after the incident. The court where the lawsuit could be started can allow more time. You ask by motion, before or after the 120 days run out. There are rules for how the notice must be served, in section 33 of the Insurance Act. The notice must tell that person that, if they are insured, they must give their insurer a copy within seven days of getting it. You must also give the person you plan to sue the information the regulations require, by the deadline the regulations set. If the person you plan to sue asks within 90 days after getting your notice, you must go to examinations. That person picks the examiners, who are regulated health professionals, and pays for the examinations. You must answer the examiner's questions that relate to the examination. An examination can't be repeated without need, and it can't use a procedure that is unreasonable or dangerous. If the examiner gives a report to the person you plan to sue, that person must make sure you get a copy within 60 days after they get the report. If the person you plan to sue asks, you must give them a statutory declaration that describes what happened and your claim. If that person asks, you must also give them proof of who you are.
```

### `answer:before-filing:notice-vehicle-injury:your-deadline`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / before-filing:notice-vehicle-injury
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I was hurt by a car, truck or bus — is there something I have to do before I sue?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90i08

```
Serve written notice of your intention to sue on the person you will sue. You have 120 days after the incident. The court where the lawsuit could be started may allow a longer time, on a motion made before or after the 120 days run out.

The general deadline to start a court case. You have 2 years after the day the claim was discovered. The last day is the anniversary of that day, 2 years later. If that day was February 29, the anniversary is February 28, except in a leap year. This applies unless the Limitations Act, 2002 provides otherwise. For example, a claim based on a sexual assault has no limitation period. The other side may admit in writing, and sign, that they owe a fixed sum of money. The same goes for an admission that they must return personal property. It also goes for enforcing a charge on personal property, or relief from that. Then the act or omission is treated as happening on the day of that admission. This counts only if it was made before the time ran out. It must be made to you, your agent, or an official receiver or trustee under the Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act (Canada). For a fixed sum of money, a part payment by the other side or their agent works the same way as a written, signed admission.

A deadline in an Ontario statute is counted under the Legislation Act, 2006, unless the statute shows otherwise. When a period is described as starting after a day, that day is not counted (s. 89 (5)). If the last day is a Sunday or a holiday, the deadline moves to the next day that is not a holiday (s. 89 (1)). Saturday is not a holiday under that Act, so a Saturday does not by itself move the deadline. Some deadlines are for doing something at a place, such as filing at an office. If that place is not open during its regular hours on the last day, the deadline moves to the next day it is open during its regular hours (s. 89 (2)).
```

### `answer:before-filing:notice-vehicle-injury:what-happens-after`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / before-filing:notice-vehicle-injury
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I was hurt by a car, truck or bus — is there something I have to do before I sue?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90i08

```
You can still start the lawsuit without doing these steps. But the court must take that into account when it decides costs. In every lawsuit like this, no prejudgment interest under section 128 of the Courts of Justice Act is awarded for the time before you served your notice. Unless the Limitations Act, 2002 says otherwise, you can't start a lawsuit about the claim more than two years after the day it was discovered. A claim is discovered on the earlier of two days. One is the day you first knew four things. First, that the injury, loss or damage happened. Second, that something someone did, or failed to do, caused it or helped cause it. Third, that it was the act or omission of the person you are suing. Fourth, that a court case is a fitting way to try to remedy it, given the kind of injury, loss or damage. The other is the first day a reasonable person with your abilities and in your circumstances ought to have known those things. You are presumed to have known them on the day of the act or omission, unless it is proved otherwise.
```

### `answer:civil:defendant:served-defence-period-running:whats-happening`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:defendant:served-defence-period-running
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I was served with a statement of claim — what do I have to do, and by when?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
You have been served with a statement of claim, so you are a defendant in this action. If you want to defend, the rules set a time for you to deliver a statement of defence (Form 18A). Deliver means serve and file with proof of service. If you are a corporation, you must have a lawyer, unless the court gives leave. If you are under disability, such as a minor, or you act in a representative capacity, you must also have a lawyer.
```

### `answer:civil:defendant:served-defence-period-running:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:defendant:served-defence-period-running
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I was served with a statement of claim — what do I have to do, and by when?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
Your defence must briefly state the key facts you rely on, but not the evidence that proves them. You must admit every fact in the claim that you do not dispute. Any fact you do not deny is treated as admitted, unless you say you have no knowledge of it. In a claim for damages, the amount is treated as in dispute unless you admit it. If your version of the facts is different, denying theirs is not enough, and you must set out your own version. You must also plead anything you rely on to defeat the claim that might surprise the plaintiff, or raise a new issue, if you left it out. You may first deliver a notice of intent to defend (Form 18B) within the time for your defence. If you do, you get 10 more days to deliver the defence. If you have a claim against the plaintiff, you may make a counterclaim. A counterclaim (Form 27A or 27B) must be in the same document as your defence, titled a statement of defence and counterclaim.
```

### `answer:civil:defendant:served-defence-period-running:your-deadline`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:defendant:served-defence-period-running
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I was served with a statement of claim — what do I have to do, and by when?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
Deliver a statement of defence (Form 18A). You have 20 days after the day you were served with the statement of claim. This is the time if you were served in Ontario. If you were served elsewhere in Canada or in the United States, it is 40 days. If you were served anywhere else, it is 60 days. If you deliver a notice of intent to defend (Form 18B) in that time, you get 10 more days for the defence. Deliver means serve it on the other parties and file it with proof of service. If the claim was left at a home with an adult and a copy mailed, service takes effect on the fifth day after mailing. If it was mailed with an acknowledgment of receipt card, service takes effect on the day the sender gets the card back. If a corporation was served by mail to its last recorded address, service takes effect on the fifth day after mailing. A counterclaim against the plaintiff goes in the same document as your defence, by the same time. Your counterclaim may also name someone who is not yet a party. If so, issue it within the same time as your defence, or before you are noted in default, or later with the court's leave. Then serve and file it, with proof of service, within 30 days after it is issued. A crossclaim against a co-defendant goes with your defence, by the same time. It can also go in at any time before you are noted in default, or later with leave. The court must give that leave unless it would prejudice the plaintiff. The time can be extended by filing a consent, or by the court. You can still deliver a defence at any time before you are noted in default. But once the time is up, the plaintiff can have you noted in default without telling you. After that, you get no notice of further steps. If the claim is under the simplified procedure and you say it does not fit Rule 76, say so in your defence. An action under the simplified procedure is not tried with a jury, so no jury notice can be delivered in it, unless the claim arises from slander, libel, malicious arrest, malicious prosecution or false imprisonment. In any other action, a jury notice must be delivered before pleadings close.

You can bring in someone who is not yet a party if they are or may be liable to you for all or part of the plaintiff's claim. You can also do it for a related claim, or if they should be bound by the result. To do this, issue a third party claim (Form 29A). You have 10 days after the day you delivered your statement of defence. You can also issue it at any time before you are noted in default. Or you can issue it within 10 days after the plaintiff delivers a reply to your defence. After that, you can issue it at any time with the plaintiff's consent or the court's leave. The court must give leave unless it would prejudice the plaintiff. You must serve it within 30 days after it is issued. The two-year limitation period still applies to your claim against the third party. For a claim for contribution and indemnity, the Limitations Act, 2002 treats the day you were served with the plaintiff's claim as the day of the act or omission.

Times set by the Rules of Civil Procedure are counted under those rules. The first day is not counted. If a time counted forward ends on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, it ends on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (c)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the safe course is to act by the last day before it that is not a holiday. For a period of seven days or less, holidays are not counted at all (r. 3.01 (1) (b)). Except for the document that starts a case, a document served after 4 p.m. or on a holiday counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (d)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
```

### `answer:civil:defendant:served-defence-period-running:what-happens-after`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:defendant:served-defence-period-running
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I was served with a statement of claim — what do I have to do, and by when?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
The plaintiff may then deliver a reply within 10 days after your defence is served, or within 20 days if you made a counterclaim. If your defence is not delivered in time, the plaintiff may ask the registrar to note you in default. If you are noted in default, you are taken to admit every fact stated in the claim. Until then, you may still deliver a defence at any time.
```

### `answer:civil:plaintiff:claim-drafted-not-issued:whats-happening`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:plaintiff:claim-drafted-not-issued
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "How do I start my action in the Superior Court?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
Your action does not start until the document that starts it is issued. Under the Limitations Act, 2002, most cases cannot start more than 15 years after the act or omission they are based on. This limit does not cover claims with no limitation period, such as a case to enforce a court order or one based on a sexual assault. There is also none for other sexual misconduct if, at the time, the person was a minor. The same applies if the other person had charge of them or was in a position of trust or authority over them. It also applies if the person depended on the other person in some way. There is no time limit for a claim based on an assault if, at the time, the person was a minor. The same applies if the two had an intimate relationship, or the person depended on the other person in some way. That 15-year period does not run during some times. One is when the person with the claim cannot sue because of their condition and has no litigation guardian. A time limit in another Act has no effect on a claim covered by the Limitations Act, 2002, with two exceptions. One is a time limit listed in the Schedule to that Act. The other is one that existed on January 1, 2004 and refers to a listed provision. Being listed does not by itself mean that the time limit applies to your claim. Section 6 of the Libel and Slander Act is listed. For libel in a newspaper or broadcast, section 5 (1) of that Act first requires written notice to the defendant of what you complain of. You must give it within six weeks after you learn of the libel. It must be served like a statement of claim, or given to a grown-up person at the defendant's chief office. Section 6 says the case itself must start within three months after the person defamed learns of the libel. Sections 5 (1) and 6 apply only to newspapers printed and published in Ontario and to broadcasts from a station in Ontario.
```

### `answer:civil:plaintiff:claim-drafted-not-issued:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:plaintiff:claim-drafted-not-issued
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "How do I start my action in the Superior Court?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
The usual document to start an action is a statement of claim (Form 14A, or Form 14B for a mortgage action). If there is not enough time to write one, you may start with a notice of action (Form 14C) that says in short what the claim is about. You must then file a statement of claim (Form 14D) within 30 days after the notice of action is issued. After those 30 days, a statement of claim can be filed only with the defendant's written consent, or the court's leave obtained on notice to the defendant. File an Information for court use (Form 14F) with a Form 14A, 14B or 14C, unless you file online through one of the court portals the rule names. Rule 76 sets out a simplified procedure. It is not used for a class proceeding, a Construction Act action other than a trust claim, or an action with a jury notice. Otherwise, you must use it if your claim is only for money, real property or personal property. The money claimed plus the fair market value of the property on the day you start must also be $200,000 or less, not counting interest and costs. If so, your claim must say that the action is brought under Rule 76. If there are two or more plaintiffs, each plaintiff's claim is checked on its own. If you sue more than one defendant, your claim against each one is checked on its own. The Small Claims Court can hear a claim for money up to a set amount, not counting interest and costs, or to recover personal property worth up to that amount. That amount is $50,000. If your claim is within that limit, it can only be started in the Superior Court with that court's leave. A claim above it needs no such leave. You may ask for leave by motion without notice, unless the court orders otherwise. The court may grant it only if it is in the interest of justice.
```

### `answer:civil:before-filing:notice-required-before-suing:whats-happening`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:before-filing:notice-required-before-suing
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "Do I have to send a notice before I sue the government, the city, a property owner or a newspaper?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/19c07

```
You cannot sue the Ontario Crown for damages unless you serve a notice of the claim on the Crown at least 60 days before you start. A claim is different if it is about the Crown's duty as owner, occupier, possessor or controller of property. Its notice must be served no later than 10 days after the event. If a municipality did not keep a road or bridge in repair, you must give its clerk written notice within 10 days after the injury. A sidewalk can be part of a municipal road. If snow or ice on such a sidewalk hurt you, the same 10-day notice to the clerk applies. There, the municipality is liable only for gross negligence. If snow or ice on someone's premises hurt you, you must give written notice to the occupier or their snow contractor. You have 60 days after the injury. For a libel in a newspaper or broadcast from Ontario, you must give the defendant written notice. You have six weeks after you learn of the libel.
```

### `answer:civil:before-filing:notice-required-before-suing:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:before-filing:notice-required-before-suing
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "Do I have to send a notice before I sue the government, the city, a property owner or a newspaper?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/19c07

```
Leave the notice to the Crown with an employee at the Crown Law Office (Civil Law) of the Ministry of the Attorney General. The notice to a municipality must give the date, time and place. Serve it on the clerk or send it by registered mail. If two or more municipalities share the duty to repair the road or bridge, give notice to the clerk of each. In Toronto, the City of Toronto Act, 2006 sets the same 10-day notice, given to the city clerk. For snow or ice, the notice must also give the date, time and place. It must be personally served on, or sent by registered mail to, the occupier or the contractor. For a libel, the notice must say what you complain of. Serve it like a statement of claim, or give it to a grown-up person at the defendant's chief office. You must then start the libel action within three months after you learned of the libel. This shorter time counts because the Schedule to the Limitations Act, 2002 lists section 6 of the Libel and Slander Act.
```

### `answer:civil:before-filing:notice-required-before-suing:your-deadline`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:before-filing:notice-required-before-suing
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "Do I have to send a notice before I sue the government, the city, a property owner or a newspaper?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/19c07

```
If you are claiming damages from the Ontario Crown, serve a notice of claim on the Crown. Do this at least 60 days before the day you start the action. A claim against the Crown or a Crown officer or employee for misfeasance in public office or bad faith needs the court's leave. Until leave is given, it is stayed. Earlier is fine. Serve the notice as section 15 of the Act requires. That means leaving a copy with an employee at the Crown Law Office (Civil Law) of the Ministry of the Attorney General. The notice must give enough detail to identify the event the claim came from. The Attorney General may ask for more details to look into the claim. The 60 days count back from the day the action starts. So serving later, even because of a Sunday or holiday, leaves fewer than 60 days. An action started without the notice has no effect (it is a nullity). A claim about a duty that comes with owning, occupying, possessing or controlling property is different. Its notice must be served no later than 10 days after the event. The notice requirement does not apply to a counterclaim, crossclaim or set-off. Sometimes the notice is served before the limitation period ends, but the 60 days end after it. Then the limitation period is extended to the end of the seventh day after the 60 days.

If a municipality did not keep a highway (road) or bridge in repair and you claim damages, give written notice of the claim to the municipal clerk. You have 10 days after the day of the injury. This covers all damages a person suffers because of the failure to repair. The same section covers injury from snow or ice on a municipal sidewalk. There, the municipality is liable only for gross negligence. If you were hurt on a municipal sidewalk, this 10-day notice to the clerk may be the one that applies, not the 60-day notice to an occupier. The notice must give the date, time and place. Serve it on the clerk, or send it by registered mail. If two or more municipalities share the duty to repair the road or bridge, notify the clerk of each. In Toronto, the City of Toronto Act, 2006 sets the same 10 days, with notice to the city clerk. Missing the notice is not a bar if the injured person died from the injury. It is also not a bar if a judge finds a reasonable excuse and no prejudice to the municipality.

If the City of Toronto did not keep a highway (road) or bridge in repair and you claim damages, give written notice of the claim to the city clerk. You have 10 days after the day of the injury. The notice must give the date, time and place of the injury. Serve it on the city clerk, or send it by registered mail. For injury from snow or ice on a sidewalk, the City is liable only for gross negligence. Missing the notice is not a bar if the injured person died from the injury. It is also not a bar if a judge finds a reasonable excuse and no prejudice to the City.

If you were hurt by snow or ice on someone's premises, give written notice of the claim to an occupier or to their snow-removal contractor. You have 60 days after the day of the injury. The notice must give the date, time and place. Serve it in person or send it by registered mail. Missing the notice is not a bar if the injured person died from the injury. It is also not a bar if a judge finds a reasonable excuse and no prejudice to the defendant.

If you are suing over a libel in an Ontario newspaper or broadcast, give the defendant written notice that specifies the matter you complain of. You have 42 days after the day the libel came to your knowledge. The Act says six weeks, which is 42 days. Serve the notice the same way as a statement of claim, or give it to an adult at the defendant's chief office. This applies only to newspapers printed and published in Ontario, and to broadcasts from a station in Ontario. A newspaper cannot rely on it unless it prints its owner's and publisher's names and its address of publication. These must appear at the head of the editorials or on the front page. For a broadcast, you may ask the station by registered letter for the owner's or operator's name and address. If the station does not give them within ten days after it gets your letter, this does not apply against that owner or operator.

If you are suing over a libel in an Ontario newspaper or broadcast, start the action. You have 3 months after the day the libel came to your knowledge. This shorter time replaces the general two years, because the Limitations Act lists it in its schedule. It applies only to newspapers printed and published in Ontario, and to broadcasts from a station in Ontario. A newspaper cannot rely on it unless it prints its owner's and publisher's names and its address of publication. These must appear at the head of the editorials or on the front page. For a broadcast, you may ask the station by registered letter for the owner's or operator's name and address. If the station does not give them within ten days after it gets your letter, this does not apply against that owner or operator.

The general deadline to start a court case. You have 2 years after the day the claim was discovered. The last day is the anniversary of that day, 2 years later. If that day was February 29, the anniversary is February 28, except in a leap year. This applies unless the Limitations Act, 2002 says otherwise. For example, a claim based on a sexual assault has no time limit. A claim is discovered on the earlier of two days. The first is the day you knew four things: you had a loss, an act or omission caused it, whose act or omission it was, and that a court case was a proper way to fix it. The second is the day a reasonable person in your place ought to have known those things. You are presumed to have known them on the day of the act or omission, unless you prove otherwise. Separately, no case can start more than 15 years after the act or omission, except in some cases the Act lists. Some other Acts, listed in a schedule to the Limitations Act, set shorter times. For example, a case for libel in an Ontario newspaper or broadcast must start within three months after you learned of the libel. The other side may admit in writing, and sign, that they owe a fixed sum of money. The same goes for an admission that they must return personal property. It also goes for enforcing a charge on personal property, or relief from that. Then the act or omission is treated as happening on the day of that admission. This counts only if it was made before the time ran out. It must be made to you, your agent, or an official receiver or trustee under the Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act (Canada). For a fixed sum of money, a part payment by the other side or their agent works the same way as a written, signed admission.

A deadline in an Ontario statute is counted under the Legislation Act, 2006, unless the statute shows otherwise. When a period is described as starting after a day, that day is not counted (s. 89 (5)). If the last day is a Sunday or a holiday, the deadline moves to the next day that is not a holiday (s. 89 (1)). Saturday is not a holiday under that Act, so a Saturday does not by itself move the deadline. Some deadlines are for doing something at a place, such as filing at an office. If that place is not open during its regular hours on the last day, the deadline moves to the next day it is open during its regular hours (s. 89 (2)).
```

### `answer:civil:before-filing:notice-required-before-suing:what-happens-after`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:before-filing:notice-required-before-suing
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "Do I have to send a notice before I sue the government, the city, a property owner or a newspaper?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/19c07

```
An action against the Crown started without the notice is a nullity for that claim. Missing the notice to a municipality is not a bar if the injured person died from the injury. It is also not a bar if a judge finds a reasonable excuse and no prejudice to the municipality in its defence. For snow or ice on someone's premises, failure to give notice is not a bar if the injured person died from the injury. It is also not a bar if a judge finds a reasonable excuse and no prejudice to the defendant in its defence. Apart from these notices, a case generally cannot be started more than two years after the day the claim was discovered. Also, a case can't start more than 15 years after the act or omission it is based on, with some exceptions. For example, there is no time limit for a claim based on a sexual assault. There is also none for other sexual misconduct if, at the time, the person was a minor. The same applies if the other person had charge of them or was in a position of trust or authority over them. It also applies if the person depended on the other person in some way. There is no time limit for a claim based on an assault if, at the time, the person was a minor. The same applies if the two had an intimate relationship, or the person depended on the other person in some way.
```

### `answer:civil:plaintiff:served-awaiting-defence:whats-happening`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:plaintiff:served-awaiting-defence
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I served the defendant — how long do they have to respond?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
The defendant now has a set time to deliver a statement of defence (Form 18A). Deliver means serve and file with proof of service. The time is 20 days after service if the defendant was served in Ontario. It is 40 days if they were served elsewhere in Canada or in the United States, and 60 days if they were served anywhere else. A defendant who intends to defend may first deliver a notice of intent to defend (Form 18B) in that time, and then gets 10 more days for the statement of defence.
```

### `answer:civil:plaintiff:served-awaiting-defence:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:plaintiff:served-awaiting-defence
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I served the defendant — how long do they have to respond?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
Count the days from the day service took effect, leaving out that first day. Suppose personal service was tried at the defendant's home and failed. The claim may then have been left there in a sealed envelope with an adult member of the household, with another copy mailed there the same day or the next day. Service done that way took effect on the fifth day after mailing. If it was mailed with an acknowledgment of receipt card (Form 16A), service took effect on the day the card came back to the sender. Service may be proved by an affidavit of service (Form 16B) from the person who served the claim. The time for the statement of defence may be extended by filing a consent. The court may also extend it by order.
```

### `answer:civil:plaintiff:served-awaiting-defence:your-deadline`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:plaintiff:served-awaiting-defence
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I served the defendant — how long do they have to respond?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
The defendant's time to deliver a statement of defence. They have 20 days after the day the defendant was served with the statement of claim. This is the time if the defendant was served in Ontario. If they were served elsewhere in Canada or in the United States, it is 40 days. If they were served anywhere else, it is 60 days. A defendant who delivers a notice of intent to defend in that time gets 10 more days. If the claim was left at a home with an adult and a copy mailed, service takes effect on the fifth day after mailing. If it was mailed with an acknowledgment of receipt card, service takes effect on the day the sender gets the card back. If a corporation was served by mail to its last recorded address, service takes effect on the fifth day after mailing. The time can be extended by filing a consent, or by the court.

Set the action down for trial, or the registrar will dismiss it for delay. You have 5 years after the day the action was started. The last day is the anniversary of that day, 5 years later. If that day was February 29, the anniversary is February 28, except in a leap year. This does not apply if the action has already ended some other way. It does not apply if a party files a timetable signed by all parties, and a draft order, at least 30 days before the time ends. The timetable must give a date, no more than two years after the time ends, by which the action will be set down or restored. If the parties do not agree on a timetable, any party can ask for a status hearing before the time ends. It does not apply if you are under a disability at that time. It does not apply to Commercial List actions or class actions. The court can order otherwise. A dismissal can be set aside on a motion under rule 37.14.

Times set by the Rules of Civil Procedure are counted under those rules. The first day is not counted. If a time counted forward ends on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, it ends on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (c)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the safe course is to act by the last day before it that is not a holiday. For a period of seven days or less, holidays are not counted at all (r. 3.01 (1) (b)). Except for the document that starts a case, a document served after 4 p.m. or on a holiday counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (d)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
```

### `answer:civil:plaintiff:served-awaiting-defence:what-happens-after`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:plaintiff:served-awaiting-defence
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I served the defendant — how long do they have to respond?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
If a statement of defence is delivered, any reply must be delivered within ten days after it is served. If the defendant also counterclaims against you, you must deliver a defence to counterclaim (Form 27C) within twenty days after the statement of defence and counterclaim is served. Any reply then goes in that same document, within the same twenty days. If the time runs out and no statement of defence has been delivered, you may file proof of service of the statement of claim and require the registrar to note the defendant in default. Until then, the defendant may still deliver a statement of defence. A party under disability may be noted in default only with a judge's leave.
```

### `answer:civil:both:motion-scheduled:whats-happening`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:both:motion-scheduled
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "There is a motion in my case — what do I have to file, and when?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
A motion is made by a notice of motion (Form 37A), unless the rules or the situation make one unnecessary. The notice must state the exact order asked for, the grounds, and the documents that will be used as evidence. When a motion is made on notice, the notice of motion must be served at least seven days before the hearing. The notice of motion must also be filed with proof of service at least seven days before the hearing, in the court office where the motion will be heard. The moving party may propose in the notice that the motion be heard in writing. If so, the motion must be made on at least 14 days notice.
```
