### `answer:civil:both:motion-scheduled:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:both:motion-scheduled
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "There is a motion in my case — what do I have to file, and when?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
If you are bringing the motion, you must serve a motion record on every other party, unless the court orders otherwise. File it with proof of service at least seven days before the hearing. The motion record has a table of contents, the notice of motion, and all affidavits and other material served for the motion. It also has a list of all relevant transcripts of evidence, and any other material in the court file needed for the hearing. If you are bringing a motion on notice, you must also confer or try to confer with the other party. Then, no later than 2 p.m. five days before the hearing date, give the registrar a confirmation of motion (Form 37B). Email it to the court office or leave it there, and email a copy to the other party. If no confirmation is given, the motion is not heard and is treated as abandoned, unless the court orders otherwise. If you propose a hearing in writing, serve a motion record, a draft order and a factum for a motion in writing with the notice of motion. File them right away, with proof of service. In a simplified procedure action, you must serve a motion form (Form 76B) as rule 37.07 requires. For a motion on notice, that means at least seven days before the hearing. You must also submit the form to the court before the motion is brought and heard. There, the motion may be made with or without supporting material or a motion record, depending on what the situation needs. If you are responding and think the motion record is incomplete, you may serve and file your own responding party's motion record, with proof of service. Do this at least four days before the hearing. It holds a table of contents and any material you will use that is not in the moving party's record. If you are responding to a motion proposed to be heard in writing, you must serve and file a response, with proof of service. Do this within 10 days after you are served with the moving party's material. Your response can be a consent to the motion, or a notice that you do not oppose it. It can be your motion record, a notice that you agree to a hearing in writing, and a factum for a motion in writing. Or it can be a notice that you intend to make oral argument, with any material you will rely on. Either party may serve a factum on every other party. If you do, you must also file it with proof of service. Do this at least seven days before the hearing if you brought the motion. If you are responding, do it at least four days before the hearing.
```

### `answer:civil:both:motion-scheduled:your-deadline`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:both:motion-scheduled
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "There is a motion in my case — what do I have to file, and when?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
If you are bringing the motion, serve the notice of motion and motion record on the other parties. File them with proof of service. Do this at least 7 days before the date the motion will be heard. This is the latest it can be done; earlier is fine. Because the period is seven days or less, Saturdays, Sundays and holidays are not counted. Your factum, if you have one, is due by the same day. On a motion for summary judgment, a factum is required. The court can order otherwise for the motion record. A document served after 4 p.m., or on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday. On a motion about refusals or undertakings, your refusals and undertakings chart (Form 37C) is due by the same day. You may propose that the motion be heard in writing, without the parties attending. If so, give at least 14 days notice. Serve your motion record, a draft order and a factum for a motion in writing with the notice of motion, and file them right away. In a simplified procedure action, you serve a motion form (Form 76B). The motion may be made with or without supporting material or a motion record.

If you are bringing the motion, talk or try to talk with the other party. Then give the registrar a confirmation of motion (Form 37B), and email a copy to the other party, by 2 p.m. on the day. Do this at least 5 days before the date the motion will be heard. Because the period is seven days or less, Saturdays, Sundays and holidays are not counted. If no confirmation is given, the motion is not heard. It is treated as abandoned, unless the court orders otherwise.

If you are responding to the motion, serve your factum on the other parties and file it with proof of service. Do this at least 4 days before the date the motion will be heard. A factum is optional on most motions, but required on a motion for summary judgment. This is the latest it can be done; earlier is fine. Because the period is seven days or less, Saturdays, Sundays and holidays are not counted. On a motion about refusals or undertakings, your completed chart is due by the same day. A document served after 4 p.m., or on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday.

If you are responding and think the motion record is incomplete, serve a responding party's motion record on the other parties. File it with proof of service. Do this at least 4 days before the date the motion will be heard. This is the latest it can be done; earlier is fine. Because the period is seven days or less, Saturdays, Sundays and holidays are not counted.

If you are responding and the moving party did not email you their confirmation of motion, you may give the registrar your own (Form 37B). Email a copy to the moving party, by 10 a.m. on the day. Do this at least 4 days before the date the motion will be heard. Because the period is seven days or less, Saturdays, Sundays and holidays are not counted.

If the moving party asked for the motion to be heard in writing, serve and file your response, with proof of service. It is one of these: a consent; a notice that you do not oppose; your motion record, a notice that you agree to a hearing in writing, and a factum for a motion in writing; or a notice that you want to make oral argument, with your material. You have 10 days after the day you were served with the moving party's material. This applies when the moving party proposed in the notice of motion that the motion be heard in writing.

If you did not appear on the motion through accident, mistake or insufficient notice, serve a notice of motion to set aside or vary the order. The rule sets no fixed number of days. Serve the notice of motion forthwith (right away) after the order comes to your attention. It must name the first available hearing date at least three days after you serve it.

Times set by the Rules of Civil Procedure are counted under those rules. The first day is not counted. If a time counted forward ends on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, it ends on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (c)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the safe course is to act by the last day before it that is not a holiday. For a period of seven days or less, holidays are not counted at all (r. 3.01 (1) (b)). Except for the document that starts a case, a document served after 4 p.m. or on a holiday counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (d)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
```

```
At the hearing, the judge or officer may grant the order asked for, or dismiss or adjourn the motion, in whole or in part. If you did not appear on the motion through accident, mistake or insufficient notice, you may move to set aside or vary the order. Serve that notice of motion right away after the order comes to your attention. It must name the first available hearing date that is at least three days after you serve it.
```

### `answer:family:respondent:served-time-to-answer-running:whats-happening`

```
An application, or a claim in another party's answer, has been made against you in a family case. You must serve an answer on every other party and file it. When the application was filed, the clerk had to set a court date, except in some cases. In the Ontario Court of Justice, and in a fast track case in the Family Court, the clerk acts on or before the first court date. If no answer to the application has been filed, the clerk sends the case to a judge to decide on affidavit evidence, or sets a case conference if the applicant asks.
```

### `answer:family:respondent:served-time-to-answer-running:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:respondent:served-time-to-answer-running
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I was served with family court papers — what do I have to do, and by when?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
The answer is Form 10. The other forms rule 10 (1) lists are for child protection cases and other cases under the Child, Youth and Family Services Act, 2017. Your answer may include a claim against the applicant, or against another person, who then also becomes a respondent. The application may claim support, property, or exclusive possession of the matrimonial home and its contents. If it does, you must serve and file a financial statement (Form 13 or 13.1) within the time for your answer, even if you do not serve an answer. If your own answer makes one of those claims, you must serve and file a financial statement with your answer. You do not need one for your claim if your only support claim is for child support in the table amount. That exception does not apply if your answer also has a property claim or a claim for the matrimonial home. You also do not need one if your only claim is about a family arbitration, unless the court orders otherwise. Use Form 13 for a support claim with no property claim and no claim for the matrimonial home. Use Form 13.1 if there is a property claim or a claim for the matrimonial home, with or without a support claim. If your answer claims decision-making responsibility, parenting time or contact with a child, it must come with the documents rule 35.1 lists. Some cases need the mandatory information program. In those cases, you may not take any other step until your certificate of attendance is filed. You may still serve and file an answer, and make an appointment for a case conference.
```

### `answer:family:respondent:served-time-to-answer-running:your-deadline`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:respondent:served-time-to-answer-running
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I was served with family court papers — what do I have to do, and by when?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
Serve an answer on every other party and file it. You have 30 days after the day of being served with the application. If you were served outside Canada and the United States, you have 60 days. If another party’s answer added you as a respondent, you have 14 days. That becomes 30 days if you were served outside Canada and the United States. Other times apply to an application to dispense with a parent’s consent before adoption placement. Service rules decide when your time starts. Papers left at your home with an adult, with a copy mailed, count as served on the fifth day after mailing. Papers left with you after 4 p.m. count as served the next day. If that day is one when court offices are closed, service counts on the next open day. For mail with an acknowledgment card, the rules set no separate start day. The general rule for mail is the fifth day after mailing. That service counts only once the card you signed is filed. If the application claims support, property or the matrimonial home against you, your financial statement is due in the same time. For a support claim with no property claim, serve the income papers in r. 13 (3.1) with it. If your answer claims decision-making responsibility, parenting time or contact, serve and file an affidavit in Form 35.1 with it, and the other papers rule 35.1 requires. If the application made a claim about parenting, property or support, the rules say an automatic order is served together with the application, so look for it in what you were served. Only if no automatic order has been issued in the case does the clerk issue one for a claim in your answer. Then serve it on every other party promptly, and no later than 7 days after it is issued. If you miss the time, then unless the court orders otherwise, you lose the right to notice of further steps. Any order must still be served on you. You cannot take part in the case. The court may decide the case without you. A date may be set for an uncontested trial. The court office will refuse a late answer. It will take one only if the other parties agree in writing or the court gives more time. The parties can agree in writing to change the time. The court can also give more time.

If the application or your answer has a property claim, serve the other party with the property papers the rule lists. You have 30 days after the day your financial statement was due, which is the last day for your answer. For a claim under Part I of the Family Law Act, the rule lists the papers. One example is the statement closest to the valuation date for each bank or other account. For any other property claim, serve the information needed to support the claim. If there is also a support claim, serve the income papers in r. 13 (3.1) with it. Serve a certificate of financial disclosure (Form 13A) with the papers. The court can order otherwise. If the property claim is your own claim in your answer, your financial statement is due with the answer. So if you serve your answer early, count the 30 days from that day.

Attend the mandatory information program. You have 45 days after the day the case was started. This applies only to some cases. They are cases about parenting, support, net family property, the matrimonial home or a restraining order. It also covers a motion to change that is not only about child or spousal support. It does not apply to a case on consent. It does not apply where the only claims are for a divorce, costs, or putting an agreement or order into an order. It does not apply where the only claims are about a family arbitration, unless the court orders otherwise. It does not apply in an international child abduction case. It does not apply to the Director of the Family Responsibility Office, or to an agency under s. 33 (3) of the Family Law Act. It does not apply to a person who has already attended. File your certificate of attendance as soon as you can. File it no later than 2 p.m. on the second day before the case conference. The court can excuse a party because of urgency or hardship, or for another reason in the interest of justice. The applicant books your appointment and serves notice of it with the application. The 45 days run from the day the application was filed, not the day you were served. Until your certificate is filed, you cannot take other steps. You can still serve and file an answer. You can also book a case conference.

Times set by the Family Law Rules are counted under those rules. The first day is the day after the event (r. 3 (1)). If the last day of a period falls on a day court offices are closed, the period ends on the next day they are open (r. 3 (3)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the rules do not clearly say how this applies, so the safe course is to act by the last open day before it. For a period of less than seven days, Saturdays, Sundays and other days when all court offices are closed are not counted (r. 3 (2)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
```

> Defence, Form 9A), whether it speaks _to_ you or _about_ you, and who served
> whom. If it has those the wrong way round, nothing else about it matters.

### `answer:family:before-filing:deciding-where-to-start:whats-happening`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:before-filing:deciding-where-to-start
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "Which court do I go to for my family case, and where?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
Nothing has been filed yet. You are working out which court hears your family case and in which place it starts. The Family Law Rules cover family cases in three courts. They are the Family Court of the Superior Court of Justice, the Superior Court of Justice, and the Ontario Court of Justice. The rules list 24 municipalities where the Family Court sits. The regional municipalities are Durham, Haldimand-Norfolk, Niagara, Waterloo and York. The cities are Hamilton, Kawartha Lakes and Ottawa. The counties are Elgin, Frontenac, Haliburton, Hastings, Lanark, Lennox and Addington, Middlesex, Northumberland, Peterborough, Prince Edward, Renfrew and Simcoe. The united counties are Leeds and Grenville, Prescott and Russell, and Stormont, Dundas and Glengarry. The last is the Territorial District of Muskoka.
```

### `answer:family:before-filing:deciding-where-to-start:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:before-filing:deciding-where-to-start
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "Which court do I go to for my family case, and where?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
In the parts of Ontario where the Family Court sits, some family cases must be started, heard and decided there. These are the cases on a list in the Courts of Justice Act, except appeals and prosecutions. The list includes cases under the Divorce Act and the Family Law Act, except Part V. It also includes cases under the Children's Law Reform Act, except sections 59 and 60. For a divorce, the court in Ontario is the Superior Court of Justice. An Ontario court can hear a divorce if you or your spouse has been habitually resident in Ontario for at least one year. That year must be the one right before the case starts. The Ontario Court of Justice is not a court for family property claims under Part I of the Family Law Act. It is not one for matrimonial home claims under Part II either. As for where, the case must start in one of the places the rules list. This is subject to the Family Court sections of the Courts of Justice Act. One place is the municipality where a party lives. A case about decision-making responsibility, parenting time or contact with a child may also start where the child habitually lives. That is subject to section 22 of the Children's Law Reform Act. Or all parties can choose a municipality. But the court in that place must give its permission first.
```

```
There is an exception for urgent danger. It applies if a child may be taken out of Ontario right away. It also applies if a child's or a party's health or safety is in immediate danger. Then a party may start the case in any municipality, still subject to the Family Court sections of the Courts of Justice Act. After the urgent request is heard there, the case must be moved to one of the usual places, unless the court orders otherwise.
```

### `answer:family:applicant:application-filed-not-served:whats-happening`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:applicant:application-filed-not-served
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I filed my application — how do I get it to the other parent or my ex?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
You have filed your application, but it has not been served on the respondent yet. When an application is filed, the clerk must seal it with the court seal. The clerk must also set a court date, except in two kinds of cases. In the Family Court, a claim for divorce, a property claim or a family arbitration claim makes the case a standard track case. In a standard track case, no court date is set when the application is filed. In the Superior Court of Justice outside the Family Court, no court date is set when the application is filed either. In both kinds of cases, the clerk must schedule a case conference if any party asks.
```

### `answer:family:applicant:application-filed-not-served:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:applicant:application-filed-not-served
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I filed my application — how do I get it to the other parent or my ex?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
You must serve the application on every other party right away. You must use special service, unless the party is one of those listed in r. 8 (6). Someone other than you must carry out the special service, unless the court orders otherwise, and that person must be at least 18 years old. The rule that someone other than you must serve it also does not apply if you or the person served is one of the officials or agencies in r. 8 (6) (c). The person serving must always be at least 18. One way to do special service is to leave a copy with the person to be served. Another way is to leave a copy at their home, in an envelope addressed to them, with an adult who appears to live there. Then, on the same day or the next, another copy is mailed to them at that address. A copy can also be mailed to the person with a prepaid return postcard (Form 6). Both must go in an envelope addressed to the person that has the sender's return address. That way is valid only once the postcard, signed by the person, is filed in the continuing record. You must also prepare the continuing record, serve it on all other parties, and file it with proof that it was served.
```

```
Serve the application on every other party right away, by special service. The rule sets no number of days. It says the application must be served immediately. Someone other than you must do the special service, unless the court orders otherwise. Serve the continuing record on all other parties too. File it with proof of service. Some papers must go with the application. In a case about parenting, net family property, the matrimonial home or support, include the automatic order (Form 8.0.1). Include your financial statement if one is required. For a support claim with no property claim, also include the income papers in r. 13 (3.1) and a certificate of financial disclosure (Form 13A). The clerk will not accept a financial statement for a support claim without proof of your income. You need proof of your current income and of your income for the past three years. For a claim about decision-making responsibility, parenting time or contact, include the papers rule 35.1 requires. If you are not the child's parent and ask for decision-making responsibility, attach a police records check to Form 35.1. If you only have proof that you asked for the check, serve and file the check within 10 days after you get it. If the application is not served by its court date, the clerk must set a new date if you ask. You then serve it right away.

Attend the mandatory information program. You have 45 days after the day the case was started. This applies only to some cases. They are cases about parenting, support, net family property, the matrimonial home or a restraining order. It also covers a motion to change that is not only about child or spousal support. It does not apply to a case on consent. It does not apply where the only claims are for a divorce, costs, or putting an agreement or order into an order. It does not apply where the only claims are about a family arbitration, unless the court orders otherwise. It does not apply in an international child abduction case. It does not apply to the Director of the Family Responsibility Office, or to an agency under s. 33 (3) of the Family Law Act. It does not apply to a person who has already attended. File your certificate of attendance as soon as you can. File it no later than 2 p.m. on the second day before the case conference. The court can excuse a party because of urgency or hardship, or for another reason in the interest of justice. You book your own appointment and the respondent’s. Serve notice of the respondent’s appointment with the application. Until your certificate is filed, you cannot take another step in the case. The one exception is booking a case conference. The court can order otherwise on a motion.

If your application makes a property claim, serve the respondent with the property papers the rule lists. You have 30 days after the day your financial statement was due, which is the day you served the application. For a claim under Part I of the Family Law Act, the rule lists the papers. One example is the statement closest to the valuation date for each bank or other account. For any other property claim, serve the information needed to support the claim. If there is also a support claim, serve the income papers in r. 13 (3.1) with it. Serve a certificate of financial disclosure (Form 13A) with the papers. The court can order otherwise.

Times set by the Family Law Rules are counted under those rules. The first day is the day after the event (r. 3 (1)). If the last day of a period falls on a day court offices are closed, the period ends on the next day they are open (r. 3 (3)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the rules do not clearly say how this applies, so the safe course is to act by the last open day before it. For a period of less than seven days, Saturdays, Sundays and other days when all court offices are closed are not counted (r. 3 (2)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
```

### `answer:family:both:case-conference-scheduled:whats-happening`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:both:case-conference-scheduled
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I have a case conference coming up — what do I have to file, and when?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
One purpose of a case conference is to explore settling the case. Other purposes include finding which issues are in dispute and which are not, and looking at ways to resolve them. It is also meant to make sure the relevant evidence is shared, including financial information needed for any support or property issue. It can set the date for the next step in the case. No motion may be served or heard until a conference on the main issues is done. That does not apply if the court finds there is urgency or hardship. It also does not apply if the court finds a case conference is not needed for another reason in the interest of justice. Nor does it apply to certain motions listed in rule 14 (6). These include any motion in a child protection case. They also include a motion made without notice, made on consent, or unopposed. Another is a motion limited to procedural, uncomplicated or unopposed matters.
```

### `answer:family:both:case-conference-scheduled:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:both:case-conference-scheduled
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I have a case conference coming up — what do I have to file, and when?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
If you are the one who asked for the case conference, you must serve and file a case conference notice (Form 17). Each party must serve and file a case conference brief (Form 17A or 17B). Each party must also give the clerk a confirmation of conference (Form 17F). Before that, give a copy to every other party by mail, fax, email or any other way, except in a child protection case. You can give it to the clerk by delivering it to the court office, by email, or through the Justice Services Online website or the Ontario Courts Public Portal, whichever is available. Unless the court orders otherwise, the conference will not be held if the clerk does not get it by 2 p.m. three days before the conference date. Rule 13 (3.1), (3.3), (3.4) and (5.0.1) list extra financial disclosure documents for a support claim, a property claim, and a motion to change support. If you had to serve those documents, you must serve a certificate of financial disclosure (Form 13A) with them and file the certificate. The parties must come to the conference, unless the court orders otherwise. A party who has a licensed representative must also bring that representative, with full knowledge of and authority in the case.
```

### `answer:family:both:case-conference-scheduled:your-deadline`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:both:case-conference-scheduled
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I have a case conference coming up — what do I have to file, and when?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
If you served the case conference notice (Form 17), serve and file your case conference brief. If no one asked for the conference, this time is for the applicant or the party who made the motion. Do this at least 6 days before the date of the case conference. Your last financial statement may be more than 60 days old by the conference. If so, update it by this same day. Serve and file an affidavit saying nothing has changed, an affidavit with the changes, or a new statement. If there is a support claim, give the other party the income papers in r. 13 (3.1) before the case conference, unless you already served them. Before the conference, talk or write to every other party, or make your best effort to. Discuss requests for financial disclosure and settling the issues for now. You do not have to if a court order forbids it. You also do not have to if there is a risk of domestic violence by a party with no licensed representative. The parties can agree in writing to change this time. The court can also change it.

If you are the other party, serve and file your case conference brief. Do this at least 4 days before the date of the case conference. The extra steps listed above apply to you too. Where they say "by the same day", your day is this 4-day one. The parties can agree in writing to change this time. The court can also change it.

Give a copy of the confirmation of conference (Form 17F) to every other party. Then give it to the clerk no later than 2 p.m. Do this at least 3 days before the date of the case conference. The parties cannot change this time by agreement. Unless the court orders otherwise, the conference will not go ahead without it.

If you are the applicant or the party who made the motion, and you had to serve financial disclosure, file your certificate of financial disclosure (Form 13A). Do this at least 6 days before the date of the case conference. You also serve the certificate with the disclosure papers. The parties can agree in writing to change this time. The court can also change it.

If you are the other party and had to serve financial disclosure, file your certificate (Form 13A). Do this at least 4 days before the date of the case conference. You also serve the certificate with the disclosure papers. The parties can agree in writing to change this time. The court can also change it.

File your information program certificate of attendance as soon as you can, and no later than 2 p.m. Do this at least 2 days before the date of the case conference. This applies only if the program applies to the case. The parties can agree in writing to change this time. The court can also change it.

Times set by the Family Law Rules are counted under those rules. The first day is the day after the event (r. 3 (1)). If the last day of a period falls on a day court offices are closed, the period ends on the next day they are open (r. 3 (3)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the rules do not clearly say how this applies, so the safe course is to act by the last open day before it. For a period of less than seven days, Saturdays, Sundays and other days when all court offices are closed are not counted (r. 3 (2)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
```

### `answer:family:both:case-conference-scheduled:what-happens-after`

- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I have a case conference coming up — what do I have to file, and when?"

```
At the conference, the judge may, if it is right to do so, order document disclosure or questioning, set times for steps in the case, or give directions for the next steps. If notice has been served, the judge may also make a final order or a temporary order. An agreement reached at a conference does not take effect until the parties sign it and it is witnessed, and in some cases the court must approve it. A case cannot be set for trial unless a settlement conference has been held or a judge has ordered it.
```

### `answer:family:both:financial-disclosure-missing:whats-happening`

```
You think the other party's financial papers do not give enough information to fully understand their finances. A party who finds that a financial disclosure paper they served is wrong, incomplete or out of date must serve a new or corrected one right away. They must also file it, if that applies. A party who finds they did not serve one of the extra disclosure documents rule 13 requires must serve it as soon as they find out.
```

### `answer:family:both:financial-disclosure-missing:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:both:financial-disclosure-missing
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "The other side's financial disclosure is incomplete — how do I get the rest?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
First, you must ask the other party in writing for the extra information you need. If any of it is not given within seven days of your request, the court may order them to give it or to serve and file a new financial statement. The court can do this on a motion, or at a case or settlement conference. When you ask for this order, you must list in your motion or conference brief the information you asked for but did not get. No motion may be served or heard until a conference on the main issues is done. That does not apply if the court finds there is urgency or hardship. It also does not apply if the court finds a case conference is not needed for another reason in the interest of justice. It also does not apply to certain motions listed in rule 14 (6). These include any motion in a child protection case. They also include a motion made without notice, made on consent, or unopposed. Another is a motion limited to procedural, uncomplicated or unopposed matters. A motion form (Form 14B) may be used to ask for this order. A party may be questioned on their financial statement under rule 20, but only after a written request for information has been made. Outside a child protection case, questioning needs the other party's consent or a court order. The court can order it on a motion only if three things are true. It would be unfair to go on without it. The information is not easy to get another way. And it will not cause unacceptable delay or undue expense. In a child protection case, a party is entitled to question the other party without an order. To do so, they must serve the other party with a summons to witness (Form 23) by special service. This does not apply to an application for an order under sections 53.1 to 53.5 of Ontario Regulation 155/18. To question, you must first have served and filed any answer, financial statement or net family property statement the rules require. You must also promise in writing not to serve or file more material for the next step, except in reply to what you learn.
```

### `answer:family:both:financial-disclosure-missing:your-deadline`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:both:financial-disclosure-missing
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "The other side's financial disclosure is incomplete — how do I get the rest?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
The other party's time to give the additional financial information you asked for in writing. They have 7 days after the day of the written request. If it is not given in that time, the court can order it. It can do so on a motion or at a case or settlement conference. In your motion or conference brief, say what you asked for and did not get.

Times set by the Family Law Rules are counted under those rules. The first day is the day after the event (r. 3 (1)). If the last day of a period falls on a day court offices are closed, the period ends on the next day they are open (r. 3 (3)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the rules do not clearly say how this applies, so the safe course is to act by the last open day before it. For a period of less than seven days, Saturdays, Sundays and other days when all court offices are closed are not counted (r. 3 (2)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
```

### `answer:civil:before-filing:deciding-whether-to-sue:whats-happening`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:before-filing:deciding-whether-to-sue
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "Can I sue over this in the Superior Court, and am I still in time?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
Nothing has been filed yet. You are working out whether the Superior Court of Justice is the place for your dispute, and whether you are still in time. Which court can hear a claim for money depends on the amount claimed, not counting interest and costs. For a claim to get back personal property, it depends on the value of the property. The most the Small Claims Court can hear is a claim for $50,000.
```

### `answer:civil:before-filing:deciding-whether-to-sue:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:before-filing:deciding-whether-to-sue
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "Can I sue over this in the Superior Court, and am I still in time?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
A case that is within the Small Claims Court's limits must not be started in the Superior Court of Justice unless the Superior Court gives leave. The court may give that leave only if it is in the interest of justice. You may ask for this leave without notice, unless the court orders otherwise. Leave is not needed for a counterclaim, a crossclaim, or a third or later party claim, if the main case was started in the Superior Court. In the Superior Court, a set of steps called the simplified procedure must be used if two things are true. First, your claim is only for money, real property or personal property, or some of these. Second, the total is $200,000 or less, not counting interest and costs. The total is the money claimed plus the fair market value of any property on the day the case starts. If there are two or more plaintiffs or defendants, each claim is considered separately. The simplified procedure does not apply to some cases, such as cases under the Class Proceedings Act, 1992. It also stops applying if a party delivers a jury notice. A party may do that only if the case involves a claim arising from slander, libel, malicious arrest, malicious prosecution or false imprisonment.
```

### `answer:civil:before-filing:deciding-whether-to-sue:your-deadline`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:before-filing:deciding-whether-to-sue
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "Can I sue over this in the Superior Court, and am I still in time?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
The general deadline to start a court case. You have 2 years after the day the claim was discovered. The last day is the anniversary of that day, 2 years later. If that day was February 29, the anniversary is February 28, except in a leap year. This applies unless the Limitations Act, 2002 says otherwise. For example, a claim based on a sexual assault has no time limit. A claim is discovered on the earlier of two days. The first is the day you knew four things: you had a loss, an act or omission caused it, whose act or omission it was, and that a court case was a proper way to fix it. The second is the day a reasonable person in your place ought to have known those things. You are presumed to have known them on the day of the act or omission, unless you prove otherwise. Separately, no case can start more than 15 years after the act or omission, except in some cases the Act lists. Some other Acts, listed in a schedule to the Limitations Act, set shorter times. For example, a case for libel in an Ontario newspaper or broadcast must start within three months after you learned of the libel. The two years do not run while the person with the claim is a minor and has no litigation guardian. They also do not run while a physical, mental or psychological condition keeps the person from starting a case, and they have no litigation guardian. A person is presumed able to start a case unless shown otherwise. If that condition ends with less than six months left, the time runs to six months after it ends. The 15 years also do not run while the other side wilfully hides from you that the loss happened, that an act or omission caused it, or that it was theirs. Nor do they run while the other side wilfully misleads you about whether a court case is a proper way to fix it. You must prove this. The two years and the 15 years also stop while the parties have agreed to have an independent third party resolve the claim or help resolve it. The other side may admit in writing, and sign, that they owe a fixed sum of money. The same goes for an admission that they must return personal property. It also goes for enforcing a charge on personal property, or relief from that. Then the act or omission is treated as happening on the day of that admission. This counts only if it was made before the time ran out. It must be made to you, your agent, or an official receiver or trustee under the Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act (Canada). For a fixed sum of money, a part payment by the other side or their agent works the same way as a written, signed admission. For a debt payable on demand, the loss happens on the first day it is not paid after a demand for payment.

A deadline in an Ontario statute is counted under the Legislation Act, 2006, unless the statute shows otherwise. When a period is described as starting after a day, that day is not counted (s. 89 (5)). If the last day is a Sunday or a holiday, the deadline moves to the next day that is not a holiday (s. 89 (1)). Saturday is not a holiday under that Act, so a Saturday does not by itself move the deadline. Some deadlines are for doing something at a place, such as filing at an office. If that place is not open during its regular hours on the last day, the deadline moves to the next day it is open during its regular hours (s. 89 (2)).
```

### `answer:civil:before-filing:deciding-whether-to-sue:what-happens-after`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:before-filing:deciding-whether-to-sue
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "Can I sue over this in the Superior Court, and am I still in time?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
Unless the Limitations Act, 2002 provides otherwise, a case cannot be started more than two years after the day the claim was discovered. Some proceedings fall outside the Limitations Act, 2002. One example is a proceeding the Real Property Limitations Act applies to. Even if the two years have not run out, no case can be started more than 15 years after the day the act or omission it is based on took place. Some claims have no time limit at all, such as a claim based on a sexual assault. There is also none for other sexual misconduct if, at the time, the person was a minor. The same applies if the other person had charge of them or was in a position of trust or authority over them. It also applies if the person depended on the other person in some way. There is no time limit for a claim based on an assault if, at the time, the person was a minor. The same applies if the two had an intimate relationship, or the person depended on the other person in some way. That 15-year period does not run during some times, including these two. One is while you are a minor and have no litigation guardian. The other is while a physical, mental or psychological condition makes you unable to start a case, and you have no litigation guardian. Some time limits in other Acts are listed in the Schedule to the Limitations Act, 2002. One is section 6 of the Libel and Slander Act. It covers a case for libel in a newspaper or broadcast. That case must be started within three months after the person defamed learned of the libel. First, you must give the defendant written notice of what you complain of. You must give it within six weeks after you learned of the libel. The notice must be served the same way as a statement of claim, or given to a grown-up person at the defendant's chief office. These two time limits apply only to newspapers printed and published in Ontario and to broadcasts from a station in Ontario. The Libel and Slander Act also sets conditions a newspaper or broadcaster must meet to rely on them.
```

### `answer:civil:before-filing:limitation-period-may-have-passed:whats-happening`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:before-filing:limitation-period-may-have-passed
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "This happened years ago — is it too late to sue?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/02l24

```
More than two years seem to have passed since the events. But the day the claim was discovered has not been worked out yet. Unless the Limitations Act, 2002 provides otherwise, you have two years from the day the claim was discovered to start a case. Some proceedings fall outside the Limitations Act, 2002. One example is a proceeding the Real Property Limitations Act applies to. A claim is discovered on the earlier of two days. The first is the day you first knew four things. First, that the injury, loss or damage happened. Second, that an act or omission caused it or helped cause it. Third, that it was the act or omission of the person you would sue. Fourth, that given the kind of loss, a court case would be a fitting way to try to fix it. The second is the first day a reasonable person with your abilities, in your circumstances, ought to have known those things. You are presumed to have known them on the day of the act or omission, unless it is proved otherwise. Some claims are about a demand obligation created on or after January 1, 2004. For those, the loss happens on the first day the obligation is not performed after a demand is made.
```

### `answer:civil:before-filing:limitation-period-may-have-passed:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:before-filing:limitation-period-may-have-passed
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "This happened years ago — is it too late to sue?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/02l24

```
The two years do not run while you are a minor and have no litigation guardian for the claim. They also do not run while a physical, mental or psychological condition makes you unable to start a case, and you have no litigation guardian for the claim. You are presumed to have been able to start a case at all times, unless it is proved otherwise. If a pause for such a condition ends with less than six months left, the time is extended to six months after the day it ends. Time also stops while you and the other person have agreed to have an independent third party resolve the claim or help you resolve it. It starts again when the claim is resolved, when that process ends, or when one of you ends or withdraws from the agreement. This pause covers both the two years and the 15 years described below. The other person, or their agent, may have admitted liability in writing and signed it. For some claims, the act or omission is then treated as taking place on the day of that admission. These include a claim for a fixed sum of money or to get back personal property. This counts only if the admission was made before the time ran out. It must also have been made to you, your agent, or an official receiver or trustee under the Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act (Canada). For a fixed sum of money, a part payment by the other person or their agent has the same effect.
```

### `answer:civil:plaintiff:claim-issued-not-served:whats-happening`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:plaintiff:claim-issued-not-served
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "My claim was issued — how do I serve the defendant, and by when?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
The registrar has issued your claim. That means it was dated, signed, sealed with the court's seal and given a court file number. The next step is to serve it on each defendant. If you started with a notice of action, you must first file your statement of claim. That is because the notice may not be served separately from the statement of claim. A statement of claim must be served within six months after it is issued. If you started with a notice of action, the notice and the statement of claim must be served together. That must be done within six months after the notice of action was issued.
```

### `answer:civil:plaintiff:claim-issued-not-served:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:plaintiff:claim-issued-not-served
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "My claim was issued — how do I serve the defendant, and by when?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
If you used a notice of action, you must file your statement of claim (Form 14D) within 30 days after the notice was issued. After that, you can file it only with the defendant's written consent, or with the court's permission asked for on notice to the defendant. In Ontario, the claim must be served personally, or by one of the alternatives to personal service in the rules. To serve a person personally, leave a copy with that person, unless they are under a disability. To serve a corporation that is not a municipality, leave a copy with an officer, director or agent of it. Or leave it at any of its places of business with a person who appears to control or manage that place. Other kinds of parties are served personally in other ways, such as a municipality, a minor, a partnership or a sole proprietorship. One alternative is to mail a copy, with an acknowledgment of receipt card (Form 16A), to the person's last known address. That service counts only from the date you receive the card back. Another alternative applies if you try to serve personally at the person's home and cannot. You may leave a copy, in a sealed envelope addressed to them, at the home with anyone who appears to be an adult member of the same household. For this method, you must also mail another copy to them at that home on the same day or the next day. Service this way takes effect on the fifth day after the copy is mailed. If the defendant has a lawyer, you may leave a copy with the lawyer or an employee in the lawyer's office. This works only if the lawyer writes on the document, or a copy, that they accept service and the date they accept it. A corporation's head office, registered office or main place of business may not be found at the last address recorded with the Ministry of Public and Business Service Delivery. If so, you may mail a copy to the corporation at that address. For an extra-provincial corporation, the same applies to its attorney for service in Ontario. If prompt service is impractical for any reason, the court may order substituted service. Where needed in the interest of justice, it may excuse service instead. Service may be proved by an affidavit of the person who served the claim (Form 16B). If the defendant is outside Ontario, other rules apply. In some cases you need the court's permission to serve them there. Some countries are contracting states under the Convention on the Service Abroad of Judicial and Extrajudicial Documents, signed at The Hague in 1965. In one of those countries, the claim must be served in one of two ways. One is through that country's central authority. The other is a way the Convention permits that these rules would also permit in Ontario.
```

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:plaintiff:claim-issued-not-served
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "My claim was issued — how do I serve the defendant, and by when?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
Serve the statement of claim on the defendant. You have 6 months after the day the statement of claim was issued. If you started with a notice of action, serve the notice and the statement of claim together within six months after the notice was issued. The time can be extended by filing a consent. The court can also extend it, before or after the time runs out. If you do not serve the claim in time, a defendant who is not in default can ask the court to dismiss the action for delay.

If you started with a notice of action, file your statement of claim (Form 14D). You have 30 days after the day the notice of action was issued. This applies only if you started with a notice of action. After the 30 days, you can file the statement of claim only with the defendant's written consent or the court's permission. You must ask for that permission on notice to the defendant.

Set the action down for trial, or the registrar will dismiss it for delay. You have 5 years after the day the action was started. The last day is the anniversary of that day, 5 years later. If that day was February 29, the anniversary is February 28, except in a leap year. This does not apply if the action has already ended some other way. It does not apply if a party files a timetable signed by all parties, and a draft order, at least 30 days before the time ends. The timetable must give a date, no more than two years after the time ends, by which the action will be set down or restored. If the parties do not agree on a timetable, any party can ask for a status hearing before the time ends. It does not apply if you are under a disability at that time. It does not apply to Commercial List actions or class actions. The court can order otherwise. A dismissal can be set aside on a motion under rule 37.14.

Times set by the Rules of Civil Procedure are counted under those rules. The first day is not counted. If a time counted forward ends on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, it ends on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (c)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the safe course is to act by the last day before it that is not a holiday. For a period of seven days or less, holidays are not counted at all (r. 3.01 (1) (b)). Except for the document that starts a case, a document served after 4 p.m. or on a holiday counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (d)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
```

### `answer:civil:plaintiff:claim-issued-not-served:what-happens-after`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:plaintiff:claim-issued-not-served
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "My claim was issued — how do I serve the defendant, and by when?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
After service, the defendant has a set time to deliver a statement of defence (Form 18A). The time depends on where they were served. A defendant who delivers a notice of intent to defend (Form 18B) within that time gets 10 more days to deliver a defence. To deliver means to serve and file with proof of service. If a defendant fails to deliver a defence in time, you may file proof of service of the statement of claim and require the registrar to note that defendant in default.
```

### `answer:civil:plaintiff:defence-period-expired-no-defence:whats-happening`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:plaintiff:defence-period-expired-no-defence
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "The defendant's time is up and they never filed a defence — what can I do?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
The defendant's time to deliver a statement of defence has run out, and no defence has been delivered. To deliver means to serve and file with proof of service. The defendant has not been noted in default yet, so they may still deliver a defence at any time until that happens.
```

### `answer:civil:plaintiff:defence-period-expired-no-defence:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:plaintiff:defence-period-expired-no-defence
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "The defendant's time is up and they never filed a defence — what can I do?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
Because no defence was delivered in time, you may require the registrar to note the defendant in default. To do this, you file proof of service of the statement of claim with the registrar. The defendant may never have been served but may have delivered a notice of intent to defend or notice of appearance. If so, they are treated as served as of the date they delivered it. You then file proof of that instead. One way to prove service is an affidavit of the person who served the claim (Form 16B). If the defendant is under a disability, such as being a minor, they may be noted in default only with a judge's permission. That permission is asked for on a motion under rule 7.07. A defendant who is not in default may move to have the action dismissed for delay. They may do this if you have not had a defendant who failed to deliver a defence noted in default within 30 days after the default.
```

```
If there is more than one defendant, have the one who did not defend noted in default. Do this by filing proof of service of the statement of claim with the registrar. If you do not, a defendant who is not in default can ask the court to dismiss your action for delay. You have 30 days after the day the defendant's time to deliver a defence ran out. Only a defendant who is not in default can bring this motion. So it matters mainly where there is more than one defendant. Until a defendant is noted in default, they can still deliver a defence.

Set the action down for trial, or the registrar will dismiss it for delay. You have 5 years after the day the action was started. The last day is the anniversary of that day, 5 years later. If that day was February 29, the anniversary is February 28, except in a leap year. This does not apply if the action has already ended some other way. It does not apply if a party files a timetable signed by all parties, and a draft order, at least 30 days before the time ends. If the parties do not agree on a timetable, any party can ask for a status hearing before the time ends. It does not apply if you are under a disability at that time. It does not apply to Commercial List actions or class actions. The court can order otherwise. A dismissal can be set aside on a motion under rule 37.14.

Times set by the Rules of Civil Procedure are counted under those rules. The first day is not counted. If a time counted forward ends on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, it ends on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (c)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the safe course is to act by the last day before it that is not a holiday. For a period of seven days or less, holidays are not counted at all (r. 3.01 (1) (b)). Except for the document that starts a case, a document served after 4 p.m. or on a holiday counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (d)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
```

### `answer:civil:plaintiff:defence-period-expired-no-defence:what-happens-after`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:plaintiff:defence-period-expired-no-defence
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "The defendant's time is up and they never filed a defence — what can I do?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
Once a defendant is noted in default, you may require the registrar to sign judgment on some kinds of claims. These are a claim for a debt or liquidated demand in money (Form 19A), for the recovery of possession of land (Form 19B) or personal property (Form 19C), or for foreclosure, sale or redemption of a mortgage. Before the registrar signs, you must file a requisition for default judgment (Form 19D). For any claim without a signed default judgment, you may move before a judge for judgment. A defendant noted in default is deemed to admit the facts in your statement of claim. On a motion for judgment, that alone does not entitle you to judgment unless the facts do.
```

### `answer:civil:plaintiff:defence-received:whats-happening`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:plaintiff:defence-received
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "The defendant served a statement of defence — what happens now?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
The defendant has answered your claim with a statement of defence. In an action, the pleadings are the statement of claim, the statement of defence and a reply (Form 25A), if there is one. Pleadings close when two things are true. First, you have delivered a reply to every defence, or the time to deliver a reply has run out. Second, every defendant who did not deliver a defence in time has been noted in default.
```

### `answer:civil:plaintiff:defence-received:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:plaintiff:defence-received
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "The defendant served a statement of defence — what happens now?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
Deliver means serve and file with proof of service. You must deliver a reply if you plan to prove a version of the facts that is different from the one in the defence, unless your claim already sets it out. You must also deliver a reply to raise a matter that might take the other side by surprise, or that raises an issue no earlier pleading raised. But a new ground of claim, or a fact that conflicts with your claim, must not go in the reply. It must be made by amending your claim. In any other case, you must not deliver a reply. A reply is due within 10 days after service of the statement of defence. If the defendant also made a counterclaim, you must deliver a defence to counterclaim (Form 27C) within 20 days after service of the statement of defence and counterclaim. Any reply is due within the same 20 days. If you deliver a reply as well, the reply and defence to counterclaim go in one document. If you deliver a reply, you must admit every fact in the defence that you do not dispute. If you do not deliver a reply in time, you are taken to deny the facts set out in the defence. Any party may ask for a jury by delivering a jury notice (Form 47A) at any time before pleadings close. This does not apply if section 108 of the Courts of Justice Act or another statute requires a trial without a jury. An action under the simplified procedure (Rule 76) cannot be tried with a jury. A party may still deliver a jury notice if the action involves a claim arising from slander, libel, malicious arrest, malicious prosecution or false imprisonment. If they do, the action no longer goes under the simplified procedure. The party who delivered the jury notice must also deliver a notice (Form 76A) saying the action goes on as an ordinary action.
```

### `answer:civil:plaintiff:defence-received:your-deadline`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:plaintiff:defence-received
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "The defendant served a statement of defence — what happens now?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
If a reply is required, deliver it. You have 10 days after the day the statement of defence was served on you. A reply is needed only if you will prove a different version of the facts than the defence pleads, or must raise a matter that could take the other side by surprise. Otherwise you must not deliver one. If the defendant also counterclaimed, you have 20 days instead for a reply and defence to counterclaim. Deliver means serve it on the other parties and file it with proof of service. Your action may be under the simplified procedure, and the defence may object that your claim does not fit it. Then the action stays under that procedure only if your reply gives up the parts of the claim that do not fit. The time can be extended by filing a consent, or by the court.

If your action is under the simplified procedure, serve every other party with an affidavit of documents. Include copies of the documents in its Schedule A. You pay the cost. You have 10 days after the day pleadings closed. This applies only to an action under the simplified procedure. Pleadings close when every defence has been replied to, or the time for a reply has run out, and every defendant who did not defend has been noted in default. The affidavit must also list the people who might know about the issues, unless the court orders otherwise. A person not named in it cannot be a witness at trial unless the court orders otherwise. The time can be extended by filing a consent, or by the court.

If your action is under the simplified procedure, meet or talk by phone with the other parties. Discuss whether all relevant documents have been shared, and whether any issue can be settled. You have 60 days after the day the first statement of defence or notice of intent to defend was filed. This applies only to an action under the simplified procedure. The general rules for actions also apply to it, unless Rule 76 says otherwise.

If your action is under the simplified procedure, set it down for trial. Do this by serving a notice of readiness for pre-trial conference (Form 76C) on every party and filing it with proof of service. You have 180 days after the day the first statement of defence or notice of intent to defend was filed. This applies only to an action under the simplified procedure. It replaces the usual way of setting down. If you do not do it, any other party may. You must certify in the notice that there was a settlement discussion. The court can extend the time.

If you want a jury, deliver a jury notice (Form 47A) before pleadings close. The rule fixes no number of days. The cut-off is the close of pleadings. That can come 10 days after the defence if no reply is delivered. If a reply is delivered sooner, pleadings close when it is delivered, as long as every defendant has delivered a defence or been noted in default. Some statutes require a trial without a jury. A simplified procedure action cannot have a jury. The exception is a claim for slander, libel, malicious arrest, malicious prosecution or false imprisonment.

If any party wants evidence through discovery, such as documents, an examination, an inspection or a medical exam, agree on a written discovery plan with the other parties. You have 60 days after the day pleadings closed. The parties can agree to a longer time. But the plan must be agreed before anyone tries to get the evidence, if that comes first. The plan must be in writing. It must set dates for serving each party's affidavit of documents.

If a third party delivered a statement of defence in the main action and you want to reply to it, deliver a reply. You have 10 days after the day the third party's statement of defence was served on you. This applies only where a defendant brought in a third party who has also defended the main action. A reply is needed only if you will prove a different version of the facts than the defence pleads, or must raise a matter that could take the other side by surprise. Otherwise you must not deliver one.

Set the action down for trial. If you do not, a defendant who is not in default can ask the court to dismiss the action for delay. You have 6 months after the day pleadings closed. This is not an automatic dismissal. It is a motion a defendant may bring. The registrar's own dismissal comes at five years. Once you set the action down, you cannot start or continue discovery or motions without leave. If your action is covered by mandatory mediation, one party must first file with the mediation co-ordinator the notice naming the mediator and date (Form 24.1A), or the mediator's report. If your action is under the simplified procedure, it is set down another way. That is by a notice of readiness for pre-trial conference (Form 76C), within 180 days after the first defence.

If your action is covered by mandatory mediation, choose a mediator with the other parties and hold the mediation session. You have 180 days after the day the first defence was filed. This applies only to actions that Rule 24.1 covers. For example, it covers actions started in Ottawa, Toronto or the County of Essex on or after January 1, 2010. Some kinds of action are left out. The court can exempt an action, or set a different time. The parties can put off the session by filing their written consent with the mediation co-ordinator. Some actions are covered only because they were moved to Ottawa, Toronto or Essex. For those, the 180 days do not apply, and the court can set the date. The co-ordinator assigns a mediator if, within the 180 days, they receive none of these: a notice of the mediator and date, a mediator's report, a consent, an order, or a notice of settlement.

Set the action down for trial, or the registrar will dismiss it for delay. You have 5 years after the day the action was started. The last day is the anniversary of that day, 5 years later. If that day was February 29, the anniversary is February 28, except in a leap year. This does not apply if the action has already ended some other way. It does not apply if a party files a timetable signed by all parties, and a draft order, at least 30 days before the time ends. The timetable must give a date, no more than two years after the time ends, by which the action will be set down or restored. If the parties do not agree on a timetable, any party can ask for a status hearing before the time ends. It does not apply if you are under a disability at that time. It does not apply to Commercial List actions or class actions. The court can order otherwise. A dismissal can be set aside on a motion under rule 37.14.

Times set by the Rules of Civil Procedure are counted under those rules. The first day is not counted. If a time counted forward ends on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, it ends on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (c)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the safe course is to act by the last day before it that is not a holiday. For a period of seven days or less, holidays are not counted at all (r. 3.01 (1) (b)). Except for the document that starts a case, a document served after 4 p.m. or on a holiday counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (d)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
```

```
If your action is under the simplified procedure, the defence may object that your claim does not fit it. If your reply does not give up the claims or parts that do not fit, the action goes on as an ordinary action. You must then deliver a notice (Form 76A) saying so, after all the pleadings have been delivered. A claim or part of a claim that you give up cannot be brought in any other proceeding. ### `answer:civil:defendant:noted-in-default:whats-happening`
```

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:defendant:noted-in-default
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I have been noted in default — can I still defend?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
The registrar has noted you in default. You are now taken to admit that every fact in the statement of claim is true. You must not deliver a statement of defence or take any other step in the action. The exception is with the court's leave or the plaintiff's consent. Without either, the one step you may take is a motion to set aside the noting of default. The same motion can also cover any judgment obtained because of the default. A step that needs a defendant's consent may now be taken without yours.
```

### `answer:civil:defendant:noted-in-default:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:defendant:noted-in-default
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I have been noted in default — can I still defend?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
If you want to defend, you may bring a motion asking the court to set aside the noting of default. The court may set it aside on terms that are just. A motion is made by a notice of motion (Form 37A). The exception is where the kind of motion or the facts make one unneeded, or the rules say otherwise. On a motion to set aside the results of default, you may show that a document served on you did not come to your notice. You may also show that it came to your notice only later than when it was served or deemed served. Another way is to get the plaintiff's consent, or the court's leave, to deliver a statement of defence (Form 18A). If you deliver a statement of defence with the plaintiff's consent, the noting of default is treated as set aside. Deliver means serve and file with proof of service.
```

### `answer:civil:defendant:noted-in-default:your-deadline`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:defendant:noted-in-default
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I have been noted in default — can I still defend?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
If you want to defend, bring a motion to set aside the noting of default. Or get the plaintiff's consent to deliver a defence. The rule sets no fixed number of days. If you deliver a defence with the plaintiff's consent, the noting of default is treated as set aside. You are not entitled to notice of further steps, so the plaintiff can seek judgment without telling you.
```

### `answer:civil:defendant:noted-in-default:what-happens-after`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:defendant:noted-in-default
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I have been noted in default — can I still defend?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
While you are noted in default, you have no right to notice of any step in the action. You also need not be served with any document in it. There are exceptions, such as when the court orders otherwise, when a party requires you to attend personally, when the statement of claim against you is amended, or when another party's counterclaim names you as a defendant to it. The plaintiff may ask the registrar to sign judgment against you on some kinds of claim, such as a debt, or getting back land or personal property. For any claim with no signed default judgment, the plaintiff may move before a judge for judgment.
```

### `answer:civil:defendant:default-judgment-against-me:whats-happening`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:defendant:default-judgment-against-me
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "There is a default judgment against me — what can I do?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
You were noted in default. Then a judgment was signed or granted against you. Being noted in default means you are deemed to admit that every fact in the statement of claim is true. You must not deliver a statement of defence or take any other step in the action. To do so, you need the court's leave or the plaintiff's consent. One step needs neither: a motion to set aside the noting of default or any judgment obtained because of it.
```

### `answer:civil:defendant:default-judgment-against-me:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:defendant:default-judgment-against-me
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "There is a default judgment against me — what can I do?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
You may bring a motion to set aside the judgment. Who decides it depends on how the judgment was made. The registrar may have signed it, or the court may have granted it on a motion under rule 19.04. If so, the court may set it aside or change it on terms that are just. Or it may have come from a motion for judgment under rule 19.05, or after a trial. Then a judge may set it aside or change it on terms that are just. If the judgment is set aside, the court or judge may also set aside the noting of default. A document may have been served on you in a way the rules allow. Even so, on that motion you may show that it never came to your notice. Or you may show that you learned of it only after it was served or deemed served.
```

### `answer:civil:defendant:default-judgment-against-me:your-deadline`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:defendant:default-judgment-against-me
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "There is a default judgment against me — what can I do?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
If you want the default judgment set aside, bring a motion to set it aside. The rule sets no fixed number of days. The court can set aside a judgment the registrar signed, or one the court granted on a motion under rule 19.04. A judge can set aside one granted on a motion for judgment under rule 19.05, or after a trial. An appeal from a final order of a judge must start within 30 days after the order is made. Appealing a refusal to set aside a default judgment does not by itself stop the judgment from being enforced.
```

### `answer:civil:defendant:default-judgment-against-me:what-happens-after`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:defendant:default-judgment-against-me
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "There is a default judgment against me — what can I do?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
If the court refuses to set aside the judgment, an appeal from that refusal does not by itself put the judgment on hold. Putting it on hold is called a stay. The judgment may be stayed by an order, on terms that are just. The order may come from the court whose decision is being appealed, or from a judge of the court where the appeal or a motion for leave to appeal is brought. A stay from the court whose decision is being appealed ends if no notice of appeal, or notice of motion for leave to appeal, is delivered in time.
```
