### `answer:civil:both:discovery:whats-happening`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:both:discovery
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "What is discovery, and what do I have to hand over?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
Pleadings close when two things are done. First, the plaintiff has delivered a reply to every defence, or the time for a reply has run out. Second, every defendant who is in default of a defence has been noted in default. If any party wants to get evidence in one of five ways, the parties must agree to a discovery plan. The five are documents, examination for discovery, inspection of property, a medical exam, and examination by written questions. If the court has set a plan for the parties, they do not need to agree on one.
```

### `answer:civil:both:discovery:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:both:discovery
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "What is discovery, and what do I have to hand over?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
You must agree on the plan before the earlier of two times. One is 60 days after pleadings close, or a longer time the parties agree to. The other is when anyone first tries to get the evidence. The plan must be in writing. It must say what the document discovery will cover, given relevance, costs, and how important and complex the issues are. It must give the dates for each party to serve an affidavit of documents (Form 30A or 30B). It must say when and how documents will be produced, and what that will cost. It must name who will be examined orally for discovery, and say when and for how long. It must add anything else that helps finish discovery quickly, in a way that fits how important and complex the case is. You must serve an affidavit of documents on every other party. In it, list every document relevant to any issue in the action that is or was in your possession, control or power. List them as fully as you know or believe. Documents you claim privilege for must be listed too, in a separate schedule, with your grounds. Documents you no longer have go in another schedule. Say when and how you lost them, and where they are now. Do not file the affidavit unless it is relevant to an issue on a pending motion or at trial. Later, you may get a relevant document that is not privileged, or find the affidavit is wrong or incomplete. Then you must serve a supplementary affidavit right away. Another party may serve you with a request to inspect documents (Form 30C). It lets them see the documents your affidavit says you have, except privileged ones. It may also cover documents you have that are named in your originating process, pleadings or a served affidavit. If you get one, you must at once name a date within five days after it was served. You must also name a time between 9:30 a.m. and 4:30 p.m., and a place. The place is your lawyer's office or some other convenient place. You must then have the documents there at that time. Unless the parties agree otherwise, the documents you listed that are not privileged must be produced at your examination for discovery and at trial. So must any document you have already produced for inspection. No party may spend more than seven hours in all on oral examinations for discovery, however many people are examined. More time needs the consent of the parties or the court's leave. A person examined must answer any proper question about an issue in the action, or about other matters the rules open to discovery. They answer as best they know or believe.
```

### `answer:civil:both:discovery:your-deadline`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:both:discovery
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "What is discovery, and what do I have to hand over?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
If any party wants evidence through discovery, such as documents, an examination, an inspection or a medical exam, agree on a written discovery plan with the other parties. You have 60 days after the day pleadings closed. The parties can agree to a longer time. But the plan must be agreed before anyone tries to get the evidence, if that comes first. The plan must be in writing. It must set dates for serving each party's affidavit of documents.

If you gave an undertaking or took a question under advisement at an examination for discovery, answer it. You have 60 days after the day you gave that response at the examination. If you do not answer in that time, you cannot use that information at trial without the trial judge's permission. You still have to keep an undertaking.

If you are the plaintiff, set the action down for trial. If you do not, a defendant who is not in default can ask the court to dismiss the action for delay. You have 6 months after the day pleadings closed. This is not an automatic dismissal. It is a motion a defendant may bring. The registrar's own dismissal comes at five years. Once you set the action down, you cannot start or continue discovery or motions without leave. If your action is covered by mandatory mediation, one party must first file with the mediation co-ordinator the notice naming the mediator and date (Form 24.1A), or the mediator's report. If your action is under the simplified procedure, it is set down another way. That is by a notice of readiness for pre-trial conference (Form 76C), within 180 days after the first defence.

If you are the plaintiff, set the action down for trial, or the registrar will dismiss it for delay. You have 5 years after the day the action was started. The last day is the anniversary of that day, 5 years later. If that day was February 29, the anniversary is February 28, except in a leap year. This does not apply if the action has already ended some other way. It does not apply if a party files a timetable signed by all parties, and a draft order, at least 30 days before the time ends. The timetable must give a date, no more than two years after the time ends, by which the action will be set down or restored. If the parties do not agree on a timetable, any party can ask for a status hearing before the time ends. It does not apply if the plaintiff is under a disability at that time. It does not apply to Commercial List actions or class actions. The court can order otherwise. A dismissal can be set aside on a motion under rule 37.14.

If your action is covered by mandatory mediation, choose a mediator with the other parties and hold the mediation session. You have 180 days after the day the first defence was filed. This applies only to actions that Rule 24.1 covers. For example, it covers actions started in Ottawa, Toronto or the County of Essex on or after January 1, 2010. Some kinds of action are left out. The court can exempt an action, or set a different time. The parties can put off the session by filing their written consent with the mediation co-ordinator. Some actions are covered only because they were moved to Ottawa, Toronto or Essex. For those, the 180 days do not apply, and the court can set the date. The co-ordinator assigns a mediator if, within the 180 days, they receive none of these: a notice of the mediator and date, a mediator's report, a consent, an order, or a notice of settlement.

Times set by the Rules of Civil Procedure are counted under those rules. The first day is not counted. If a time counted forward ends on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, it ends on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (c)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the safe course is to act by the last day before it that is not a holiday. For a period of seven days or less, holidays are not counted at all (r. 3.01 (1) (b)). Except for the document that starts a case, a document served after 4 p.m. or on a holiday counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (d)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
```

### `answer:civil:both:discovery:what-happens-after`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:both:discovery
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "What is discovery, and what do I have to hand over?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
A question counts as not answered if it is refused. It also counts if it is taken under advisement or promised (an undertaking), and no answer comes within 60 days. Then that party may not bring in the information at trial unless the trial judge gives leave. A promise to answer must still be kept. This is in addition to other orders the court may make when a person refuses to answer a proper question. These include dismissing the party's proceeding or striking out its defence. Say you leave a document out of your affidavit, or fail to produce it as required. If it is favourable to your case, you may not use it at trial without the trial judge's leave. If it is not favourable to your case, the court may make any order that is just. A party may fail to serve an affidavit of documents, or to produce a document as the rules or a court order require. Then the court may take away or suspend that party's right to start or continue an examination for discovery. It may also dismiss a plaintiff's action or strike out a defendant's defence, or make any other order that is just.
```

### `answer:civil:both:mandatory-mediation:whats-happening`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:both:mandatory-mediation
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "Do we have to go to mediation, and what do I need to do for it?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
Mandatory mediation applies to some actions. These include actions started in the City of Ottawa, the City of Toronto or the County of Essex on or after January 1, 2010. Some kinds of action are left out, such as mortgage actions and actions on the Commercial List in Toronto. The court may also exempt an action from mediation if a party brings a motion asking for that. In mediation, a neutral person helps the parties talk to each other, to help them reach a result they all accept.
```

### `answer:civil:both:mandatory-mediation:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:both:mandatory-mediation
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "Do we have to go to mediation, and what do I need to do for it?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
The parties must choose a mediator. It can be a person on the county's list whom the parties agree on, or a person not on the list if the parties consent. Before the action is set down for trial, one of the parties must file a notice (Form 24.1A) with the mediation co-ordinator. The notice gives the mediator's name and the date of the session. The filing can instead be the mediator's report saying the mediation is over. At least seven days before the session, every party must prepare a statement in Form 24.1C. By then you must also give a copy to every other party and to the mediator. The statement must name the factual and legal issues in dispute, and briefly set out your position and interests. You must attach any documents you think are of central importance in the action. If you are the plaintiff, you must also put a copy of the pleadings with the mediator's copy of your statement. The parties, and their lawyers if they have them, must attend the session unless the court orders otherwise. An insurer may have to pay all or part of a judgment for a party, or pay the party back for it. If so, someone for the insurer must attend, and that party does not have to, unless the court orders otherwise. You may need someone else's okay before you agree to settle. If so, you must arrange before the session to be able to reach that person by phone the whole time.
```

### `answer:civil:both:mandatory-mediation:your-deadline`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:both:mandatory-mediation
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "Do we have to go to mediation, and what do I need to do for it?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
If your action is covered by mandatory mediation, choose a mediator with the other parties and hold the mediation session. You have 180 days after the day the first defence was filed. This applies only to actions that Rule 24.1 covers. For example, it covers actions started in Ottawa, Toronto or the County of Essex on or after January 1, 2010. Some kinds of action are left out. The court can exempt an action, or set a different time. The parties can put off the session by filing their written consent with the mediation co-ordinator. Some actions are covered only because they were moved to Ottawa, Toronto or Essex. For those, the 180 days do not apply, and the court can set the date. The co-ordinator assigns a mediator if, within the 180 days, they receive none of these: a notice of the mediator and date, a mediator's report, a consent, an order, or a notice of settlement.

Prepare a statement of issues (Form 24.1C) and give a copy to every other party and to the mediator. Do this at least 7 days before the date of the mediation session. This is the latest it can be done; earlier is fine. Because the period is seven days or less, Saturdays, Sundays and holidays are not counted. The plaintiff must also include a copy of the pleadings with the mediator's copy. A party may fail to do this, so that holding the session is not practical. Then the mediator cancels it and files a certificate of non-compliance. The matter then goes to a judge or associate judge. The judge can dismiss the action of a plaintiff who did not comply. The judge can strike out the defence of a defendant who did not comply, or make other orders.

Times set by the Rules of Civil Procedure are counted under those rules. The first day is not counted. If a time counted forward ends on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, it ends on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (c)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the safe course is to act by the last day before it that is not a holiday. For a period of seven days or less, holidays are not counted at all (r. 3.01 (1) (b)). Except for the document that starts a case, a document served after 4 p.m. or on a holiday counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (d)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
```

### `answer:civil:both:mandatory-mediation:what-happens-after`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:both:mandatory-mediation
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "Do we have to go to mediation, and what do I need to do for it?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
A party may fail to attend within the first 30 minutes, so that holding the session is not practical. Then the mediator must cancel it and file a certificate of non-compliance (Form 24.1D). The matter then goes to a judge or associate judge. The judge may hold a case conference. The judge may also set a timetable, strike out any document a party filed, or order a party to pay costs. The judge may dismiss the action if the party who did not comply is a plaintiff, or strike out the defence if that party is a defendant. Or the judge may make any other order that is just. Within 10 days after the mediation ends, the mediator must give the co-ordinator and the parties a report on it. Any agreement that settles some or all of the issues must be signed by the parties or their lawyers.
```

### `answer:civil:both:trial-date-set:whats-happening`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:both:trial-date-set
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "My trial is coming up — what do I need to do to be ready?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
Once an action is placed on a trial list, every party is treated as ready for trial. The trial goes ahead when the action is reached on the list, unless a judge orders otherwise. An expert may speak at trial on an issue only if the substance of that evidence is in a report served on time under the rules, unless the trial judge gives leave.
```

### `answer:civil:both:trial-date-set:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:both:trial-date-set
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "My trial is coming up — what do I need to do to be ready?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
If you need a person in Ontario to come to the trial as a witness, you may serve them with a summons to witness (Form 53A). The summons tells them the time and place of the trial. It may also require them to bring documents or other things they have about the case, if the summons lists them. You need the court's leave to serve a summons for an original record or document that can be proved by a certified copy. The summons must be served on the witness personally, not by an alternative to personal service. At the same time, you must pay or offer the witness attendance money set under Tariff A.
```

### `answer:civil:both:trial-date-set:your-deadline`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:both:trial-date-set
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "My trial is coming up — what do I need to do to be ready?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
If your expert will testify on something not in their report, serve a supplementary report on every other party. Do this at least 45 days before the first day of trial. This is the latest it can be done; earlier is fine. A responding supplementary report must be served at least 15 days before trial. Otherwise the expert cannot testify on that issue without the trial judge's leave. The time can be extended by the judge at a pre-trial conference, by the court on a motion, or by the parties' written consent. But consent cannot move the trial date.

If your action is under the simplified procedure and you set it down for trial, serve a trial record on every party and file it with proof of service. Do this at least 10 days before the first day of trial. This applies only to an action under the simplified procedure, and only to the party who set it down. It is the latest it can be done; earlier is fine. Witness affidavits, including any outstanding expert affidavits, must be delivered by the dates the pre-trial judge fixed.

If you want to use business records, such as invoices or account records, under the Evidence Act's business-records rule, give every other party notice that you plan to. Do this at least 7 days before the day you tender the records in evidence. The Act requires at least seven days notice of your plan. It does not name the trial date. The notice must come before the records are offered in evidence. So notice given at least 7 days before the first day of trial covers every day of the trial. Giving notice later, even because of a Sunday or holiday, leaves fewer than 7 days. This notice is set by a statute, the Evidence Act. So it is counted under the Legislation Act, 2006, not under the court rules' counting described below. The day the notice is given is not counted, and the day the evidence is offered is. Without the notice, the business-records rule does not apply. Any other party can have the records produced for inspection within five days after giving notice to produce them.

If you want to use a report signed by a doctor or other health practitioner, give every other party notice. Do this at least 10 days before the day you tender the report in evidence. The Act requires at least ten days notice to all other parties before the report is admitted. It does not name the trial date. Notice given at least 10 days before the first day of trial covers every day of the trial. Giving notice later, even because of a Sunday or holiday, leaves fewer than 10 days. This notice is set by a statute, the Evidence Act. So it is counted under the Legislation Act, 2006, not under the court rules' counting described below. The day the notice is given is not counted, and the day the report is offered is. The report also needs the court's leave to be admitted. When notice is given, the other parties can get a copy of the report, unless the court orders otherwise. A practitioner who signed a report cannot testify at trial unless the report was given to the other parties this way. The trial judge can allow it anyway.

If you claim special damages and have further amounts or details not in your pleading, deliver notice of them. Do this at least 10 days before the first day of trial. The notice must be delivered right away once the amounts become known, and in any event not less than ten days before trial.

You may want to call the other side as a witness, or its officer, director, employee, sole proprietor or partner. If so, serve them with a summons to witness. Or serve a notice of intention to call them on the other side or its lawyer. Do this at least 10 days before the first day of trial. The 10 days apply to the notice of intention. Attendance money under Tariff A must be paid or offered at the same time. If the person is already at the trial, no summons or attendance money is needed.

If your action is under the simplified procedure and you want to examine or cross-examine someone who gave an affidavit, give notice to the party who filed the affidavit. Do this at least 10 days before the first day of trial. This applies only to an action under the simplified procedure. The party who filed the affidavit then arranges for that person to attend. It is the latest it can be done; earlier is fine.

Times set by the Rules of Civil Procedure are counted under those rules. The first day is not counted. If a time counted forward ends on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, it ends on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (c)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the safe course is to act by the last day before it that is not a holiday. For a period of seven days or less, holidays are not counted at all (r. 3.01 (1) (b)). Except for the document that starts a case, a document served after 4 p.m. or on a holiday counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (d)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
```

### `answer:family:applicant:served-waiting-for-answer:whats-happening`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:applicant:served-waiting-for-answer
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "My ex has been served — how long do they have to answer?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
Your application has been served on the respondent, and their time to answer has not run out yet. The respondent must serve an answer on every other party and file it within 30 days after being served with the application. If the application was served outside Canada or the United States, that time is 60 days. In an application to dispense with a parent's consent before adoption placement, the time is 20 days. It is 40 days if served outside Canada or the United States. To count the days, day one is the day after the respondent was served. If the last day falls on a day when court offices are closed, the time ends on the next day they are open.
```

### `answer:family:applicant:served-waiting-for-answer:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:applicant:served-waiting-for-answer
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "My ex has been served — how long do they have to answer?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
If your application claims support, property, or exclusive possession of the matrimonial home and its contents, the respondent must serve and file a financial statement. They must do it within the same time as the answer, even if they do not serve an answer. If your application makes a property claim under Part I of the Family Law Act, you must serve the respondent with the papers rule 13 (3.3) lists, unless the court orders otherwise. You must do this no later than 30 days after the day your financial statement had to be served. One of those papers is the statement closest to the valuation date for each account you had then. This covers each bank or other financial account, pension, retirement or other savings plan, and any other savings or investment. For any other property claim, you must serve the information needed to support the claim within the same 30 days, unless the court orders otherwise. With those papers you must serve a certificate of financial disclosure (Form 13A). You must also file that certificate no later than six days before a case conference. Some cases need the mandatory information program. One example is a case with a claim about parenting, support, net family property or the matrimonial home. Some parties are not covered, such as parties in a case going ahead on consent, or where the only claims are for a divorce or costs. Where the program applies, each party must attend no later than 45 days after the case is started. Until your certificate of attendance is filed, you must not take any step in the case. The exception is making an appointment for a case conference. The court may, on a motion, excuse a party from this because of urgency or hardship, or for another reason in the interest of justice.
```

> whom. If it has those the wrong way round, nothing else about it matters.

### `answer:family:applicant:served-waiting-for-answer:your-deadline`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:applicant:served-waiting-for-answer
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "My ex has been served — how long do they have to answer?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
The respondent's time to serve an answer on every other party and file it. They have 30 days after the day the respondent was served with the application. If the respondent was served outside Canada and the United States, the time is 60 days. A respondent added by another party’s answer has 14 days. That becomes 30 days if they were served outside Canada and the United States. Other times apply to an application to dispense with a parent’s consent before adoption placement. Service rules decide when the time starts. Papers left at the home with an adult, with a copy mailed, count as served on the fifth day after mailing. Papers left with the respondent after 4 p.m. count as served the next day. If that day is one when court offices are closed, service counts on the next open day. For mail with an acknowledgment card, the rules set no separate start day. The general rule for mail is the fifth day after mailing. That service counts only once the card signed by the respondent is filed. If the application claims support, property or the matrimonial home, the respondent’s financial statement is due in the same time. The parties can agree in writing to change the time. The court can also give more time.

Attend the mandatory information program. You have 45 days after the day the case was started. This applies only to some cases. They are cases about parenting, support, net family property, the matrimonial home or a restraining order. It also covers a motion to change that is not only about child or spousal support. It does not apply to a case on consent. It does not apply where the only claims are for a divorce, costs, or putting an agreement or order into an order. It does not apply where the only claims are about a family arbitration, unless the court orders otherwise. It does not apply in an international child abduction case. It does not apply to the Director of the Family Responsibility Office, or to an agency under s. 33 (3) of the Family Law Act. It does not apply to a person who has already attended. File your certificate of attendance as soon as you can. File it no later than 2 p.m. on the second day before the case conference. The court can excuse a party because of urgency or hardship, or for another reason in the interest of justice. You book your own appointment and the respondent’s. Serve notice of the respondent’s appointment with the application. Until your certificate is filed, you cannot take another step in the case. The one exception is booking a case conference. The court can order otherwise on a motion. If you claim support and no property, the income papers in r. 13 (3.1) should have gone with your financial statement. If they did not, serve them now. In any case, serve them before the case conference.

If your application makes a property claim, serve the respondent with the property papers the rule lists. You have 30 days after the day your financial statement was due, which is the day you served the application. For a claim under Part I of the Family Law Act, the rule lists the papers. One example is the statement closest to the valuation date for each bank or other account. For any other property claim, serve the information needed to support the claim. If there is also a support claim, serve the income papers in r. 13 (3.1) with it. Serve a certificate of financial disclosure (Form 13A) with the papers. The court can order otherwise.

Times set by the Family Law Rules are counted under those rules. The first day is the day after the event (r. 3 (1)). If the last day of a period falls on a day court offices are closed, the period ends on the next day they are open (r. 3 (3)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the rules do not clearly say how this applies, so the safe course is to act by the last open day before it. For a period of less than seven days, Saturdays, Sundays and other days when all court offices are closed are not counted (r. 3 (2)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
```

> Defence, Form 9A), whether it speaks _to_ you or _about_ you, and who served
> whom. If it has those the wrong way round, nothing else about it matters.

- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "My ex has been served — how long do they have to answer?"

If the respondent's answer makes a claim against you, you may serve and file a reply (Form 10A) within 10 days after being served with the answer. If the answer claims support, property, or exclusive possession of the matrimonial home against you, you must serve and file a financial statement. You must do it within those same 10 days, even if you do not serve a reply. If the respondent does not serve and file an answer, some things follow unless a court orders otherwise. They are not entitled to further notice of steps in the case, except service of an order, and may not take part in the case in any way. The court may deal with the case without them, and a date may be set for an uncontested trial.

### `answer:family:applicant:no-answer-filed:whats-happening`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:applicant:no-answer-filed
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "The time is up and my ex never answered — what happens now?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
The respondent's time to serve and file an answer has passed, and no answer has been filed. When a respondent does not serve and file an answer, some things follow unless a court orders otherwise. The respondent is not entitled to further notice of steps in the case, except service of an order. They may not take part in the case in any way. The court may deal with the case without them, and a date may be set for an uncontested trial. An uncontested trial is a trial where only the party making the claim gives evidence and makes submissions. Court office staff must refuse an answer the respondent asks to file late. Late means after the time the rules set. But a later time may be set by a written consent of the parties, a statute that applies to the case, or a court order. Then late means after that later time.
```

### `answer:family:applicant:no-answer-filed:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:applicant:no-answer-filed
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "The time is up and my ex never answered — what happens now?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
In the Ontario Court of Justice, the clerk acts on or before the first court date. If no answer has been filed, the clerk sends the case to a judge to decide on affidavit evidence. Or, if you ask, the clerk sets a case conference instead. The same applies to a fast track case in the Family Court of the Superior Court of Justice. A case there is fast track unless the application claims a divorce, makes a property claim, or makes a family arbitration claim. These steps do not apply to enforcements or to cases under the Child, Youth and Family Services Act, 2017. Rules 39 (2) and 40 (2) list a few other cases they do not cover. Under the conference rule, when no answer is filed, the clerk must, if you ask, schedule a case conference or set a date for an uncontested trial. In an uncontested divorce case, you can instead ask the clerk to prepare the documents for a judge. A settlement conference or trial management conference is held only if the court orders it. At an uncontested trial, evidence may be given by affidavit in Form 14A or Form 23C. Forms 35.1 and 35.1A may also be used if they apply. But the court may direct that oral evidence must be given. In a divorce case, you must file an affidavit in Form 36, because the respondent filed no answer. It must confirm that the facts in your application are correct, except as the affidavit says. It must also give the other facts rule 36 (5) lists. With the affidavit you must file three copies of a draft divorce order (Form 25A) and a stamped envelope addressed to each party. Will the divorce order have a support order in it? Then also file an extra copy of the draft divorce order and two copies of a draft support deduction order. Where the mandatory information program applies, you must not take any step until your certificate of attendance is filed, except making an appointment for a case conference.
```

### `answer:family:applicant:no-answer-filed:what-happens-after`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:applicant:no-answer-filed
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "The time is up and my ex never answered — what happens now?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
If your application claims a divorce, two papers must be filed before the divorce is granted. One is a marriage certificate or marriage registration certificate. The other is a report on earlier divorce cases started by either spouse. The certificate is not needed if your application says it is impractical to get one and explains why. In that case, your Form 36 affidavit must give enough facts to prove the marriage. Once those papers and the affidavit papers are filed, the clerk prepares a certificate (Form 36A) and presents the documents to a judge. The judge may grant the divorce as set out in the draft order, or have the clerk return the documents to you to make needed corrections. The judge may also change the draft order or refuse the divorce. Before doing either, the judge must first let you file another affidavit, or come to court to explain why the order should be made without change.
```

### `answer:family:respondent:answer-time-missed:whats-happening`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:respondent:answer-time-missed
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I missed the deadline to answer — can I still take part in my family case?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
The time to serve and file your answer has passed, and you have not filed one. Because you did not serve and file an answer, four results apply, with the changes needed to fit, unless a court orders otherwise. First, you are not entitled to any more notice of steps in the case. But an order made in the case must still be served on you, unless the court orders otherwise. Second, you are not entitled to take part in the case in any way. Third, the court may deal with the case without you. Fourth, a date may be set for an uncontested trial of the case.
```

### `answer:family:respondent:answer-time-missed:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:respondent:answer-time-missed
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I missed the deadline to answer — can I still take part in my family case?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
Court office staff must refuse a document filed after the time set in the rules. They must also refuse it after any later time set in a written consent of the parties. The same applies after a later time set by a court order or by a statute that applies to the case. The parties may agree in writing to change a time set in the rules, but rule 3 (6) lists some times they cannot change. The court may make an order to lengthen or shorten a time set in the rules, subject to any limits the rules set. You may be able to show that a document was served on you as the rules allow, but did not come to your notice. Or you may show that it came to your notice only after the date that service took effect. If you show either one, the court may, on motion, lengthen a time or set aside the results of missing a step. It may also adjourn, or make any other order that is just. The application may claim support, or make a property claim. Or it may claim exclusive possession of the matrimonial home and its contents. If that claim is made against you, you had to serve and file a financial statement within the time for an answer, whether or not you serve an answer. If you have not served or filed it, the court may, on motion, order you to do so. If the court makes that order, it must also order you to pay costs.
```

### `answer:family:both:settlement-conference-scheduled:whats-happening`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:both:settlement-conference-scheduled
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "We have a settlement conference — what do I need to file and bring?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
One purpose of a settlement conference is to explore settling the case. Other purposes include settling or narrowing the issues in dispute. Another is making sure the relevant evidence is shared. It can also settle or narrow issues about expert evidence or reports the parties plan to use at trial. If the case does not settle, it can name the witnesses and other evidence for trial. It can also estimate how long the trial will take, and schedule it. The conference may be run by someone other than a judge, unless a party asks for a judge. That person must be named for this by the regional senior judge. One kind of person who can do it is a lawyer with at least 10 years of family law work, whose licence is not suspended.
```

### `answer:family:both:settlement-conference-scheduled:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:both:settlement-conference-scheduled
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "We have a settlement conference — what do I need to file and bring?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
Each party must serve and file a brief for the conference. If you asked for the conference, do this no later than six days before it. If no party asked, the six-day time is for the applicant or the party who made the motion. The other party must do it no later than four days before the conference. The general brief is Form 17C. Form 17D is the brief for a protection application or status review. Your last financial statement may be more than 60 days old by the time the conference is held. If so, you must update it by the same six-day or four-day time as your brief. If nothing has changed, serve and file an affidavit saying it has not changed and is still true. If the changes are only minor, serve and file an affidavit with the details. Otherwise, serve and file a new financial statement. If you are a party to a property claim under Part I of the Family Law Act, you must also serve and file a net family property statement (Form 13B) by that same time. If you already served one and it has not changed, you can instead serve and file an affidavit saying it is still true. This does not apply if the property claim arises within a claim under the Arbitration Act, 1991 or the Family Law Act about a family arbitration, its agreement or its award. Once the parties have served and filed these statements, they must file a joint comparison of net family property statements (Form 13C) no later than six days before the conference. If you cannot agree on a joint one, each party must serve and file their own Form 13C by the same six-day or four-day time as the brief. You may have served a corrected, updated or new version of certain financial disclosure documents, or extra documents. If so, you must serve and file an updated certificate of financial disclosure (Form 13A) by the same six-day or four-day time as your brief. Before the conference, you must talk or write to every other party, or make your best efforts to. Cover requests for financial disclosure. Also cover settling the issues in dispute, both for now and for good. You do not have to do this if a court order forbids that contact. You also do not have to if there is a risk of domestic violence by a party who has no licensed representative. If a party does not do this, the court may make orders that fit. These include putting off the conference until it is done, and ordering costs whether or not the conference is put off. You must also give a confirmation of conference (Form 17F). First give a copy to every other party by mail, fax, email or any other way, except in a child protection case. Then give it to the clerk no later than 2 p.m., three days before the conference. You can deliver it to the court office or email it there. You can also submit it through the Justice Services Online website or the Ontario Courts Public Portal, whichever is available. Unless the court orders otherwise, the conference will not be held if the clerk does not get it this way and on time. In a property claim under Part I of the Family Law Act, bring any document that supports your position on a disputed property value or debt amount. Also bring any document rule 13 requires to be served, if there is a dispute about whether it was served. The parties must come to the conference, unless the court orders otherwise. If you have a licensed representative, they must come too. They must have full knowledge of and authority in the case. You may want to call a litigation expert as a witness at trial. If so, at least six days before the conference, you must serve the expert's signed report on all other parties and file it. The report must contain at least what rule 20.2 (2) lists. When you serve it, include any written statement of facts the opinion is based on. Also include any document the expert relied on. You do not need to include papers already served on that party. On a claim about decision-making responsibility, parenting time or contact with a child, a litigation expert's opinion can only be given by a joint litigation expert, unless the court orders otherwise. The same applies to any other matter the court names. To call a participant expert at trial, serve notice of that on all other parties at least six days before the conference. If you want to use that expert's written opinion at trial, also serve it on all other parties and file it by then. If another party asks, serve them a copy of any papers that support that expert's opinion evidence.
```

### `answer:family:both:settlement-conference-scheduled:your-deadline`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:both:settlement-conference-scheduled
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "We have a settlement conference — what do I need to file and bring?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
If you asked for the settlement conference, serve and file your settlement conference brief. If no one asked for the conference, this time is for the applicant or the party who made the motion. Do this at least 6 days before the date of the settlement conference. Your last financial statement may be more than 60 days old by the conference. If so, update it by this same day. Serve and file an affidavit saying nothing has changed, an affidavit with the changes, or a new statement. If there is a property claim under Part I of the Family Law Act, also serve and file your net family property statement (Form 13B) by the same day. Or serve and file an affidavit that it has not changed. If you have served corrected, updated or extra financial disclosure, serve and file an updated certificate of financial disclosure (Form 13A) by the same day. Before the conference, talk or write to every other party, or make your best effort to. Discuss requests for financial disclosure and settling the issues for now, and settling them for good. You do not have to if a court order forbids it. You also do not have to if there is a risk of domestic violence by a party with no licensed representative. In a Part I property claim, bring to the conference any paper that supports your side on a disputed property value or debt amount. Also bring any financial disclosure paper whose service is disputed. The parties can agree in writing to change this time. The court can also change it.

If you are the other party, serve and file your settlement conference brief. Do this at least 4 days before the date of the settlement conference. The extra steps listed above apply to you too. Where they say "by the same day", your day is this 4-day one. The parties can agree in writing to change this time. The court can also change it.

Give a copy of the confirmation of conference (Form 17F) to every other party. Then give it to the clerk no later than 2 p.m. Do this at least 3 days before the date of the settlement conference. The parties cannot change this time by agreement. Unless the court orders otherwise, the conference will not go ahead without it.

If there is a property claim under Part I of the Family Law Act, file a joint comparison of net family property statements (Form 13C). Do this at least 6 days before the date of the settlement conference. If the parties cannot agree on a joint one, each party serves and files their own. The party who asked for the conference does it 6 days before. If no one asked, that is the applicant or the party who made the motion. The other party does it 4 days before. The parties can agree in writing to change this time. The court can also change it.

If you want to call a litigation expert at trial, serve the expert's signed report on all other parties and file it. Do this at least 6 days before the date of the settlement conference. For a participant expert, serve notice on all other parties by the same day. Also serve and file any written opinion from that expert that you want to use. The parties cannot change this time by agreement. It can be extended only by an order made at the settlement conference, with an order about costs. The trial judge or the judge managing the case can order otherwise.

Times set by the Family Law Rules are counted under those rules. The first day is the day after the event (r. 3 (1)). If the last day of a period falls on a day court offices are closed, the period ends on the next day they are open (r. 3 (3)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the rules do not clearly say how this applies, so the safe course is to act by the last open day before it. For a period of less than seven days, Saturdays, Sundays and other days when all court offices are closed are not counted (r. 3 (2)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
```

- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
If a judge runs the conference, the judge may, if it is right to do so, order document disclosure or questioning. The judge may also set times for steps in the case, or give directions for the next steps. If notice has been served, the judge may also make a final order or a temporary order. Costs are awarded at a conference only if a party was not prepared, did not serve required papers, or did not make required disclosure. The same goes if a party helped make the conference unproductive, or did not follow the rules in some other way. In that case, if a judge runs the conference, the judge must order that party to pay the costs of the conference right away. An agreement reached at the conference does not take effect until the parties sign it and it is witnessed. In a case with a special party or a child party, the court must also approve it. No brief or evidence prepared for the conference may be shown to any other judge. The same goes for anything said at it. The only exceptions are an agreement reached at the conference, or an order. A judge who runs the conference on an issue may not hear that issue, except as rule 17 (25) allows. A case cannot be scheduled for trial unless a settlement conference has been held or a judge has ordered it.
```

### `answer:family:both:bringing-a-motion:whats-happening`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:both:bringing-a-motion
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I need a temporary order before the case is over — how do I bring a motion?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
You may make a motion if you want a temporary order for a claim made in an application. You may also make one to get directions on how to carry on the case, or to change a temporary order. A motion may be made by a party to the case or by a person with an interest in the case. In most cases, no motion papers may be served and no motion may be heard until a conference on the main issues in the case is done. That wait does not apply if the court finds there is urgency or hardship. It also does not apply if the court finds a case conference is not needed for another reason in the interest of justice. Nor does it apply to the motions listed in rule 14 (6). These include a motion made without notice, made on consent, or unopposed, or one limited to procedural, uncomplicated or unopposed matters. They also include a motion for summary judgment and any motion in a child protection case.
```

### `answer:family:both:bringing-a-motion:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:both:bringing-a-motion
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I need a temporary order before the case is over — how do I bring a motion?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
A motion needs a notice of motion (Form 14) and an affidavit (Form 14A), and it may be supported by more evidence. If your motion is only about procedural, uncomplicated or unopposed matters, you may use a motion form (Form 14B) instead. An affidavit must, as much as possible, contain only what the person signing it knows personally. Unless the court orders otherwise, you must serve all the evidence in support of the motion with the notice of motion. For a motion with notice, you must serve these papers on all other parties no later than six days before the motion date. You must file them as soon as possible after you serve them, but no later than four days before the motion date. You must also talk or write to every other party about the issues in dispute in the motion, or make your best efforts to. You do not have to if a court order forbids it, or if there is a risk of domestic violence by a party who has no licensed representative. Before you give the clerk the confirmation of motion (Form 14C), you must give a copy to every other party by mail, fax, email or any other method. That copy step does not apply in child protection cases, except applications for an order under sections 53.1 to 53.5 of Ontario Regulation 155/18. You must give the clerk the confirmation of motion no later than 2 p.m. three days before the motion date. You can deliver it to the court office, email it to the court office, or submit it through the Justice Services Online website or the Ontario Courts Public Portal, whichever is available. Unless the court orders otherwise, the motion will not be heard if the clerk does not get the confirmation on time. A motion may be made without notice in the cases rule 14 (12) lists. These include when the nature or circumstances of the motion make notice unnecessary or not reasonably possible. For a motion without notice, you must file the papers on or before the motion date, unless the court orders otherwise.
```

### `answer:family:both:bringing-a-motion:your-deadline`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:both:bringing-a-motion
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I need a temporary order before the case is over — how do I bring a motion?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
Serve your notice of motion and affidavit (or your motion form) on all other parties. Do this at least 6 days before the date the motion will be heard. In most cases, you cannot serve a motion or have it heard until a conference on the main issues is done. The court can allow it sooner for urgency, hardship or another reason in the interest of justice. The wait does not apply to the motions the rule lists. Examples are motions without notice, on consent, unopposed or procedural (Form 14B). It also does not apply to a motion for summary judgment, or to change an order for fraud, mistake or lack of notice. Before the motion, talk or write to every other party about the issues, or make your best effort to. You do not have to if a court order forbids it. You also do not have to if there is a risk of domestic violence by a party with no licensed representative. Where the information program applies, you cannot bring a motion until your certificate is filed. The court can order otherwise, for example for urgency or hardship. Your last financial statement may be more than 30 days old when the motion is heard. If so, update it by this same day with an affidavit or a new statement. If the motion claims support, property or exclusive possession of the matrimonial home, serve and file a financial statement with it. Do the same if it asks to change temporary support. For a motion without notice, file the papers on or before the motion date. If the court then makes an order, serve it right away on every party affected. Serve all the motion papers with it, unless the court orders otherwise. The order sets a return date within 14 days, or on a date the court chooses. The parties can agree in writing to change this time. The court can also change it.

File your motion papers. File them as soon as you can after you serve them. Do this at least 4 days before the date the motion will be heard. The parties can agree in writing to change this time. The court can also change it.

Give a copy of the confirmation of motion (Form 14C) to every other party. Then give it to the clerk no later than 2 p.m. Do this at least 3 days before the date the motion will be heard. The parties cannot change this time by agreement. Unless the court orders otherwise, the motion will not be heard without it. If you used a notice of motion and got a response, any reply is due by this same time. If you used a motion form (Form 14B), you cannot reply to a response.

Times set by the Family Law Rules are counted under those rules. The first day is the day after the event (r. 3 (1)). If the last day of a period falls on a day court offices are closed, the period ends on the next day they are open (r. 3 (3)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the rules do not clearly say how this applies, so the safe course is to act by the last open day before it. For a period of less than seven days, Saturdays, Sundays and other days when all court offices are closed are not counted (r. 3 (2)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
```

A response to a notice of motion must be served and filed no later than four days before the motion date. If you used a motion form (Form 14B), you may not serve or file a reply. - **Status:** draft

- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I was served with a motion — how do I respond, and by when?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
If you were served with a notice of motion, you must serve and file your response no later than four days before the motion date. If you were served with a motion form, you must serve and file your response no later than seven days after it was served on you. Unless the court orders otherwise, you must serve all your evidence in response to the motion. Evidence on a motion may be given by an affidavit or other written evidence the court can accept, or by a transcript of questioning under rule 20. With the court's permission, it may also be given by oral evidence. An affidavit must, as much as possible, contain only what the person signing it knows personally. It may also contain what the person learned from someone else, but only if it names that source and says the person signing believes it is true. For a contempt motion under rule 31, rule 14 (19) adds one more condition for this kind of information.
```

### `answer:family:both:responding-to-a-motion:your-deadline`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:both:responding-to-a-motion
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I was served with a motion — how do I respond, and by when?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
If you were served with a notice of motion (Form 14), serve and file your response. Do this at least 4 days before the date the motion will be heard. Your last financial statement may be more than 30 days old when the motion is heard. If so, update it by this same day with an affidavit or a new statement. The motion may claim support, property or exclusive possession of the matrimonial home against you. If so, serve and file your financial statement by this same day, even if you do not respond. If the motion asks to change temporary support, see the rule below as well. Meet whichever time is earlier. The parties can agree in writing to change this time. The court can also change it.

If you were served with a motion form (Form 14B), serve and file your response. You have 7 days after the day the motion form was served on you. Every day counts, including Saturdays and Sundays. The parties can agree in writing to change this time. The court can also change it.

If the motion asks to change temporary support, serve and file your financial statement as soon as you can after you are served. Serve and file your affidavit in response at the same time. Do this at least 2 days before the date the motion will be heard. The rule for this kind of motion sets 2 days before the motion for both papers. The general rule for a response sets 4 days. To be safe, serve and file both by the 4-day date. The parties can agree in writing to change this time. The court can also change it.

Times set by the Family Law Rules are counted under those rules. The first day is the day after the event (r. 3 (1)). If the last day of a period falls on a day court offices are closed, the period ends on the next day they are open (r. 3 (3)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the rules do not clearly say how this applies, so the safe course is to act by the last open day before it. For a period of less than seven days, Saturdays, Sundays and other days when all court offices are closed are not counted (r. 3 (2)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
```

### `answer:family:both:asking-to-change-final-order:whats-happening`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:both:asking-to-change-final-order
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "Things have changed since the final order — how do I ask the court to change it?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
You want the court to change a final order. The same steps apply to a support agreement filed under section 35 of the Family Law Act. They also apply to a family arbitration award filed under section 59.9 of that Act. They do not apply to an order under the Child, Youth and Family Services Act, 2017. The one exception is a final order under section 102 of that Act. You can ask for the change only by a motion to change under rule 15, if that rule allows it. There are two exceptions. First, rule 25 (19) lets the court change an order on a motion in some cases. Examples are an order made by fraud, one with a mistake, or one made without notice. Second, you may want to make related claims that fall outside rule 15 as well. Then you may file an application to deal with the change and those claims together. A motion to change starts where rule 5 says a new case would start. The places rule 5 names include the town or city where a party lives. Is the case about decision-making responsibility, parenting time or contact with a child? Then it starts where the child usually lives. The one exception is set out in section 22 of the Children's Law Reform Act.
```

### `answer:family:both:asking-to-change-final-order:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:both:asking-to-change-final-order
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "Things have changed since the final order — how do I ask the court to change it?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
Unless the parties and any assignee all agree to the change, you must serve and file a motion to change (Form 15). Add all required attachments. Attach a copy of any order or agreement that deals with decision-making responsibility, parenting time, contact or support. Does your motion make a claim about decision-making responsibility, parenting time or contact with a child? Then you must also include the papers rule 35.1 requires. With the motion, you must serve the other party a blank response (Form 15B). You must also serve a blank consent motion to change (Form 15C). These papers must be served by special service, and not by regular service. But you may use regular service on the people listed in rule 8 (6). They include foster parents, band or First Nations, Inuit or Métis community representatives, and certain officials and agencies. Someone other than you must carry out special service of the motion to change. That does not apply if the court orders otherwise. It also does not apply if you or the person served is one of the officials or agencies named in rule 8 (6) (c). An assignee is an agency or person a support order or agreement has been assigned to. If the order or agreement was assigned, you must serve the assignee as if it were a party. You may ask to change child support set out in an order under the Divorce Act (Canada). If that support was recalculated under section 39.1 of the Family Law Act in the 35 days before you file, there is one more step. You must also serve the motion papers on the Director of the Family Responsibility Office. Do you ask to change a final support order or a support agreement? Then you must serve and file a financial statement (Form 13 or 13.1) with your motion. You do not need one if your only support claim is for child support in the table amount. But you do need one if the motion also makes a property claim. You also need one if it claims exclusive possession (sole use) of the matrimonial home and its contents. With the financial statement, you must serve other papers, unless the court orders otherwise. They include the papers in rule 13 (3.1) and a current list of what is owed from the Family Responsibility Office. If you ask to change or cancel arrears, you must also serve proof of your income for each of those years. This is your income tax return with your notice of assessment, and any notice of reassessment. If those notices are unavailable for a year, use the Canada Revenue Agency's Income and Deductions printout with the return instead. If you do not have to file a tax return and chose not to because of the Indian Act (Canada), serve some other proof of income. Serve a certificate of financial disclosure (Form 13A) with those papers. File the certificate no later than six days before a case conference. If your motion is not on consent, you may use an affidavit instead of Parts C and D of Form 15. It must have the facts the court needs to make the order you ask for. Rules 14 (18) and (19) also apply to that affidavit. If the parties and any assignee all agree to the change, the steps are different. The parties must then file a consent motion to change (Form 15C) and the other papers rule 15 (17) lists. If the agreed change is to a final support order or support agreement, each party must file a financial statement with Form 15C. This does not apply if you both say in the form that you agree not to. If the agreed change is only about child support, they must file Form 15D and the papers rule 15 (18) lists. With Form 15D, no financial statements need to be served or filed.
```

### `answer:family:both:asking-to-change-final-order:your-deadline`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:both:asking-to-change-final-order
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "Things have changed since the final order — how do I ask the court to change it?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
Serve and file your motion to change (Form 15). Include all required attachments, a blank response (Form 15B) and a blank consent (Form 15C). If you ask to change decision-making responsibility, parenting time or contact, include the papers rule 35.1 requires. Serve it by special service, not regular service. Someone other than you must serve it, unless the court orders otherwise. If the other party and any assignee agree to the change, you do not serve a motion to change. Instead the parties file a consent motion to change (Form 15C), with the papers the rule lists. If only child support is changing, use Form 15D. If you ask to change support, serve and file your financial statement with the motion. You do not need one if the only support claim is child support in the table amount. Serve the papers the rule lists with it. Examples are the income papers in r. 13 (3.1) and a current schedule of arrears from the Family Responsibility Office. Add a certificate of financial disclosure (Form 13A). If the order or agreement was assigned, serve the assignee as if it were a party.

If the order is a support order under the Family Law Act, you cannot apply to vary it within six months after it was made. The same is true within six months after the last decision on an application to vary it. The court can give permission (leave). This is section 37 (3) of the Family Law Act. The six months are counted under the Legislation Act, 2006 (s. 89 (6)). They end on the day with the same number as the start day. If that month has no such day, they end on its last day.

The other party's time to serve and file a response, or return a signed consent. They have 30 days after the day the other party receives the motion to change and its supporting documents. It is 60 days if they do not live in Canada or the United States. The parties can agree in writing to change the time. The court can also give more time.

If your motion to change makes a claim about parenting, property or support and the clerk gave you an automatic order, serve it on every other party. You have 7 days after the day the automatic order was issued. Serve it promptly after the clerk gives it to you.

Attend the mandatory information program. You have 45 days after the day the case was started. This applies only to some cases. They are cases about parenting, support, net family property, the matrimonial home or a restraining order. It also covers a motion to change that is not only about child or spousal support. It does not apply to a case on consent. It does not apply where the only claims are for a divorce, costs, or putting an agreement or order into an order. It does not apply where the only claims are about a family arbitration, unless the court orders otherwise. It does not apply in an international child abduction case. It does not apply to the Director of the Family Responsibility Office, or to an agency under s. 33 (3) of the Family Law Act. It does not apply to a person who has already attended. File your certificate of attendance as soon as you can. File it no later than 2 p.m. on the second day before the case conference. The court can excuse a party because of urgency or hardship, or for another reason in the interest of justice. Until your certificate is filed, you cannot take another step in the case. The one exception is booking a case conference. The court can order otherwise on a motion. The rule counts the 45 days from when the case started. It says nothing more exact for a motion to change.

Times set by the Family Law Rules are counted under those rules. The first day is the day after the event (r. 3 (1)). If the last day of a period falls on a day court offices are closed, the period ends on the next day they are open (r. 3 (3)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the rules do not clearly say how this applies, so the safe course is to act by the last open day before it. For a period of less than seven days, Saturdays, Sundays and other days when all court offices are closed are not counted (r. 3 (2)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
```

The other party then has time to serve and file a response, or return a signed consent. It is 30 days after they get your motion and its papers, if they live in Canada or the United States. In any other case, it is 60 days. If they do neither, you may file a motion form (Form 14B) asking the court to make the order you asked for in your papers. ### `answer:family:both:served-with-motion-to-change:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft

- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "My ex wants to change our final order — what do I have to do, and by when?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
Do you disagree with the change, or want the court to make an added or different change? Then you must serve and file a response to motion to change (Form 15B), with all required attachments. You must do this within 30 days after you get the motion to change and its papers, if you live in Canada or the United States. In any other case, the limit is 60 days. Do you agree to the change, or have you and the other party agreed to a different change? Then you must fill in the parts of the consent motion to change (Form 15C) that apply to you. Within the same 30 or 60 days, you must return a signed copy to the party making the motion. You must also give a copy of the signed consent to the assignee, if there is one. An assignee is an agency or person a support order or agreement has been assigned to. If the order or agreement was assigned, you must serve your response on the assignee as if it were a party. You may use an affidavit to give the facts that support your side. It can replace Parts C and D of Form 15B, or add to them. Rules 14 (18) and (19) apply to that affidavit. Does the motion ask to change a final support order or a support agreement? Then you must serve and file a financial statement within the same time as your response or consent. Your response (Form 15B) must be served and filed at the same time as the financial statement. This is subject to rule 13 (1.3). Under it, a party making a claim does not have to file a financial statement in one case. That is when their only support claim is for child support in the table amount. That does not apply if there is also a property claim. It also does not apply if there is a claim for exclusive possession (sole use) of the matrimonial home and its contents. The motion may not need a financial statement, but your response may ask to change a support order or support agreement. If so, the financial statement rules apply to you too. With a financial statement, you must serve other papers, unless the court orders otherwise. They include the papers in rule 13 (3.1) and a current list of what is owed from the Family Responsibility Office. If you are the one asking to change or cancel arrears, you must also serve proof of your income for each of those years. This is your income tax return with your notice of assessment, and any notice of reassessment. If those notices are unavailable for a year, use the Canada Revenue Agency's Income and Deductions printout with the return instead. If you do not have to file a tax return and chose not to because of the Indian Act (Canada), serve some other proof of income. Serve a certificate of financial disclosure (Form 13A) with those papers. File the certificate no later than four days before a case conference. Your response may make a claim about decision-making responsibility or parenting time, net family property, a matrimonial home, or support. If it does, the clerk may give you an automatic order (Form 8.0.1). If the clerk gives you one, you must serve it on every other party. Serve it promptly, and no later than seven days after it is issued.
```

### `answer:family:both:served-with-motion-to-change:your-deadline`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:both:served-with-motion-to-change
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "My ex wants to change our final order — what do I have to do, and by when?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
If you do not agree, or want the court to make an added or different change, serve and file a response (Form 15B). If you agree, return a signed consent motion to change (Form 15C) to the party making the motion. Give a copy to any assignee. You have 30 days after the day you receive the motion to change and its supporting documents. It is 60 days if you do not live in Canada or the United States. The motion may ask to change support, or your response may ask for a support change. If so, your financial statement is due in the same time. Serve the papers the rule lists with it. Examples are the income papers in r. 13 (3.1) and a current schedule of arrears from the Family Responsibility Office. Add a certificate of financial disclosure (Form 13A). Your response may ask for its own change to parenting, property or support. If the clerk then issues an automatic order, serve it promptly, and no later than 7 days after it is issued. Where the information program applies, your certificate must be filed before you serve the response. This is explained below. The parties can agree in writing to change the time. The court can also give more time.

Attend the mandatory information program. You have 45 days after the day the case was started. This applies only to some cases. They are cases about parenting, support, net family property, the matrimonial home or a restraining order. It also covers a motion to change that is not only about child or spousal support. It does not apply to a case on consent. It does not apply where the only claims are for a divorce, costs, or putting an agreement or order into an order. It does not apply where the only claims are about a family arbitration, unless the court orders otherwise. It does not apply in an international child abduction case. It does not apply to the Director of the Family Responsibility Office, or to an agency under s. 33 (3) of the Family Law Act. It does not apply to a person who has already attended. File your certificate of attendance as soon as you can. File it no later than 2 p.m. on the second day before the case conference. The court can excuse a party because of urgency or hardship, or for another reason in the interest of justice. Until your certificate is filed, you cannot take any step in the case except booking a case conference. The rule's other exception is for an answer. It does not mention a response to a motion to change. So where the program applies, attend it and file your certificate before your response is due. Or ask the court on a motion to excuse you. The rule counts the 45 days from when the case started. It says nothing more exact for a motion to change.

Times set by the Family Law Rules are counted under those rules. The first day is the day after the event (r. 3 (1)). If the last day of a period falls on a day court offices are closed, the period ends on the next day they are open (r. 3 (3)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the rules do not clearly say how this applies, so the safe course is to act by the last open day before it. For a period of less than seven days, Saturdays, Sundays and other days when all court offices are closed are not counted (r. 3 (2)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
```

Say you do not serve and file a response, or return a consent, as required. Then these things apply, unless a court orders otherwise. You do not get notice of more steps in the case, except service of an order. You cannot take part in the case in any way. The court may deal with the case without you, and a date may be set for an uncontested trial. The party making the motion may also file a motion form (Form 14B) asking the court to make the order they asked for in their papers. They cannot do this if an assignee has filed a notice of financial interest and opposes the change. If the motion is opposed, a judge must hold at least one conference. Even after you serve and file a response, the parties and any assignee may still agree before the hearing. They may then go ahead on consent by filing the papers rule 15 (19) lists.
