### `answer:family:both:trial-scheduled:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:both:trial-scheduled
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "Our family case is going to trial — what do I have to file before it starts?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
If you are the applicant, you must serve and file a trial record at least 20 days before the trial starts, or before the trial sitting if that is earlier. It must have a table of contents and the documents the rule lists. They include the application, answer and reply, if any, any agreed statement of facts, and any temporary order about a matter still in dispute. If you are a respondent, you may serve, file and add any listed document that is not already in the trial record, no later than seven days before the trial starts. Your last financial statement may be more than 40 days old by the start of the trial or trial sitting, whichever is earlier. If so, you must serve and file an update no later than 30 days before that date. If nothing has changed, the update is an affidavit saying the last statement has not changed and is still true. If the changes are only minor, it is an affidavit with details of the changes. For any other change, it is a new financial statement. If there is a property claim under Part I of the Family Law Act, each party must serve and file a net family property statement (Form 13B) no later than 30 days before the trial or trial sitting, whichever is earlier. If you already served one and it has not changed, you may instead serve and file an affidavit by then saying it has not changed and is still true. This does not apply if the property claim arises within a claim about a family arbitration, arbitration agreement or arbitration award. If you want a witness to give evidence in court, or to be questioned and bring documents or other things, you must serve them with a summons to witness (Form 23). A summons to a witness outside Ontario under the Interprovincial Summonses Act uses Form 23A instead. The summons and the witness fee must be served at least seven days before the witness must be in court or at a questioning. For a person outside Ontario who will not come here to be questioned, the court may set a different notice time. Unless the court orders otherwise, the summons must be served by leaving a copy with the witness. For a child, or a person who is or appears to be mentally incapable in respect of an issue in the case, a copy also goes to certain others, as rule 6 (3) (a) sets out. Someone other than you must serve it, unless the court orders otherwise or an exception for officials and agencies applies. The witness fee includes $50 for each day the witness is needed, plus travel money. It also includes $100 a night for meals and a place to stay, if the witness lives outside the city or town of the trial and must stay overnight. To call the other party as a witness, you may serve them with a summons, or serve their lawyer with a notice of intention to call them at least 10 days before the trial starts. You may ask the court for an order letting a party or witness give evidence by affidavit or another way that does not need them to come in person. That evidence may be used at trial only if it follows that order and is served at least 30 days before the trial starts. It must also be evidence that would have been allowed if the person gave it in court. A supplementary report by a litigation expert must be signed by the expert, served on all other parties and filed. This must be done at least 30 days before the trial starts, or at least 14 days before in a child protection case.
```

### `answer:family:both:trial-scheduled:your-deadline`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:both:trial-scheduled
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "Our family case is going to trial — what do I have to file before it starts?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
If you are the applicant, serve and file a trial record with a table of contents and the documents the rule lists. Do this at least 20 days before the start of the trial or of the trial sitting, whichever is earlier. The parties can agree in writing to change this time. The court can also change it. Separately, an offer to settle counts under the costs rule in r. 24 (12) only if it is made at least 7 days before the trial. It must also stay open until the trial starts.

If you are the respondent and want to add a document that is not already in the trial record, serve and file it. Do this at least 7 days before the start of the trial. Only papers of the kinds listed for the trial record can be added. The parties can agree in writing to change this time. The court can also change it.

Update your financial information by serving and filing an affidavit or a new financial statement. Do this at least 30 days before the start of the trial or of the trial sitting, whichever is earlier. This applies only if your last financial statement would be more than 40 days old by then. That is the start of the trial or trial sitting, whichever is earlier. The parties can agree in writing to change this time. The court can also change it.

If there is a property claim under Part I of the Family Law Act, serve and file a net family property statement (Form 13B), or an affidavit that your last one has not changed. Do this at least 30 days before the start of the trial or of the trial sitting, whichever is earlier. The parties can agree in writing to change this time. The court can also change it.

If your litigation expert has a supplementary report, serve it on all other parties and file it, signed by the expert. Do this at least 30 days before the start of the trial. In a child protection case it is 14 days. The parties cannot change this time by agreement. It can be extended only by an order made at the settlement conference. The trial judge or the judge managing the case can order otherwise.

If you need a witness, serve a summons to witness (Form 23) with the witness fee by leaving it with the witness personally. Do this at least 7 days before the day the witness must be in court or at a questioning. Someone other than you must serve it, unless the court orders otherwise. The court can also order another way of serving it. The opposing party may have a lawyer. To call that party as a witness, you can instead serve their lawyer with a notice of intention to call them. Do that at least 10 days before the trial starts. The parties can agree in writing to change this time. The court can also change it.

If the court ordered that evidence be given by affidavit or another way without coming to court, serve that evidence. Do this at least 30 days before the start of the trial. If you do not, it cannot be used at trial. The parties can agree in writing to change this time. The court can also change it.

Times set by the Family Law Rules are counted under those rules. The first day is the day after the event (r. 3 (1)). If the last day of a period falls on a day court offices are closed, the period ends on the next day they are open (r. 3 (3)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the rules do not clearly say how this applies, so the safe course is to act by the last open day before it. For a period of less than seven days, Saturdays, Sundays and other days when all court offices are closed are not counted (r. 3 (2)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
```

```
A summons stays in effect until the witness has given evidence or been questioned. It ends sooner if it is set aside, if notice is given that it is no longer needed, or if the witness is otherwise no longer needed. If a summons is no longer needed, the party who served it must give the witness written notice as soon as possible, with the reason. ### `answer:family:both:support-order-not-paid:whats-happening`
```

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:both:support-order-not-paid
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "There is a support order but the payments are not being made — who enforces it?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/96f31

```
Ontario has a Director of the Family Responsibility Office. The Director's job is to enforce support orders filed in the Director's office. This applies when the order, and any support deduction order that goes with it, are filed there. The Director pays what is collected to the person it is owed to. The clerk or registrar of the court that made a support order must file it there promptly once it is signed.
```

### `answer:family:both:support-order-not-paid:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:both:support-order-not-paid
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "There is a support order but the payments are not being made — who enforces it?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/96f31

```
While a support order is filed there, only the Director may enforce it. The one exception is someone given the Director's powers under section 4 of the Act. The Director may refuse to enforce all or part of a filed order in some cases the Act lists. They include an order whose meaning is unclear. They also include when the person owed support has not met reasonable requests for facts the Director needs. An order that was withdrawn from the Director's office may be filed there again at any time. The payor or the recipient does this by signing a written notice. A support order and any support deduction order that goes with it must be filed again together. Whoever files or refiles a support order there must give notice right away. It goes to the clerk at any court office where the recipient is enforcing the order. It can be sent by mail or email. It can also be sent online, through Justice Services Online or the Ontario Courts Public Portal, whichever is available. A person owed support who files the order there may have started to enforce it on their own. If the Director asks, they must hand that over to the Director. A payment order is a temporary or final order to pay money to another person, such as a support order. It does not include a provisional order. The Family Law Rules list ways to enforce a payment order. Who uses these ways depends on where the order is. While a support order is filed in the Director's office, only the Director may use them, apart from the exception above. If it is not filed there, the person owed the money may. The ways include a request for a financial statement, seizure and sale, and garnishment. A default hearing can also be used if the order is a support order. When the Director enforces an order, the rules for the person the order favours apply to the Director. Other orders may be enforced in three ways. They are a writ to seize property for a time, a contempt order, and naming a receiver. All of these are in addition to other ways the law provides.
```

```
Using one way to enforce a support order does not stop other ways at the same time or at other times. The Director may enforce arrears that built up before the order was filed there. If an order is withdrawn, the Director must stop enforcing it. But the Director may keep enforcing to collect arrears owed to an agency from a past assignment.
```

### `answer:civil:plaintiff:service-attempted-failed:whats-happening`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:plaintiff:service-attempted-failed
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I cannot find the defendant to serve them — what now?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
Your claim has been issued, and you have tried to serve it on the defendant without success. Under the Rules of Civil Procedure, a statement of claim must be served in one of two ways. One is personal service. The other is one of the alternatives to personal service set out in those rules. A statement of claim must be served within six months after it is issued. If you started with a notice of action, the notice and the statement of claim must be served together within six months after the notice was issued.
```

### `answer:civil:plaintiff:service-attempted-failed:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:plaintiff:service-attempted-failed
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I cannot find the defendant to serve them — what now?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
If you tried to serve the defendant personally at their home and could not, you may leave a copy at that home instead. The copy must be in a sealed envelope addressed to them, left with anyone who appears to be an adult member of the same household. For this method, you must also mail another copy to them at that home on the same day or the next day. Service this way takes effect on the fifth day after the copy is mailed. Another alternative is to mail a copy, with an acknowledgment of receipt card (Form 16A), to the defendant's last known address. That service counts only from the date you get the card back. A corporation's head office, registered office or main place of business may not be found at the last address recorded with the Ministry of Public and Business Service Delivery. If so, you may serve the corporation by mailing a copy to it at that address. For an extra-provincial corporation, the same applies to its attorney for service in Ontario: if the attorney cannot be found at that address, you may mail a copy to the attorney there. If prompt service is impractical for any reason, the court may make an order for substituted service. Where needed in the interest of justice, the court may instead dispense with service, which means excuse it. An order for substituted service must say when service under the order takes effect. If the court dispenses with service, the claim is treated as served on the date of the order, for counting time under the rules. You may have served the claim in a way other than one the rules or an order authorize. If so, the court may make an order validating that service. It may do so if it is satisfied that the claim came to the defendant's notice. It may also do so if the claim was served in a way that it would have come to their notice, except for their own attempts to evade service. The court may by order extend the time to serve, on terms that are just. A motion to extend the time may be made before or after the time runs out.
```

### `answer:civil:plaintiff:service-attempted-failed:your-deadline`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:plaintiff:service-attempted-failed
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I cannot find the defendant to serve them — what now?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
Serve the statement of claim on the defendant. You have 6 months after the day the statement of claim was issued. If you started with a notice of action, serve the notice and the statement of claim together within six months after the notice was issued. The time can be extended by filing a consent. The court can also extend it, before or after the time runs out. If you do not serve the claim in time, a defendant who is not in default can ask the court to dismiss the action for delay.

Set the action down for trial, or the registrar will dismiss it for delay. You have 5 years after the day the action was started. The last day is the anniversary of that day, 5 years later. If that day was February 29, the anniversary is February 28, except in a leap year. This does not apply if the action has already ended some other way. It does not apply if a party files a timetable signed by all parties, and a draft order, at least 30 days before the time ends. The timetable must give a date, no more than two years after the time ends, by which the action will be set down or restored. If the parties do not agree on a timetable, any party can ask for a status hearing before the time ends. It does not apply if you are under a disability at that time. It does not apply to Commercial List actions or class actions. The court can order otherwise. A dismissal can be set aside on a motion under rule 37.14.

Times set by the Rules of Civil Procedure are counted under those rules. The first day is not counted. If a time counted forward ends on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, it ends on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (c)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the safe course is to act by the last day before it that is not a holiday. For a period of seven days or less, holidays are not counted at all (r. 3.01 (1) (b)). Except for the document that starts a case, a document served after 4 p.m. or on a holiday counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (d)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
```

### `answer:civil:plaintiff:service-attempted-failed:what-happens-after`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:plaintiff:service-attempted-failed
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I cannot find the defendant to serve them — what now?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
Service may be proved by an affidavit of the person who served the claim (Form 16B). A defendant who was not served but delivers a defence, notice of intent to defend or notice of appearance is treated as served on the date they deliver it. To deliver means to serve and file with proof of service. Once served, the defendant has a set time to deliver a statement of defence (Form 18A), which depends on where they were served. A defendant who delivers a notice of intent to defend within that time gets 10 more days to deliver a defence.
```

### `answer:civil:plaintiff:defendant-noted-in-default:whats-happening`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:plaintiff:defendant-noted-in-default
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "The defendant was noted in default — how do I get judgment?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
The registrar has noted the defendant in default, and no judgment has been signed or granted yet. A defendant noted in default is deemed to admit the truth of all the facts stated in your statement of claim. They may not deliver a defence or take any other step in the action unless the court gives leave or you consent. The one step they may take without that is a motion to set aside the noting of default, or any judgment obtained because of the default. A defendant noted in default is not entitled to notice of any step in the action, and need not be served with documents in it. There are exceptions. They include when the court orders otherwise, or when a party requires the defendant to attend personally. They also include some documents the rules list, such as an amended pleading or a counterclaim.
```

> **Read this as the person at this stage.** Does every instruction apply to
> you, and could you follow it? Check whose step it is (a plaintiff asks the
> clerk to note a defendant in default with Form 9B; a defendant files the
> Defence, Form 9A), whether it speaks _to_ you or _about_ you, and who served
> whom. If it has those the wrong way round, nothing else about it matters.

### `answer:civil:plaintiff:defendant-noted-in-default:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:plaintiff:defendant-noted-in-default
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "The defendant was noted in default — how do I get judgment?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
For some kinds of claims, you may require the registrar to sign judgment against the defendant. One kind is a claim for a debt or liquidated demand in money (Form 19A). This includes interest, if you claimed it in the statement of claim. Another is a claim to recover possession of land (Form 19B). Another is a claim to recover possession of personal property (Form 19C). The last is a claim for foreclosure, sale or redemption of a mortgage (Forms 64B to 64D, 64G to 64K and 64M). Before the registrar signs, you must file a requisition for default judgment (Form 19D) with the registrar. It must state that the claim is one of the kinds for which default judgment may properly be signed. It must state whether any part of the claim has been paid, and give the date and amount of any partial payment. If you claimed prejudgment interest in the statement of claim, it must set out how the interest is calculated. If you claimed postjudgment interest at a rate other than the one in section 129 of the Courts of Justice Act, it must set out that rate. It must also state whether you want the registrar to fix your costs or want them assessed. If part of the claim has been paid, the default judgment is limited to the rest of the claim. The registrar may decline to sign if unsure whether the claim is one of those kinds. The registrar may also decline if unsure of the amount or rate of interest that can properly be recovered. If the registrar declines, you may move before a judge for judgment under rule 19.05. If the registrar declines and your claim is one of the kinds listed above, you may instead make a motion to the court for default judgment. For any claim with no signed default judgment, you may move before a judge for judgment against the defendant on the statement of claim. If the claim is for unliquidated damages, the motion must be supported by evidence given by affidavit. On a motion for judgment, the facts in your claim being deemed admitted does not by itself entitle you to judgment, unless those facts entitle you to it.
```

### `answer:civil:plaintiff:defendant-noted-in-default:your-deadline`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:plaintiff:defendant-noted-in-default
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "The defendant was noted in default — how do I get judgment?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
Set the action down for trial, or the registrar will dismiss it for delay. You have 5 years after the day the action was started. The last day is the anniversary of that day, 5 years later. If that day was February 29, the anniversary is February 28, except in a leap year. This does not apply if the action has already ended some other way. It does not apply if a party files a timetable signed by all parties, and a draft order, at least 30 days before the time ends. The timetable must give a date, no more than two years after the time ends, by which the action will be set down or restored. If the parties do not agree on a timetable, any party can ask for a status hearing before the time ends. It does not apply if you are under a disability at that time. It does not apply to Commercial List actions or class actions. The court can order otherwise. A dismissal can be set aside on a motion under rule 37.14.

Times set by the Rules of Civil Procedure are counted under those rules. The first day is not counted. If a time counted forward ends on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, it ends on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (c)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the safe course is to act by the last day before it that is not a holiday. For a period of seven days or less, holidays are not counted at all (r. 3.01 (1) (b)). Except for the document that starts a case, a document served after 4 p.m. or on a holiday counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (d)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
```

### `answer:civil:plaintiff:defendant-noted-in-default:what-happens-after`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:plaintiff:defendant-noted-in-default
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "The defendant was noted in default — how do I get judgment?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
When the registrar signs default judgment, the registrar must fix your costs under Tariff A and include them in the judgment. This does not apply if the judgment directs a reference. It also does not apply if you said in the requisition that you want costs assessed. In those cases, the judgment includes costs to be decided on the reference or assessment. On a motion for judgment, the judge may grant judgment, dismiss the action, or order that the action go to trial with oral evidence. If the action goes to trial, a motion for judgment on the statement of claim against the defendant noted in default may be made at the trial. The court may set aside the noting of default on terms that are just. A judgment against a defendant noted in default does not stop you from going after the same defendant for any other relief.
```

### `answer:civil:plaintiff:served-with-counterclaim:whats-happening`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:plaintiff:served-with-counterclaim
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "The defendant is suing me back in the same case — do I have to respond?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
The defendant has made a claim against you in the same case. This is called a counterclaim. A defendant may use it to make any claim against the plaintiff in the main action. The counterclaim goes in the same document as the defence, called a statement of defence and counterclaim.
```

### `answer:civil:plaintiff:served-with-counterclaim:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:plaintiff:served-with-counterclaim
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "The defendant is suing me back in the same case — do I have to respond?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
Deliver means serve and file with proof of service. You must deliver a defence to counterclaim (Form 27C) within 20 days after the statement of defence and counterclaim was served on you. A reply to the defence is required in two cases, and allowed only then. One is if you plan to prove a version of the facts that differs from the one in the defence, unless your claim already sets it out. The other is to raise a matter that might take the defendant by surprise, or that raises an issue no earlier pleading raised. But a new ground of claim, or a fact that conflicts with your claim, must not go in a reply. It must be made by amending your claim. In any other case, you must not deliver a reply. If you do not deliver a reply in time, you are taken to deny the facts set out in the defence. If you do deliver a reply, it must go in one document with your defence to counterclaim, called a reply and defence to counterclaim. That one document is due within the same 20 days. In your defence to counterclaim, you must admit every fact in the counterclaim that you do not dispute. Any fact you do not deny is taken as admitted, unless you say you have no knowledge of it. If the counterclaim is for damages, the amount stays in dispute unless you specifically admit it. If you plan to prove a different version of the facts, denying theirs is not enough. You must set out your own version. You must also set out any point you will rely on to defeat the counterclaim, if it might take the defendant by surprise or raise a new issue. If the 20 days pass, you may still deliver your defence to counterclaim at any time before you are noted in default.
```

### `answer:civil:plaintiff:served-with-counterclaim:your-deadline`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:plaintiff:served-with-counterclaim
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "The defendant is suing me back in the same case — do I have to respond?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
Deliver a defence to counterclaim (Form 27C). You have 20 days after the day the statement of defence and counterclaim was served on you. If you also deliver a reply, put both in one document called a reply and defence to counterclaim. If you do not deliver a defence to counterclaim in time, the defendant can have you noted in default on the counterclaim. You would then be treated as admitting the facts it alleges. Judgment could then be given against you on it. The time can be extended by filing a consent, or by the court.

If you want a jury, deliver a jury notice (Form 47A) before pleadings close. The rule fixes no number of days. The cut-off is the close of pleadings. With a counterclaim, that is not before the defendant replies to your defence to counterclaim, or the 10 days for that reply run out. Delivering the jury notice with your defence to counterclaim avoids any doubt. Some statutes require a trial without a jury. A simplified procedure action cannot have a jury. The exception is a claim for slander, libel, malicious arrest, malicious prosecution or false imprisonment.

If your action is under the simplified procedure, serve every other party with an affidavit of documents. Include copies of the documents in its Schedule A. You pay the cost. You have 10 days after the day pleadings closed. This applies only to an action under the simplified procedure. Pleadings close when every defence has been replied to, or the time for a reply has run out, and every defendant who did not defend has been noted in default. The affidavit must also list the people who might know about the issues, unless the court orders otherwise. A person not named in it cannot be a witness at trial unless the court orders otherwise. The time can be extended by filing a consent, or by the court.

If your action is under the simplified procedure, meet or talk by phone with the other parties. Discuss whether all relevant documents have been shared, and whether any issue can be settled. You have 60 days after the day the first statement of defence or notice of intent to defend was filed. This applies only to an action under the simplified procedure. The general rules for actions also apply to it, unless Rule 76 says otherwise.

If your action is under the simplified procedure, set it down for trial. Do this by serving a notice of readiness for pre-trial conference (Form 76C) on every party and filing it with proof of service. You have 180 days after the day the first statement of defence or notice of intent to defend was filed. This applies only to an action under the simplified procedure. It replaces the usual way of setting down. If you do not do it, any other party may. You must certify in the notice that there was a settlement discussion. The court can extend the time.

If your action is covered by mandatory mediation, choose a mediator with the other parties and hold the mediation session. You have 180 days after the day the first defence was filed. This applies only to actions that Rule 24.1 covers. For example, it covers actions started in Ottawa, Toronto or the County of Essex on or after January 1, 2010. Some kinds of action are left out. The court can exempt an action, or set a different time. The parties can put off the session by filing their written consent with the mediation co-ordinator. Some actions are covered only because they were moved to Ottawa, Toronto or Essex. For those, the 180 days do not apply, and the court can set the date. The co-ordinator assigns a mediator if, within the 180 days, they receive none of these: a notice of the mediator and date, a mediator's report, a consent, an order, or a notice of settlement.

If any party wants evidence through discovery, such as documents, an examination, an inspection or a medical exam, agree on a written discovery plan with the other parties. You have 60 days after the day pleadings closed. The parties can agree to a longer time. But the plan must be agreed before anyone tries to get the evidence, if that comes first. The plan must be in writing. It must set dates for serving each party's affidavit of documents.

Set the action down for trial. If you do not, a defendant who is not in default can ask the court to dismiss the action for delay. You have 6 months after the day pleadings closed. This is not an automatic dismissal. It is a motion a defendant may bring. The registrar's own dismissal comes at five years. Once you set the action down, you cannot start or continue discovery or motions without leave. If your action is covered by mandatory mediation, one party must first file with the mediation co-ordinator the notice naming the mediator and date (Form 24.1A), or the mediator's report. If your action is under the simplified procedure, it is set down another way. That is by a notice of readiness for pre-trial conference (Form 76C), within 180 days after the first defence.

Set the action down for trial, or the registrar will dismiss it for delay. You have 5 years after the day the action was started. The last day is the anniversary of that day, 5 years later. If that day was February 29, the anniversary is February 28, except in a leap year. This does not apply if the action has already ended some other way. It does not apply if a party files a timetable signed by all parties, and a draft order, at least 30 days before the time ends. The timetable must give a date, no more than two years after the time ends, by which the action will be set down or restored. If the parties do not agree on a timetable, any party can ask for a status hearing before the time ends. It does not apply if you are under a disability at that time. It does not apply to Commercial List actions or class actions. The court can order otherwise. A dismissal can be set aside on a motion under rule 37.14.

Times set by the Rules of Civil Procedure are counted under those rules. The first day is not counted. If a time counted forward ends on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, it ends on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (c)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the safe course is to act by the last day before it that is not a holiday. For a period of seven days or less, holidays are not counted at all (r. 3.01 (1) (b)). Except for the document that starts a case, a document served after 4 p.m. or on a holiday counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (d)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
```

### `answer:civil:plaintiff:served-with-counterclaim:what-happens-after`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:plaintiff:served-with-counterclaim
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "The defendant is suing me back in the same case — do I have to respond?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
If the defendant delivers a reply to your defence to counterclaim (Form 27D), it is due within 10 days after your defence to counterclaim is served. A counterclaim is tried at the trial of the main action, unless the court orders otherwise. But if the counterclaim may unduly complicate or delay that trial, or cause undue prejudice to a party, the court may order separate trials. It may instead order the counterclaim to go ahead as a separate action.
```

### `answer:civil:plaintiff:ready-to-set-down:whats-happening`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:plaintiff:ready-to-set-down
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "How do I get my action set down for trial, and is there a deadline?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
After pleadings close, a party who is ready for trial may set the action down for trial. That party must not be in default under the rules or a court order. Any counterclaim or crossclaim in the action is set down with it. Once it is set down, the registrar at the place of trial must put the action on the right trial list.
```

### `answer:civil:plaintiff:ready-to-set-down:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:plaintiff:ready-to-set-down
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "How do I get my action set down for trial, and is there a deadline?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
If your action is covered by mandatory mediation, one party must file a paper with the mediation co-ordinator before it is set down. It is either a notice (Form 24.1A) naming the mediator and the date of the session, or a mediator's report saying the mediation has ended. In a defended action, you set it down by serving a trial record on every party to the action or to a counterclaim or crossclaim. You also serve it on any third or later party. Then you file the trial record with proof of service right away. If the court orders the trial of an undefended action, you set it down by just filing a trial record. The trial record must hold these items, in this order. First comes a table of contents that describes each document by what it is and its date. Next come a copy of any jury notice, and a copy of the pleadings, including those for any counterclaim or crossclaim. Next comes a copy of any demand or order for particulars of a pleading, and the particulars given in answer. Next comes a copy of any notice of amounts and particulars of special damages that was delivered. Next comes a copy of any order about the trial, including an order made under Rule 6.1. Last comes a signed certificate. If you have no lawyer and act for yourself, you sign it. It states that the record holds the required documents and that the time to deliver pleadings has run out. Where it applies, it also states that a defendant who did not deliver a defence has been noted in default. Where it applies, it also states that judgment was obtained against a defendant, or that the action was discontinued or dismissed against one. Before the trial, you must also add to the record a copy of some later papers. These are any notice of special damages, or any order about the trial, made after you filed the record. They also include any order under rule 50.07 and the pre-trial conference report under rule 50.08. In an undefended action, they include any affidavit to be used as evidence. The way of setting down is different for an action under the simplified procedure (Rule 76). There, you must set it down within 180 days after the first statement of defence or notice of intent to defend is filed. This is done by serving a notice of readiness for pre-trial conference (Form 76C) on every party to the action and to any counterclaim, crossclaim or third party claim. You then file it with proof of service right away.
```

### `answer:civil:plaintiff:ready-to-set-down:what-happens-after`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:plaintiff:ready-to-set-down
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "How do I get my action set down for trial, and is there a deadline?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
Once you set the action down, you must not start or continue any motion or discovery without the court's leave. Setting down does not end your duty to keep the undertakings you gave on an examination for discovery. Duties under some other rules also still apply. One is the discovery plan (rule 29.1.03). Others are telling of documents or errors found later (rule 30.07), and giving up a claim of privilege (rule 30.09). Others are the rule on failing to answer on discovery (rule 31.07), and telling of facts learned later (rule 31.09). The last are answering a request to admit (rule 51.03), and serving expert reports (rule 53.03). You may also still serve a request to admit facts or documents under rule 51.02. Some motions do not need leave. One is a motion to make a party meet a duty under rule 29.1.03, 30.07, 30.09, 31.07, 31.09, 51.03 or 53.03. Another is a motion for a separate hearing on some issues under rule 6.1.01. When the action is on a trial list, all parties are taken to be ready for trial, and the trial goes ahead when the action is reached, unless a judge orders otherwise. Unless the court orders otherwise, the parties must book a pre-trial conference with the registrar within 180 days after the action is set down. The date and time must suit all parties. Unless a court order or practice direction says otherwise, the date must be 30 to 120 days before the later of two days. One is the first day fixed for the trial, and the other is the first day of the sitting when the trial is expected. If they do not, the registrar sets a date and time and tells the parties, subject to any earlier order. Within 60 days after the action is set down, the parties must also agree on dates for serving experts' reports, unless the court orders otherwise.
```

### `answer:civil:plaintiff:judgment-unpaid:whats-happening`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:plaintiff:judgment-unpaid
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I have a judgment but they will not pay — how do I collect?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
You have a judgment for money, by default or after a hearing, and it has not been paid. The rules call a person who is entitled to enforce an order for money the creditor. The person it can be enforced against is called the debtor. Besides any other method the law provides, an order for money may be enforced in four ways. They are a writ of seizure and sale (Form 60A), garnishment, a writ of sequestration (Form 60B), and the appointment of a receiver.
```

### `answer:civil:plaintiff:judgment-unpaid:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:plaintiff:judgment-unpaid
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I have a judgment but they will not pay — how do I collect?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
To get a writ of seizure and sale, file a requisition with the registrar where the case was started. The requisition says how much is owing and the rate of postjudgment interest. It also lists the date and amount of any payment made since the order. Include a copy of the order as entered. Also include any other proof needed to show the amount awarded and your right to it. A lawyer or a person licensed by the Law Society may instead ask for the writ through the Teranet software. You need the court's leave first in two cases. One is if six years or more have passed since the date of the order. The other is if enforcing the order is subject to a condition. If the order is for payment at or after a set future time, the writ cannot be issued until that time has passed. You may file the writ with a sheriff. You may then file a direction to enforce (Form 60F) with the sheriff, with a copy of the order as entered. The direction tells the sheriff to enforce the writ. Garnishment lets you collect debts that other people owe to the debtor. To use it, file a requisition for garnishment (Form 60G) with the registrar where the case was started. Include a copy of the order as entered, and an affidavit. Also include any other proof needed to show the amount awarded and your right to it. The affidavit must state several things the rule lists, such as the amount owing with postjudgment interest. It must also name each person the notice is to go to, and say why you believe they owe or will owe the debtor money. The same two cases need the court's leave before a notice of garnishment is issued. The registrar then issues a notice of garnishment (Form 60H) for each person named, who is called a garnishee. You must serve the notice on the debtor with a copy of your affidavit. You must also serve it on the garnishee with a blank garnishee's statement (Form 60I). It must be served by ordinary mail, by personal service, or by an alternative to personal service. If the garnishee is a financial institution, serve it at the branch where the debt is payable. You may also examine the debtor. You can ask about things such as why they have not paid, their income and property, and the debts owed to and by them. If the debtor is a corporation, an officer or director may be examined for it. For a partnership or sole proprietorship, a partner or sole proprietor whom the order can be enforced against may be examined. Only one such examination of a debtor may be held in a 12-month period in the same case, unless the court orders otherwise. The debtor must be served with a notice of examination personally or by an alternative to personal service. A person examined on the debtor's behalf must be served with a notice of examination in one of two ways. It may be served on the debtor's lawyer of record. Or it may be served on that person personally, and not by an alternative to personal service.
```

### `answer:civil:plaintiff:judgment-unpaid:your-deadline`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:plaintiff:judgment-unpaid
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I have a judgment but they will not pay — how do I collect?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
If you have a writ of seizure and sale, renew it before it expires. You have 6 years after the day the writ was issued. The last day is the anniversary of that day, 6 years later. If that day was February 29, the anniversary is February 28, except in a leap year. A writ filed with a sheriff is renewed by filing a request to renew (Form 60E) with the sheriff. A writ not filed with a sheriff is renewed with the registrar who issued it. A renewal can be filed only in the six years before the expiry it relates to. A notice of garnishment also lasts six years and can be renewed before it expires.

Times set by the Rules of Civil Procedure are counted under those rules. The first day is not counted. If a time counted forward ends on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, it ends on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (c)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the safe course is to act by the last day before it that is not a holiday. For a period of seven days or less, holidays are not counted at all (r. 3.01 (1) (b)). Except for the document that starts a case, a document served after 4 p.m. or on a holiday counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (d)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
```

### `answer:civil:plaintiff:judgment-unpaid:what-happens-after`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:plaintiff:judgment-unpaid
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I have a judgment but they will not pay — how do I collect?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
A garnishee who admits owing the debtor money must pay it to the sheriff as the notice sets out, subject to section 7 of the Wages Act. Some garnishees dispute the garnishment, or pay less than the notice says. Within 10 days after being served, such a garnishee must serve you and the debtor with a garnishee's statement (Form 60I), and file it. Under a writ, you may not take any step to sell land until four months after the writ was filed with the sheriff. No sale of land may be held until six months after it was filed. If the writ was withdrawn, these times run from when it was filed again. If a notice of appeal is delivered, the parts of the order for paying money are put on hold. The hold lasts until the appeal is decided. It does not cover parts that award support or enforce a support order. A judge of the appeal court may order that the hold does not apply. While an order is on hold, no steps may be taken under it or to enforce it, except as a judge of the appeal court orders or as the rules allow. A writ of execution can still be issued and filed in a sheriff's office or land registry office. But no instruction or direction to enforce the writ may be given to a sheriff until the hold ends. An appeal from an order refusing to set aside a default judgment does not put that judgment on hold, but a court order may do so. You are entitled to the costs of your enforcement steps, unless the court orders otherwise on a motion. These costs are on a partial indemnity scale.
```

### `answer:civil:defendant:defence-delivered:whats-happening`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:defendant:defence-delivered
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I delivered my statement of defence — what happens next?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
You have served and filed your statement of defence. Discovery has not started. In these rules, to deliver a document means to serve it and file it with proof of service. Pleadings close when two things are true. First, the plaintiff has delivered a reply to every defence, or the time for a reply has run out. Second, every defendant whose time to deliver a defence has run out without delivering one has been noted in default.
```

### `answer:civil:defendant:defence-delivered:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:defendant:defence-delivered
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I delivered my statement of defence — what happens next?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
You may start a third party claim (Form 29A) against a person who is not a party to the action, in any of three cases. First, that person is or may be liable to you for all or part of the plaintiff's claim. Second, that person is or may be liable to you for a separate claim for damages or other relief. That claim must arise out of the events in the action, or related events. Third, that person should be bound by the decision on an issue between the plaintiff and you. If you bring a third party claim, it must be issued within 10 days after you deliver your defence, or at any time before you are noted in default. It may also be issued within 10 days after the plaintiff delivers a reply to your defence. It may be issued at any time with the plaintiff's consent or the court's leave. The court must give leave unless it would prejudice the plaintiff. You must serve it on the third party within 30 days after it is issued. Serve the third party personally or by an alternative to personal service. Include all the pleadings delivered so far in the action. This includes those in any counterclaim, crossclaim or other third party claim. You must also serve it on every other party in the same time, but personal service is not needed for them. You may crossclaim against another defendant in the same three cases. If you claim contribution from another defendant under the Negligence Act, you must do it by crossclaim. A crossclaim (Form 28A) must be in the same document as your defence, called a statement of defence and crossclaim. A statement of defence and crossclaim must be delivered within the time for delivering your defence, or at any time before you are noted in default. After that, it may be delivered with the court's leave. The court must give leave unless the plaintiff would be prejudiced. If your defence has no crossclaim and you want to add one, you may amend your defence. You may amend without leave before pleadings close, if the change does not add, remove or replace a party. Otherwise you need the consent of all parties, or the court's leave. If the change adds or replaces a party, that person must also consent, unless the court gives leave. You may ask for a jury to decide the facts, the damages, or both. To do so, deliver a jury notice (Form 47A) at any time before pleadings close. You cannot do this if section 108 of the Courts of Justice Act or another statute requires a trial without a jury. An action under the simplified procedure cannot be tried with a jury. In such an action, no party may deliver a jury notice, with one exception. A party may deliver one if the action involves a claim arising from slander, libel, malicious arrest, malicious prosecution or false imprisonment. If a party does that, the action can no longer go on under the simplified procedure. That party must also deliver a notice (Form 76A) saying the action and any related proceedings go on as an ordinary action. The parties must agree to a discovery plan if any party intends to get evidence under the discovery rules. These rules cover discovery of documents, examination for discovery, and inspection of property. They also cover medical examination, and examination for discovery by written questions. The plan must be agreed within 60 days after pleadings close, or a longer time the parties agree to. But it must be agreed before anyone tries to get the evidence, if that comes first.
```

### `answer:civil:defendant:defence-delivered:your-deadline`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:defendant:defence-delivered
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I delivered my statement of defence — what happens next?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
You can bring in someone who is not yet a party if they are or may be liable to you for all or part of the plaintiff's claim. You can also do it for a related claim, or if they should be bound by the result. To do this, issue a third party claim (Form 29A). You have 10 days after the day you delivered your statement of defence. You can also issue it at any time before you are noted in default. Or you can issue it within 10 days after the plaintiff delivers a reply to your defence. After that, you can issue it at any time with the plaintiff's consent or the court's leave. The court must give leave unless it would prejudice the plaintiff. You must serve it within 30 days after it is issued. The two-year limitation period still applies to your claim against the third party. For a claim for contribution and indemnity, the Limitations Act, 2002 treats the day you were served with the plaintiff's claim as the day of the act or omission.

If you issued a third party claim, serve it on the third party with all the pleadings delivered so far, and on every other party. You have 30 days after the day the third party claim was issued. The third party must be served personally or by an alternative to personal service. The other parties to the main action must be served in the same time, but not personally. The time can be extended by filing a consent, or by the court.

If you want a jury, deliver a jury notice (Form 47A) before pleadings close. The rule fixes no number of days. The cut-off is the close of pleadings. That can come 10 days after the defence if no reply is delivered. If a reply is delivered sooner, pleadings close when it is delivered, as long as every defendant has delivered a defence or been noted in default. Some statutes require a trial without a jury. A simplified procedure action cannot have a jury. The exception is a claim for slander, libel, malicious arrest, malicious prosecution or false imprisonment.

If your action is under the simplified procedure, serve every other party with an affidavit of documents. Include copies of the documents in its Schedule A. You pay the cost. You have 10 days after the day pleadings closed. This applies only to an action under the simplified procedure. Pleadings close when every defence has been replied to, or the time for a reply has run out, and every defendant who did not defend has been noted in default. The affidavit must also list the people who might know about the issues, unless the court orders otherwise. A person not named in it cannot be a witness at trial unless the court orders otherwise. The time can be extended by filing a consent, or by the court.

If any party wants evidence through discovery, such as documents, an examination, an inspection or a medical exam, agree on a written discovery plan with the other parties. You have 60 days after the day pleadings closed. The parties can agree to a longer time. But the plan must be agreed before anyone tries to get the evidence, if that comes first. The plan must be in writing. It must set dates for serving each party's affidavit of documents.

If you counterclaimed and want to reply to the defence to counterclaim, deliver a reply to defence to counterclaim (Form 27D). You have 10 days after the day the defence to counterclaim was served on you. This applies only if you counterclaimed. A reply is needed only if you will prove a different version of the facts than the defence pleads, or must raise a matter that could take the other side by surprise. Otherwise you must not deliver one. If you crossclaimed, you have the same 10 days to reply to a defence to crossclaim (Form 28C). If you brought a third party claim, you also have 10 days to reply to the third party defence (Form 29C). Each runs from service of that defence.

If your action is under the simplified procedure, meet or talk by phone with the other parties. Discuss whether all relevant documents have been shared, and whether any issue can be settled. You have 60 days after the day the first statement of defence or notice of intent to defend was filed. This applies only to an action under the simplified procedure. The general rules for actions also apply to it, unless Rule 76 says otherwise.

If your action is covered by mandatory mediation, choose a mediator with the other parties and hold the mediation session. You have 180 days after the day the first defence was filed. This applies only to actions that Rule 24.1 covers. For example, it covers actions started in Ottawa, Toronto or the County of Essex on or after January 1, 2010. Some kinds of action are left out. The court can exempt an action, or set a different time. The parties can put off the session by filing their written consent with the mediation co-ordinator. Some actions are covered only because they were moved to Ottawa, Toronto or Essex. For those, the 180 days do not apply, and the court can set the date. The co-ordinator assigns a mediator if, within the 180 days, they receive none of these: a notice of the mediator and date, a mediator's report, a consent, an order, or a notice of settlement.

If the action is under the simplified procedure, the plaintiff sets it down for trial by serving and filing a notice of readiness for pre-trial conference (Form 76C). They have 180 days after the day the first statement of defence or notice of intent to defend was filed. This applies only to an action under the simplified procedure. If the plaintiff does not do it, any other party may.

Times set by the Rules of Civil Procedure are counted under those rules. The first day is not counted. If a time counted forward ends on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, it ends on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (c)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the safe course is to act by the last day before it that is not a holiday. For a period of seven days or less, holidays are not counted at all (r. 3.01 (1) (b)). Except for the document that starts a case, a document served after 4 p.m. or on a holiday counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (d)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
```

### `answer:civil:defendant:defence-delivered:what-happens-after`

- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I delivered my statement of defence — what happens next?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
The plaintiff may deliver a reply within 10 days after your defence was served. If you counterclaimed, the time for a reply and defence to counterclaim is 20 days after your defence and counterclaim was served. If the plaintiff does not deliver a reply in time, the plaintiff is treated as denying the facts in your defence.
```

### `answer:civil:defendant:defence-period-expired-not-noted:whats-happening`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:defendant:defence-period-expired-not-noted
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I missed the time to file my defence — is it too late?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
The time to deliver your statement of defence has run out. But you have not been noted in default yet. Since your time has run out, the plaintiff may ask the registrar to note you in default. To do that, the plaintiff files proof that the statement of claim was served on you, or was deemed served. If the plaintiff has not done so, another defendant who has delivered a statement of defence may move to have the court order you noted in default. That motion must be on notice to the plaintiff. If you are under a disability, such as being a minor, you may be noted in default only with a judge's leave.
```

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:defendant:defence-period-expired-not-noted
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I missed the time to file my defence — is it too late?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
If you want to defend, you may still deliver a statement of defence (Form 18A) at any time before you are noted in default. Deliver means serve and file with proof of service. The time to deliver it may be extended by filing a consent in writing. The court may also extend the time by order, on terms that are just. A motion to extend time may be made before or after the time has run out. A motion is made by a notice of motion (Form 37A). The exception is where the kind of motion or the facts make one unneeded, or the rules say otherwise.
```

```
If you want to defend, deliver your statement of defence. The rules set no further fixed number of days. But you can deliver it only until you are noted in default. The plaintiff can have that done at any time by filing proof of service. After that, you get no notice of further steps. The time can also be extended by filing a consent, or by the court.
```

```
If you are noted in default first, you are deemed to admit that every fact in the statement of claim is true. You then must not deliver a defence or take any other step, except a motion to set aside the noting of default or a judgment obtained because of it, unless the court gives leave or the plaintiff consents. You also get no notice of further steps, with some exceptions, such as when the court orders otherwise or a party requires you to attend personally.
```

### `answer:civil:defendant:judgment-being-enforced:whats-happening`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:defendant:judgment-being-enforced
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "There is a judgment against me and they are trying to collect — what can they do?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
A judgment to pay money has been made against you. In the rules, you are the debtor, and the person entitled to enforce it is the creditor. The rules list four ways to enforce an order to pay money. They are a writ of seizure and sale (Form 60A), garnishment, a writ of sequestration (Form 60B), and appointing a receiver. A writ of sequestration may be issued only with the court's leave, obtained on a motion. The court may grant leave only if it is satisfied that other ways of enforcing the order are not working, or are not expected to work. Any other method the law provides may also be used.
```

### `answer:civil:defendant:judgment-being-enforced:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:defendant:judgment-being-enforced
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "There is a judgment against me and they are trying to collect — what can they do?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
Garnishment means the creditor collects debts that other people owe you. The creditor must serve the notice of garnishment on you, with a copy of the creditor's affidavit. Each notice names one garnishee, a person the creditor believes owes or will owe you money. A garnishee who admits owing you money must pay it to the sheriff, as the notice says. This is subject to section 7 of the Wages Act. You may bring a motion for a garnishment hearing. At the hearing, the court may, for example, change or pause periodic payments. A copy of your notice of motion must be served on the sheriff by ordinary mail, by personal service, or by an alternative to personal service. Once the sheriff gets it, the sheriff must pause payments to the creditor under the notice until the motion is decided or abandoned. The creditor may also examine you about things such as why the order is not paid, your income and property, and the debts you owe and that others owe you. The notice of examination must be served on you personally or by an alternative to personal service. Only one such examination may be held in a 12 month period in the same case, unless the court orders otherwise. If six years or more have passed since the order, or its enforcement depends on a condition, the creditor needs the court's leave first. That applies before a writ of seizure and sale or a notice of garnishment is issued.
```

### `answer:civil:defendant:judgment-being-enforced:your-deadline`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:defendant:judgment-being-enforced
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "There is a judgment against me and they are trying to collect — what can they do?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
If you want to appeal a final order, serve a notice of appeal with a certificate respecting evidence (Form 61C). You have 30 days after the day the order was made. File the notice, with proof of service, within 10 days after you serve it. Which court hears the appeal depends on the order. Some final orders of a Superior Court judge go to the Divisional Court. These include an order to pay one sum of $50,000 or less, or payments of $50,000 or less in the first 12 months, not counting costs. They also include an order dismissing a claim for $50,000 or less. So does an order dismissing a larger claim where the judge or jury says the award would have been $50,000 or less. Other final orders of a Superior Court judge go to the Court of Appeal. A final order of an associate judge goes to the Divisional Court. An appeal only about costs, or from an order made with everyone's consent, needs leave first. An order extending the time can be made only by a judge of the appeal court. Delivering a notice of appeal pauses the parts of the order that say to pay money, until the appeal is decided. This does not apply to support.

Times set by the Rules of Civil Procedure are counted under those rules. The first day is not counted. If a time counted forward ends on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, it ends on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (c)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the safe course is to act by the last day before it that is not a holiday. For a period of seven days or less, holidays are not counted at all (r. 3.01 (1) (b)). Except for the document that starts a case, a document served after 4 p.m. or on a holiday counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (d)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
```

### `answer:civil:defendant:judgment-being-enforced:what-happens-after`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:defendant:judgment-being-enforced
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "There is a judgment against me and they are trying to collect — what can they do?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
If you deliver a notice of appeal from the order, any part of it that says to pay money is put on hold until the appeal is decided. This does not apply to support. It also does not apply to an appeal from an order refusing to set aside a default judgment. But in that case, the default judgment may be put on hold by an order. A judge of the appeal court may also order that the hold does not apply. If the judgment was made after you were noted in default, it may be set aside or changed on terms that are just. The court or a judge decides that, depending on how the judgment was made. When the amount owing is paid, a creditor using garnishment must right away serve a notice of termination of garnishment (Form 60J) on the garnishee and the sheriff.
```

### `answer:civil:both:summary-judgment-motion:whats-happening`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:both:summary-judgment-motion
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "The other side brought a motion for summary judgment — what do I have to file?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
A motion for summary judgment asks the court to decide all or part of the claim on affidavits or other evidence. When a plaintiff brings it, it asks for judgment on all or part of the claim. When a defendant brings it, it asks that all or part of the claim be dismissed. The court must grant summary judgment if it is satisfied there is no genuine issue that needs a trial on a claim or defence. It must also grant it if the parties agree to have all or part of the claim decided this way, and the court is satisfied that is appropriate.
```

### `answer:civil:both:summary-judgment-motion:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:both:summary-judgment-motion
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "The other side brought a motion for summary judgment — what do I have to file?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
If you are responding, you cannot rest only on what your pleading says or denies. You must set out specific facts, in affidavits or other evidence, that show there is a genuine issue that needs a trial. An affidavit on this motion may state what the person swearing it was told and believes, if it names the source and says that they believe it. But at the hearing, the court may, if appropriate, draw an adverse inference when a party does not give evidence from a person who has personal knowledge of facts in dispute. On this motion, each party must serve a factum on every other party to the motion, and it must meet the requirements of rule 4.06.1. If you are responding, you must serve your factum and file it with proof of service at the court office where the motion will be heard, at least four days before the hearing. If you brought the motion, you must serve and file your factum the same way at least seven days before the hearing. If you brought the motion, then unless the court orders otherwise, you must also serve a motion record on every other party at least seven days before the hearing. You must file it with proof of service at that court office by the same time. If you are responding, the moving party's motion record holds the affidavits and other material any party has served for use on the motion. The court file is not put before the judge unless the judge asks for it or a party requisitions it. If material you will use on the motion is not in the moving party's motion record, you may put it in a responding party's motion record. Serving and filing it are one step. You serve it on every other party and file it, with proof of service, in the court office where the motion will be heard, at least four days before the hearing. It holds a table of contents and a copy of any material you will use on the motion that is not in the motion record.
```

### `answer:civil:both:summary-judgment-motion:your-deadline`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:both:summary-judgment-motion
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "The other side brought a motion for summary judgment — what do I have to file?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
If you are bringing the motion for summary judgment, serve the notice of motion, motion record and your factum on the other parties. File them with proof of service. Do this at least 7 days before the date the motion will be heard. A factum is required on this motion. This is the latest it can be done; earlier is fine. Because the period is seven days or less, Saturdays, Sundays and holidays are not counted. A document served after 4 p.m., or on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday. You must also give the registrar a confirmation of motion (Form 37B) by 2 p.m. five days before the hearing. If you do not, the motion is not heard.

If you are responding to a motion for summary judgment, serve your factum on the other parties and file it with proof of service. Do this at least 4 days before the date the motion will be heard. A factum is required on this motion. You cannot rely only on what your pleading says or denies. You must set out specific facts, in affidavits or other evidence, showing there is a genuine issue that needs a trial. This is the latest it can be done; earlier is fine. Because the period is seven days or less, Saturdays, Sundays and holidays are not counted. A document served after 4 p.m., or on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday.

If you are responding, serve your affidavits and other evidence on the other parties. If the moving party's motion record does not include them, serve and file a responding party's motion record containing them, with proof of service. Do this at least 4 days before the date the motion will be heard. This is how your evidence of specific facts reaches the court. This is the latest it can be done; earlier is fine. Because the period is seven days or less, Saturdays, Sundays and holidays are not counted. If the moving party did not email you a copy of their confirmation of motion, you may give the registrar your own confirmation of motion (Form 37B) by 10 a.m. four days before the hearing.

Times set by the Rules of Civil Procedure are counted under those rules. The first day is not counted. If a time counted forward ends on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, it ends on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (c)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the safe course is to act by the last day before it that is not a holiday. For a period of seven days or less, holidays are not counted at all (r. 3.01 (1) (b)). Except for the document that starts a case, a document served after 4 p.m. or on a holiday counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (d)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
```

### `answer:civil:both:summary-judgment-motion:what-happens-after`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:both:summary-judgment-motion
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "The other side brought a motion for summary judgment — what do I have to file?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
To decide if there is a genuine issue that needs a trial, the court must consider the evidence the parties gave. A judge may weigh the evidence and judge how believable a person who swore an affidavit is. The judge may also draw reasonable inferences from the evidence. But a judge does not use these powers if the interest of justice means they should be used only at a trial. For this, a judge may also order one or more parties to give oral evidence, with or without time limits. If summary judgment is refused or granted only in part, the court may set out the facts not in dispute and the issues to be tried. It may also order the case to go to trial quickly. The court may order a party to pay the costs of the motion on a substantial indemnity basis in two cases. One is if the party acted unreasonably in making or responding to the motion. The other is if the party acted in bad faith to cause delay.
```

### `answer:civil:both:offer-to-settle:whats-happening`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:both:offer-to-settle
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "How do offers to settle work, and does the timing matter?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
A party may serve an offer to settle one or more of the claims in the case on any other party, on the terms the offer sets out (Form 49A). Rule 49 applies to actions and applications, and with needed changes to motions, counterclaims, crossclaims and third or later party claims. In this rule, a plaintiff includes an applicant, and a defendant includes a respondent. An offer to settle is treated as an offer of compromise made without prejudice. No pleading may say that an offer was made. If an offer is not accepted, nothing about it may be told to the court at the hearing until liability and the relief, other than costs, have been decided. An offer must not be filed until then either.
```

### `answer:civil:both:offer-to-settle:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:both:offer-to-settle
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "How do offers to settle work, and does the timing matter?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
You may make an offer at any time, but if it is made less than seven days before the hearing starts, the costs results in rule 49.10 will not apply. You may withdraw your offer at any time before it is accepted, by serving written notice of withdrawal on the party you made it to. That notice may be in Form 49B. If an offer sets a time to accept it and it is not accepted or withdrawn in that time, it is treated as withdrawn when the time ends. You may accept an offer by serving an acceptance of offer (Form 49C) on the party who made it, before it is withdrawn or the court decides the claim. If you rejected an offer, or made a counter-offer that was not accepted, you may still accept the first offer. This is so unless it was withdrawn or the court has decided the claim. A plaintiff's offer to settle for money may say the defendant must pay the money into court or to a trustee. If it does, the defendant may accept only by paying the money as the offer says and telling the plaintiff about the payment. A party under disability, such as a minor, may make, withdraw and accept an offer. But if they accept an offer, or their own offer is accepted, it is not binding on them without a judge's approval under rule 7.08, except as that rule provides.
```
