### `answer:civil:defendant:served-with-crossclaim:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:defendant:served-with-crossclaim
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "Another defendant has crossclaimed against me — do I have to respond?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
Unless the exception below applies, you must deliver a defence to crossclaim (Form 28B) within 20 days after the statement of defence and crossclaim is served on you. Deliver means serve and file with proof of service. You do not need to deliver one only if all three of these things are true. First, the crossclaim asks only for contribution or indemnity under the Negligence Act. Second, you have delivered a statement of defence in the main action. Third, you rely on the facts in that statement of defence. You do not rely on a different version of the facts, or on anything that might take the co-defendant by surprise. In that case, you are deemed to deny the facts in the crossclaim and to rely on the facts in your statement of defence. Otherwise, if you are noted in default on the crossclaim, you are deemed to admit all the facts it alleges. The co-defendant may then get judgment against you only at the trial of the main action or on a motion to a judge. In a defence to crossclaim, you may defend against the crossclaim. Where it fits, you may also defend against the plaintiff's claim against the co-defendant. You may then raise any defence open to that co-defendant. If you do, that must be a separate part titled defence to plaintiff's claim against crossclaiming defendant. You then have the same rights and duties as a defendant to that claim. This includes those for discovery, trial and appeal. Whether or not you defend against that claim, you are bound by any order or finding in the main action between the plaintiff and the co-defendant.
```

### `answer:civil:defendant:action-discontinued-counterclaim-pending:whats-happening`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:defendant:action-discontinued-counterclaim-pending
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "The plaintiff dropped the case against me — what happens to my counterclaim?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
The plaintiff has discontinued, or dropped, the action against you. You had made a counterclaim. A plaintiff may discontinue all or part of an action in one of three ways. Before the close of pleadings, the plaintiff serves a notice of discontinuance (Form 23A) on all parties served with the claim. The plaintiff then files it with proof of service. After the close of pleadings, the plaintiff needs the leave, or permission, of the court. At any time, the plaintiff can file the consent of all parties. But if a party to the action is under disability, the action may be discontinued by or against that party only with a judge's leave, asked for by motion.
```

### `answer:civil:defendant:action-discontinued-counterclaim-pending:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:defendant:action-discontinued-counterclaim-pending
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "The plaintiff dropped the case against me — what happens to my counterclaim?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
To go on with your counterclaim, you may deliver a notice of election to proceed with the counterclaim (Form 23B) within 30 days after the discontinuance. To deliver means to serve and file with proof of service. If you do not deliver it in time, your counterclaim is treated as discontinued, without costs. You may also have made a crossclaim or a third party claim. If so, it is treated as dismissed 30 days after the discontinuance, unless the court orders otherwise in those 30 days. Any party to the action may make a motion about the costs of the action within 30 days after it is discontinued.
```

### `answer:civil:defendant:plaintiff-delaying:whats-happening`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:defendant:plaintiff-delaying
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "The plaintiff is not moving the case forward — can I get it dismissed?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
The plaintiff has let a time in the rules pass. You are thinking about asking the court to dismiss the action for delay. In two cases, the court must dismiss an action for delay, unless the plaintiff shows that this would be unjust. One is where the action was not set down for trial or ended by the fifth anniversary of its start. The other is where it was struck off a trial list. Then, by the second anniversary of that, it was not put back on a list or ended. A special rule applies if the plaintiff is under disability, set out below.
```

### `answer:civil:defendant:plaintiff-delaying:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:defendant:plaintiff-delaying
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "The plaintiff is not moving the case forward — can I get it dismissed?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
If you are not in default under the rules or a court order, you may make a motion to have the action dismissed for delay. You may do this where the plaintiff has failed to do one of four things. The first is to serve the claim on all the defendants within the time set by the rules. The second is to have a defendant who did not deliver a defence noted in default within 30 days after that default. The third is to set the action down for trial within six months after the close of pleadings. The fourth is to move for leave to put the action back on a trial list within 30 days after it was struck off. If the plaintiff is under disability, you must serve your notice of motion on the plaintiff's litigation guardian. If that guardian is not the Children's Lawyer or the Public Guardian and Trustee, you must also serve one of them. Serve the Children's Lawyer if the plaintiff is a minor, and the Public Guardian and Trustee in any other case. If one of them was served but is not the guardian, the action may be dismissed only if they confirm to the court that they were served and take no position. That applies unless a judge orders otherwise.
```

### `answer:civil:defendant:plaintiff-delaying:what-happens-after`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:defendant:plaintiff-delaying
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "The plaintiff is not moving the case forward — can I get it dismissed?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
If your motion succeeds, you must serve a copy of the order dismissing the action on every defendant who has crossclaimed against you. Their crossclaim against you is then treated as dismissed 30 days after the order is served on them. That applies unless the court orders otherwise in those 30 days. If you made a counterclaim, you may deliver a notice of election to proceed with it (Form 23B) within 30 days after the dismissal. If you do not, the counterclaim is treated as discontinued, without costs. If you made a crossclaim or a third party claim, it is treated as dismissed, unless the court orders otherwise. Any party to the action may make a motion about the costs of the action within 30 days after the dismissal. The dismissal is not a defence to a later action, unless the order dismissing the action says otherwise.
```

### `answer:civil:defendant:action-dismissed-counterclaim-pending:your-deadline`

- **Status:** draft

- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "The plaintiff's case was dismissed for delay — what happens to my counterclaim?"

```
If you want to go on with your counterclaim, deliver a notice of election to proceed with the counterclaim (Form 23B). You have 30 days after the day the action was dismissed. If you do not, the counterclaim is treated as discontinued, without costs. This applies to a dismissal by the registrar as well as by the court. The time can be extended by filing a consent, or by the court.

If the action was dismissed for delay, you can ask the court to deal with the costs of the action. Do this by making a motion about the costs. You have 30 days after the day the action was dismissed. Any party to the action can make this motion. The rule's own words cover any action "dismissed for delay". The registrar's five-year order is a dismissal for delay. The only doubt comes from rule 48.14 (9). That rule applies the dismissal rules to a registrar's order, but it names only rules 24.03 to 24.05. So the rules' text does not settle whether this rule, 24.05.1, reaches that order. Bringing the motion within the 30 days avoids the doubt. The time can be extended by filing a consent, or by the court.

Times set by the Rules of Civil Procedure are counted under those rules. The first day is not counted. If a time counted forward ends on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, it ends on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (c)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the safe course is to act by the last day before it that is not a holiday. For a period of seven days or less, holidays are not counted at all (r. 3.01 (1) (b)). Except for the document that starts a case, a document served after 4 p.m. or on a holiday counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (d)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
```

### `answer:civil:both:lawyer-removed-from-record:whats-happening`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:both:lawyer-removed-from-record
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "My lawyer got off the record — what do I have to do now?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
The court has made an order removing your lawyer from the record. The order must include your contact details and the text of the rules that apply to you. Your lawyer must serve the order on you. They may do this in person or by an alternative to personal service. Or they may mail it to your last known address. They also mail it to any other address where they believe it will come to your notice. Your lawyer stays your lawyer of record until one of two things happens. You deliver a notice changing that, or the order is entered and your lawyer has met the rules for serving and filing it.
```

### `answer:civil:both:lawyer-removed-from-record:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:both:lawyer-removed-from-record
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "My lawyer got off the record — what do I have to do now?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
If you are not a corporation, not under disability and not acting in a representative role, you must do one of two things within 30 days after being served with the order. You must either appoint a new lawyer by serving a notice in Form 15B, or serve a notice of intention to act in person (Form 15C). To appoint a lawyer, serve a notice of appointment of lawyer (Form 15B) on every other party, and file it with proof of service. A notice of intention to act in person sets out your address for service and phone number. You serve it on your former lawyer and every other party, and file it with proof of service. If you do neither in time, the court may dismiss your case or strike out your defence. In an appeal, a judge of the appeal court may, on motion, dismiss your appeal, or the court hearing the appeal may refuse to hear you. A corporation must have a lawyer unless the court gives leave. Within 30 days after being served with the order, a corporation must do one of two things. It must appoint a new lawyer (Form 15B), or get and serve on every other party an order letting someone who is not a lawyer act for it. If it does not, the court may dismiss its case or strike out its defence, and in an appeal the same results as above can follow. If you act in a representative role, or are the litigation guardian of a party under disability, you must appoint a new lawyer (Form 15B) within 30 days after being served with the order. If that is not done, another party must ask the court for directions or ask for a case conference. Until that motion has been heard or that case conference has been held, no party may take a further step in the case, unless the court orders otherwise. A claim started for a minor under section 61 of the Family Law Act is different. There, the rule above for other clients who miss the 30 days applies, with needed changes.
```

- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
If you are an individual, do one of two things. Appoint a new lawyer by serving a notice (Form 15B). Or serve a notice of intention to act in person (Form 15C). You have 30 days after the day you were served with the order removing your lawyer. If you do not, the court may dismiss your case or strike out your defence. In an appeal, a judge of the appeal court may dismiss the appeal, or the court hearing it may refuse to hear you. A corporation has 30 days to do one of two things instead. It can appoint a new lawyer. Or it can get and serve an order letting someone who is not a lawyer represent it. The same results follow if it does not. A party acting in a representative role, or the litigation guardian of a party under disability, has 30 days to appoint a new lawyer. The time can be extended by the court.

Times set by the Rules of Civil Procedure are counted under those rules. The first day is not counted. If a time counted forward ends on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, it ends on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (c)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the safe course is to act by the last day before it that is not a holiday. For a period of seven days or less, holidays are not counted at all (r. 3.01 (1) (b)). Except for the document that starts a case, a document served after 4 p.m. or on a holiday counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (d)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
```

### `answer:civil:both:served-with-amended-pleading:whats-happening`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:both:served-with-amended-pleading
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "The other side served an amended claim or defence — do I have to respond again?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
Another party has changed one of its pleadings and served the amended version on you. Unless the court orders otherwise, it must be served right away on every party. That includes parties to a counterclaim, crossclaim or third party claim in the action. A party may amend without the court's permission before pleadings close, if the change does not add, remove or replace a party. Otherwise, it needs the filed consent of all parties, or the court's permission. If a person is being added or replaced as a party, that person's consent must be filed too. The changes must be underlined, so you can tell the new wording from the original. If a pleading has been amended more than once, each later change has one more underline.
```

### `answer:civil:both:served-with-amended-pleading:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:both:served-with-amended-pleading
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "The other side served an amended claim or defence — do I have to respond again?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
Unless the court orders otherwise, your time to respond to the amended pleading is the longer of two times. One is the time that was left to respond to the original pleading. The other is 10 days after the amended pleading was served on you. If you responded to the original and do not respond to the amended pleading in time, you are treated as relying on your original pleading. It then stands as your answer to the amended one. An originating process is a document that starts a proceeding, such as a statement of claim. Is the amended pleading an originating process? Then the way it is served depends on whether you responded to the original. If you were served with the original and responded to it, it does not have to be served on you personally. If you did not respond to the original, it must be served on you personally or by an alternative to personal service. This applies even if you were noted in default.
```

### `answer:civil:both:simplified-procedure-after-defence:whats-happening`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:both:simplified-procedure-after-defence
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "My case is under the simplified procedure — what are the steps after the defence?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
Your action is going ahead under the simplified procedure in Rule 76, and a defence or notice of intent to defend has been filed. The usual rules for an action still apply to it, unless Rule 76 says otherwise. Pleadings close when the plaintiff has delivered a reply to every defence, or the time for a reply has run out. Also, every defendant who is in default in delivering a defence must have been noted in default.
```

### `answer:civil:both:simplified-procedure-after-defence:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:both:simplified-procedure-after-defence
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "My case is under the simplified procedure — what are the steps after the defence?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
Within 10 days after pleadings close, you must serve an affidavit of documents (Form 30A or 30B) on every other party. You pay the cost. It must disclose every relevant document you have or once had in your possession, control or power. Disclose them as fully as you know and believe. Within the same 10 days, you must also serve copies of the documents listed in its Schedule A. Unless the court orders otherwise, the affidavit must list people who might reasonably be expected to know about the issues. Give their names and addresses. Unless the court orders otherwise, a party may not call a witness at trial who is not named in that party's affidavit of documents. Being named in a supplementary one also counts. Within 60 days after the first defence or notice of intent to defend is filed, the parties must meet or talk by phone. They must consider whether all relevant documents have been disclosed, and whether any or all issues can be settled. Some steps are not allowed. One is examination for discovery by written questions and answers under Rule 35. Another is cross-examining someone on an affidavit under rule 39.02. A third is examining a witness on a motion under rule 39.03. Oral examinations for discovery are limited. No party may examine for more than three hours in total, no matter how many people are examined. If you bring a motion, you must serve a motion form (Form 76B) under rule 37.07, and submit it to the court before the motion is brought and heard. If you plan to call expert evidence at trial, you must comply with rule 53.03. An expert's report served under rule 53.03 must be attached to the expert's affidavit. In that affidavit, the expert adopts the report as evidence in the action. If you are the plaintiff, you must set the action down for trial within 180 days after the first defence or notice of intent to defend is filed. You do this by serving a notice of readiness for pre-trial conference (Form 76C). Serve it on every party to the action and to any counterclaim, crossclaim or third party claim. You must then file the notice right away, with proof of service. If the plaintiff has not set the action down, any other party may do it. Whoever sets the action down must certify in the notice that there was a settlement discussion.
```

### `answer:civil:both:simplified-procedure-after-defence:your-deadline`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:both:simplified-procedure-after-defence
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "My case is under the simplified procedure — what are the steps after the defence?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
If your action is under the simplified procedure, serve every other party with an affidavit of documents. Include copies of the documents in its Schedule A. You pay the cost. You have 10 days after the day pleadings closed. This applies only to an action under the simplified procedure. Pleadings close when every defence has been replied to, or the time for a reply has run out, and every defendant who did not defend has been noted in default. The affidavit must also list the people who might know about the issues, unless the court orders otherwise. A person not named in it cannot be a witness at trial unless the court orders otherwise. The time can be extended by filing a consent, or by the court.

If your action is under the simplified procedure, meet or talk by phone with the other parties. Discuss whether all relevant documents have been shared, and whether any issue can be settled. You have 60 days after the day the first statement of defence or notice of intent to defend was filed. This applies only to an action under the simplified procedure. The general rules for actions also apply to it, unless Rule 76 says otherwise.

If your action is covered by mandatory mediation, choose a mediator with the other parties and hold the mediation session. You have 180 days after the day the first defence was filed. This applies only to actions that Rule 24.1 covers. For example, it covers actions started in Ottawa, Toronto or the County of Essex on or after January 1, 2010. Some kinds of action are left out. The court can exempt an action, or set a different time. The parties can put off the session by filing their written consent with the mediation co-ordinator. Some actions are covered only because they were moved to Ottawa, Toronto or Essex. For those, the 180 days do not apply, and the court can set the date. The co-ordinator assigns a mediator if, within the 180 days, they receive none of these: a notice of the mediator and date, a mediator's report, a consent, an order, or a notice of settlement.

If you are the plaintiff, set the action down for trial. Do this by serving a notice of readiness for pre-trial conference (Form 76C) on every party and filing it with proof of service. You have 180 days after the day the first statement of defence or notice of intent to defend was filed. This applies only to an action under the simplified procedure. If you are not the plaintiff, this is not your duty. If the plaintiff does not do it, any other party may. The party who sets it down must certify that there was a settlement discussion. The court can extend the time.

If you gave an undertaking or took a question under advisement at an examination for discovery, answer it. You have 60 days after the day you gave that response at the examination. If you do not answer in that time, you cannot use that information at trial without the trial judge's permission. You still have to keep an undertaking.

If any party wants evidence through discovery, such as documents, an examination, an inspection or a medical exam, agree on a written discovery plan with the other parties. You have 60 days after the day pleadings closed. The parties can agree to a longer time. But the plan must be agreed before anyone tries to get the evidence, if that comes first. The plan must be in writing. It must set dates for serving each party's affidavit of documents.

If you are the plaintiff, set the action down for trial, or the registrar will dismiss it for delay. You have 5 years after the day the action was started. The last day is the anniversary of that day, 5 years later. If that day was February 29, the anniversary is February 28, except in a leap year. This does not apply if the action has already ended some other way. It does not apply if a party files a timetable signed by all parties, and a draft order, at least 30 days before the time ends. The timetable must give a date, no more than two years after the time ends, by which the action will be set down or restored. If the parties do not agree on a timetable, any party can ask for a status hearing before the time ends. It does not apply if the plaintiff is under a disability at that time. It does not apply to Commercial List actions or class actions. The court can order otherwise. A dismissal can be set aside on a motion under rule 37.14.

Times set by the Rules of Civil Procedure are counted under those rules. The first day is not counted. If a time counted forward ends on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, it ends on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (c)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the safe course is to act by the last day before it that is not a holiday. For a period of seven days or less, holidays are not counted at all (r. 3.01 (1) (b)). Except for the document that starts a case, a document served after 4 p.m. or on a holiday counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (d)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
```

- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "My case is under the simplified procedure — what are the steps after the defence?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
A pre-trial conference is then scheduled under rule 50.02. At least 30 days before it, the parties must agree to a proposed trial management plan. The plan lists every witness, including experts, that a party plans to call at trial. It also divides the trial time between the parties, and the total may not be more than five days. It sets each party's time for an opening statement and for evidence in chief, given by affidavit and under rule 31.11. It also sets time to cross-examine, to re-examine, and for oral argument.
```

- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I got a request to admit — what happens if I do not answer?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
Another party has served you with a request to admit (Form 51A). It asks you to admit that a fact is true, or that a document is authentic. For example, authentic includes that a document said to be a copy is a true copy of the original. Any admission counts for this case only.
```

### `answer:civil:both:served-with-request-to-admit:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:both:served-with-request-to-admit
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I got a request to admit — what happens if I do not answer?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
Within 20 days after the request is served on you, you must serve a response to request to admit (Form 51B) on the party who sent it. If you do not serve a response in time, you are treated as admitting the facts or documents in the request, for this case only. In your response, you may specifically deny that a fact is true or that a document is authentic. Or you may refuse to admit it, but your response must then set out your reason for refusing. Anything in the request that your response does not deny, or refuse with a reason, is treated as admitted for this case.
```

For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the safe course is to act by the last day before it that is not a holiday. Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
```

Say you deny or refuse to admit something, and it is later proved at the hearing. The court may take your denial or refusal into account when it decides costs. Any party may bring a motion to a judge in this case for the order they say the admission entitles them to, and the judge may make the order that is just.
```

### `answer:civil:both:interlocutory-order-made:whats-happening`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:both:interlocutory-order-made
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "A judge decided a motion against me — can I appeal it, and by when?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
Where your appeal goes depends on who made the order. An appeal from an interlocutory order of an associate judge goes to the Superior Court of Justice. An appeal from an interlocutory order of a Superior Court judge goes to the Divisional Court, but only with leave as the rules provide. Those Divisional Court appeal rights do not apply to an order made under section 137.1 of the Courts of Justice Act. Instead, an appeal from an order made under section 137.1 goes to the Court of Appeal.
```

### `answer:civil:both:interlocutory-order-made:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:both:interlocutory-order-made
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "A judge decided a motion against me — can I appeal it, and by when?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
To appeal an interlocutory order of a Superior Court judge, you must first get leave from a panel of the Divisional Court. To ask for it, serve a notice of motion for leave to appeal (Form 61A). You must serve it within 15 days after the order was made, unless a statute provides otherwise. Then file it, with proof of service, in the Registrar's office within five days after you serve it. You must also serve a motion record, a factum, and any transcripts of evidence. Within 30 days after filing the notice, you must file the motion record, factum, and any transcripts and book of authorities, with proof of service. Your factum must be limited to facts, issues, law and authorities that relate to a ground on which leave may be granted. The motion for leave is heard in writing, without the parties or lawyers attending. Leave from an interlocutory order is not granted unless one of two things is shown to the panel. One is a conflicting decision by another judge or court on the same matter, where the panel thinks leave is desirable. The other is good reason to doubt the order is correct. For that one, the appeal must also involve matters so important that, in the panel's view, leave should be granted. For an interlocutory order of an associate judge, the appeal goes to a judge. You start it by serving a notice of appeal (Form 62A). Serve it on all parties whose interests may be affected, within seven days after the order was made. The notice must state what you are asking for and your grounds of appeal. At the hearing, you may not rely on other grounds unless the judge hearing the appeal gives leave. The notice must name the first available hearing date that is not less than seven days after you serve it. File it, with proof of service, in the court office where the appeal will be heard, no later than seven days before the hearing date. You must also serve an appeal record and a factum on every other party. Serve them, and file them there with proof of service, no later than seven days before the hearing. A judge may excuse you from that step, in whole or in part, before or at the hearing.
```

### `answer:civil:both:interlocutory-order-made:your-deadline`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:both:interlocutory-order-made
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "A judge decided a motion against me — can I appeal it, and by when?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
If you want to appeal an interlocutory order of a Superior Court judge, serve a notice of motion for leave to appeal to the Divisional Court (Form 61A). You have 15 days after the day the order was made. File the notice, with proof of service, within five days after you serve it. A panel of the Divisional Court hears the leave motion in writing. The same leave process applies to a final order of a Superior Court judge that is only about costs. Within 30 days after filing the notice of motion, file your motion record, factum, any transcripts and any book of authorities, with proof of service. If leave is granted, deliver the notice of appeal, with your certificate respecting evidence (Form 61C), within seven days after leave is granted.

If you want to appeal an interlocutory order of an associate judge, serve a notice of appeal (Form 62A) on all parties whose interests may be affected. You have 7 days after the day the order was made. This appeal goes to a judge, not to the Divisional Court. Because the period is seven days or less, Saturdays, Sundays and holidays are not counted. The notice must name the first available hearing date at least seven days after you serve it. File it with proof of service no later than seven days before that hearing date.

If you are appealing an associate judge's order, serve your appeal record and factum on every other party and file them with proof of service. Do this at least 7 days before the date the appeal will be heard. This is the latest it can be done; earlier is fine. Because the period is seven days or less, Saturdays, Sundays and holidays are not counted.

If you are responding to an appeal from an associate judge's order, serve your factum, and any more material needed, on every other party. File it with proof of service. Do this at least 4 days before the date the appeal will be heard. This is the latest it can be done; earlier is fine. Because the period is seven days or less, Saturdays, Sundays and holidays are not counted.

If the other side asks the Divisional Court for leave to appeal and you oppose it, file your factum, any motion record and any book of authorities. File them with proof of service. You have 25 days after the day you were served with the moving party's motion record. This applies to a motion for leave to appeal an interlocutory order or a costs order of a Superior Court judge.

Times set by the Rules of Civil Procedure are counted under those rules. The first day is not counted. If a time counted forward ends on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, it ends on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (c)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the safe course is to act by the last day before it that is not a holiday. For a period of seven days or less, holidays are not counted at all (r. 3.01 (1) (b)). Except for the document that starts a case, a document served after 4 p.m. or on a holiday counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (d)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
```

### `answer:civil:both:interlocutory-order-made:what-happens-after`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:both:interlocutory-order-made
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "A judge decided a motion against me — can I appeal it, and by when?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
If the Divisional Court grants leave, you must deliver the notice of appeal and your certificate respecting evidence within seven days after leave is granted. From then on, Rule 61 applies to the appeal. Delivering a notice of appeal stays any part of the order for paying money. The stay lasts until the appeal is decided. It does not cover a part that awards support or enforces a support order. A judge of the appeal court may order, on terms that are just, that this stay does not apply. If the order refused to set aside a default judgment, a notice of appeal does not stay that judgment, but it may be stayed by order.
```

### `answer:civil:both:pretrial-scheduled:whats-happening`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:both:pretrial-scheduled
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "My action has been set down for trial — what has to happen before the pre-trial conference?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
Your action has been set down for trial. The pre-trial conference has not happened yet. At this conference, the parties go before a judge or associate judge. It is a way to settle some or all of the issues without a hearing. For issues that do not settle, the court can give orders or directions to help the case end fairly, quickly and at the least cost. If your action was set down before March 31, 2022, rule 50.02 as it read on March 30, 2022 still applies.
```

### `answer:civil:both:pretrial-scheduled:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:both:pretrial-scheduled
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "My action has been set down for trial — what has to happen before the pre-trial conference?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
Unless the court orders otherwise, the parties must book the conference with the registrar within 180 days after the action was set down. The time must suit all the parties. The date must be 30 to 120 days before the first trial day, unless an order or practice direction says otherwise. If the trial sittings start later, count back from the first day of the sittings. Subject to any earlier order, if the parties do not book it in time, the registrar books it and tells them when to come. Unless the court orders otherwise, the parties must agree on dates for serving expert reports within 60 days after the action was set down. If you will call an expert at trial, you must serve the expert's signed report on every other party at least 90 days before the conference. It must include set details, such as the expert's opinion and reasons, and a signed form on the expert's duty (Form 53). If your expert will answer another party's expert, you must serve that report on every other party at least 60 days before the conference. Without the trial judge's leave, an expert may not testify on an issue unless it is in a report served under this rule. A supplementary report also counts if it is served on every other party at least 45 days before trial. So does a responding supplementary report served on every other party at least 15 days before trial. At least 30 days before the conference, you must deliver a certificate of readiness (Form 50A). Deliver means serve and file with proof of service. It says if you will call expert evidence at trial. If so, it says for each expert if the report was served in time, and if not, why. At least five days before the conference, you must file a pre-trial conference brief with proof of service. It gives short statements of set matters, without argument. They are what the case is about, the issues and your position, and the witnesses you expect to call and how long each will take. They also include the steps still needed before the action is ready for trial, and how long those steps will take. If any party plans to ask for separate hearings under rule 6.1.01, the brief also gives your position on that. Some of this is different if your action is under the simplified procedure. Then the parties must agree on a proposed trial management plan at least 30 days before the conference. And instead of a brief, at least five days before the conference you must file a copy of that plan. By then you must also file your affidavit of documents and the documents you rely on. You must also file any expert affidavit, other than a supplementary one, and any other material needed. You must also deliver a statement of the issues and your position, of no more than three pages. You must also deliver a trial management checklist (Form 76D). If any party plans to ask for separate hearings, you must also deliver your position on that.
```

### `answer:civil:both:pretrial-scheduled:your-deadline`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:both:pretrial-scheduled
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "My action has been set down for trial — what has to happen before the pre-trial conference?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
Schedule a pre-trial conference date with the registrar, agreed among the parties. You have 180 days after the day the action was set down for trial. If the parties do not schedule it in that time, the registrar schedules it and tells the parties. The court can order otherwise. The date must be 30 to 120 days before the first trial day, or before the first day of the trial sittings, whichever is later. An order or practice direction can say otherwise.

Agree with the other parties on a schedule of dates for serving experts' reports. You have 60 days after the day the action was set down for trial. The court can order otherwise.

If you will call an expert witness at trial, serve the expert's signed report on every other party. Do this at least 90 days before the date of the pre-trial conference. This is the latest it can be done; earlier is fine. A report from an expert who answers another party's expert must be served at least 60 days before the pre-trial conference. An expert cannot testify on an issue that is not in a report served in time, unless the trial judge allows it. The time can be extended by the pre-trial judge, by the court on a motion, or by the parties' written consent. But consent cannot move the trial date.

Deliver a certificate of readiness (Form 50A) saying whether you will call expert evidence at trial. Do this at least 30 days before the date of the pre-trial conference. For each expert, say whether their report was served in time and, if not, why. This applies even if the time to serve the report was extended. This is the latest it can be done; earlier is fine. If the pre-trial conference is moved, count from the new date.

If your action is under the simplified procedure, agree with the other parties on a proposed trial management plan. Do this at least 30 days before the date of the pre-trial conference. This applies only to an action under the simplified procedure. The plan lists every witness, including experts, and divides the trial time between the parties, to a total of no more than five days. This is the latest it can be done; earlier is fine.

File a pre-trial conference brief, with proof of service. Do this at least 5 days before the date of the pre-trial conference. This is the latest it can be done; earlier is fine. Because the period is seven days or less, Saturdays, Sundays and holidays are not counted. In a simplified procedure action, each party files other things instead. These are the proposed trial management plan, the party's affidavit of documents and the documents it relies on, any expert affidavit, and any other material needed. Each party also delivers a statement of no more than three pages on the issues and its position, and a trial management checklist (Form 76D). For the form to use for the brief, check the notice of the pre-trial conference or the court's order.

Times set by the Rules of Civil Procedure are counted under those rules. The first day is not counted. If a time counted forward ends on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, it ends on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (c)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the safe course is to act by the last day before it that is not a holiday. For a period of seven days or less, holidays are not counted at all (r. 3.01 (1) (b)). Except for the document that starts a case, a document served after 4 p.m. or on a holiday counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (d)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
```

### `answer:civil:both:missed-trial:whats-happening`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:both:missed-trial
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I missed my trial — is my case over?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
Your action was called for trial and a party did not attend. When that happens, the trial judge may go ahead with the trial without that party. If the plaintiff attends and the defendant does not, the judge may dismiss any counterclaim and let the plaintiff prove the claim. If the defendant attends and the plaintiff does not, the judge may dismiss the action and let the defendant prove any counterclaim. The judge may also make any other order that is just.
```

### `answer:civil:both:missed-trial:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:both:missed-trial
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I missed my trial — is my case over?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
If you did not attend the trial and a judgment was made against you, a judge may set it aside or change it, on terms that are just. An appellate court means the Court of Appeal or the Divisional Court, as the case requires. If you appeal an order to an appellate court, you must start by serving a notice of appeal within 30 days after the order was made, unless a statute or the rules say otherwise. The notice is Form 61A.2 for the Court of Appeal or Form 61A.3 for the Divisional Court. With it, you must serve and file, with proof of service, an appellant's certificate respecting evidence (Form 61C). The certificate sets out only the parts of the evidence that you think the appeal needs. Serve them on every party whose interest may be affected by the appeal, and on anyone a statute allows to be heard on it. You do not need to serve a defendant who was noted in default.
```

### `answer:civil:both:missed-trial:your-deadline`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:both:missed-trial
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I missed my trial — is my case over?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
If you want to appeal a final order, serve a notice of appeal with a certificate respecting evidence (Form 61C). You have 30 days after the day the order was made. File the notice, with proof of service, within 10 days after you serve it. Which court hears the appeal depends on the order. Some final orders of a Superior Court judge go to the Divisional Court. These include an order to pay one sum of $50,000 or less, or payments of $50,000 or less in the first 12 months, not counting costs. They also include an order dismissing a claim for $50,000 or less. So does an order dismissing a larger claim where the judge or jury says the award would have been $50,000 or less. Other final orders of a Superior Court judge go to the Court of Appeal. A final order of an associate judge goes to the Divisional Court. An appeal only about costs, or from an order made with everyone's consent, needs leave first. An order extending the time can be made only by a judge of the appeal court. You can also ask a judge to set aside the judgment under rule 52.01 (3). That rule sets no fixed time. If no party attended and the action was struck off the trial list, other steps apply. There are 30 days to move for leave to restore it, and two years before the registrar dismisses it.

Times set by the Rules of Civil Procedure are counted under those rules. The first day is not counted. If a time counted forward ends on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, it ends on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (c)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the safe course is to act by the last day before it that is not a holiday. For a period of seven days or less, holidays are not counted at all (r. 3.01 (1) (b)). Except for the document that starts a case, a document served after 4 p.m. or on a holiday counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (d)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
```

### `answer:civil:both:judgment-given:whats-happening`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:both:judgment-given
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "The judge decided my case and I disagree — can I appeal, and by when?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
A final order of an associate judge is appealed to the Divisional Court. Some final orders of a Superior Court judge also go to the Divisional Court. One kind is an order to pay one sum of $50,000 or less, not counting costs. Another is an order for payments that add up to $50,000 or less in the first 12 months, not counting costs. A third is an order that dismisses a claim for $50,000 or less. The last is an order that dismisses a larger claim, where the judge or jury says the award would have been $50,000 or less. Other final orders of a Superior Court judge go to the Court of Appeal. The exception is when another Act sends the appeal to the Divisional Court. An order made under section 137.1 of the Courts of Justice Act also goes to the Court of Appeal.
```

### `answer:civil:both:judgment-given:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:both:judgment-given
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "The judge decided my case and I disagree — can I appeal, and by when?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/90c43

```
If you want to appeal, serve a notice of appeal within 30 days after the order was made. This applies unless a statute or the rules say otherwise. Use Form 61A.2 for the Court of Appeal, or Form 61A.3 for the Divisional Court. Serve it on every party whose interest may be affected by the appeal, and on anyone a statute allows to be heard on the appeal. You do not have to serve a defendant who was noted in default. You also do not have to serve a respondent who did not deliver a notice of appearance. This does not apply if that respondent was heard at the hearing with leave. With the notice, you must serve and file an appellant's certificate respecting evidence (Form 61C), with proof of service. It lists only the parts of the evidence that you think are needed for the appeal. The notice of appeal must state what you are asking for, your grounds of appeal, and why the appeal court can hear it. That last part includes whether leave to appeal is needed and, if so, whether it was granted. File the notice of appeal, with proof of service, in the Registrar's office within 10 days after you serve it. If you serve it but do not file it in that time, you are treated as having given up the appeal, unless the court orders otherwise. An appeal only about costs that the judge had the choice to award needs leave of the appeal court first. So does an appeal from an order made with the consent of the parties. To ask for leave, serve a notice of motion for leave to appeal within 15 days after the order was made, unless a statute says otherwise. Use Form 61A.1 for the Court of Appeal, or Form 61A for the Divisional Court. File it with proof of service in the Registrar's office within five days after you serve it. If leave is granted, deliver the notice of appeal within seven days after leave is granted. If the Divisional Court granted leave under rule 62.02, also deliver the appellant's certificate respecting evidence (Form 61C) with it within those seven days. You may want to add a costs-only appeal to an appeal that needs no leave. If so, ask for leave in the notice of appeal, or in a supplementary notice of appeal. The panel that hears the main appeal decides whether to grant leave. Maybe the other side appealed, and you want the order set aside or changed. If so, serve a notice of cross-appeal (Form 61E) within 15 days after you were served with their notice of appeal. The same applies if you will ask for a different result should their appeal succeed. File it, with proof of service, within 10 days after you serve it. If your cross-appeal is under a statute that needs leave to appeal, you must get leave. An order extending a time limit for an appeal can be made only by a judge of the appeal court.
```

Delivering the notice of appeal puts part of the order on hold until the appeal is decided. The hold covers any part for paying money. It does not cover a part that awards or enforces support. ### `answer:civil:both:appeal-in-progress:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:both:appeal-in-progress
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "An appeal has been started — what has to be done next, and by when?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
If you are the appellant, file the notice of appeal, with proof of service, in the Registrar's office within 10 days after you served it. If you do not, you are treated as having given up the appeal, unless the court orders otherwise. Within 30 days after filing it, file proof that you ordered a transcript of all oral evidence the parties have not agreed to leave out. If it is needed in the interest of justice, a judge of the appeal court may give special directions about the transcript. Perfect the appeal within 30 days after filing the notice of appeal if no transcript is needed. If a transcript is needed, you have 60 days after you get notice that the evidence has been transcribed. To perfect it, serve the appeal book and compendium, the exhibit book, any transcript and your factum. Serve them on every other party and anyone else entitled to be heard. File them with the Registrar, with proof of service. Then serve and file a certificate of perfection, with proof of service. If you are the respondent, serve a respondent's certificate respecting evidence (Form 61D) on the appellant. Do this within 15 days after you were served with the appellant's certificate. File it with proof of service. It confirms the appellant's certificate, or lists things to add or remove. If you do not serve and file it in time, you are treated as confirming the appellant's certificate. Instead of these certificates, the parties may make an agreement about the documents and transcript within 30 days after the notice of appeal was served. As respondent, deliver your factum and compendium within 60 days. The time starts when you are served with the appeal book and compendium, exhibit book, any transcript and the appellant's factum. Deliver means serve and file with proof of service. If you are the respondent and want the order set aside or changed, serve a notice of cross-appeal (Form 61E). Do this within 15 days after you were served with the notice of appeal. The same applies if you will ask for a different result should the appeal succeed. File it, with proof of service, within 10 days after you serve it. If your cross-appeal is under a statute that needs leave to appeal, you must get leave. If you do not deliver a notice of cross-appeal, no cross-appeal can be heard without leave of the court hearing the appeal. If you cross-appeal, you also deliver a factum as appellant in the cross-appeal, with your factum or as part of it. The appellant then delivers a factum as respondent to the cross-appeal within 10 days after your factum is served. Your cross-appeal factum is late if it is not delivered within 60 days after the appeal book, transcript and appellant's factum were served. Then the appellant may ask the Registrar, on five days notice, to dismiss the cross-appeal for delay.
```

### `answer:civil:both:appeal-in-progress:your-deadline`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / civil:both:appeal-in-progress
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "An appeal has been started — what has to be done next, and by when?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/900194

```
If you are the appellant, file the notice of appeal, with proof of service, in the Registrar's office. You have 10 days after the day you served the notice of appeal. The 30 days to file proof that you ordered a transcript, and the 30 days to perfect an appeal that needs no transcript, are both counted from the day you file it. An order extending the time can be made only by a judge of the appeal court.

If you are the respondent, serve a respondent's certificate respecting evidence (Form 61D) on the appellant. File it with proof of service. You have 15 days after the day you were served with the appellant's certificate, which comes with the notice of appeal. It confirms the appellant's certificate, or sets out additions or deletions. If you do not serve and file it in time, you are treated as confirming the appellant's certificate. A notice of cross-appeal has the same 15 days. It must be filed with proof of service within 10 days after it is served.

If you are the appellant, file proof that you have ordered a transcript of all oral evidence the parties have not agreed to leave out. You have 30 days after the day you filed the notice of appeal. If you do not, the respondent can ask the Registrar, on ten days notice, to dismiss the appeal for delay. If the problem is not fixed before that motion is heard, the Registrar dismisses the appeal. Costs are then fixed at $750. A judge of the appeal court can allow more time.

If you are the appellant and no transcript is needed, perfect the appeal by serving and filing the appeal documents. You have 30 days after the day you filed the notice of appeal. If you do not, the respondent can move to have the appeal dismissed for delay. Or the Registrar can give notice that it will be dismissed unless it is perfected within 10 days. If the problem is not fixed in time, the Registrar dismisses the appeal, with costs fixed at $750. A judge of the appeal court can allow more time after a Registrar's notice. If there is a cross-appeal, deliver your factum as respondent to it within 10 days after the respondent's factum is served.

If you are the appellant and a transcript is needed, perfect the appeal by serving and filing the appeal documents. You have 60 days after the day you received notice that the evidence has been transcribed. If you do not, the respondent can move to have the appeal dismissed for delay. The Registrar can also give notice that the appeal will be dismissed unless it is perfected within 10 days. The Registrar can do this if the transcript is not filed within 60 days after the Registrar was told it was ready. The Registrar can also do it if the appeal is not perfected within one year after the notice of appeal was filed. If the problem is not fixed in time, the Registrar dismisses the appeal, with costs fixed at $750. If there is a cross-appeal, deliver your factum as respondent to it within 10 days after the respondent's factum is served.

If you are the respondent, deliver your factum and compendium. You have 60 days after the day you were served with the appeal book and compendium, exhibit book, any transcript and the appellant's factum. Deliver means serve it on the other parties and file it with proof of service. An order extending the time can be made only by a judge of the appeal court.

Times set by the Rules of Civil Procedure are counted under those rules. The first day is not counted. If a time counted forward ends on a Saturday, Sunday or holiday, it ends on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (c)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the safe course is to act by the last day before it that is not a holiday. For a period of seven days or less, holidays are not counted at all (r. 3.01 (1) (b)). Except for the document that starts a case, a document served after 4 p.m. or on a holiday counts as served on the next day that is not a holiday (r. 3.01 (1) (d)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
```

```
The appellant may miss the time to file proof of the transcript order, or the time to perfect. Then the respondent may ask the Registrar to dismiss the appeal for delay, on 10 days notice. The Registrar may also warn that the appeal will be dismissed unless it is perfected within 10 days. One case is when the appeal is not perfected within one year after the notice of appeal was filed. If the problem is not fixed in time, the Registrar must dismiss the appeal, with costs fixed at $750. A judge of the appeal court can allow more time. Once the appeal is perfected, the Registrar lists it to be heard and sends a notice of listing for hearing (Form 61G).
```

- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I missed my conference, or forgot to confirm it — what happens now?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
Each party must confirm a conference with the clerk by 2 p.m. three days before the conference date. Unless the court orders otherwise, a conference is not held if that confirmation was not given on time. The parties must come to each conference, unless the court orders otherwise. ### `answer:family:both:missed-or-unconfirmed-conference:what-to-do-next`
```

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:both:missed-or-unconfirmed-conference
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I missed my conference, or forgot to confirm it — what happens now?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
For any conference that is set, each party must give the clerk a confirmation of conference (Form 17F). It is due no later than 2 p.m. three days before the conference date. You can deliver it to the court office, email it to the court office, or submit it online through Justice Services Online or the Ontario Courts Public Portal, whichever is available. Before you give it to the clerk, you must give a copy to every other party by mail, fax, email or any other method, except in a child protection case. Costs are not awarded at a conference unless a party was not prepared or did not serve the required documents, or one of the other cases below applies. The other cases are a party who did not make required disclosure, made the conference unproductive in some other way, or did not follow the rules. In that case, the judge must order that party to pay the costs of the conference right away, decide the amount, and give any directions needed.
```

### `answer:family:both:missed-or-unconfirmed-conference:your-deadline`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:both:missed-or-unconfirmed-conference
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I missed my conference, or forgot to confirm it — what happens now?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
If the clerk serves a notice of approaching dismissal, take one of the five steps below, or the case is dismissed without further notice. You have 60 days after the day the notice of approaching dismissal was served. Step one: get an order giving more time. Step two: file an agreement signed by all parties and their licensed representatives, if any, for a final order on all issues. File it with a notice of motion for an order carrying it out. Step three: serve and file a notice of withdrawal (Form 12) of all outstanding claims. Step four: schedule or adjourn the case for trial. Step five: arrange a case conference or settlement conference for the first available date. After a missed conference, the clerk serves that notice if three things are true. It was a case or settlement conference. It was set for 365 days or more after the case started. And a judge did not adjourn it. The clerk also serves one if the case was not settled, withdrawn, or scheduled or adjourned for trial before day 365. If a conference arranged as step five also does not go ahead, and a judge did not adjourn it, the case is dismissed without further notice. A judge can set aside the clerk's dismissal order on a motion. These rules do not apply to an enforcement. They do not apply to cases under rules 37, 37.1 and 37.2. Those cover support across borders, provisional orders and child abduction across borders. In the Superior Court and the Family Court, they do not apply to a request to enforce a family arbitration award (rule 32.1). In the Ontario Court of Justice and the Family Court, they do not apply to a child protection case.

Times set by the Family Law Rules are counted under those rules. The first day is the day after the event (r. 3 (1)). If the last day of a period falls on a day court offices are closed, the period ends on the next day they are open (r. 3 (3)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the rules do not clearly say how this applies, so the safe course is to act by the last open day before it. For a period of less than seven days, Saturdays, Sundays and other days when all court offices are closed are not counted (r. 3 (2)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
```

### `answer:family:both:order-made-without-notice:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:both:order-made-without-notice
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "A judge made an order against me and I was never told about the motion — what can I do?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
An order made without notice must send the matter back to court, to the same judge if possible, within 14 days or on a date the court chooses. If you respond to a motion made with a notice of motion (Form 14), your response must be served and filed no later than four days before the motion date. Unless the court orders otherwise, the order must be served right away on every party affected, along with all the documents used on the motion. You may bring a motion asking the court to change the order, because the court may change an order that was made without notice. Usually no motion can be served or heard before a conference on the main issues in the case is done. A motion to change a temporary order made without notice is an exception, so it can be brought before then. A motion needs a notice of motion (Form 14) and an affidavit (Form 14A), and may have more evidence. If it is only about procedural, simple or unopposed matters, you may use a motion form (Form 14B) instead. For a motion with notice, the steps you must take include serving the papers on all other parties no later than six days before the motion date, and filing them no later than four days before it. They also include giving the clerk a confirmation of motion (Form 14C) by 2 p.m. three days before the motion date.
```

```
The order must send the matter back to court within 14 days after the day the order was made. This is the court's timetable, not a step you take. The court can choose another date instead. The matter goes back to the same judge if possible. The order sets the return date. Unless the court orders otherwise, the other party must serve you right away. They must serve the order and all the papers used on the motion. You can also bring a motion to change the order because it was made without notice. That motion does not have to wait for a conference.

Times set by the Family Law Rules are counted under those rules. The first day is the day after the event (r. 3 (1)). If the last day of a period falls on a day court offices are closed, the period ends on the next day they are open (r. 3 (3)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the rules do not clearly say how this applies, so the safe course is to act by the last open day before it. For a period of less than seven days, Saturdays, Sundays and other days when all court offices are closed are not counted (r. 3 (2)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
```

### `answer:family:both:motion-to-change-response-time-missed:whats-happening`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:both:motion-to-change-response-time-missed
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "Nobody responded to the motion to change in time — what happens now?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
A person served with a motion to change who does not agree must serve and file a response (Form 15B). The same applies if they want the court to make an added or a different change. A person who agrees must instead sign a consent (Form 15C) and return it to the person who made the motion. They must also give a copy of the signed consent to the assignee, if there is one. They have 30 days after they get the motion and its papers if they live in Canada or the United States. In any other case, they have 60 days. Here, that time has passed and neither was done.
```

### `answer:family:both:motion-to-change-response-time-missed:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:both:motion-to-change-response-time-missed
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "Nobody responded to the motion to change in time — what happens now?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
Then, unless a court orders otherwise, the person who did not respond loses the right to notice of later steps in the case. The one exception is that they must still be served with any order made. They also may not take part in the case in any way. The court may deal with the case without them, and a date may be set for an uncontested trial. In the Ontario Court of Justice, the clerk must send the case to a judge by the first court date. This happens if no response, consent or notice of financial interest was filed. The judge decides on the evidence filed in the motion. In the Family Court of the Superior Court of Justice, a motion to change is a fast track case. There, the clerk must do the same. Neither of these two clerk steps applies to enforcements, to cases under rule 37, 37.1 or 37.2, or to cases under the Child, Youth and Family Services Act, 2017. In the Family Court, the clerk step also does not apply to cases under rule 32.1. If you made the motion, you may also file a motion form (Form 14B). In it, you ask the court to make the order you asked for in your papers. You cannot do this if an assignee has filed a notice of financial interest and opposes the change. Court staff must refuse a late document. They may take it only by a later time set by a statute, a court order or the parties’ written consent. The parties may agree in writing to change most times set in the rules. The court may also make an order to lengthen a time, subject to any limits in the rules. Sometimes a person is served under the rules but never sees the papers. Or they see them only after the date service took effect. If that is you, you may bring a motion. The court may then lengthen the time, set aside the results of missing it, or make any other order that is just.
```

### `answer:family:both:case-in-wrong-municipality:whats-happening`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:both:case-in-wrong-municipality
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "The case was started in the wrong city — or it would be easier somewhere else. Can it be moved?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
The rules say where a family case must start. This is subject to the Courts of Justice Act sections on the Family Court. The usual place is the municipality where a party lives. A case may be about decision-making responsibility, parenting time or contact with a child. Then the place is where the child usually lives, except as section 22 of the Children’s Law Reform Act provides. Child protection and adoption cases have their own rules on place. A case may also start in a place all parties choose. But the court in that place must give its permission first. These rules apply to a motion to change a final order or agreement as if it were a new case.
```

### `answer:family:both:case-in-wrong-municipality:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:both:case-in-wrong-municipality
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "The case was started in the wrong city — or it would be easier somewhere else. Can it be moved?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
The clerk must refuse to accept an application for filing unless one of four things is true. First, it is started where a party lives. Second, it is started where the child usually lives. This one is for a child protection case, or a case about decision-making responsibility, parenting time or contact with a child. Third, it is started in a place all parties chose, and the order allowing that is filed with the application. Fourth, the person filing it says in writing that the rules allow this kind of case to be started there. This one covers only a case about decision-making responsibility, parenting time or contact with a child, a child protection case, an adoption, or a case started because of immediate danger. A party may start a case in any place if there is immediate danger to a child’s or party’s health or safety. The same applies if there is immediate danger that a child may be taken out of Ontario. A motion may be heard there. Then the case must be moved right away to a place the rules name, unless the court orders otherwise. Every step in the case, except enforcement, must take place where the case was started or moved to. The court may move the case, or one step in it, to another place if that is much more convenient. You ask for this by bringing a motion.
```

```
In areas served by the Family Court, the family cases listed in the Courts of Justice Act must be started, heard and decided there. Appeals and prosecutions are not included. A Family Court judge may, on motion, move a case to the right court in an area the Family Court does not serve. The judge must find that the balance of convenience favours that place. A judge in such an area may also, on motion and on the same test, move a case to the Family Court in a particular place. Enforcing an order follows its own rules on place.
```

The clerk sends this notice by mail or email if the case was not settled, withdrawn, or scheduled or adjourned for trial before the 365th day after it started, and no order gave more time. The clerk also sends it if a case conference or settlement conference was set for the 365th day or later, but it did not take place that day and a judge did not adjourn it. Once the notice is served, the case will be dismissed without further notice unless one of the parties takes a step within 60 days.

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:both:notice-of-approaching-dismissal
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I got a notice that my family case will be dismissed — how do I stop that?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
To stop the dismissal, one of the parties must take one of five steps within 60 days after the notice is served. One step is to get an order that gives more time. The parties cannot give more time just by agreeing to it, as only an order can. A second step is to file an agreement for a final order that deals with all issues in the case. All parties and their licensed representatives, if any, must sign it. File it with a notice of motion for an order that carries out the agreement. A third step is to serve on all parties, and file, a notice of withdrawal (Form 12) that drops all claims still left in the case. A fourth step is to schedule or adjourn the case for trial. A fifth step is to arrange a case conference or settlement conference for the first available date. If you take the fifth step, the conference must go ahead on that date or be adjourned by a judge, or the case will be dismissed without further notice.
```

### `answer:family:both:notice-of-approaching-dismissal:your-deadline`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:both:notice-of-approaching-dismissal
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I got a notice that my family case will be dismissed — how do I stop that?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
Take one of the five steps below, or the case is dismissed without further notice. You have 60 days after the day the notice of approaching dismissal was served. Step one: get an order giving more time. Step two: file an agreement signed by all parties and their licensed representatives, if any, for a final order on all issues. File it with a notice of motion for an order carrying it out. Step three: serve and file a notice of withdrawal (Form 12) of all outstanding claims. Step four: schedule or adjourn the case for trial. Step five: arrange a case conference or settlement conference for the first available date. Only one party needs to take a step. The parties cannot extend this time by agreement. Only a court order can. If a conference arranged as step five does not go ahead, and a judge did not adjourn it, the case is dismissed without further notice. If the clerk dismisses the case, a judge can set aside the dismissal order on a motion. These rules do not apply to an enforcement. They do not apply to cases under rules 37, 37.1 and 37.2. Those cover support across borders, provisional orders and child abduction across borders. In the Superior Court and the Family Court, they do not apply to a request to enforce a family arbitration award (rule 32.1). In the Ontario Court of Justice and the Family Court, they do not apply to a child protection case. If the notice came by mail, it counts as served on the fifth day after mailing. If it came by email, it counts as served on the date in the email, or the next day if sent after 4 p.m. To be safe, count from the day it was mailed or emailed.

Times set by the Family Law Rules are counted under those rules. The first day is the day after the event (r. 3 (1)). If the last day of a period falls on a day court offices are closed, the period ends on the next day they are open (r. 3 (3)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the rules do not clearly say how this applies, so the safe course is to act by the last open day before it. For a period of less than seven days, Saturdays, Sundays and other days when all court offices are closed are not counted (r. 3 (2)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
```

```
If no step is taken in time, the clerk dismisses the case by preparing and signing an order, with no costs payable by any party. The clerk serves that order on each party by mail or email. ### `answer:family:both:served-with-notice-of-default-hearing:whats-happening`
```

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:both:served-with-notice-of-default-hearing
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "A notice of default hearing has been issued about unpaid support — what do I have to do?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
At a default hearing, the payor must come to court. The payor must explain why support was not paid as the order requires. The payor is the person who must pay under the order. The clerk issues the notice (Form 30) when the party enforcing the order files a statement of money owed. If the recipient is enforcing, the recipient also files a request (Form 30A). The Director of the Family Responsibility Office may be enforcing instead. If so, the rules on enforcement by the recipient apply to the Director. The notice must be served on the payor by special service, and filed. When the payor could face jail, the notice may be served only by leaving a copy with the payor, unless the court orders otherwise. Someone other than the party who must serve it has to do the serving. That does not apply if the court orders otherwise, or if the party serving is the Director of the Family Responsibility Office.
```
