### `answer:family:both:served-with-notice-of-default-hearing:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:both:served-with-notice-of-default-hearing
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "A notice of default hearing has been issued about unpaid support — what do I have to do?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
If you are the payor, you have 10 days after you were served with the notice. In that time, you must serve two forms on the party enforcing the order and file them. That party is the recipient, or the Director if the Director is enforcing. The two forms are a financial statement and a default dispute (Form 30B). If the recipient is enforcing, the Act says the financial statement must be in the form the court rules set. Under the rules, that is Form 13. If the Director is enforcing, its notice may ask you to give the Director a financial statement and proof of income. In that case, the Act says the financial statement must be in the form set by the regulations. You are presumed to admit that the statement of money owed is correct. That changes only if you file a default dispute that says it is wrong and gives detailed reasons. You must also appear in court to explain the default. If you do not file the financial statement or do not appear, the court may issue a warrant for your arrest to bring you to court. If you are the recipient enforcing the order, you must serve and file a new statement of money owed. Do this not more than seven days before the hearing. If the Director is enforcing, it must do this only in two cases. One is if it asks the court to enforce more than the notice shows. The other is if the court directs it.
```

- **Status:** draft

- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "A notice of default hearing has been issued about unpaid support — what do I have to do?"

```
If you are the payor, serve a financial statement and a default dispute (Form 30B) on the party enforcing the order, and file them. You have 10 days after the day you were served with the notice of default hearing. The party enforcing is the recipient, or the Director of the Family Responsibility Office. Use Form 13 for the financial statement. If the Director is enforcing, use the form the regulations require, as the notice will say. Also give the Director the proof of income the notice asks for. You are presumed to agree that the statement of money owed is correct. That changes only if you file a default dispute saying it is wrong and giving detailed reasons. You must also come to court to explain the default. If you do not file the financial statement or do not come, the court can issue a warrant for your arrest. At the hearing, you are presumed able to pay unless you show otherwise. Unless the court finds you cannot pay for valid reasons, it can order payments, security, or jail for up to 180 days. The court can decide and enforce the amount owing up to the hearing date.

If you are the recipient enforcing the order, serve and file a new statement of money owed no more than 7 days before the default hearing. That means within the last 7 days before it, not earlier. If the Director of the Family Responsibility Office is enforcing, the Director must do this only in two cases. One is if it asks the court to enforce more than the notice shows. The other is if the court directs it.

Times set by the Family Law Rules are counted under those rules. The first day is the day after the event (r. 3 (1)). If the last day of a period falls on a day court offices are closed, the period ends on the next day they are open (r. 3 (3)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the rules do not clearly say how this applies, so the safe course is to act by the last open day before it. For a period of less than seven days, Saturdays, Sundays and other days when all court offices are closed are not counted (r. 3 (2)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
```

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:both:served-with-notice-of-default-hearing
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "A notice of default hearing has been issued about unpaid support — what do I have to do?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
At the hearing, the court may decide and enforce the amount owing as of the hearing date. Unless shown otherwise, the payor is presumed able to pay the arrears and later payments. A statement of arrears the Director prepared and served is also presumed correct for arrears that built up while the order was filed with it. The court may make orders unless it is satisfied the payor cannot pay for valid reasons. These orders include paying all or part of the arrears, and giving security. They also include jail for up to 180 days, or until the arrears are paid, if sooner. The court may suspend a jail order on conditions. These orders do not stop arrears from building up. They also do not limit other ways to enforce the order.
```

### `answer:family:both:served-with-contempt-motion:whats-happening`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:both:served-with-contempt-motion
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I was served with a contempt motion for not following an order — what could happen?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
A contempt motion enforces an order that is not a payment order, in the same case the order was made in. Unless the court orders otherwise, the notice of contempt motion (Form 31) must be served together with a supporting affidavit, by special service. To bring you before the court, the court may issue a warrant for your arrest, but only if two things are true. Your attendance must be needed in the interest of justice. And it must be that you are not expected to come on your own.
```

### `answer:family:both:served-with-contempt-motion:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:both:served-with-contempt-motion
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I was served with a contempt motion for not following an order — what could happen?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
Unless the court orders otherwise, you, as the party responding, must serve all your evidence in response. After that, the party making the motion may serve evidence that replies to any new matters raised by your evidence. Unless the court orders otherwise, no other evidence may be used. Most motions must wait until a conference on the main issues in the case is completed. That wait does not apply to a motion for a contempt order. Any affidavit on this motion, including yours, must as much as possible hold only what the signer knows first-hand. It may include things the signer learned from someone else only if three things are true. The source must be named, and the signer must say they believe it is true. For a contempt motion, the information must also not be expected to be disputed.
```

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:both:served-with-contempt-motion
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I was served with a contempt motion for not following an order — what could happen?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
Rule 31 sets no separate time to respond to a notice of contempt motion (Form 31). The general rule for responding to a motion sets 4 days before the motion date. But that rule is worded for a notice of motion in Form 14, not Form 31. Under the motion rules, the party responding serves all their evidence in response. The safe course is to serve and file your evidence at least 4 days before the motion date.
```

### `answer:family:both:served-with-contempt-motion:what-happens-after`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:both:served-with-contempt-motion
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I was served with a contempt motion for not following an order — what could happen?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
If the court finds you in contempt, it may order you to go to jail for a period and on terms that are just. It may also order you to pay a fine, pay a penalty to a party, or pay costs. Or it may order you to do anything else it decides, not do what it forbids, or obey any other order. The court may also give permission to issue a writ of temporary seizure (Form 28C) against your property. Some contempt orders are made under one of three provisions. For those, the jail time and the fine cannot be more than the relevant Act allows. The first provision is s. 38 of the Children’s Law Reform Act. The second is s. 49 of the Family Law Act. The third is s. 53 of the Family Responsibility and Support Arrears Enforcement Act, 1996. An order for jail or a fine may be put on hold on conditions. A party may later say, in a Form 32C affidavit on a motion with special service, that you broke such a condition. The court may then issue a warrant of committal against you. The court may, on motion, change a contempt order.
```

### `answer:family:both:document-disclosure-requested:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:both:document-disclosure-requested
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "The other side asked me for a list of my documents — what do I have to give them, and by when?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
Within 10 days after the request, you must give the other party that affidavit. Papers that must be served under rule 13 (financial disclosure) are left out of this 10-day duty. The duty is also not on the Office of the Children’s Lawyer or on children’s aid societies. If you claim a document is protected by legal privilege, the court may, on motion, look at it and decide. You may use a document you claim is privileged at trial only in one of two ways. One is if the other party was allowed to see it and given a free copy at least 30 days before the settlement conference. The other is on the terms the trial judge thinks fit. Later, you may find a document that should have been listed, or find the list is wrong or not complete. If so, you must right away serve a new affidavit with the correct list. If you do not follow this rule or an order under it, the court may order you to give the affidavit, let the other party examine a document, or give them a free copy. It may also order that a document that helps your case cannot be used without its permission. Or it may order that you cannot get disclosure until you comply. Those orders are in addition to the court’s general powers when the rules or an order are not followed. They include an order for costs, a penalty or fine, dismissing a claim, or striking out a document a party filed.
```

The other party can then ask to see a listed document, unless it is protected by legal privilege. They can get a copy at their own cost. The parties can agree in writing to change this time. The court can also change it.

Times set by the Family Law Rules are counted under those rules. The first day is the day after the event (r. 3 (1)). If the last day of a period falls on a day court offices are closed, the period ends on the next day they are open (r. 3 (3)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the rules do not clearly say how this applies, so the safe course is to act by the last open day before it. For a period of less than seven days, Saturdays, Sundays and other days when all court offices are closed are not counted (r. 3 (2)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
```

### `answer:family:both:offer-to-settle:whats-happening`

- **Status:** draft

- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "We got an offer to settle, or want to make one — how long does it stay open?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
An offer is an offer to settle one or more claims in a case, motion, appeal or enforcement. A counter-offer is an offer too. The rule on offers applies to an offer made at any time, even before the case is started. An offer can set a time for it to be accepted. If it is not accepted in that time, it is treated as withdrawn.
```

### `answer:family:both:offer-to-settle:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:both:offer-to-settle
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "We got an offer to settle, or want to make one — how long does it stay open?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
A party may serve an offer on any other party. An offer must be signed personally by the party making it. A party may act in person, without a representative. If the party making the offer has a licensed representative, the representative must sign it too. A licensed representative is a lawyer or family legal services provider. The party who made an offer may withdraw it at any time before it is accepted, by serving a notice of withdrawal. The only valid way to accept an offer is to serve an acceptance on the party who made it. This must be done before the offer is withdrawn, and before the court begins to give a decision on a claim the offer deals with. You may accept an offer even if you rejected it before or made a counter-offer. The terms of an offer must not be mentioned in any document filed in the continuing record. They also must not be mentioned to the judge hearing the claim until the judge has dealt with all the issues except costs. A special party or a child party may make, withdraw or accept an offer. But an acceptance of their offer, or their acceptance of an offer, does not bind them until the court approves.
```

### `answer:family:both:offer-to-settle:your-deadline`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:both:offer-to-settle
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "We got an offer to settle, or want to make one — how long does it stay open?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
To accept an offer, serve an acceptance on the party who made it. Do it before the offer is withdrawn or ends, and before the court starts to give a decision on the claim it covers. An offer not accepted within the time it sets is treated as withdrawn. The party who made it can withdraw it at any time before it is accepted, by serving a notice of withdrawal. It can still be accepted after it was rejected, or after a counter-offer. The party making it must sign it personally. Their licensed representative, if they have one, must sign it too. Making, withdrawing, accepting or rejecting an offer can affect costs. The costs rule in r. 24 (12) has conditions. An offer about a motion must be made at least 1 day before the motion date. An offer about a trial or other hearing must be made at least 7 days before it. The offer must not end or be withdrawn before the hearing starts. It must not be accepted. The party who made it must get an order as good as or better than the offer.
```

- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "We got an offer to settle, or want to make one — how long does it stay open?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
Making, withdrawing, accepting and rejecting offers can have costs results under rule 24. If an accepted offer does not deal with costs, either party can ask the court for costs. If a party does not carry out the terms of an accepted offer, the other party has two choices. They may make a motion to turn the parts of the offer within the court's power into an order. Or they may go on with the case as if the offer had never been accepted.
```

### `answer:family:respondent:served-with-amended-application:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:respondent:served-with-amended-application
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "The applicant changed their application after I answered — do I have to answer again?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
You may amend your answer without the court's permission. To do so, serve and file an amended answer within 14 days after you were served with the amended application. In a child protection case, a different rule applies if something significant about the child changed after the first document was filed. Then you may serve and file an amended answer and plan of care. You have 30 days after service if you were served in Canada or the United States. It is 60 days if you were served outside them. An application for an order under sections 53.1 to 53.5 of Ontario Regulation 155/18 is an exception to that rule. In your amended answer, underline all changes. Also note in the margin of each changed page the rule or order that allows the change and the date of the change. Your amended answer may add a claim about decision-making responsibility, parenting time or contact with a child that was not in your first answer. If it does, it must come with the documents that rule 35.1 requires. Some claims need a financial statement from the person they are made against. They are a claim for support, a property claim, or a claim for exclusive possession of the matrimonial home and its contents. If the amendment adds one of these claims against you, you must serve and file a financial statement within the time for serving and filing an answer, even if you do not serve an answer.
```

### `answer:family:respondent:served-with-amended-application:your-deadline`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:respondent:served-with-amended-application
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "The applicant changed their application after I answered — do I have to answer again?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
If you want to amend your answer without the court's permission, serve and file an amended answer. You have 14 days after the day you were served with the amended application. In a child protection case, if something significant about the child has changed, the time is 30 days. It is 60 days if you were served outside Canada and the United States. After the time runs out, you need the court's permission on a motion to amend your answer. Your amended answer may add a claim about decision-making responsibility, parenting time or contact that was not in your first answer. If so, include the papers rule 35.1 requires. The amendment may add a claim for support or property against you. If so, your financial statement is due in the time for answering it. The parties can agree in writing to change this time. The court can also change it.

Times set by the Family Law Rules are counted under those rules. The first day is the day after the event (r. 3 (1)). If the last day of a period falls on a day court offices are closed, the period ends on the next day they are open (r. 3 (3)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the rules do not clearly say how this applies, so the safe course is to act by the last open day before it. For a period of less than seven days, Saturdays, Sundays and other days when all court offices are closed are not counted (r. 3 (2)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
```

### `answer:family:both:served-with-notice-of-appeal:whats-happening`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:both:served-with-notice-of-appeal
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "The other side is appealing an Ontario Court of Justice order to the Superior Court — what do I have to do?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
The other party is appealing an order of the Ontario Court of Justice to the Superior Court of Justice. They started the appeal by serving a notice of appeal (Form 38) on you. In the appeal, they are the appellant and you are the respondent. The notice of appeal must state the order the appellant wants and the legal grounds for the appeal. At the hearing, no other grounds may be argued unless the court gives permission.
```

### `answer:family:both:served-with-notice-of-appeal:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:both:served-with-notice-of-appeal
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "The other side is appealing an Ontario Court of Justice order to the Superior Court — what do I have to do?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
The appellant must decide, after talking with you, whether the appeal needs a transcript of the evidence. If you both agree on what evidence to transcribe, the appellant must order that evidence transcribed. If you cannot agree, the appellant must order a transcript of all the oral evidence from the hearing, unless the court orders otherwise. Within 60 days after the appellant serves its appeal record and factum, you must serve your respondent's factum on the appellant and anyone else entitled to be heard, and file it. In a case under the Child, Youth and Family Services Act, 2017, that time is 30 days instead. That shorter time does not apply to an appeal of an order under sections 53.1 to 53.5 of Ontario Regulation 155/18. Some material from the first court may be needed for the appeal but missing from the appellant's appeal record. If so, you must also serve and file, in the same time, a respondent's appeal record with a copy of that material. Your factum can be no more than 30 pages long, and it must be signed by your lawyer or, if you have none, by you. Its parts include your position on each issue the appellant raised and the exact order you ask the appeal court to make. You may also want to appeal the same order yourself. If you do, the same rule applies to your appeal, and the two appeals are heard together. Your notice of appeal must be served on every other party affected by the appeal or entitled to appeal, and on the clerk of the court where the order was made. Some appeals are under section 121 of the Child, Youth and Family Services Act, 2017. In those, also serve every other person entitled to notice under subsection 79 (3) of that Act who appeared at the hearing. It must be served within 30 days after the date of a final order, or seven days after the date of a temporary order. In a case under the Child, Youth and Family Services Act, 2017, it is 30 days for a temporary order too. Again, that does not apply to an appeal of an order under sections 53.1 to 53.5 of Ontario Regulation 155/18. You must then file it within 10 days after serving it. If a transcript is needed, the appellant must file proof it was ordered within 30 days after filing the notice of appeal. Sometimes the appellant does not do that, or does not serve and file its appeal record and factum in time. If so, you may file a motion form (Form 14B) to have the appeal dismissed for delay.
```

For a temporary order, it is 7 days. Count from the order, not from when you were served. Serving a notice of appeal does not stop a support order from being enforced. For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the rules do not clearly say how this applies, so the safe course is to act by the last open day before it. For a period of less than seven days, Saturdays, Sundays and other days when all court offices are closed are not counted (r. 3 (2)). ### `answer:family:both:served-with-licence-suspension-notice:whats-happening`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:both:served-with-licence-suspension-notice
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "FRO says my driver's licence may be suspended for unpaid support — what can I do, and how long do I have?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/96f31

```
A support order filed in the Director's office is in default, and the Director has served you with a first notice. It says your driver's licence may be suspended unless you act within 30 days after the day it was served. If you do not act in that time, the Director may direct the Registrar of Motor Vehicles to suspend your licence. An order to refrain is a court order that the Director not direct the suspension of your licence.
```

### `answer:family:both:served-with-licence-suspension-notice:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:both:served-with-licence-suspension-notice
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "FRO says my driver's licence may be suspended for unpaid support — what can I do, and how long do I have?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/96f31

```
Within the 30 days, you can do one of three things. You can make an arrangement the Director accepts for paying the support and the arrears. You can pay all the arrears. Or you can get an order to refrain and file it in the Director's office. If you bring a motion to change the support order, you may also bring a motion for an order to refrain, on notice to the Director. You may bring the motion to refrain first if you or your lawyer undertakes to get a court date for the motion to change within 20 days after the order to refrain. If no court date is obtained within those 20 days, the order to refrain ends automatically. You do not need a motion to change if you have started an appeal of the support order and it has not been decided. Submitting a support variation application to the designated authority in Ontario under the Interjurisdictional Support Orders Act, 2002 counts as a motion to change. So does submitting one to the Central Authority in Ontario under the International Recovery of Child Support and Family Maintenance Convention Act, 2023. The motion for an order to refrain must be made in the court that can change the support order. With the notice of motion, you must serve and file a financial statement (Form 13 or 13.1, or Form 4 under Ontario Regulation 167/97) and the proof of income set out in section 15 of that regulation. You may not be able to serve and file the proof of income before the motion is heard. If so, the court may still make the order if you or your lawyer undertakes to serve and file it within 20 days. This motion does not have to wait until a conference on the main issues in the case is over.
```

### `answer:family:both:served-with-licence-suspension-notice:your-deadline`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:both:served-with-licence-suspension-notice
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "FRO says my driver's licence may be suspended for unpaid support — what can I do, and how long do I have?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/96f31

```
To stop the suspension, do one of three things. Make an arrangement the Director accepts for paying the support and the arrears. Or get a court order to refrain and file it in the Director's office. Or pay all the arrears. You have 30 days after the day the first notice was served. For a court order to refrain, these 30 days cannot be extended. A court cannot make an order to refrain after the 30 days. It can make only one for each first notice. If the 30th day is a day court offices are closed, the time for the order does NOT move to the next open day. The order to refrain must be made by the last day court offices are open BEFORE the 30th day. To ask for an order to refrain, bring a motion to change the support order. Also bring a motion for the order to refrain, on notice to the Director. Bring both in the court that can change the support order. You can ask for the order to refrain before you bring the motion to change. To do that, you or your lawyer must give an undertaking (a formal promise) to get a court date for the motion to change. That date must be got within 20 days after the order. You do not need a motion to change if you have appealed the support order and the appeal is not decided. Serve and file a financial statement and proof of income with the notice of motion. If you cannot file proof of income before the motion is heard, the court can still make the order. You or your lawyer must then undertake to serve and file it within 20 days. This motion does not have to wait for a case conference. A motion must normally be served at least 6 days before it is heard, not counting weekends. The order must be made within the 30 days. So start right away.
```

### `answer:family:both:served-with-licence-suspension-notice:what-happens-after`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:both:served-with-licence-suspension-notice
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "FRO says my driver's licence may be suspended for unpaid support — what can I do, and how long do I have?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/statute/96f31

```
A court may make an order to refrain only within the 30 days in the first notice, which cannot be extended, and only one for each first notice. If the 30th day is a day court offices are closed, the order must be made by the last day they are open before then. The court must file a copy in the Director's office promptly after it is signed, and it takes effect only when filed there. It ends on the earliest of several days, which include six months after it is made and the day the motion to change or the appeal is decided. You may bring a motion, with notice to the Director, to extend it once for three months, or six months in some cases. The court must make the extending order before the order to refrain ends. If it ends on a day court offices are closed, the last day is the last day they are open before it ends. Payment terms in an order to refrain do not stop arrears from adding up or stop other ways of enforcing the support order.
```

### `answer:family:both:served-with-notice-of-garnishment:whats-happening`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:both:served-with-notice-of-garnishment
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I was served with a notice of garnishment for family support — can I dispute it?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
A payment order can be enforced in several ways, and garnishment is one of them. The notice of garnishment must be served on the payor and on the garnishee. The payor must also be served with the papers the recipient filed to get it. The notice covers money the garnishee owes the payor when it is served. It also covers money that becomes payable by the garnishee to the payor after that. If the garnishee is a financial institution served as rule 29 requires, the notice reaches only accounts that were open when it was served. The notice stays in effect until it is withdrawn or stopped under rule 29, or until the court orders otherwise. The notice can also cover a debt owed to the payor and another person jointly. Then the garnishee must pay half of that debt, or a larger or smaller amount the court orders. The garnishee must also right away send the other person a notice to co-owner of debt (Form 29C).
```

### `answer:family:both:served-with-notice-of-garnishment:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:both:served-with-notice-of-garnishment
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I was served with a notice of garnishment for family support — can I dispute it?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
If you are the payor or the garnishee, you may dispute the garnishment. To do so, serve a dispute on the other parties and file it within 10 days after you were served. Those 10 days run from service of the notice of garnishment or of a statutory declaration of indexed support. Form 29E is the dispute for a payor. Form 29F is the dispute for a garnishee. Filing a dispute does not by itself stop the money being paid out. The Director or clerk must pay out money received right away, even if a dispute has been filed. There are two exceptions. The court may order that this does not apply, at a garnishment hearing or on a motion to change the garnishment. And once served with the notice to co-owner of debt, the sheriff, clerk or Director must hold the money for 30 days. If you are the co-owner, it may be paid out when the 30 days end, unless you serve and file a dispute within the 30 days. The dispute for a co-owner of the debt is Form 29G.
```

### `answer:family:both:served-with-notice-of-garnishment:your-deadline`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:both:served-with-notice-of-garnishment
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I was served with a notice of garnishment for family support — can I dispute it?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
If you are the payor or the garnishee, you can dispute a notice of garnishment or a statutory declaration of indexed support. To do so, serve a dispute (Form 29E, 29F or 29G) on the other parties and file it. You have 10 days after the day you were served with the notice of garnishment or the statutory declaration of indexed support. Except for a joint debt, money taken under the garnishment is paid out even if a dispute is filed. The court can order otherwise. After a dispute is served and filed, the clerk issues a notice of garnishment hearing if asked. The payor's situation may later change in a way that affects their ability to pay. The payor can then bring a motion to change the garnishment. While the garnishment is in place, the payor may go back to work for the garnishee or start getting money from a new source. If so, the payor sends a notice to the clerk and to the recipient or the Director within 10 days. The parties can agree in writing to change this time. The court can also change it.

If you co-own a debt that was garnished and got a notice to co-owner of debt (Form 29C), you can dispute it. To stop the money being paid out, serve and file a dispute within the 30-day holding period. The sheriff, clerk or Director holds the money for 30 days. They may pay it out when the 30 days end, unless you serve and file a dispute within them. The rule does not say exactly when the 30 days start. So act as soon as you get the notice.

Times set by the Family Law Rules are counted under those rules. The first day is the day after the event (r. 3 (1)). If the last day of a period falls on a day court offices are closed, the period ends on the next day they are open (r. 3 (3)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the rules do not clearly say how this applies, so the safe course is to act by the last open day before it. For a period of less than seven days, Saturdays, Sundays and other days when all court offices are closed are not counted (r. 3 (2)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
```

### `answer:family:both:served-with-notice-of-garnishment:what-happens-after`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:both:served-with-notice-of-garnishment
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I was served with a notice of garnishment for family support — can I dispute it?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
Within 10 days after a dispute is served and filed, the clerk must issue a notice of garnishment hearing (Form 29H) on request. The clerk must serve and file that notice no later than 10 days before the hearing. At the hearing, the court may make temporary or final orders. These include an order dismissing the dispute or changing how much is garnished. They also include an order suspending the garnishment or setting aside the notice. If the payor's situation changes in a way that affects their ability to pay, the court may, on a motion, make the same kinds of orders. If you are the payor and you go back to work for or get money again from the garnishee, you must send a notice within 10 days. You must also do so within 10 days after you start work with or get money from a new income source. Send it to the clerk, and to the recipient or the Director, by mail or email.
```

### `answer:family:both:notice-case-may-be-stayed-or-dismissed:whats-happening`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:both:notice-case-may-be-stayed-or-dismissed
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "The court sent a notice that our case or motion may be stayed or dismissed as frivolous or an abuse — what happens now?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
The court may stay or dismiss a case that appears on its face to be frivolous or vexatious or otherwise an abuse of the court process. It may do this on its own, or when a party asks for it in Form 1.4. The court may do the same with a motion. When the court decides such an order may be appropriate, it has the clerk give the parties a notice in Form 1.4A. If the notice is about a case, the case is automatically stayed once the clerk gives notice to any party. It stays that way until the court makes an order staying or dismissing it, or an order declining to. Until then, no party may take any step in the case other than the steps in rule 1.4, unless the court orders otherwise. This automatic stay does not apply when the notice is about a motion.
```

### `answer:family:both:notice-case-may-be-stayed-or-dismissed:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:both:notice-case-may-be-stayed-or-dismissed
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "The court sent a notice that our case or motion may be stayed or dismissed as frivolous or an abuse — what happens now?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
These steps apply unless the court orders otherwise. If you brought the case, you may file a written submission responding to the notice, no later than 15 days after receiving it. If the notice is about a motion, this is the party who made the motion. The submission may be no more than 10 pages long. If no submission is filed in time, the court may make the order without any further notice to the parties. If a submission is filed, the court may have the clerk give a copy of it to any other party. If you are another party and you receive a copy, you may file a responding submission of no more than 10 pages, no later than 10 days after receiving it. If you do, you must give a copy to the party who brought the case and to any other party who asks for one. If a party has a lawyer in the case, the copy goes to the lawyer instead of to the party. The notice and any copy of a submission are given by regular service, and rule 6 decides when they count as received. For example, service by mail is effective on the fifth day after it was mailed.
```

### `answer:family:both:notice-case-may-be-stayed-or-dismissed:your-deadline`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:both:notice-case-may-be-stayed-or-dismissed
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "The court sent a notice that our case or motion may be stayed or dismissed as frivolous or an abuse — what happens now?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
If you brought the case or motion the notice is about, file a written submission of no more than 10 pages responding to the notice. You have 15 days after the day you received the notice (Form 1.4A). If no submission is filed in time, the court may make the order without further notice. The notice is given by regular service. Rule 6 decides when it is received. For example, a notice sent by mail is received on the fifth day after mailing. These times apply unless the court orders otherwise.

If you are another party and the clerk gives you a copy of that submission, you may file a reply submission of no more than 10 pages. You have 10 days after the day you received the copy of the submission. Give a copy of your reply to the party who brought the case or motion. Also give one to any other party who asks. These times apply unless the court orders otherwise.

Times set by the Family Law Rules are counted under those rules. The first day is the day after the event (r. 3 (1)). If the last day of a period falls on a day court offices are closed, the period ends on the next day they are open (r. 3 (3)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the rules do not clearly say how this applies, so the safe course is to act by the last open day before it. For a period of less than seven days, Saturdays, Sundays and other days when all court offices are closed are not counted (r. 3 (2)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
```

### `answer:family:both:served-with-request-to-admit:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:both:served-with-request-to-admit
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I was served with a request to admit facts or documents — what happens if I ignore it?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
If you do not serve a response (Form 22A) within 20 days, you are treated as admitting, for this case only, that the facts are true and the documents are genuine. In your response, you can deny that a particular fact is true or that a particular document is genuine. Or you can refuse to admit a particular fact or document, but you must give your reasons for each refusal. Your response must name each fact or document you deny or refuse to admit. Any fact or document your response does not deny, or refuse to admit with reasons, is treated as admitted for this case. Admitting that a document is genuine has a set meaning, which depends on what the document is said to be. For an original, it means the document was written, signed or sealed as it appears to have been. For a copy, it means the copy is complete and accurate. For a copy of something usually sent from one person to another, like a letter, fax or electronic message, it also means it was sent as it appears and was received by the person it is addressed to.
```

```
Serve a response (Form 22A) for each fact or document in the request that you do not accept. Deny it, or refuse to admit it and give your reasons. You have 20 days after the day you were served with the request to admit. If you do not respond in time, you are treated as admitting them for this case. You can withdraw an admission only if the other party agrees or the court allows it. The parties can agree in writing to change this time. The court can also change it.

Times set by the Family Law Rules are counted under those rules. The first day is the day after the event (r. 3 (1)). If the last day of a period falls on a day court offices are closed, the period ends on the next day they are open (r. 3 (3)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the rules do not clearly say how this applies, so the safe course is to act by the last open day before it. For a period of less than seven days, Saturdays, Sundays and other days when all court offices are closed are not counted (r. 3 (2)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
```

### `answer:family:both:childrens-lawyer-report:whats-happening`

- **Status:** draft

- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "The Children's Lawyer is involved or has served a report — what do I have to do?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
The Children's Lawyer is looking into decision-making responsibility, parenting time or contact for a child in your case. Before starting, the Children's Lawyer must serve notice on the parties and file it. The Children's Lawyer has the same rights as a party to see documents and to question witnesses. These rights cover the child's decision-making responsibility, parenting time, contact, support or education. The Children's Lawyer may report and make recommendations to the court on the results.
```

### `answer:family:both:childrens-lawyer-report:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:both:childrens-lawyer-report
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "The Children's Lawyer is involved or has served a report — what do I have to do?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
Once you are served with the notice, you must serve the Children's Lawyer with every paper in the case about the child. That means papers about decision-making responsibility, parenting time, contact, support or education. Serve them as if the Children's Lawyer were a party in the case. Within 90 days after serving the notice, the Children's Lawyer must serve a report on the parties and file it. The person who prepares the report must sign an affidavit that backs up the facts in it. For facts they do not know themselves, the affidavit must say where their information came from. That person must serve the affidavit on the parties, with the report attached, and file both with the court. If you dispute anything in the report, you may serve and file a statement saying so. You have 30 days after you are served with the report to do this.
```

### `answer:family:both:served-with-request-for-financial-statement:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:both:served-with-request-for-financial-statement
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I was served with a request for a financial statement because a payment order is in default — what do I have to do?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
Within 15 days after you were served with the request, you must send a completed financial statement (Form 13) to the recipient. You send it by mail, fax or email. Some parts of rule 13 also apply to your statement, with necessary changes. They are the rules on full disclosure, income tax documents, insufficient financial information, updating a financial statement, correcting and updating, and an order to file a statement. Under the rule on insufficient information, if the recipient believes your statement does not give enough information to fully understand your finances, they must ask you in writing for what is needed. If you do not give the requested information within seven days of the request, the court may order you to give it or to serve and file a new financial statement. The court may do this on motion or at a case conference or settlement conference.
```

For a period of less than seven days, Saturdays, Sundays and other days when all court offices are closed are not counted (r. 3 (2)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.

### `answer:family:both:binding-judicial-dispute-resolution:whats-happening`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:both:binding-judicial-dispute-resolution
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "We agreed to a binding judicial dispute resolution hearing — what do we file, and when?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
The purpose of this hearing is to let a judge, in a single hearing, help the parties settle issues and decide issues that are not settled. It is only available in the Superior Court of Justice, including its Family Court, in a municipality shown on the Ontario Courts website as chosen by the Chief Justice. It does not apply to cases under the Child, Youth and Family Services Act, 2017, interjurisdictional support cases (rule 37) or international child abduction cases (rule 37.2). The parties may ask for it if each party is satisfied of three things. First, the case has no major credibility issues that need cross-examination. Second, no witness who is not a party needs to give oral evidence. Third, it is reasonable to expect the issues can be settled or decided in a summary way. If those conditions are not met, the court must not order the hearing, unless it decides the hearing is right in the circumstances.
```

> whom. If it has those the wrong way round, nothing else about it matters.

### `answer:family:both:binding-judicial-dispute-resolution:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:both:binding-judicial-dispute-resolution
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "We agreed to a binding judicial dispute resolution hearing — what do we file, and when?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
To ask for the hearing, each party must serve and file a request and consent form (Form 43 or 43A) and a motion form (Form 14B). Form 43A is the version for the Office of the Children’s Lawyer. If you are serving and filing papers for a conference or other hearing, you may file the request and consent form with those papers instead of with a motion form. For the hearing, each party must serve and file a set of papers by the times below, unless the court orders otherwise. They include an affidavit (Form 43B or 14A) of no more than 12 pages, not counting exhibits. The exhibits can total no more than 10 pages, not counting the other listed papers, unless the court orders otherwise. They also include a draft order setting out what you are asking for. They also include any relevant agreements, minutes of settlement or court orders. Add any offer to settle that has not been withdrawn. Other papers depend on the claims and issues in your case. One example is an updated financial statement for a support claim. They are all listed under your deadline. The applicant, or the party who made a motion to change, must serve and file them no later than 20 days before the hearing. The respondent, or the party responding to a motion to change, must serve and file them no later than 10 days before the hearing. No later than five days before the hearing, the applicant or the party who made the motion may serve and file a reply affidavit (Form 14A) of no more than four pages. The reply may only deal with new matters raised in the other party's affidavit. The parts of an affidavit you fill in must be typed or written clearly, double spaced, in at least 12 point size. Each party must give a copy of a confirmation (Form 43C) to every other party by mail, fax, email or any other method. Then, no later than 2 p.m. three days before the hearing, you must give the confirmation to the clerk. You can deliver it to the court office, email it to the court office, or submit it through Justice Services Online or the Ontario Courts Public Portal, whichever is available. In the confirmation, you must say if you are satisfied that the other party's disclosure is enough for the issues to be settled or decided at the hearing. If you are not satisfied, you must explain why it would be unfair to go ahead without it.
```

### `answer:family:both:binding-judicial-dispute-resolution:your-deadline`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:both:binding-judicial-dispute-resolution
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "We agreed to a binding judicial dispute resolution hearing — what do we file, and when?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
If you are the applicant, or the party who made a motion to change, serve and file your hearing papers, as listed below. Do this at least 20 days before the date of the binding judicial dispute resolution hearing. Your papers are these. An affidavit (Form 43B or 14A) of no more than 12 pages, with no more than 10 pages of exhibits. A draft order. Any relevant agreements, minutes of settlement or court orders. Any offer to settle that has not been withdrawn. For a support claim, an updated financial statement and certificate of financial disclosure (Form 13A). For a property claim, updated Forms 13.1, 13B and 13C, with Form 13A. For a parenting claim, an updated Form 35.1, and Form 35.1A if it applies. If the amount or length of support is an issue, your calculations. If support arrears are an issue, a statement of money owed. If special expenses are an issue, proof of the amount. For property issues, any supporting papers and expert or professional reports. For parenting issues, any expert or professional reports. Once the court has ordered the hearing, you cannot withdraw your consent. The exception is with every other party's written consent or the court's permission. The parties can agree in writing to change this time. The court can also change it.

If you are the respondent, or the party responding to a motion to change, serve and file the same hearing papers, as listed above. Do this at least 10 days before the date of the binding judicial dispute resolution hearing. The parties can agree in writing to change this time. The court can also change it.

If you are the applicant or the party who made the motion, you may serve and file a reply affidavit of no more than four pages about new matters in the other party's affidavit. Do this at least 5 days before the date of the binding judicial dispute resolution hearing. The parties can agree in writing to change this time. The court can also change it.

Give a copy of the confirmation (Form 43C) to every other party. Then give it to the clerk no later than 2 p.m. Do this at least 3 days before the date of the binding judicial dispute resolution hearing. The parties cannot change this time by agreement.

Times set by the Family Law Rules are counted under those rules. The first day is the day after the event (r. 3 (1)). If the last day of a period falls on a day court offices are closed, the period ends on the next day they are open (r. 3 (3)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the rules do not clearly say how this applies, so the safe course is to act by the last open day before it. For a period of less than seven days, Saturdays, Sundays and other days when all court offices are closed are not counted (r. 3 (2)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
```

### `answer:family:both:binding-judicial-dispute-resolution:what-happens-after`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:both:binding-judicial-dispute-resolution
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "We agreed to a binding judicial dispute resolution hearing — what do we file, and when?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
The whole hearing is held under oath or affirmation. It starts with settlement talks, with the judge helping the parties settle issues by agreement. If the judge decides more talks are not expected to settle any more issues, the judge may decide any issue left. That decision may be temporary or final. If a party does not take part, the judge may hold the hearing based only on the evidence filed for or received at the hearing. The judge may end the hearing if the judge decides it is no longer appropriate in the circumstances. If that happens, the hearing counts as a conference in the case. The judge may also give any directions the judge thinks necessary on how the case goes on.
```

### `answer:family:both:questioning:whats-happening`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:both:questioning
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "Can I question the other side under oath, or do I have to answer their questions?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
Questioning means asking a person questions out loud, under oath or affirmation. The right to question a person includes the right to cross-examine. In a case that is not a child protection case, a party can get information from another party about any issue in two ways. One is with that party's consent, and the other is by a court order. Outside a child protection case, if you do not consent to be questioned, the party who wants to question you needs a court order. In a child protection case, a party has a right to get information from another party about any issue. No consent or court order is needed. To question the other party, the party must serve them with a summons to witness (Form 23) by special service. The party can instead get it by affidavit or another way. To do that, the party must serve them with a request for information (Form 20). There is one exception to this. It is an application for an order under sections 53.1 to 53.5 of Ontario Regulation 155/18. That regulation is made under the Child, Youth and Family Services Act, 2017. For that application, the consent-or-order rule applies instead.
```

### `answer:family:both:questioning:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:both:questioning
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "Can I question the other side under oath, or do I have to answer their questions?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
The court may, on motion, order a person to be questioned by a party, or to give information by affidavit or another way. The person can be a party or someone who is not a party. The court may make this order if three conditions are met. First, it would be unfair to make the party who wants it carry on with the case without it. Second, the information is not easily available any other way. Third, it will not cause unacceptable delay or undue expense. An order can affect someone who is not a party only if they were served by special service. They must have been served with the notice of motion, a summons to witness (Form 23) and the witness fee. If you want to question someone, you must first have served and filed any answer, financial statement or net family property statement the rules require. You must also promise in writing not to serve or file more papers for the next step in the case. The exception is papers in reply to the answers or information you get. A party can be questioned on their financial statement only after a written request for more information has been made under rule 13 (11) (a). The questioning takes place in the municipality where the person to be questioned lives. But that person and the party asking can agree to hold it in another one. They may not agree on the date and time, who records the questioning, how it is recorded, or paying a non-party's expenses. If so, the court must decide the matter on a motion. All parties must be served with notice at least three days before the questioning. The notice gives the name of the person to be questioned and the address, date and time.
```

### `answer:family:both:questioning:your-deadline`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:both:questioning
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "Can I question the other side under oath, or do I have to answer their questions?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
If you are arranging the questioning, serve every party with notice of who will be questioned, and the address, date and time. Do this at least 3 days before the date of the questioning. Before you can question anyone, you must have served and filed any answer, financial statement or net family property statement the rules require. You must also promise in writing not to serve or file more papers for the next step, except in reply. The questioning takes place in the city or town where the person lives, unless they and you agree on another. To question someone on their financial statement, you must first have asked in writing for the missing information under r. 13 (11) (a). The parties can agree in writing to change this time. The court can also change it.

Times set by the Family Law Rules are counted under those rules. The first day is the day after the event (r. 3 (1)). If the last day of a period falls on a day court offices are closed, the period ends on the next day they are open (r. 3 (3)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the rules do not clearly say how this applies, so the safe course is to act by the last open day before it. For a period of less than seven days, Saturdays, Sundays and other days when all court offices are closed are not counted (r. 3 (2)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
```

### `answer:family:both:questioning:what-happens-after`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:both:questioning
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "Can I question the other side under oath, or do I have to answer their questions?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
If a person being questioned refuses to answer a question, the court may, on motion, decide whether the question is proper. It may also give directions for the person to return, and make a contempt order. Sometimes the person who refused is a party, or is questioned for a party. Then that party cannot use the refused information as evidence unless the court gives permission. You may find that an answer you gave was wrong or incomplete, or is no longer right or complete. If so, you must give the correct and complete information in writing to all parties right away. What a party gets this way may be used only for this case. There are some exceptions. One is when the person who gave it consents.
```

- **Status:** draft

- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I want to drop my case or part of it — how do I withdraw, and does it cost me anything?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
To withdraw, serve a notice of withdrawal (Form 12) on every other party and file it. A motion is withdrawn the same way as an application or answer. There is an exception for a special party or a child party. Their application, answer or reply, in whole or in part, can be withdrawn only with the court's permission. The notice of motion for permission must be served on every other party. It must also be served on the Public Guardian and Trustee for a special party, or on the Children's Lawyer for a child party.
```

```
If you withdraw all or part of an application, answer or reply, you must pay every other party's costs. This covers their costs for the part you withdrew, up to the date you withdraw. This applies unless the court orders otherwise or the parties agree otherwise. If the party withdrawing is a government agency, costs are up to the court instead.
```

### `answer:family:applicant:amending-own-application:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:applicant:amending-own-application
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I need to change my application after I filed it — can I?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
If no answer has been filed, you may amend without the court's permission. To do so, serve and file an amended application the same way you start a case under rule 8. If an answer has been filed, you may still amend without the court's permission. To do so, serve and file the amended application the same way. Also file the consent of all parties to the change. You can also ask the court for permission to amend on a motion. The court must give it, unless the change would harm another party in a way that costs or a delay could not make up for. In your amended application, underline all changes. Also note in the margin of each changed page the rule or order that allows the change and the date of the change. Your change may add a new claim about a child that was not in your first application. If it does, it must come with the documents that rule 35.1 requires. A claim about a child here means one about decision-making responsibility, parenting time or contact. These include an affidavit in Form 35.1. A child protection case has its own rule. It applies if a significant change about the child happens after the first document is filed. Then the applicant may serve and file an amended application, an amended plan of care, or both. An application for an order under sections 53.1 to 53.5 of Ontario Regulation 155/18 is an exception to that rule.
```

### `answer:family:applicant:amending-own-application:what-happens-after`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:applicant:amending-own-application
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I need to change my application after I filed it — can I?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
Under rule 8, an application must be served right away on every other party. Special service must be used, unless the party is one of those listed in rule 8 (6). Once served, the respondent may amend their answer without the court's permission. To do so, they serve and file an amended answer within 14 days after being served. In the child protection case described above, the respondent may serve and file an amended answer and plan of care. They have 30 days after being served if served in Canada or the United States, or 60 days if served outside them.
```

### `answer:family:both:served-with-financial-examination-appointment:whats-happening`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:both:served-with-financial-examination-appointment
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I was served with an appointment for a financial examination about unpaid support — what do I have to do?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
The recipient can serve an appointment for a financial examination (Form 27C) when a payment order is in default. You have been served with one. It is served by special service. At the examination, you may be asked about many things. They include why you have not paid, your income and property, and the debts owed to and by you. You may also be asked about your ability to pay under the order, and whether you intend to obey it.
```

### `answer:family:both:served-with-financial-examination-appointment:what-to-do-next`

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:both:served-with-financial-examination-appointment
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I was served with an appointment for a financial examination about unpaid support — what do I have to do?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
The appointment requires you to come to the financial examination. You must bring any document or thing named in the appointment that meets three tests. You control it or can get it on request. It relates to enforcing the order. And it is not protected by legal privilege. You must also serve a financial statement (Form 13) on the recipient. Do this no later than seven days before the date of the examination. Some parts of rule 13 apply to this statement, such as full disclosure and income tax documents. You must be given at least 10 days' notice of the time and place. The examination is held in one of three places. It can be a place the parties and you agree on. If you live in Ontario, it can be the city or town where you live. Or it can be a place the court chooses. It is held under oath or affirmation. It is held before a person you and the recipient agree on, or as set out in rule 20 (12). The way it is recorded is chosen in the same way.
```

Serve a financial statement (Form 13) on the recipient. Do this at least 7 days before the date of the examination. You must also come to the examination. Bring any document or thing named in the appointment that you control or can get, that relates to enforcing the order, and that is not protected by legal privilege. The examination is held where the parties and you agree. If not, it is in the city or town in Ontario where you live, or where the court chooses. The parties can agree in writing to change this time. The court can also change it.

Times set by the Family Law Rules are counted under those rules. The first day is the day after the event (r. 3 (1)). If the last day of a period falls on a day court offices are closed, the period ends on the next day they are open (r. 3 (3)). For a time that must be met a number of days before a date, the rules do not clearly say how this applies, so the safe course is to act by the last open day before it. For a period of less than seven days, Saturdays, Sundays and other days when all court offices are closed are not counted (r. 3 (2)). Times set by a statute are counted differently, as stated beside them.
```

- **Status:** draft
- **Pathway / stage:** small-claims / family:both:served-with-financial-examination-appointment
- **Appears in:** Stage answer for "I was served with an appointment for a financial examination about unpaid support — what do I have to do?"
- **Source:** https://www.ontario.ca/laws/regulation/990114

```
Rule 27 (19) applies if you miss the examination or fail to serve the financial statement. It also applies if you come but fail to bring a named document or thing. And it applies if you refuse to take an oath or affirm, or to answer a question. Then the court may, on motion, order another examination and give directions. It may also require you to post a bond (Form 32). If you then fail, without sufficient excuse, to obey that order or direction, the court may act on a motion with special service. It may order you jailed for up to 40 days, all at once or in parts.
```
